en: Continuation of the *Yiqiejing yinyi*, Scroll One, with Preface.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xīlín of Chōngrén Monastery in Yānjīng. Preface:

It is heard that when the primal simplicity was discarded and virtue and morality were slighted, benevolence and righteousness gradually emerged. When the practice of binding records with knotted cords was abandoned...
The divining stalks and tortoise shells were determined; thus, written characters were created.
Looking upward, one observed the profound celestial phenomena.
As forms were shaped by looking downward,
Cang Jie first devised the ancient script (guwen),
and Shi Zhou compiled the great seal script (da zhuan).
Carried down through successive generations,
they have changed with the times; thus,
the seal script and the ancient script [evolved].
Its application was slightly different.
By the time of the *Zhouli*, the Baoshi (Master of Preservation) presided over the education of the state's sons,
instructing them in the Six Scripts (*liushu*) through these methods.
That is to say: pictographs, indexicals,
associative compounds, and phonetic-semantic characters.
Transposition (zhuanzhu) and phonetic borrowing (jiejie)—
these six are the foundations of character creation.
Although the forms of the insect-script (zhongzhuan) have varied and the texts of ancient and modern times differ,
they do not depart from these six types of writing.
Both [these views] are erroneous and delusive.
By the end of the Spring and Autumn period, the teaching of the Official for the Preservation of Ritual had fallen into disuse.
When the Qin unified the realm within the seas,
Chancellor Li Si examined and compared the *zhòu* script.
A separate script, the Small Seal (xiaozhuan),
was created for administrative purposes to facilitate speed and ease;
as its forms evolved, they gradually became corrupted.
Cheng Miao reformed the script,
which is called the Lì (Slav) script.
With the rise of the Han dynasty, the study of calligraphy flourished.
Yang Xiong composed the *Xuncuan* in eighty-nine chapters;
Ban Gu added thirteen chapters,
whereby the usage of characters across various texts was roughly complete.
Xu Shen of the Later Han dynasty compiled the various scholarly traditions of ancient script, *zhòu* script, and seal script,
producing a catalog of five hundred and forty chapters.
He took the *Liesheng* as his instructional commentary and composed the *Shuowen Jiezi*.
At that time, Cai Boga (Cai Yong) was present.
Furthermore, after the cessation of his studies,
he requested that the definitive versions of the Five Classics be engraved upon stone and erected at the gate of the National University (Taixue).
This is called the Stone Classics.
Furthermore, Lü Chen composed the *Zilin* (Forest of Characters) in five fascicles.
To supplement the omissions and brevities of Xu Cai, the study of the *Shuowen*,
the Stone Classics, and the *Zilin* was established during the Tang dynasty;
this continued until the Dali era.
He summoned the filial and incorruptible scholar Yan Chuanjing and Zhang Can,
the Director of Studies at the National Academy, and others.
He standardized the Five Classics and established the correct forms of the characters;
furthermore, there was the *Zitong*.
The *Zijing* (Mirror of Characters), the *Shiwén* (Explanations of Words) by Mr. Lù,
and the *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) by Zhāng Yǔ.
Rhyme Dictionary.
Rhyme Brilliance.
Rhyme Collection.
Regarding the *Yunlüe* (Abridged Rhymes), as compositions have become numerous, various versions—
some expanded and some abridged— have coexisted.
These works all extensively draw upon the Three Histories and provide evidence from the Nine Classics;
if such literature possesses any profound meaning, it is found herein.
The meaning of those [terms] is without distinction;
the emergence of their sounds and meanings has its own origins.
How much more so regarding the teaching of the Buddha Śākyamuni:
the wondrous scriptures of the Four Āgamas discuss the existence of marks within the provisional gate.
The Eightfold True Sect manifests the unconditioned within the limit of reality,
simultaneously upholding both the ultimate and the conventional truths.
Proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit,
he employed phonemes, phrases, and syllables as the means of expression,
and manifested bodhi and nirvāṇa as that which is realized.
Paramārtha came from India and translated [the scriptures] throughout China;
these were transmitted through successive translations over time.
In ancient and modern transcriptions,
regarding the Sanskrit sounds, there is a case where a single character serves two functions;
thus, the "erru" (誤) is placed among the twelve vowels.
Numerals converge in their essence;
one should examine the strokes and dots within the eight case endings (aṣṭavibhakti) of the nominal stems.
It is simply like the characters *zǔ* (棪), *rǎn* (冉), *shān* (掞), *shū* (舒), *zhàn* (贍), and *luàn* (亂) being confused within the "hand" radical (*shǒu*);
or *zhàng* (帳), *zhī* (知), *liàng* (亮), *chàng* (悵), *chǒu* (丑), and *zhàng* (仗) being mixed within the "heart" radical (*xīn*).
It is like *dōu* (都), *xī* (奚), *yí* (𢓎), *zhí* (直), *ní* (尼), *zhuó* (著), *hèng* (彳), and *zhuó* (著) being confused within the "man" radical (*rén*).
Nuo (naked), guan (ancient object), luo (barbarian), wa (tile): these follow the radical for clothing (衣) and the radical for manifestation (示).

Chuan (flattery): composed of tou (spit) and dao (knife); chan (flattery): composed of chou (ugly), ran (to move), and not distinguishing yao (to lift) from xiao (small) and xi (to sink)—the phonetic is yan (陷). Zhuang (mighty): side-lying liang (bright). Mu (ox): mo (not) and hou (after). Wang (net): distinguish niu (ox) from yu (speech). Qiu (seek): composed of zhuang (shoulder) and ji (sickness). Liang (measure): shao (few) and zhuo (axe). Mei (darkness): at xu (dog). Cai (exclamation): zai (this).
There are no omissions or errors in the transcription of the wealth [of the scriptures].
Instances such as these are truly numerous among the errors.
If one does not investigate and examine these matters in detail,
one will gradually deviate from the great meaning.
Thus, during the early Tang dynasty, there was a śramaṇa named Xuanying.
He alone exercised his prior awakening;
endowed by Heaven with innate knowledge,
he clearly understood the differences between the languages of Tang and India.
He identified rare characters from antiquity and the present;
he first aroused his resolve and applied himself diligently to examining them in detail.
Beginning with the ancient *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and ending with the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*,
he compiled the *Jīng yīnyì* (Meanings and Pronunciations of the Scriptures) in twenty-five fascicles.
Next, there was the śramaṇa Huìyuǎn,
who compiled the *Xīnhuáyán yīnyì* (New Avataṃsaka Phonetics and Meanings) in two fascicles.
Furthermore, there was the śramaṇa Yúnggōng.
He compiled the *Niepan yinyi* (Meanings and Pronunciations of Nirvāṇa) in two fascicles.
Furthermore, there was Master Ji of Da Cien Monastery,
who compiled the *Fahua yixun* (Pronunciations and Explanations of the Lotus Sūtra) in one fascicle.
Either they have not yet encompassed the three baskets in their entirety,
or they are merely partial and limited to a single sutra.
Upon searching and examining them, it was found that they were incomplete and compiled out of order;
this continued until the end of the Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty.
There was a śramaṇa named Huilin,
who was internally refined in the teachings and had entered the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Externally, he investigated the currents of the Mo school and refined his mastery of the essence of written characters and the subtleties of Indian phonology and grammar.
The profound mysteries of Chinese phonology have already been received by my former teacher as if poured from one vessel into another,
and they now flow forth like a spring for the benefit of later students.
Having settled his mind for twenty years,
he read through all the sutras and compiled a total of one hundred fascicles of *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciation and Meaning).
According to the Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu (Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era),
[the collection] begins with the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra and concludes with the Dhāraṇī for Protecting Life.
The total number of fascicles of all the translated scriptures is five thousand forty-eight,
comprising four hundred and eighty bundles.
Since the Kaiyuan lu, various sutras, śāstras,
as well as the Shiyi lüzhuan and other works, have been translated and transmitted in succession.
From the Mahāyāna-naya-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra, he read the entire Kaiyuan shijiao lu (Kaiyuan Record of the Buddhist Teachings),
totaling two hundred and sixty-six fascicles.
Twenty-five bundles.
These are those that were not included in the previous catalog and are now being added as continuations.
I humbly observe that the Master of Unimpeded Wisdom, the Compiler of this work,
was born with innate sagacity and endowed by the divine with brilliant intelligence.
He provided a comprehensive exposition of the various sutras and extensively compiled commentaries and digests;
he kept the transmission of the lamp of the Dharma ever in mind.
With the welfare of sentient beings as his heart’s intent,
he observed that the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings) was not yet complete and feared that the textual collation might contain omissions.
Because you have sent me this elegant letter,
you command my humble talent to face the radiance of the sun.
I have thus raised a mere firefly’s glow against a candle.
Nevertheless, there may be variations in the breadth or brevity of character explanations, and differences in the depth or shallowness of their interpretations of meaning.
Although this comparative translation of Chinese and Sanskrit terms, examining their similarities and differences across ancient and modern traditions, serves as a reliable foundation,
I await further refinement from future scholars.
I hope you will examine this in detail once more, so that there may be no further confusion.

Regarding the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-naya-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Six Pāramitās of the Mahāyāna Principle): one fascicle, ten volumes. From Volume One through Volume Ten, these volumes continue the phonetic glosses.

Volume One, Part One: The Mahāyāna-prakṛti-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra, Volume One, including the Preface. The character *dà* (大): In the *Dàpǔ* (大朴), it is pronounced as *tú* (徒) with the *gài* (葢) rhyme. The *Cāngjié piān* (蒼頡篇) states that it means "great" (*jù*). The *Yì* (易) says: "Great indeed is the Primordial Qian; all things derive their beginning from it. Below, in the *Pǔbō* (普剝), the character *fèn* (正) is read as *pǔ* (樸). The *Shuowén* (說文) states that it is the "raw state of wood. The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states: "Generally, when objects have not yet been carved or engraved, they are called *pǔ*. Wáng Bǐ (王弼) says: "*Pǔ* is the True (*zhēn*); it is like the primordial vapors before they have differentiated. The *Zhuāngzǐ* (莊子) says: "If the pure *pǔ* is not damaged, who would fashion it into a sacrificial vessel? It further says: "To damage the *pǔ* in order to make vessels is the fault of the artisan; to destroy the Way and Virtue in order to establish Benevolence and Righteousness is the error of the Sage."

"Ten thousand sounds" (*wànlài*)—the "wan" (萬) is read as *shàng wúyuàn* (上無怨), though it is combined with the character for "ten thousand" (*wàn*). The *Shùanshù jīng* (算經) states that ten thousand is called "wan. The current form is "wan" (萬). It is the name of an insect, and in the region of Zhōu, it was used as a personal name; it has been conventionally borrowed to mean the character "wan" (萬). The "xià luò dà fǎn" (下落大反) refers to the tone. It is the name of a musical instrument. The *Shuowén* (說文) states: "The *dàlài* (大籟) is the large *xiāo* (簫); the small one has sixteen tubes and is one chi two cun long. Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Ěryá* says: "The *dàxiāo* (大簫) has twenty-three tubes and is one chi four cun long; the smaller one has sixteen tubes and is one chi two cun long; it is also called *lài* (籟). The character is composed of "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "lài" (*lài*). In the preface, the character is written with "grass" (*cǎo*) as the radical, forming *háo* (𦯆), which is the name of a plant; it is not used here in this sense.

"Fen-lun" (紛綸): The *Guangya* states that "fen" means a multitude; its phonetic component indicates disorder. "Lun" (綸) is pronounced with the rhyme *chun*; the *Yi Jing* says "lun" refers to managing and organizing. The commentary on the *Tai Xuan Jing* says it means "interwoven. Examining this now, "fen-lun" describes a state of dense, interlaced abundance. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, both characters are written with the radical "silk" (糸); "fen" is pronounced as *mi*, and "lun" is the phonetic component.

*Xù* (旭): *xiōng* and *yù* are the phonetic components. The *Yùnyùn* states it means "the sun first rising. The *Shuowén* states it means "the sun rising at dawn. The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "bright radiance. It is composed of the character for "sun" (*rì*) and the number "nine" (*jiǔ*), with "nine" also serving as the phonetic component. The lower part, *rén*, has one tone. The *Shuowén* says it means "fullness. It is the essence of the great sun, which is never diminished. It is composed of the character for "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the number "one" (*shēng*). The sound of "mouth" (*kǒu*) is *yǔfēi*. Its form resembles that of a mouth encircling [something].

*Kaśmīra* (罽賓) is the name of a kingdom in the Western Regions; it is also called *Kaśmira* (个濕蜜羅) or *Kāśmīra* (迦葉彌羅), which are all corruptions of the Sanskrit term. The correct form is *Kaśmīra*, translated as "Who would dare to enter? This refers to the time when this country had not yet established a capital. There was a great dragon lake where no one dared to approach. A certain arhat, seeing that the topography and terrain were suitable for human habitation, requested from the dragon a space as large as one knee. The dragon granted this, and the arhat transformed his body, gradually increasing its size until his knee filled the dragon lake. The dragon, bound by the sanctity of his word, abandoned the land and departed. The arhat then used his supernatural powers to dry up the water completely, and subsequently built a city and walls. Everyone said, "If it were not for our holy master, who would dare to enter? Because of these words, the name of the kingdom was established.

The character 空 (kōng) [with the radical 穴 and phonetic 工]: the *Qieyun* glosses it as "great" (*dà*) and also as "universal" (*tōng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is formed from 冗 with 工 as the phonetic. The lower part, 符仲反 (*fúzhòngfǎn*), according to the *Zishu*, means "principle" (*lǐ*). The *Kaosheng* states it means "clarity" (*míng*), and also provides the reading 皮變反 (*píbiàn fǎn*). The *Qieyun* glosses it as "instruction" (*xùn*). Examining the two characters 空 and 𧦬 now, they are names for monks.

"Gěnggài" (梗槩): the upper radical is *ǎng* (杏). The *Ěryá* states that "gěng" means "straight"; the *Guǎngyá* states it means "rough outline. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lìjì* says it refers to "leveling a bushel-measure"; Bì’s commentary on the "Dōngdū Fù" says "gěnggài" means "not fine or detailed. The *Shìwén* says it means "a general outline. Both characters are composed of the "wood" radical (*mu*) with the phonetic element *jìng* (更).

*Bhagavān* (pronounced *pó-gá-wàn*; in Sanskrit it is also called *Bhagavat*, or correctly *Bhagavant*; *vān* is pronounced *pú-hè* and *vant* is pronounced *máng-fàn*). The Śramaṇa Huìlín, who translated the scriptures, states that the ancient translations rendered this as "World-Honored One" (*Shìzūn*), because he is revered by both the mundane and supramundane worlds. Furthermore, among the ten titles [of a Buddha], this is the tenth. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Honored Title of the Tathāgata has immeasurable names, which can be summarized into six types: sovereignty, brilliance, majesty, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility. Because the term *Bhagavān* possesses these six meanings, the translators of the scriptures retained the Sanskrit term.

*Kālandaka* (迦蘭多迦): both the first and second syllables are pronounced *jiàngqié* (薑佉) according to the standard reading; formerly it was transcribed as *Jiālántuó* (迦蘭陀) or *Jiālánduójiā* (迦闌鐸迦), which are all corruptions of the Sanskrit sound. The correct form is *Kalandaka*, which is translated as "the bird with a beautiful voice. This refers to a large bamboo grove on the outskirts of Rājagṛha where these birds frequently nested; the place was named after them. It is precisely at this location that the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra* was preached.

*Asaṃkhyeya* (the *saṃ* sound is light, pronounced with the *qi* rhyme; the *ye* sound is pronounced with the *zhe* rhyme; this is the correct Sanskrit term). The old translation is *asaṃkhyī*, which is translated as "innumerable" (*wúyāngshù*). This refers to the name for the exhaustion of all numbers. The *Gu Huáyán Yìnyì* states that among the one hundred and twenty numerical units, "innumerable" corresponds to the one hundred and twentieth. Furthermore, according to the numerical system of the Hīnayāna, Master Cien, citing the *Abhidharmakośa*, says that of the original sixty numbers, eight have been lost in transmission; thus, "innumerable" corresponds to the fifty-second number.

"Yi" (依): In the *Xiyan* (玉篇), it is said to mean "to lean on"; in the *Qieyun*, it means "to follow. The *Lunyu* says, "Rely upon benevolence (*ren*). The *Shuowen* explains it as a compound character formed by two people leaning against one another. "Hu" (怙): In the *Erya*, it means "to rely upon"; the *Han Shi Waizhuan* says it means "to depend on. The *Mao Shi* says, "Without a father, what is there to rely on? It is formed with the radical "heart" and the phonetic "gu" (古).

*Ji-yǎng* (羈鞅): The upper character is pronounced *jū* with the retroflex *-y* (居宜反). Lexicons state it means "a tether. The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states it is a leather strap for the horse's head. The *Shuowén* (說文) explains it as a compound character (*huìyì*) derived from the radical *gē* (革, leather) and the meaning "to restrain a horse. The lower character is pronounced *yāng* with the retroflex *-l* (於兩反). The *Yùpian* (玉篇) states it means "forceful" or "stout. The *Qièyùn* (切韻) states it is the "pole" of a carriage or "the halter on a bull's neck. The character is composed of the radical *gē* (革) and the phonetic *yāng* (央).

Regarding the character for *míng* (star/bright): the *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of 󱤒 (guǐyǒng) with 𠇾 added below; Cāi Yōng writes it with 目 (eye); the ancient script (gǔwén) writes it with 日 (sun). All three forms are valid. In the Classics, the ancient script form is most commonly used. The sound of 󱤒 is *guǐyǒng*. The character for *xīng* (star) in the ancient script is written as 曐. The *Erya* states: "The bright star is called *qìmíng*. Guò Pǔ’s commentary says: "It is the planet Venus (*tàibáixīng*). When seen in the east at dawn, it is *qìmíng*; when seen in the west at dusk, it is *tàibái*."

*Huí fù* (洄澓): The first character is pronounced *huí* (as in "return"), and the second is pronounced *fù* (as in "repeat"). The *Erya* states: "To flow upstream against the current is called *sù huí*. Guo's commentary says this refers to that which whirls. The *Sancang* says: "*Fù* means deep; it refers to places where rivers and seas form swirling currents."

*Kāruḷa* (pronounced with the *li-gu* reversed) is also called *Kālūla*, and further *Garuda*; the correct transcription is *Garuḍa*, which translates as "Wondrous Wing" (*Miaochi*) or "Golden Wing" (*Jinchi*), and is also named "Enemy of the Dragons. According to the *Qishi jing* (Sutra on the Arising of the World), both the Golden-Winged Birds and the dragons possess the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). The egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) Golden-Winged Bird eats only the egg-born dragon because its power is small; this continues up to the case of the transformation-born (*upapāduka*) Golden-Winged Bird, which eats all four types of dragons because its majestic power is great. The other two modes of birth may be understood by analogy.

"Lǔ" (hunchbacked) refers to the primary force above [the waist]. The commentary of Du on the *Zuozhuan* states that "lǔ" means "wǔ" (stooped); it means the back is curved. The *Guoyaya* states it means the body is bent. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "kuāng" (weak/crippled), composed of the radical "person" (亻) and the phonetic "lǚ" (縷) with its strokes reduced.

Regarding "nǔ" (裸): it is written with the character 華 (huā) on top and the radical 瓦 (wǎ) below; this pronunciation was altered to avoid a vulgar taboo. Its original pronunciation is *lánguǒ* (郎果反). Gu Yewang stated that "nǔ" means to strip off clothes and expose the shoulders. The *Shuowen Jiezi* uses the character 果 (guǒ) beneath the radical 衣 (yī) to form the word 裸; the *Shuowen* itself uses the radical 身 (shēn) to form the character 躶 (luò); and the *Yupian* uses the radical 人 (rén) to form the character 倮 (luò)—these three forms are all interchangeable. The text of the Classics uses the character 祼 (guàn) with the radical 示 (shì), which has the pronunciation *guàn*; this is an error in the received text of the *Shujing*.

*Nǎng* (聾): The upper radical is *lù* (祿) with the tone *dōng* (東). The *Zuǒzhuan* states: "When the ears do not hear the harmony of the five musical notes, it is called deafness (*nǎng*). Du Yu says: "Deafness implies darkness [of hearing]. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *ěr* (耳) and the phonetic *lóng* (龍). In the received text, it does not form a character when used as a rhyme. *Yà* (瘂): The lower radical is *yā* (鴉) with the tone *jiǎ* (賈). The *Kǎoshēng* says: "One who cannot speak. Though there is sound, there are no words. The standard character for this meaning throughout antiquity is *yǐn* (瘖). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒)—the sound of which is *nǚ è* (女厄)—and the phonetic *yà* (亞). In the received text, it is written with the radical *kǒu* (口) as *'a* (啞), with the pronunciation *è* (厄) meaning the sound of laughter; this is not the intended meaning of the scripture.

*Mānglǎng* (魍魎): the first character is pronounced *wǎng* and the second *liǎng*. Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that they are water-monsters and *jìguǐ* (ghosts). The *Huainanzi* says that the *mānglǎng* appear like three-year-old children, red-black in color, with red eyes, red claws, long ears, and beautiful hair; there are also versions written as *wāngliǎng* (蝄蜽), which are used interchangeably.

"Dǐ" (砥) is pronounced "zhǐ" (脂) with the "fǎn" (反) tone. Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states that "dǐ" means "level. The *Cangjie pian* states it refers to a whetstone for sharpening. The character in the script follows the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and is read as "dǐ" (抵), meaning "to strike"; it does not carry the meaning of being "as level as a palm" (*rú dǐ zhǎng*).

*Āixià* (隘陿): The first character is pronounced *yājiè*. According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "constricted. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it refers to narrow and dangerous passes; it is also written as *ài* (阸). The second character is pronounced *xiánjiǎ*. Gu Yewang says it means "constricted and narrow. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical *fù* (阜) with *qiè* (匧) as the phonetic. The text here uses *xiá* (狹), which is composed of the radical *quǎn* (犬) and means "to practice" (*xiàoxí*); this is not its usage here.

*Chánlǐ* (廛里): The first character, *chán*, has the phonetic *zhílián* (直連); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means an empty space in a market or a dwelling. The text reads *tàn* (𫮈), which is a vulgar form. The second character, *lǐ* (里), has the phonetic *liángshǐ* (良史); the *Zōulǐ* (周禮) states that five households constitute a *líng* (鄰) and five *líng* constitute a *lǐ*. The *Fēngsùtōng* (風俗通) states that *lǐ* means "to stop" (*zhǐ*), referring to fifty households stopping together.

The character for *yīng* (鸚) has the phonetic "wū" (烏) with the radical "shàng" (上), while the second form is also written as *mù* (䳇); both share the same pronunciation, *wǔ*. The *Shānhǎi jīng* states: "On Mount Huáng there is a bird with green feathers and a red beak; it has a human tongue and can speak the language of humans, and is named *yīngwǔ*. The *Lǐjì* states: "The *yīngwǔ* can speak, yet it does not depart from the category of flying birds. Both characters are examples of *xíngshēng* (phonetic-semantic) compounds.

The upper character *máo* (𤛆) is the name for a type of ox among the southwestern tribes, also known as the "long-maned ox" (*chángmáo niú*). The lower character, pronounced *qiú* (求), refers to the ox-drawn carriage. The *Shiben* states that the Yellow Emperor’s minister *Yi* attained immortality by taming oxen. The *Shiji* records that Zhou Di dragged nine oxen backward.

Regarding the term *bēngniú* (犎牛): the upper character is pronounced *fēng*. The *Shānhǎi jīng* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states that it is the wild ox of the south. The *Jízhù* (Collected Annotations) on the *Ěryǎ* says it is the "Prime Minister Ox" (*chóngxiàng niú*) presented from Jiǎozhǐ today. Guō Pǔ’s commentary on the *Shìxù* (Explanation of Domestic Animals) says: "On its neck, a fleshy protuberance rises about two feet high, like a hump of flesh; what is commonly called the *fēngniú* (peak ox) today is this. The pronunciation of *bó* (犦) is *báo*; the character *zhè* (胅) is pronounced *tiánjié*.

Regarding "bear" (*xiong*) and "brown bear" (*pí*): the *Shangyugong* (Bow of Superior Feathers) has its fur reversed; the *Shijing* says, "There are bears and brown bears"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* says they are beasts resembling wild boars that dwell in mountains and hibernate in winter. The term *lǚ* refers to their paws; the character for *páo* (paw) is pronounced *fán* (upper tone), while the lower part is pronounced *bēi*. The *Erya* states, "The brown bear is like a bear, yellowish-white in pattern. Guo Pu said: "It resembles a bear with a long head and tall legs; it is fierce and powerful, capable of uprooting trees. A bear is one that can pull down trees.

The character for *hǔ* (tiger) is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* and the final rhyme *fǎn*. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it means "the lord of beasts. It is composed of *hú* (pronounced *hū*) and the radical *rén*. Because the tiger’s feet resemble human feet, the *rén* radical is used. The character for *bão* (leopard) is pronounced with the initial *páo* and the final rhyme *fǎn*. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it resembles a tiger but has rounded patterns of black spots and is smaller than a tiger. It is composed of the radical *zhì* (pronounced *zhì*) and the abbreviated form of *páo* as its phonetic. The sound of *zhì* is like that of *zhì* (pheasant).

"When jackals and wolves go to bed, they all turn back. The *Yǐnyá* says: "The *chái* (jackal) is a type of *zǎo* (beast). The *Shuōwén* says: "It belongs to the genus *láng* (wolf); it follows the radical *zhì* (beast) and takes *cái* as its phonetic. The text of the scripture uses *quán* (dog) instead of *chái*, which is incorrect. Upon examination, there are two types of *chái*: the larger is called *cháláng* (jackal), and the smaller is called *cháinú* (jackal-puppy). The smaller ones go out first to hunt deer and roe; having killed them, they guard the prey and do not dare eat immediately, waiting for the *cháláng* to arrive later. Once the *cháláng* has eaten its fill, the *cháinú* then consume the remaining meat. Therefore, the *Yueling* states: "Five days later, the *chái* sacrifice the beasts," referring precisely to this.

*Konghou* (箜篌) is the name of a musical instrument; "kong" (空) is the upper radical and "hou" (侯) is the lower radical. The *Shiming* (釋名) states that it was created by Shi Yan and later emerged from the empty lands between Sangxian and Hanshang. It was likely preserved by the Marquis of the state of Kong. Furthermore, it is said that Shi Jian played it for the Lord of Jin, and after Zheng and Wei divided its territory and took possession of it, it came to be known as the licentious music of Zheng and Wei.

Wǎnshé (蝮蛇). The first character, wǎn, has two readings: the upper radical is wǔ (五) and the phonetic is yuán (轅, with the second tone); the lower radical is shè (社) and the phonetic is zhē (遮). *Bàopǔzǐ* says: "There are many species of snakes, but among them, the *wǎnshé* is the most dangerous when it stings a person. One must cut the flesh at the site of the sting with a knife and throw it onto the ground; the flesh will boil up of its own accord as if being roasted by fire until it is completely charred in an instant, after which the person may recover. Both characters take the "insect" radical (*chóng*) and are pronounced according to the phonetic *yuán* (元) and *tā* (它).

*Fù* (蝮): The upper character is read as *fāng* (芳) and the lower as *fú* (伏). The *Erya* states: "The *fù* is a *huǐ* (viper); its width is three inches and its head is as large as a thumb. Guo Pu’s commentary says it is like a person's thumb. The *Shiji* states that if a *fù* bites the hand, one must amputate it. The lower character is read as *xuē* (軒謁). This is a term used throughout the four quarters. The *Shuowen* calls it a venomous insect; its tail is coiled upward. The *Yupian* calls it a *chài* (scorpion). The character is composed of the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic element "xiè" (*xiē*); it is a compound of form and sound. The text uses the character *xié* (蝎), pronounced *hè*; *xié*, *qiè*, and *jué* share the same meaning, though they differ from the sense of *fù* and *xié*.

"Yú (fish)": pronounced with the initial *jū* and final rhyme *shuō*; according to the *Shuowen*, it is an aquatic insect. The *Erya* states: "The tail of a fish is called *bǐng*. Guo's commentary notes: "It resembles the seal-script character for *bǐng*; the vulgar form is written as the character for 'fish' (*yú*). "Xià (tortoise)": pronounced with the initial *biān* and final rhyme *miè*; according to the *Shuowen*, it is an amphibious aquatic insect, composed of the radical *mǐng* and the phonetic *bì*. The text of the scripture uses the character *bié* (鱉) derived from the 'fish' radical; this is a vulgar form. The pronunciation of *mǐng* is *měng*.

The character for *yuán* (黿) is pronounced with the first tone; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a large turtle. The large ones are like chariot wheels, while the small ones are like basins. They possess divine power, able to control aquatic creatures and bewitch humans to devour them. The character for *táo* (鼉) is pronounced with the second tone, *duō*. The *Shanhaijing* states that the Yangtze River (*Jiangshui*) abounds in *táos*. Guo’s commentary says they resemble lizards and have scales; the large ones are about one *zhang* in length, while the small ones are four or five feet long. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines them as "aquatic crustaceans," formed from the radical *mǐng* (黽) and the phonetic component *nà* (𠹈). The pronunciation of *mǐng* is *měng*, and *nà* is *nà*. Both characters in the scripture text are written below with the *guī* (龜) radical as *yǎo* (鼉); this is a vulgar form and is incorrect.

Fēng-huáng (Phoenix): the upper character is pronounced *fēng* (as in *fēng gòng*) and the lower is pronounced *huáng*. The *Erya* states: "The male is called fēng; its female is called huáng. Guo Pu’s commentary notes that it is a bird of auspicious response (*ruìyì*). Xu Shen’s *Shuowen Jiezi* describes it as a divine bird that emerges from the Land of the Gentleman in the East. It soars beyond the four seas; its markings are like those of a dragon, its back like a tortoise, its chin like a swallow’s, and its beak like a rooster’s. All five claws are fully displayed. It does not perch upon anything but the wú-tóng tree, nor does it eat anything but the fruit of the bamboo. Its morning cry is called *fā míng*; its midday cry is called *shàng shuò*; its evening cry is called *mǎn chāng*; and its dusk cry is called *gù cháng*. Its nocturnal cry is called *bǎo zhǎng*. When it appears, all under heaven is in great peace.

*Sùmòzhā* (蘇莫遮): The character *mào* (冒) is pronounced with the *máo* (毛) radical and the *bào* (報) phonetic. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to the head-cloth of children and the barbarians; it is derived from the phonetic *mù* (目). The character for "mouth" (*yù*) has the same pronunciation as above. The *Wenzi Jilüe* (Textual Compendium) notes that it is also written with the *jīn* (巾) radical as *mào* (帽), which is likewise acceptable. In fact, *sùmòzhā* is a term from the Hu language; its original form was *sàmozhā*, which translates here as "play" (*xì*). It originated in the kingdom of Kucha and persists to this day in the form of musical compositions, such as those of the *Dàmiàn* (Great Face) and *Bātuó* (Head-Striking) genres.

"Shuan" (船) refers to a boat; the *Fangyan* states that west of the Guanzhong region, boats are called "shuan. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "zhou" (舟) and the phonetic "yuan" (沿) in abbreviated form. The current form "shuan" is a vulgar character; the variant "huang" (舡) is incorrect. The character below, "fan" (帆), is a vulgar character meaning to bind bamboo and wood to float upon the water. The *Guangya* writes it as "qian" (𦪑) with the radical "zhou" (舟); the *Shuowen* writes it as "bo" (橃) with the radical "mu" (木) and the phonetic "fa" (發).

The character 霤 (liù) is pronounced with the *pú* and *mào* finals; the *Kǎo* (Examination of Characters) states its sound means "sudden rain. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "swiftly falling rain," and further notes it is also "a shower. The character is composed of the radical 水 (water), 曰 (mouth/sun), 出 (to emerge), and 廾 (two hands joined, phonetic *gǒng*), and from the element 丰 (fēng), which has the phonetic value *tāo*.

Regarding the characters *máo* (毫) and *cǎo* (𣯛): the first character is pronounced with the initial *hú* (胡) and the final *gāo* (高) [in the ancient reading], while the second is pronounced with the initial *lì* (力) and the final *chí* (馳). The *Jiuzhang suanjing* (Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art) states: "In all measurements, it begins with the *hū* (忽); ten *hū* make one *sī* (絲), ten *sī* make one *máo* (毫), and ten *máo* make one *cǎo* (𣯛). The *Shuowen jiezi* states that both characters *máo* and *cǎo* are derived from *máo* (毛). The character *máo* is formed by omitting a portion of *háo* (豪), and the character *cǎo* is formed by omitting a portion of *cè* (𣺶). The forms *háo* (豪) and *cǎo* (󱶩) found in the current text are erroneous.

"Qingmei" (to despise). The *Shuowen* states: "To treat with contempt. It is composed of the radical for the mind (*xin*), with the phonetic "bian" (變) modified to "zhi" (忄). The character "meng" (薎) has the same pronunciation as above. The text of this scripture uses the bamboo radical to form "mian" (篾), meaning bamboo bark; this does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. There are versions where it is written with the hand radical to form "mie" (蔑), which is the name of a musical instrument; this is not accepted here.

Volume Two, Part Two: The Mahāyāna-prakṛti-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra, Volume Two. *Kacalin-dika*: Both the first and second characters are pronounced with the *jiàngqié* (薑佉) rhyme; the final character *dǐ* (底) is pronounced with the *dīngyǐ* (丁以) rhyme. This is the name of an auspicious bird found in the Western Regions. Its body is covered in downy feathers that are exceptionally light and soft; they were spun into cloth for the use of a Cakravartin King. Only such a king may wear this garment. Today, descendants of that species are still seen in that country, though their feathers are coarse and do not equal those obtained during the time of a Cakravartin King.

"不瞚" (bù shùn): "下" is pronounced with the *rùn* rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "瞚 refers to the frequent opening and closing and shaking of the eyes; it is composed of '目' (eye) and '寅' (yín), which also serves as the phonetic. The vulgar form is "瞬" (*shùn*), and the archaic form is "眒" (*shèn*). In current scriptural texts, it is written as "眴" (*xiùn*) with "旬" (*xún*) below "目," which is also acceptable. The *Spring and Autumn Annals* of the Lu state records: "Ten thousand generations are as if but a single blink (*yī xiàn*)."

*Utpala* (the *u* and *bo* of "烏骨" are corrected; it is a Sanskrit term). Formerly it was called *youpoluo* or *youpoluo*; this is translated as "blue lotus. It is the most fragrant and largest [of lotuses], absolutely non-existent among humans, and appears only in the Anavatapta Lake (Lake of No Heat) in the Great Snowy Mountains.

*Padma* is an incorrect transcription of the Sanskrit term; it is also called *pātuma* or *paṇuma*. The correct form is *padma*, which is translated as "red lotus," referring to the finest among flowers.

*Kumuda*—sometimes called *kumudhu*, sometimes called *kumāna*—are all corruptions of the Sanskrit term; it is correctly spelled *kumudā*. This is translated as "red lotus. They are rare in the human world, but they grow abundantly in those ponds.

*Puṇḍarīka* was formerly called *fen-tuo-li*; both are corruptions. The correct pronunciation is *bèn* (fourth tone) and *tè* (with the *nuo-ya* rhyme). *Li-ka* means "white lotus. It does not exist among humans, but grows in that pond.

Maṇḍala, or as it is sometimes called maṇḍara, should properly be rendered mahā-maṇḍala; this is translated as "Great Altar" (Dàtán), which refers to the place where the assembly of all sages gathers. According to the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, there are seventeen great maṇḍalas, each of which possesses four maṇḍalas, as explained in detail therein.

*Ōng-yü*: The first character is pronounced *wǔ* (with the initial *k-*) and the second is pronounced *wēn-lǜ*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "yù" refers to fragrant grass; it is composed of the radical "lín" (forest), the phonetic "fǒu" (*fāng jiǔ*), and the elements "mìng" (*rén mìng*), "chī", and "shān". The character is written as "yù," though the scriptural text uses "yù"; the common usage [of the latter] is incorrect. The *Hanshu* records that Sima Xiangru described it as "蓊鬱" (*wǒng yù*), meaning the lush and flourishing appearance of plants and trees.

Āṃ: the first character is pronounced with the initial *wū* (烏) and the final *gān* (甘), reversed; the second is pronounced with the initial *yú* (于) and the final *yín* (淫). These are characters found within mantras. Hīḥ:
the first character is pronounced with the initial *xīng* (馨) and the final *yǐ* (以), reversed; the second is pronounced with the initial *hū* (呼) and the final *jī* (雞). Ṇu-mi:
the first character is pronounced with the initial *nú* (奴) and the final *gōu* (溝); according to the character, it means "rabbit."
*Akṣa*: The first character, *kǔ*, is pronounced with a retroflex stop;
the character *àn* means "white-bald. *Nikha*: The second character, *xī*, has the phonetic value *hǔ xī*;

it is a word found within a mantra. From *āṃ* to *vakṣa*, these are all direct transliterations of the Indic script (*saṃskṛta*) using shadow-phonetics (*yǐngfàn*), without seeking the semantic meaning of the words.

Regarding "zhǐxī" (賑恤): the first character, zhǐ, is pronounced with the initial *r* and the final *-en* (as in 刃). The *Erya* states: "Zhǐ means wealthy. The second character, xī, is pronounced with the final *-lǜ* (as in 律). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* says: "Zhǐxī means to take pity upon the poor. Gu Yewang says: "Zhǐ means to rescue; xī means to have compassion. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "xī" is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "blood" (*xue*).

Regarding the heart (*xin*), the *Baihutong* states: "The heart is *li* (ritual). It is the essence of Fire in the South; it is red and pointed, with lobes like an unfurled lotus flower. Wang Bi’s *Maijing* says: "The heart and the small intestine (*xiaochang*) combine to form the *fu* (receptacle); its spirit is the *shen*; its external manifestation is the mouth. When the heart is diseased, one loses their voice and cannot speak. [In the text, *xiang* is read as *fang* and *fei*. Regarding the lungs (*fei*), the *Baihutong* states: "The lungs are *yi* (righteousness). They are the essence of Metal in the West; they are white in color. Wang Bi’s *Maijing* says: "The lungs and the bladder (*pangguang*) combine to form the *fu*; their spirits are the *po*; their external manifestations are the nose and the throat. Therefore, when the lungs are diseased, the nose cannot perceive fragrances or stenches. The *Shuowen* explains that the character is formed from "flesh" (*rou*) and the phonetic "yu"; "yu" is pronounced *feiwei*. The classical text uses the character with the "market" radical (*shi*), whereas the vulgar usage is incorrect.

The character for *cháng* (intestines) is pronounced with the initial *l* in *liángfǎn*. The *Shìmíng* (*Explanation of Names*) states: "It is the palace within the abdomen where the qi flows freely. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *ròu* (flesh) and the phonetic *chǎng* in abbreviated form. The lower part is sometimes written as *yǒu*, which is a vulgar variant. The correct form is *wèi* (stomach). The *Báihùtōng* (*General Discourse on the White Tiger*) states: "It is the palace of the spleen; its color is black. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is the palace of grain; it is a pictographic character composed of the radical *ròu* (flesh).

The upper character 肝 (gān) is pronounced with the initial *g* and final *-an*. The *Baihutong* states: "The liver is benevolence (*ren*); it is the essence of Wood in the East. The *Wangshi Maijing* states: "The liver and gallbladder combine to form a *fu*; its spirit is the *hun*, and its clinical manifestation is the eyes; therefore, when the liver is heated, the eyes turn red. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical 月 (moon) and the phonetic 干 (*gan*). The lower character 膽 (*dǎn*) is pronounced with the initial *d* and final *-an*. The *Baihutong* states: "The gallbladder is the *fu* of the liver and presides over benevolence; thus, the benevolent person possesses courage. The *Wangshi Maijing* states: "When the gallbladder is diseased, the spirit does not maintain its seat. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical 肉 (flesh) and the phonetic 詹 (*zhān*), where *zhān* is pronounced like *zhān*.

The spleen and kidneys are "upper female" (*shàng bì*, *bì* pronounced as *mí*). The *Báihù Tōng* states: "The spleen is associated with trustworthiness; it is the essence of the Central Earth, its color yellow. The *Wáng Shì Mài Jīng* states: "The spleen and stomach combine to form a *fǔ* (organ-vessel); its clinical manifestation is the tongue. Therefore, when the spleen has heat, the tongue becomes diseased and the lips cannot be retracted. The *Báihù Tōng* states: "The kidneys are associated with wisdom; they are the essence of the Northern Water, their color black, and their form is paired. The *Mài Jīng* states: "The kidneys and the *sān jiāo* (triple burner) combine to form a *fǔ*; its clinical manifestation is the ears. Therefore, when the kidneys are depleted, the ears become deaf. According to the *Shuōwén*, [the character for kidney] is composed of "flesh" (*ròu*) and "qian" (*xián*, pronounced *qǐ xián*).

Volume Three. The Third Fascicle of the Mahāyāna-ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā-sūtra (The Sūtra of the Six Pāramitās of the Mahāyāna Path). Fascicle Three. Regarding the character *xié* (脇) [in the term *chuānxī*]: the commentary on the characters states that it refers to the two sides of the abdomen (*dù*). It is composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and the phonetic *xié* (劦). The pronunciation of *xié* is *xié*. It is composed of three *lì* (力). It is incorrect for the sūtra text to use three *dāo* (刀) to form the character *lí* (刕).

*Zhuó* (upper tone, pronounced *chuò*): The *Guǎngyǎ* states that it means "to peck and bite. The *Shuowén* states that it means "a bird eating"; it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "pig" (*zhī*), which is pronounced *chǔ lù* (with the final tone reversed). The text here uses the character *huàn* (composed of "tuan"), which is pronounced *xū wèi*; it refers to the beak of a bird and does not carry this specific meaning. *Táng* (lower tone, pronounced *lán*): *Dàn* also means "to eat. It may also be written as *dàn*, which is identical.

The character for *jiǎn* (鉆) [pronounced with the initial *jiǎn* and final *-yán*] is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "an iron clamp used to seize objects," composed of the radical 金 (*jīn*) and the phonetic 占 (*zhàn*). In the sutra text, it is written with 苷 (*gān*) as the phonetic, which refers to an iron collar for infants and does not carry the meaning of "seizing. The character for *nián* (黏) [pronounced with the initial *nián* and final *-zhuó*] is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as: "A *jiǎn* (鉆); also a *jié* (攝, to grasp). Composed of the radical 金 (*jīn*) and the phonetic 取 (*qǔ*). The pronunciation of 取 is the same as above. In the sutra text, it is written with 三耳 (*sān'ěr*) as the phonetic, which refers to an iron hairpin for a carriage and is not the original character.

*Zhālè* (磔裂): The first character is pronounced *zhé* (with the radical *shè*, meaning "to split open" according to the *Zìshū*; it also means "to spread. The *Shuowén* states: "To kill and then stretch out the carcass. The pronunciation is *pǐ gè*. This refers to cutting the flesh. The *Zhou Lǐ* states: "Tearing apart sacrificial animals in a ritual to ward off calamities. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "In current vernacular usage, dogs are torn apart in the middle of a great road to stop the wind."
Fénliào (焚燎): *liao* reversed [is pronounced] *dǎo*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Liji* says it means "to illuminate. The *Shuowen* says it means "to set fire to";

it is a compound character formed from the radical *huǒ* (fire) and the phonetic *láo*. Xiāngcà (相拶): *la* reversed [is pronounced] *là*. The *Jixun* says it means "to press closely. The *Kaosheng* says it means "to push aside. The *Shuowen* says it is formed from the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *zǎo*; *zǎo* is pronounced *cái-là*, and *là* is pronounced *lán-dá*.

*Yǎnpù* (偃仆): The upper character is read as *qiàn* (蹇) according to the *Guǎngyá*, which states it means "to stretch out" (*yǎn'ǎng*). It is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) and the phonetic element *yàn*. The lower character is read as *míngběi* (明北). It is also written as *pú* (踣), which has the same meaning. The *Kǎośēng* states it means "to fall face-forward. The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to lean and collapse. It is also read as *fāngyù* (芳遇).

Regarding the character *zhú* (斸): the upper radical is *lù* (綠) with the phonetic *kǎo* (考); the *Kǎo Shēng* dictionary states it means "to dig up" (*zhú jué*). The *Shuōwén Jiězì* defines it as "to chop" (*zhú zhāo*), composed of the radical *jīn* (斤) and the phonetic *shǔ* (屬). The text here uses *zhú*, which is a vulgar form; the lower part is pronounced *ruò* (若), meaning "to hack with a blade."

The character *jiāng* (韁) has the phonetic *jiāng* (薑) for its upper radical and *bì* (祕) for its lower radical. Gu Yewang states that it refers to the bridle used to control carriage horses. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is a phono-semantic compound. The character *jiǎn* (𨊥), from which the lower part of *jiāng* is derived, is a semantic compound consisting of the radicals "silk" (糸) and "to guard" (衛, pinyin: wèi). There is also a variant form with "mouth" (口) and "perish" (亡), which is incorrect.

"Biàn-tà" (鞭撻): "Biàn" (鞭) is glossed in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "a whip for horses," following the radical "metal" (革) with the phonetic "biàn" (便), read as "tá-gé" (他葛). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states it means "chì" (抶); "chì" (抶) likewise means to strike. It is read as "chǐ-lì" (恥栗). In the *Shuowen*, "tà" (撻) follows the radical "hand" (手) with the phonetic "dá" (達).

*Bi* (upper tone *bei*) refers to hanging hair; according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *biao* with the phonetic *pi*. *Biao* is pronounced *biyao fan*. *Yan* (upper tone) and *yu* (lower tone): The *Erya* states that the *shuyan* is the *mù*; *mù* is pronounced *mu*. Guo Pu’s commentary says it is a duck.

The *Kaoseng* says it is the smaller variety of wild duck. The character is composed of the bird radical with the phonetic *ji*; *ji* is pronounced *shuji*. "Short-winged" (*duanyu*) means when flying, its wings are held close together (*jijiran*). This is a combination of form and sound. The lower character is pronounced *yanjian fan*. The *Commentary on the Mao Shi* says: "The large are called *hong* (wild geese); the small are called *yan* (wild geese). They are birds that follow the sun. The *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) states: "In the month of late autumn, the *hong* and *yan* arrive as guests. According to the *Shuowen*, *yan* is a type of goose (*e*), also known as *ge* (pronounced *go*).

Regarding "yìxī" (蜥蜴): the first character is pronounced *yì* (亦) and the second is pronounced *xīlì* (西歷). The *Erya* states: "The *xīxī* (蜥蜴) is the *wàndiǎn* (蝘蜓), which is the *shǒugōng* (守宮). The *Shuowen* states: "That which dwells on walls is called *wàndiǎn*; that which dwells in grass is called *xīxī*. The *Fangyan* states: "In Qin and Jin it is called *shǒugōng*; in Nan Chu it is called *shéyī*, or sometimes *yíngyuán*. The *Shuowen* further notes that the character for *xī* may be written as *yì*, and the character *xī* is composed of the radical "insect" (*虫*) and the phonetic "xié" (*析*). The text here uses the character *qiè* (蚚) with the radical "axe" (*斤*), which is pronounced *qī* (祈) and is not the character for *xīxī*.

Regarding "jīshì" (lice): the upper character is pronounced *jǐ* (as in *yǐ*)—the *Yùnyīng* states it refers to the eggs of lice; the lower character is pronounced *shì* (as in *suǒ yǐ*)—the *Shuōwén* defines it as a biting insect, written with the radical for insects (*wēn*) and the component *xùn*; the form used in the scriptures with *xùn* is correct, whereas the common usage is not. *Xùn* is pronounced *xìn*, and *wēn* is pronounced *kūn*.

The character 𧎮 (pronounced *zào*, with the variant *zàng lǎo*) is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "a jumping insect that bites humans," composed of the radical 䖵 (insect) and the element 叉 (*chā*), which also serves as the phonetic. The text of the sutra uses 蚤, a vulgar character; the pronunciation of 叉 is *zhǎo*.

*Mínglíng* (螟蛉): the initial *míng* is pronounced with the *shàng* (rising) tone, and the final *líng* is pronounced with the *fǎn* (reversal) tone of *dīng*. The *Erya* calls it the "mulberry insect" (*sānchóng*). The *Mao Shi Chongyu Shu* (Explanations of Insects and Fish in the Mao Odes) states: "It is a small green insect on mulberries, resembling the *bùqū* (step-curl); it is that which the *guǒlǚ* (wasp) carries about as its offspring. The *guǒlǚ* is a wasp, also known as the *yīwēng* (wasp). Xu Shen says it is a "slender-waisted wasp. Guo Pu says: "In common parlance, the *mínglíng* is called the *sānwàn* (mulberry-worm). *Guǒ*: pronounced *guǒ*. *Lǚ*: pronounced *lǔ guǒ fǎn*. *Yī*: pronounced *yān*. *Wēng*: pronounced *wū gōng fǎn*. *wàn*: pronounced *wàn*.

*Móu* (upper character pronounced *mòhóu*, lower character pronounced *téngdé*) and *téng* are both types of locusts. The *Mao Shih Zhuan* states: "The *móu* eats the roots; the *téng* eats the leaves. It is also written as *yí* or *bǐ*. The *Erya* writes it as *bǐ*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "When officials and functionaries beg and extort (*qītè*), then the *yí* arises. Both characters are examples of *xiángxīng* (phonetic-semantic) compounds.

The character for *fǒu* (蛗) has the upper radical *fù* (負) and the lower part *zhōng* (終); the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *yǒu* (󱲡), with the same pronunciation. Xu Shen states: "Fǒuzhōng is a type of locust that dwells among the grasses and does not eat the sprouts. The *Mao Shi* says, "Tì tì fǒuzhōng" (The fǒuzhōng insects leap about). The *Erya* also uses the term *fǒuzhōng*; these are all characters formed through both shape and sound. *Tì* (趯) is pronounced *tālì* (他曆反).

*Jiébò* (蛺蝶): The upper character is read as *jiān* (兼) with the fanqie *yè* (叶); the lower character is read as *tiánjié* (恬頰). According to the *Shuowen*, it is the name of an insect; it is also called *húdié* (胡蝶), that which Zhuang Zhou dreamed of. Both characters are composed of the "insect" radical (*chóng*, pronounced *xǔguǐ*). The character *jiá* (夾) has the phonetic *shēng* (聲) of *jiā* (古洽反); the character *yè* (枼) has the phonetic *shēng* of *yè* (叶).

Regarding the *qiāngliáng* (蜣蜋): the first character is pronounced *qiāng* (上佉良反) and the second has the sound *liáng* (下音良). The *Erya* states: "The *qǐqiāng* is the *qiāngliáng*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "It is a black-shelled insect that feeds on dung and soil. The character *qǐ* (蛣) is pronounced *qì* (音詰).

Regarding the character *yíng* (蠅): the upper radical is *zhòng* (孕) with the *zhèng* (蒸) rhyme, and the lower part is *mài* (麥) with the *péng* (彭) rhyme. Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "As for the insect called *yíng*, it is white when moist and black when dry. The *Fān yǔ* says: "In the regions between Qin, Jin, Chen, and Chu, it is called *yíng*; in Dongqi, it is called *yáng*. This is a phonetic corruption and shift. Guo Pu notes: "In Jiangdong, they call a *yáng* that resembles a fly [a *yíng*]."

The upper character is written as 馲 (also pronounced *tángluò* or *lánggè*) and the lower character is also written as 駞 (pronounced *tánghé*). The *Kǎoshēng* states that it is a beast of burden from the land of the Hu. The *Shānhǎijīng* says: "On its back there is a fleshy saddle; it can carry a thousand *jīn* and travel three hundred *lǐ* in a day. It knows the location of springs and water sources. The *Shuōwén* states that both characters are phono-semantic compounds (*xíngshēng*). The text of the sutra uses the character 駱 (pronounced *luò*), which according to the *Ērjiá* refers to a white horse with a black mane and is not the word for a *bactrian camel*.

*Kuāng* (尫): The upper radical is *wū guāng* (烏光). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) says it means "broken. Duan Yucai’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* says it refers to emaciation and illness. The *Shuōwén* says it refers to crooked legs; it is composed of the radical *quàn* (犬), which graphically represents a dog with one leg bent and leaking, and the phonetic *wáng* (王). The text erroneously uses *wù* (兀) instead of *kuāng*. The lower part is read as *lì zhuī* (力追). Jia Gongyan’s commentary on the *Guóyuè* says it means "emaciated and ill. Duan Yü’s commentary on the *Zuǒ Zhuan* says it means "weak. The *Shuōwén* defines *léi* (羸) as "slim"; it is composed of *yáng* (羊) and *lí* (𣎆), where *lí* has the phonetic value *lì gē* (力戈).

Regarding "㓟剝" (gāo bō): the upper character "㓟" has the phonetic "pí" (as in "pí xià"), with the rhyme category "bāng jiǎo. Lexicons define it as "to peel off" or "to injure. The upper character "㓟" is traditionally read as "pí," yet upon examining lexicons, this character does not exist. This remains unresolved; however, it should be written as "㱟" (with the phonetic "pǐ mǐ"), meaning "to injure" or "to break off."

*Jūn-pī*: The upper radical *jūn* is pronounced *chǐ* (反). The *Běicāng* states that it means "cracking skin" (*qì*). The phonetic for *qì* is *chǐ-lüè* (反). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "frozen cracks. The *Shuōwén* explains it as a compound character formed from *pí* (skin) and *jùn* (the form and the phonetic), where *jùn* is pronounced *chǐ-xún* (反). The lower part, *pī*, is pronounced *pǐ-yì* (反). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to split open. The *Shuōwén* defines *pī* as "to break," formed from *dāo* (knife) and *bì* (phonetic). The archaic form is written as *bǐ*, formed from *piàn* (tablet/split) and *lǐ* (the shape of being dispersed).

"Qi-kai" (乞匃): The second character is pronounced *gài* (垓礙). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "When a person loses their wealth and property, they go out to beg; thus, 'qi-kai' means to beg. 'Kai' also means to seek. This character is composed of 'ren' (人, person) and 'wang' (亾, to lose), and does not derive from 'bao' (包, to wrap)."

"Laojuan" (勞倦): "Qian" (卷) is pronounced as *quǎn* (with the initial *qù*). It means exhaustion and indolence. The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) uses the term "yanjuan" (厭倦). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "ren" (人) with the phonetic "quan" (卷); it may also be written as "quàn" (勌), which is likewise acceptable. The text of the scripture uses "juan" (倦), a character not found [in the aforementioned sources].

Regarding "gōngshāo" (弓弰): the *Pīcāng* states that it refers to the two ends of a bow. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "shāo" refers to the two tips of a bow; it follows the radical "gōng" (弓) and takes "xiào" (肖) as its phonetic. Regarding "gūqióng" (孤惸): the upper character "gū" (孤) is pronounced with the ancient sound *hú*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "gū" means solitary. The *Shuowén* states: "One without a father is called 'gū';

it follows the radical 'jíe' (孑) [pronounced jié] and takes the abbreviated form of 'gū' (觚) as its phonetic. The lower character "qióng" (惸) is pronounced with the sound *kuíyíng*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that "qióng" means alone. The *Wenzìdiǎnshuō* states: "One without brothers is called 'qióng'. The *Shuowén* writes this as "quín" (煢), following the radical "xùn" (卂) and taking the abbreviated form of "yíng" (營) as its phonetic; alternatively, it is written as "quín" (煢) with the radical "rén" (人), or as "qíng" (𠋫), all of which are interchangeable.

Regarding "gǒu" (widower) and "guǎ" (widow): "gǒu" is pronounced with the upper radical *guǎn* (頑). The *Líjì* states, "One who is old and without a wife is called a gǒu. The *Shàngshū* states, "There was a gǒu below," referring to Shùn being past the age for marriage yet without a wife. "Guǎ" is pronounced with the lower radical *guān* (關) or *wǎ* (瓦). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "solitary," referring to a woman without a husband. Regarding the character "guǎ," the lower part is "fēn" (分); the scriptural text uses "bì yáo" (必遙) as its phonetic, which is written as "biàn" (󱺀), though this is a scribal error.

*Liṅyǔ*: The first character is pronounced *dīng* (with the level tone) and the second is pronounced *yǔ* (with the rising tone). This was the name of prisons during the Zhou dynasty; in the Xia it was called Xiàtái, in the Yīn it was called Yǒulǐ, and in the Zhōu it was called Liṅyǔ. It refers to the place where criminals are confined and imprisoned. Both characters are formed through the method of "phonetic-semantic" (*xíngshēng*) composition.

*Fuyue* (斧鉞): The first character, *fu*, is pronounced as *fǔ* (with the alternative reading *yú*). In the *Liji* (Book of Rites), it states that only after a feudal lord is granted an axe and a battle-axe may he have the authority to execute. Zheng Xuan’s commentary says: "Only when one possesses the instruments does one dare to carry out the action. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines *fu* as "to chop," written with the radical *jin* (metal) and the phonetic *fu*. The second character, *yue*, is pronounced as *jué*. Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* (Notes on Ancient and Modern Times) states that a feudal lord who receives a yellow battle-axe is permitted to execute a general holding a ceremonial tablet. The *Shuowen* defines *yue* with the radical *jin* and the phonetic *zhué*. The character *zhué* consists of the element *jue* (pronounced *jué*) and the element *go* (spear). It is incorrect for the received text to write this as *wù*; its correct pronunciation is *mào*.

Regarding the character *gǔ* (蠱): its upper radical is pronounced *yě*. The Zhouli commentary by Zheng Xuan states that it refers to "wild venomous insects. The Shuowen jiezi states: "It is a worm within the belly that can cause painful harm to people; it is formed from the radical 'insect' (*chóng*) with the phonetic component *míng*. Some say it refers to 'poisonous *gǔ*'. The character *gǔ* is pronounced *gǔ*.

The two characters "Hù-mó" (護魔) mean "protecting against māras," though some say they are a transliteration of the Sanskrit term *homa*, which in the Tang language means "fire sacrifice. According to the *Yogācāra-homa-sūtra* (*Yújiā hù mó jīng*), there are four types of hearths: the crescent moon shape, the full moon shape, the square, and the octagonal, corresponding to four types of rites—namely, summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), pacification (*śāntika*), and attraction (*pauṣṭika*). Although the consecrations differ, all involve burning offerings such as the three white foods and various flowers and fruits within the hearth to sacrifice to the worthy and holy ones; this is precisely what is meant by the ancient rite of burning sacrificial wood.

The character [jiǎo] (with the radical *qù* and the phonetic *xiáng* [yán-fǎn]) is pronounced as *jiǎo*. The *Kǎo Shēng* states that it means "to boil" (*shān zhǔ*), referring to pouring hot water over hair to cause it to come loose. The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical *huǒ* with the phonetic *tán*. The form appearing in the scripture is a vulgar variant; the correct form is [jiǎo], and its archaic form is [jiǎo]. These are rarely used by people today.

*Zōngmáo* (騣髦): The first character, *zōng*, is pronounced with the initial *zi* and the final *jiǎn* (substitute *jiǎn*). Cāi Yōng stated that it refers to the hair on the back of a fine horse. Classical texts from both ancient and modern times refer to it as the mane of a horse (*mǎ zōng*). It is composed of the radical "horse" (*mǎ*) and the phonetic element "zhēn" (*zhēn*). The second character, *máo*, has the pronunciation *máo*; the phonetic element *zhēn* has the same pronunciation as above.

*Wan* (剜) [eye]: *shang* with the phonetic *wan* (莞). The *Beicang* states: "To carve and pare. The *Kaosheng* states: "To *wan* is to engrave. The *Shuowen* states: "It follows the radical *dao* (刀);

it is a compound of form and sound. *Ri* (刵) [ear]: *shang* with the phonetic *er* (而). Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states: "To *ri* is to cut off the ear. The *Guoyaya* also states: "To cut off the ear. The *Shuowen* states: "To sever the ear. It follows the radical *dao* (刀) and has *er* (耳) as its phonetic.

*Ni* (劓): *bí* (鼻) with the phonetic *yí* (宜). The Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that *ni* means "to cut. The *Shuowén* says it means "to sever," composed of the radical *dāo* (刀) and the phonetic *bí* (鼻). *Kuáihuì* (魁膾): The first character, *kuái* (魁), has the reading *kǔguī* (苦瓌).

The Master Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that *kuái* refers to "the army. The Master Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states it means "the head. The *Shījì* states it refers to "male spirits. It is composed of the radical *dòu* (斗) and the phonetic *guǐ* (鬼). The second character, *huì* (膾), has the reading *wàiguī* (外反). The *Guǎngyá* states that *huì* means "to mince. Examining the term *kuáihuì*, it refers to the commanders who slaughter the wicked and cruel; it is composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and the phonetic *huì* (會).

Regarding "fou" (罘) in the phrase "bound by a fou-net" (*fou wang shang bo*), the *Liji zhengyi* states that it is a net for catching beasts. The *Yunying* says it is a "jia" (罝). The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as a net for catching rabbits, formed from the radical "zi" (𠔿) with "bu" (不) as its phonetic component; "fu" (罘) is pronounced *gu*, while "jia" (罝) is pronounced *jie-ye* (姐耶反), and the latter [radical] is pronounced *wu-fang* (無倣反). It is also written as "wang" (网), though the correct form is "wang" (罔).

Regarding "zéjiǎo" (矰繳): when it appears above, it is read as "dēngfǎn" (登反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Tying silk floss to an arrow is called a *zé*. The *Kaogong ji* says: "*Zé* arrows are those used with bows," and further: "It is a name for the feathers of an arrow. The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "arrow" (*shì*) with the phonetic "zēng" (*zēng shēng*). The text here writes it as "zēng" (繒), pronounced "jílíngfǎn" (疾陵反), which is an erroneous transcription. In the following chapter, it is read as "kǔfǎn" (苦反). The *Guǎngyá* states: "Jiǎo means to entwine. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "It is raw silk thread. It is composed of the radical "silk" (*mì*) with the phonetic "jiǎo" (*jiǎo shēng*). "Jiǎo" is pronounced "yángzhuófǎn" (羊灼反). The character "jìn" (𦅾) is also used interchangeably.

*Pretas* (薜茘多): the first character is pronounced *pí* (鼙) with the *bì* (閉) tone, and the second is pronounced *lì* (𥟦) with the *dì* (帝) tone; this is a corruption of the Sanskrit term. The correct form is *Pretas*, which translates here as "hungry ghosts" (*èguǐ*). It is also the general name for the realm of ghosts within the three miserable paths of existence.

Scroll Four, Part Four: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Six Pāramitās of the Path of Reasoning. Regarding the character *pǔ* (乳哺): following the *Hǔnmànzǐ* with Xu Shen’s commentary, it states that chewing food in the mouth and giving it to [an infant] is called *bù* (哺), as in the expression "feeding a bird or a child. The *Shuowén* explains this character as being composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "fǔ" (*fǔ*). However, the current text uses the character *bù* (餔) from the "food" (*shí*) radical, which refers to rice porridge. It also has two pronunciations, *bō* and *bù*, neither of which carries the meaning of "breast-feeding" (*rǔbǔ*).

*Pinqi* (the first character pronounced with the *bi* and *yin* finals; the second with the *zi* and *liu* finals). The *Wenzi Jilüe* states that "pin" refers to knitting the eyebrows. Gu Yewang says it is the appearance of one who is sorrowful, anxious, or displeased. The archaic form is written as *pin*, and it is also written as *pin*; the second character is sometimes written as *wu*. The scriptural text uses the character for "to contract" (*cu*) with the "foot" radical, which is incorrect.

*Kǐ* (溪): Upper radical *shàng* (上), phonetic *qǐ xī fǎn* (啟奚反). The *Erya* says: "Water that flows into a river (*chuān*). The *Shuowen* says: "A river (*chuān*) is that which has no further outlet; it takes the radical *gǔ* (谷) and the phonetic *xī* (奚); it is also written as the character *xī*. Lower radical *xià* (下), phonetic *jiàn yàn fǎn* (閒晏反). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says: "When mountains flank water, it is called a *jiàn* (㵎). The *Shuowen* says: "It takes the radical *shuǐ* (水) and the phonetic *jiàn* (閒). It is also written as *yǎo* (𡼏) or *yì* (𧯑); all are interchangeable.

The character 漲 (zhàng) is pronounced with the upper radical *fáng* (fan) and the phonetic *wáng*. Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that it means "to soak" (*yān*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "pure," formed from the water radical and the phonetic *fán*. The lower part is pronounced *zhāng* (liàng). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Jiangfu* states that it refers to "swelling waters. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further explains it is formed from the water radical and the phonetic *zhāng*.

"Thi" (噏): The first character is read as *xīn* (急, qí) and *guàn* (顧, guàn). Yě Wáng says it means "to draw in the breath. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "internal respiration," composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "xi" (*xī*). It is also written as the character "xi" (吸). The pronunciation of "xīn" (歆) is *xǔ jīn* (許金).

*Huán* (滑, pinyin: huá; *guān*, pinyin: guǎn): *Bóyǎ* states it refers to a finger ring. *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states it is a ring for the little finger. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic element "huán" with its final sound abbreviated. Below is *chuānjuàn* (pinyin: chuānjuàn). *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* states it is an arm bracelet. According to the *Shuowén*, it is a wrist ring composed of the radical "metal" and the phonetic element "chuān."

Regarding "ěr dāng" (ear-ornament): the *Shìmíng* states that to pierce the ear and attach a bead is called a *dāng*; the *Bīcāng* says it is an ear ornament; the *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical "wáng" with the phonetic "dāng.

Regarding "páiyóu" (actor/entertainer): the *Bóyǎ* states that "pái" is also "yōu"; the *Shuōwén* says it means "performance" (*xì*), composed of the radical "rén" with the phonetic "fēi. The lower character is pronounced "yōu. Gù Yěwáng says that an "yōu" is what a person who provides entertainment does for amusement. Dú's commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* says it means "jesting" (*tiáo xì*). The *Cāngjiépiān* says "yōu" is also "amusement" (*lè*); the *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical "rén" with the phonetic "yōu."

*Upaniṣad-bhāga* (Níshātán fēn) is the ultimate limit of numerical divisions in the Sanskrit language; some call it *upaniṣada*. In the *Yìyì* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings), Master Huìyuàn cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, translating it as "subtle division" (*weixì fēn*). It is like dividing a single hair into one hundred parts, then further dividing one of those parts into ten million parts, and continuing to divide each subsequent part as before until reaching the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal particle), which is the point where no further division is possible; this is called the *upaniṣad-bhāga*.

*Stūpa* (the initial *sū* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṣ*, as indicated by the character 反; it is a Sanskrit term) is sometimes called *stūpa* or *tapa*; these are merely different dialectal variations of the Sanskrit word. Translated [into Chinese], it means "lofty and supreme square mound. It refers to a stupa that enshrines the relics (*śarīra*) of the Tathāgata, such as those made of stone, iron, or wood. In vernacular speech, it is sometimes called a *futu*.

"Nǎn" (赧) and above: pronounced *niǎn* (拏揀反). The *Fāngyán* states that "nǎn" also means shame (*kuì*). The *Shuowén* states it refers to the face turning red with shame; the character is formed with the phonetic element *jiǎn* (㞋), which has the pronunciation *jiǎn*. The form in the scripture using "pí" (皮) to form "nǎn" (𧹞) is a scribal error.

*Chuáng* (瘡): Pronounced *chǔ* (霜) with a retroflex initial. The *Lǐjì* states: "If there is a sore on the head, one washes it. The *Shuōwén* says: "A wound or injury. In ancient script, it is written as 用, representing the shape of a knife entering [the flesh]. Below, it is pronounced *qiú* (求). The *Cāngjiépiān* says: "It means illness. Furthermore, small ones are called *wòu* (疣) and large ones are called *zhuì* (贅). The *Gǔjīn zhèngzì* also writes it as 𤴨. *Zhuì* (贅) is pronounced *jiārùì* (佳芮).

Fascicle Five. *Mahāyāna-nyāya-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*, Fascicle Five. Regarding "dream" (*mèng*): The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains this character as being composed of the radical *mián* (roof) and the phonetic *zhuàng*. In the *Zhouli*, it is stated that one divines the good or bad fortune of the six types of dreams by means of the sun, moon, and stars: first, the dream of reality (*zhèng-mèng*); second, the dream of transformation (*guǐ-mèng*); third, the dream of thought (*sī-mèng*); fourth, the dream of awakening (*wù-mèng*); fifth, the dream of joy (*xǐ-mèng*); and sixth, the dream of fear (*jù-mèng*). Regarding "sleep" (*mí*): This is pronounced with the final *-pǐ* (as in *mípì*). It refers to lying down to rest. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical *mèng* with *wèi* as the phonetic, which has been abbreviated.

The character *wù* (寤) is also written as *jué* (覺) with the same pronunciation; the *Jiàobóyǎ* states that it means "to perceive. The lower radical is pronounced *wù* (五故反). The *Máoshī* states that *wù* also means "to awaken," and the *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the abbreviated form of *mèng* (㝱) with *wú* (吾) as the phonetic component.

*Xiàn* (陷): The upper radical is *xián* (咸) with the phonetic *jiàn* (鑒). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "a pit" (*xué*). Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says it means "to sink" (*mò*). It is composed of the radical *fù* (阜) and the phonetic *xiàn* (臽); it may also be written simply as the character *xiàn* (臽), with the pronunciation *qíng xìng* (情性). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* says it refers to digging the ground to create a deep pit for capturing birds and beasts. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical *xué* (穴) and the phonetic *jǐng* (井); it may also be written as *jìng* (阱) or *lǐng* (汬), all of which are archaic forms.

"Yǒng" (swimming): the radical is *shui* (water) and the phonetic is *you* (with the pinyin *yǒu*). Gù Yěwáng says it means "floating upon the water while moving forward. Zhèng’s commentary on the *Zōuliǎo* states it is for the purpose of preventing drowning. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of *shui* and the phonetic *you*. The *Máo Shī* says "to move secretly within the water is *yǒng*. Guō’s commentary on the *Ěryá* says "walking at the bottom of the water. The *Shuowén* further explains it as being composed of *shui* and the abbreviated form of the phonetic *yǒng*.

"Hou-er" (hook-bait): the character "er" is pronounced as *réng* or *lì*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "flour cake" and also "food. According to this, hook-bait refers to using food that fish eat, placed upon a hook, in order to catch them.

Regarding "black bee" (hēifēng): the reading for the second character is *xià* (with the phonetic *fú* and *róng*). The *Erya* states: "earth-bee" (*tǔfēng*) and "wood-bee" (*mùfēng*). Guo’s commentary says: "In present-day Jiangdong, those large bees that build nests in the ground are called 'horse-bees' (*mǎfēng*), which devour their [other insects'] larvae. The *Erya* correctly uses the character 蠭; nowadays the common form is 蜂, or it is pronounced *péng* in colloquial usage.

*Xuānlán* (旋嵐): The second character, *lán*, is pronounced with the *là* and *nán* finals; it is a term from the Sanskrit language (*vāyu*), referring to the great violent winds that arise at the time of a kalpa-ending disaster.

*Tánxiè* (談謔): The first character, *tán*, is pronounced with the *dào* and *nán* finals. Gu Yewang states that it means "discourse" or "speech. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic element "flame" (*yán*). The second character, *xiè*, is pronounced with the *xiāng* and *nuò* finals. The *Erya* states: "To laugh, frolic, and act wantonly is 'playful mockery' (*xièláo*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* also defines it as "play," explaining it as being composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic element "oppression" (*nuò*).

*Kugǎo* (with the first character *kū* pronounced with the *gǔ* rhyme and the second *gǎo* pronounced with the *lǎo* rhyme): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "kū" and "gǎo" are synonymous; it is formed from the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "old" (*gǔ*). The lower character is pronounced with the *lǎo* rhyme; the *Kaosheng* states that "gǎo" means "dry. The *Shuowen* writes it as *gǎo*, meaning "the wood is withered," formed from the radical "wood" and the phonetic "high" (*gāo*); it is also written as the character *cè*.

Regarding "jing" (睛): the *Yingyin Yiqie Jing Yin* states it refers to the eyeball. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "qing" (靑). Although there are instances in the script where it is written as "jing" (精), this carries the meanings of "excellent" or "correct," and does not carry the meaning of "eyeball."

"Sì" (厮): Upper radical *xi* (息), lower radical *zi* (資). He Xiu’s commentary on the *Gongyang zhuan* states: "A person of lowly status. The *Guangya* defines it as "one who dispatches messengers. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "It follows the radical *guǎn* (广) and takes *si* (斯) as its phonetic; it is also written as *wēi* (㒋)."

Volume Six. *Mahāyāna-nyāya-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*, Volume Six. *Caṇḍāla* is a Sanskrit term; it is also called *caṇḍāla*, which is translated as "Fierce and Blazing. This is a name for the class of people who are butchers. One account says they are the executioners and wardens of hell. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that when such a person walks, they ring a bell to identify themselves, or carry a bamboo staff with a severed head upon it; otherwise, the king would punish them.

*Děng* (隥): The upper radical is *tǐ* (隹) with the phonetic *xí* (奚). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "ladder" (*tījī*). The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it similarly, stating it is composed of the radical *mù* (木) with *dì* (第) as the phonetic. The lower part is *dēng* (登) with the phonetic *dèng* (鄧). The *Bōyá* states it means "a step" (*lǚ*) or "to ascend by relying upon it. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical *fù* (阜) with *dēng* (登) as the phonetic.

"Ant-hole" (yì xué): "yì" is pronounced as *yǐ* (with the *shàng* tone). The *Erya* states: "The large ant is called *bífú*; the small one is called *yì*. Guo's commentary notes that the larger ones are colloquially called *mǎ bífú*, and according to the *Shuowen*, this character is formed with the radical for insects and the phonetic *qǐ*. The forms "蟻" (*yǐ*) and "𧑃" (*yì*) found in the scriptures are both vulgar characters.

The upper character, *juān* (with the phonetic *xuán* reversed), the *Kǎośēng* says means "to discard. The common form is written with the radical 手 (*shǒu*) and the phonetic *juān* abbreviated. The lower character, *qì*, has the reading *qīngyì*. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to abandon. It is composed of 廾 (*kǒng*, meaning "to join the hands") and 枼 (*bō'ān*, meaning "a leaf"), with 云 (*tǔgǔ*, meaning "an orphaned child") added; it is a compound character (*huìyì zì*) formed by writing the character for "child" upside down to signify pushing [the child] away and discarding it.

*Géxié* (革𩌦): The upper character is read as *gēng* (額) and the lower as *suǒ* (所). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states that footwear which does not secure the heel is called *géxié*. According to the *Shuōwén*, it belongs to the category of *dī* (鞮). It is composed of the radical "leather" (*gé*) and the phonetic element "move" (*xǐ*). In the received text, it is written with the radical "corpse" (*shī*) as *xiě* (屣) or *xié* (𩌦), both of which are vulgar characters. *Dī* (鞮) is pronounced *dūxī* (都奚).

*Kuì* (媿) and *nù* (恧): The former is pronounced *guī* (歸) with the *fǎn* (反) [classifier]; Duan’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuan* states that *kuì* means shame (*cán*) or disgrace (*chǐ*). The *Shuowen* says it is composed of "woman" (*nǚ*) and "ghost" (*guǐ*) as phonetic components, or it may also be written with "heart" (*xīn*), in which case it is also valid; the latter is pronounced *liù* (六).
