Regarding "xiāng" (fragrance) at the top [of the character]: it is pronounced with six different tones. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that "xiāng" means "to sell. Gu Yewang says it means "to sell goods. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of "lǐn" (𩰲) and the phonetic "yù" (毓). "Lǐn" is pronounced "gé" (格), and "yù" is pronounced "yù" (育). Below, "xiāng" (fragrance) is correctly written as "jì" (𪏽), composed of "shǔ" (黍) and "gān" (甘).

*Qiào* (竅): The upper radical is *qì* (啟, pronounced with the *jiào* tone). Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that it means "aperture" (*kǒng*). The *Shuowen* states it means "void" (*kōng*), formed from the radical *xué* (穴) and the phonetic *jiǎo* (敫). The lower radical is *xiàng* (鄉, pronounced with the *nì* tone). The *Guoyaya* states it means "crack" (*liè*). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "fissure" (*xì*). The *Shuowen* states it means "a small hole in the wall," formed from the radicals *fù* (阜) and *bái* (白), indicating something small at the top and bottom. The text of the scripture uses *xī* (隟), which is incorrect.

"Cāng" (倉): The *Qiēyùn* reads "gāng" (崗) as the initial and final rhymes; it is defined as a granary (*cānglǐn*). The *Shìmíng* states that a granary is a place where grain is stored. "Xià" (下): The *Qiēyùn* reads "yuán" (緣) as the initial and final rhymes; it also notes that "chuán" (篅) is likewise a granary. According to the *Shuōwén*, this character is composed of the radical "bamboo" (竹) with "chuán" (遄) in abbreviated form as the phonetic. In the canonical texts, it is sometimes written as "chuí" (圌), which is a vulgar variant.

*Tian* (挻) and *zhi* (埴): the former is pronounced *shang* with the *yan* rhyme; the latter is pronounced *cheng* with the *li* rhyme. The *Huainanzi* states: "The potter *tian-zhi* [molds] the clay. Xu’s commentary explains that *tian* means to press down. Kong’s commentary on the *Shangshu* explains that *zhi* is sticky clay. Ru Chun says: "*Tian* means to strike; *zhi* means softness and harmony," referring to fashioning vessels from soft earth. In the *Shuowen*, the character *tian* is composed of the radical for hand (*shou*) and the phonetic element *yan*, while *zhi* is composed of the radical for earth (*tu*) and the phonetic element *zhi*; both are phono-semantic compounds. In the text of the scripture, both characters are written as *shen* (埏) and *zhi* (埴), but the upper character is erroneous.

*Huài* (壞): The *Fāngbēi* (芳盃) Rhyme Dictionary states this refers to unbaked earthenware. The *Shuowén* (說文) writes it as *huài* (坏), with the second character pronounced *jì* (冀). The *Shǐjì* (史記) states that Shùn fashioned various vessels (*shíqì*) at Shòuqīu. The *Shuowén* defines it as "vessels" (*qǐngmì*); it is a general term for utensils used for food and drink. It is composed of the radical *quán* (犬, dog) and the phonetic *jí* (㗊, sound *zhuānglì*). *Jí* (㗊) signifies a multitude of vessels, while the dog is there to guard them; thus, it is a word formed through the combination of meanings (*huìyì zì*).

"Zào" (燥) [is pronounced with the upper radical *sū* and the *hào* fanqie]. The *Yùnyùn* states it means "dry. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to dry by fire," composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "sāo" (*shēng*), with the lower part pronounced *rù*. The *Yùnyùn* states it means "moistened by water. The text of the scripture uses "shī" (濕); this is not the standard usage.

*Xiū* (恤) [upper radical: 示, phonetic: 新, lüèqiè: lǎn; lower radical: 心, phonetic: 葵, yīng]: *Kāoshēng* states it means "orphaned and solitary"; *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as "having no brothers. *Zhèn* (賑) [upper radical: 示, phonetic: 新, lüèqiè: lǎn]: *Yuànyùn* states it means "to provide relief. *Xiū* (恤) [lower radical: 心, phonetic: 葵, yīng]: *Kāoshēng* states it means "solitary"; *Wénzìdiǎn* explains it as "having no brothers."

*Dí* (嫡): Upper radical *shàng* (上), *dīng* (丁) with the phonetic *lì* (歷); the *Qièyùn* defines it as "correct. Lexicons state it means "eldest" (*zhǎng*). The *Erya* says: "The eldest wife is called *dí*. Lower radical *xiáng* (祥), *zhì* (志) with the phonetic *fǎn* (反). The *Erya* states: "*Sì* (嗣)" means "succession."

The character *jì* (日躋) is read as *shàng rén* (one who ascends); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "real" (*shí*), signifying that the essence of the great sun is never diminished. The character *xī* (兮) is read as *zǔ* (ancestral); according to the *Erya*, it means "to ascend. The *Gongyang Zhuan* asks: "What is *jì*? It says, "It is to climb. Sometimes it is written as *jí* (隮), with the pronunciation *shēng* (ascend).

*Jià* (駕): In the *Shànggǔ Yà* (上古訝) rhyme-cut, it means to mount or ride. The *Máoshī* (毛詩) says, "I shall mount my carriage" (*jià wǒ qí jì*). *Jì* (其) is read as *xīlì* (息利); *jì* (𮩴) refers to four horses riding together. The *Erya* (爾雅) states, "The *Tiānsì* (天駟) is the *Fáng* (房) [constellation]. Guō Pǔ’s commentary notes that because the dragon is the heavenly horse, the four stars of the *Fáng* are called the *Tiānsì*. Lǐ Chūnfēng’s commentary on the *Tiānwén Jīng* (天文經) states: "The *Tiānsì* is also named *Tiānmǎ* (天馬). Two stars constitute the right yoke-horse and the right side-horse; two stars constitute the left yoke-horse and the left side-horse. *Mǎ* (馬) is read as *wénjù* (文句).

Volume 12, Fascicle 12, New Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Fascicle 12. Regarding "Cí" (Sacrifice): the upper radical is *cí* (pronounced *zī*); the *Erya* states, "The spring sacrifice is called *cí*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes that the word for *cí* is *sì* (to feed). *Sì* is pronounced *sì*; the lower character is *zǐ* with the *lì* rhyme. According to the *Qieyun*, it means to offer food. The *Erya* further states: "The sacrifice to Heaven is called *fánchái* (burning wood as an offering); the sacrifice to Earth is called *chénméi* (burying the offerings). The *Lunyu* says: "When sacrificing to the spirits, act as if the spirits were present. In the *Shuowen*, the character for sacrifice (*jì*) is composed of "moon" (phonetic *ròu*, meaning meat), "hand" (phonetic *shǒu*), and "divinity" (phonetic *shì*). This signifies holding meat in the hand to display it, which constitutes a sacrifice. The form used in this scripture is not the original character.

Regarding "xúnshòu" (巡狩): the upper character "xún" (巡) is pronounced according to the rhyme scheme as *xiánglún* (上祥倫), meaning "to go everywhere" (*biàn*) and "to inspect" (*chá*). The lower character "shòu" (狩) is pronounced according to the rhyme scheme as *shūjiù* (舒救); the *Yīngyùn* (韻英) states it means "hunting. The *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents) says: "In the second month, he made a tour of inspection to the east, reaching Mount Dàizōng to offer the *chái* sacrifice. Kǒng’s commentary states: "The feudal lords guard the land for the Son of Heaven; therefore, he tours them. He proceeds to the east first because he follows the spring; the same applies to summer, autumn, and winter in turn. After touring the four peaks, he returns to report to the Grand Ancestral Temple. It further says: "Every five years there is one tour of inspection; the various lords perform the four audiences."

"Qìngzhì" (罄志): "Qìng" (罄) is pronounced with the initial *kǔ* and final *dìng* (according to the *Erya*, it means "exhausted"); Gu Yewang says it means "the interior of a vessel is empty. "Zhì" (志) is pronounced with the initial *zhí* and final *lì* (according to Sūn Miǎn, it means "thought," "intention," or "sincerity"). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "zhī" (之), where "zhī" has the sound *zhī*. According to the commentary, "qìngzhì" means to empty one's mind and exhaust one's sincerity.

Regarding calendrical calculation, the "Canon of Yao" states: "The calendar models the sun and moon, reverently transmitting the seasons to the people. Kong Yingda’s commentary explains: "The calendar models its divisions and nodes, reverently recording the celestial seasons to transmit them to the people" (the character *su* in *sujiàn* [reverently record] is pronounced *fǎn*). The *Shiben* states that it was created by Shishou during the time of the Yellow Emperor. Liu Hui’s *Jiuzhang*, *Sūnzǐ*, and *Wúcáo* are all arts of calculation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "The *suàn* (calculus) is six inches long; it is used by those who calculate the chronology of the calendar."

The upper character *tiáo* (髫) is pronounced as *tiáo* (the first tone); the *Kǎośēng* states it refers to a child’s shaved head with two tufts left on the sides. The *Zìshū* says: "Tiáo" means the hanging hair of a small child; it follows the radical *biāo* (髟) and uses *zhào* (召) as its phonetic component. The lower character, read as *chūjìn* (初覲), is explained by Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhōulǐ*: "Boys at eight years of age and girls at seven years of age undergo the 'destruction of teeth' (*huǐchǐ*). The *Shuowén* states that this character follows the radical *chǐ* (齒) and uses *qī* (七) as its phonetic. Alternatively, it may be written as *chèn* (齔) using the radicals *bǐ* (匕) and *yǐn* (乚); both of these forms are not the original characters.

The *Weihou* (緯候) states above that "noble" (*gui*) refers to the warp and woof; "warp" (*jing*) has the phonetic *gu* (古定反) and "woof" (*wei*) has the phonetic *hu* (胡遘反). The *Yunpu* (韻譜) says it means "to observe. According to the *Wuxingli* (五星曆), the twenty-eight lunar mansions constitute the warp, while the sun, moon, and five planets constitute the woof. Because their movements and degrees follow a sequential order, one observes and divines good fortune and misfortune based upon them.

*Bìxié* (弼諧): "Bì" (弼) is pronounced with the upper radical *fáng* and the final *mì* (反); the *Erya* states that "bì" means "to assist. The *Guǎngyùn* states it means "to prepare. In archaic script, it is written as *jí* (㢸). "Xié" (諧) is pronounced with the lower radical *hù* and the final *jiē* (反); the *Erya* states that "xié" means "to harmonize. The *Shujing* says: "Truly following his virtue; his plans were brilliant and his assistants were harmonious. This refers to being harmonious in assisting [the ruler].

*Yuán-xí*: "Yuán" (原) has the phonetic *niú-yuán* (牛袁) as its reading. The *Erya* states: "That which is broad and level is called *yuán*. It further states: "That which is suitable for cultivation is called *yuán*. Guo’s commentary notes: "It means that which can be planted with grain to provide food. "Xí" (隰) has the phonetic *xi-sì-rù* (似入). The *Erya* states: "That which is low and damp is called *xí*. Guo’s commentary cites the *Gongyang Zhuan*, saying: "That which is low and level is called *xí*."

Regarding the characters 𢤱 (upper part: lóng dǒng; lower part: yīn lì) and 戾 (also written as 悷), the *Qieyun* states that they denote an appearance of being ill-regulated. Both are vulgarly used characters; according to the *Zishu*, these characters do not originally exist.

*Xiōngcán* (兇殘): The upper character is pronounced *xǔ róng* (許容). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "obstinate. The *Shuowén* says it means "evil," composed of the radical "person" (*rén*) above and "dangerous" (*xiōng*) below. The lower character is pronounced *zuó gān* (昨竿). The *Yùpǔ* says it means "to wound" or "to harm. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical "bad" (*dài*) with the phonetic component *zān*. *Dài* is pronounced *wǔ gē* (五割) and *zān* is pronounced *cán* (殘). The *Yìjīng* says: "The bundles of silk are *zānzān* (戔戔)."

"Deng" (登) means ascending; in the *Fangyong* it is glossed as "to return," and in the *Yupian* it means "abundant. The *Yunjí* states it means "great" or "much," with the phonetic transcription "dōu téng. The *Chèyùn* defines it as "accomplished" or "to rise. According to the "Monthly Ordinances" (*Yueling*) of the *Lǐjì*, in the second month of autumn, "the grain then ascends" (*hé nǎi dēng*).

*Yí* (pronounced *yú lì* in reverse): The character and its gloss state that *yí* refers to the appearance of towering mountain peaks; it means standing upright and straight like a mountain peak. *Qiāo*: Pronounced *jù qiáo* in reverse. The *Shuowen* says it refers to a horse six feet high.

The *Xiaojing* says, "One who is in a position of authority must not be arrogant. The Imperial Commentary states, "To lack propriety is arrogance. *Chě*: Pronounced *chǐ shì* in reverse; also written as *zhā*. The *Shuowen* says it means extravagance. The *Qieyun* says it means abundance.

"Thighs and arms" (*gǔhóng*)—the upper character means the buttocks (pì), the lower character means the arms (bì). The *Shàngshū* says, "Thighs and arms constitute a human being," and Kǒng's commentary states, "Only when hands and feet are complete does one become a person. It further says, "How excellent are these thighs and arms!"

"Non-gu" (非辜): "Gu" (辜) is pronounced with the *gǔ* rhyme (下古胡反). The *Erya* states: "Gu means 'crime' (*zuì*, pronounced *zuì*). This means that if a person brings suffering upon themselves, they are guilty. Because the First Emperor of Qin hoped to achieve the title of "Huang" (Emperor) for successive generations, he disliked the character "gu" because it resembled the character "huang. Therefore, it was changed to "zui" (罪). Regarding "gu," the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of a simplified form of "zuì" (辠) with the phonetic element "gu" (古). The character in the received text, written with the hand radical and the element "sheng" (𢪿), is an error in transcription; it does not appear in standard dictionaries of characters.

The character for *bēi* (韛) is pronounced *pái* (排) with a retroflex initial. The *Cāngjié piān* states that *bēi* refers to oxhide (*wéipí*). Gu Yewáng says it means to blow upon a large forge to make it blaze; it is composed of the radical *wéi* (韋) and the phonetic *lín* (𤰇), where *lín* has the pronunciation *bèi* (備).

"Rangbi" (攘臂) means to roll up the sleeves; the "shang" (上) is pronounced as "yangfan" (羊反). Mencius said, "He rolled up his sleeves and descended from his carriage. Yu Wang (顧野王) stated that this refers to removing the cuffs of the garment to expose the arm. "Mie" (袂) is pronounced as "milifan" (彌勵反); it refers to the sleeve.

Regarding the character *niè* (齧): the upper radical is *jié* (結) with the reversed stroke; the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "to bite" or "to gnaw. The *Shuōwén* (說文) explains it as being composed of the radical for "teeth" (*chǐ*) and the phonetic element *qiè* (契) in abbreviated form. In the scriptural text, it is written as *niè* (嚙) with the radical for "mouth" (*kǒu*). The pronunciation of *qiè* is *kǔjié* (苦結).

*Yuē* (with the phonetic component *shàng* and *yú*, reversed; according to the *Erya*, it means "to cut off the feet"). Guo’s commentary states: "It refers to having one's feet severed. The *Shuowen* writes it as *wéi* (meaning "a punishment for the feet"). Below is *tǔdiāo* (reversed); it is also written as *biè*, a vulgar character meaning "to pull" according to the *Yunpu*.

*Páng* (䏺脹): The upper character is read as *pó* (璞邦反). The *Bīcāng* states that *gāng* (胮) is also "swelling. The *Wénzìdiǎnshuō* explains that it is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic "fēng" (夆), with the pronunciation *fāngféng* (芳逢反). The received text uses *féng* (逢) instead of *péng* (膖), which is a vulgar variant. The lower character is read as *zhāngliàng* (張亮反). Du’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "It means the abdomen is distended and full."

The upper part of the *cháng* (intestines) is pronounced *zhú* (with the radical *艮*). The *Báihùtōng* states: "The small intestine (*xiǎocháng*) is the palace (*fǔ*) of the heart; the [large] intestine (*cháng*) is the palace of the lungs. The *Shìmíng* says: "It means 'to cause the qi within the abdomen to flow freely (*shāngchàng*'); it refers to the palace where the qi within the belly circulates. The lower part is pronounced *wèi* (with the radical *韋*). The *Báihùtōng* states: "The stomach (*wèi*) is the palace of the spleen. The *Shuōwén* says: "The palace of grain (*gǔfǔ*); it is formed with the radical *月* (meat/moon), the form of the stomach, and the phonetic *胃*. The character may also be written as *胃*."

The sinews (*jin*) reside above [the flesh]. In the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), it says: "The physician nourishes the sinews with pungent flavors. The *Shuowen* states: "It is the strength of the flesh. It is composed of 'flesh' (*rou*) and 'bamboo' (*zhu*), for bamboo is among things that have many sinews; it is composed of 'strength' (*li*), as the form of 'strength' resembles the shape of a sinew. In the scriptures, some versions write it with the radical "grass" (*cao*) as *qiu*, or with the radical "horn" (*jiao*) as *jin*; these are not the correct characters. The lower part is pronounced *bo*. In the *Zhouli*, it says: "One nourishes the vessels (*mai*) with salty flavors. The *Shuowen* says: "The channels through which blood flows throughout the body are called vessels (*mai*). It correctly consists of "blood" (*xue*) and "breast" (*bi*); the character *bi* is pronounced *pu-mai*. In the scriptural texts, those written with the radical "permanence" (*yong*) are vulgar forms.

Regarding "biān" (whip/lashing): it is read as *miánfǎn* (綿反). Yě Wáng says it refers to using leather to strike offenders. The *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters) states it is a staff for striking horses. The *Shuowén* says it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jié*) and the phonetic "piàn" (*piàn*), with the final rhyme being *chǒuzhī* (丑之反). The *Lǜshū* (Book of Laws) states: "Corporal punishment, flogging, penal servitude, banishment, and death"—this is what is meant. As for the lowest form of corporal punishment for those who have committed offenses, the *Shuowén* defines "tái" (笞) as "to lash," composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "tái" (*tái*), with the pronunciation *yí* (音怡).

Volume 13, Fascicle Thirteen. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Thirteen. *Chéng yùn*: The upper character (垽) is pronounced with the initial *zhí* and the final *líng*; it refers to the clarity of water. The lower character (垽) is pronounced with the initial *yú* and the final *jìn*. The *Erya* states: "Sediment is called *yùn*. Guo’s commentary says: "It is dregs and sediment; in Jiangdong, it is called *yùn*."
*Ōng-yù* (蓊鬱): The first character is pronounced *wǔ* (烏孔反) and the second *yùn* (蘊勿反). Dictionaries state that this describes the lush appearance of grasses and trees;

it should be written as *yù* (欝), and the version in the sutra as *yù* (欝) is incorrect. *Bǐ-ní* (俾倪): The first character is pronounced *pǔ* (普米反) and the second *wǔ* (五禮反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *pěi-nì* (壀堄) or *dài-nì* (隦𨺙). The *Guoyaya* states it refers to small parapets on a city wall. Regarding the phonetic analysis, it refers to a *nǚqiáng* (女牆, "women's wall"). The *Shiming* states that one observes for emergencies through holes in the wall. Both characters may also be read with the fourth tone (*qùshēng*). Some versions of the sutra write this as *pí-àn* (脾腉), which is incorrect.

*Bǎo qiàn* (寶塹): The lower character is pronounced *qiàn* (with the initial *q* and final *-an*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that a *qiàn* is a moat or ditch. Some editions of the sutra write this with the water radical (*quàn*), which is erroneous. *Zhōuzhǔ* (洲渚):

The upper character is pronounced *zhōu*, and the lower is *zhǔ* (with the initial *ch* and final *-u*). The *Erya* states: "That which can be inhabited within the water is called a *zhōu*; a small *zhōu* is called a *zhǔ*. It is sometimes written as the character *zhǔ* (陼); a small *zhǔ* is called a *zhǐ* (沚), pronounced *zhǐ*.

"Nǔlù" (nǔ, with the tone of huā wǎ; this pronunciation is used to avoid vulgar taboos; its original phonetic is láng guǒ). Gù Yěwáng says it means "to strip off clothes and bare the torso. The *Shuowen Jiezi* [explains it] as being composed of the radical "clothing" (衣) and the phonetic "guǒ. Lexicons [also] compose it with the radical "body" (身) as "luǒ," while the *Yupian* composes it with the radical "person" (人) as "lě"; these are identical to the text of the sutra.

The character for "to eat" (啗) is also written as 啖, with the same pronunciation (dú lǎn). It is sometimes written as 噉, pronounced tú gǎn. Lexicons all define these characters as "to consume food. They also mean "to chew and swallow. It is composed of the radical "mouth" (口) and the phonetic "xuàn" (臽), with the character for "meat" (肉) below; this "meat" correctly depicts the form of muscle and sinew.

*Chǎnkuǎng* (諂誑): The first character, *chǎn*, is pronounced with the initial *chǒu* and the final *yàn* (also written as *chèn*); it is synonymous with *yú* (flattery). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "xuàn" (*xiàn*). The scriptural text uses the character *tǎo* (舀) with the pronunciation *tā* and *lì*; this does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. *Tǎo* has the pronunciation *yǐ* and *zhǎo*. The second character, *kuǎng*, is pronounced with the initial *jū* and the final *kuàng*. It means to deceive. According to dictionaries, it is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "kuáng. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "mind" (*xīn*) to form *qiè* (㤮), which has the same meaning.

Volume 14, Scroll Fourteen. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Fourteen. Regarding the character 竊 (*qiè*): Guo’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it means "shallow" (*qiǎn*). The *Qieyun* states it means "to steal. Dictionaries state it means "private" or "clandestine. It is formed with the radical 穴 (cave) and the phonetic component 釆 (biàn), with the sound 𦵮 (yì). There are instances in the sūtra text where the character is written as 竊; this is incorrect.

Kuśinagara is the name of a city in the Western Regions according to the Sanskrit language; in this [Chinese] language, it is called the City of Soft Grass, or alternatively, the City of Fragrant Grass, because such grass grows there in abundance. It is located within the borders of Central India and measures over one thousand *li* in circumference; it is the very place where the Tathāgata entered Great Parinirvāṇa.

*Parinirvāṇa* (the first syllable pronounced *bǔ mò* as a transcription of the Sanskrit) is an ancient term; *nìhuán* (Nirvana) is a corruption and abbreviation of it. The correct term is *mahāparinirvāṇam*, which is translated here as "Great Perfect Quiescence. This refers to the perfection of the three dots (*bindu*) and the letter *ī*, as well as the perfection of the four virtues and the fruit of enlightenment.

*Lù* (諸上盧谷反): The *Yun* dictionary states it means "to drip. Guo's commentary on the *Erya* says it means "to strain out saliva and foam. It is also written as *lèi* (𥂖); the *Yunyīng* dictionary states it means "to remove water."

The character 㧌 (upper radical *hu* with the phonetic *gāo*) is a vulgar form; its correct form is 撓 (*qièyùn*: *jiǎo*, also meaning "to move"). The pronunciation of 撓 is *nú qiǎo*. This [vulgar form] is not accepted here.

*Chán* (upper radical *zhí*, *lián* rhyme; meaning "dwelling"). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that an open space in the market is called a *chán*. (Lower radical *dōu*, *niàn* rhyme). The *Qiè Yùn* defines it as a shop or stall. Cui Bao’s *Gǔjīn Zhù* says: "A *diàn* is a 'placing' (*zhì*); it is so called because goods are placed there for sale. It is formed with the radical *guǎng* (pronounced *yǎn*) and the phonetic *zhàn*. *Guǎng* is a compound character consisting of both form and sound. *Yù* (in the term *zhùyù*) is pronounced *yáng jù* rhyme. *Diàn*: The upper radical is *zhí*, *lián* rhyme; the meaning is "dwelling. The *Kǎo Shēng* says: "An empty space in the marketplace is called a *chán*. The lower radical is *dōu*, *niàn* rhyme. According to the *Qiè Yùn*, it refers to a shop or stall. Cui Bao’s *Gǔjīn Zhù* states: "A *diàn* is a 'placing' (*zhì*); it is used for placing goods for sale. It is composed of the radical *guǎng* and the phonetic *zhàn*. *Guǎng* is pronounced *yǎn*; it is a character formed from both shape and sound. *Yù* is pronounced *yáng jù* rhyme.

Regarding "yán-xiù" (巖岫): the *Wǔxián Fǎnqiè Yùn* states that it means "a precipitous peak. The *Mao Shi* says, "The stones are yán-yán," with the commentary noting it means "steep. The lower character is pronounced as in "sì-yòu" (似右). The *Erya* states, "A mountain with a hollow is called a xiù," and Guo Pu explains it as meaning "rocky caves."

The character for "to sell" (鬻) is now commonly written as "yu" (鬻), with the same pronunciation as "yú" (余六反). Lexicons state it means "to sell. The character for "incense" (香) is correctly written as "xiāng" (𪏽). The *Shijing* (Classic of Poetry) says, "The millet and grain are fragrant," and the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that it is a compound character formed from the meanings of "millet" (黍) and "sweetness" (甘).

The character *guǐ* (晷) has the upper radical *guǐ* (軌); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the shadow of the sun," composed of the radicals for "sun" (日) and "old" (舊, with the phonetic *jiù*). In the scriptural text, it is written as *guò* (各), which is a vulgar error. The lower part is pronounced *lú* (盧各反). The *Erya* states that "xiáng" (降) means "to descend," and "yīn" (湮) means "to fall down. According to the scripture, *guǐ luò* (晷落) means the sun's shadow sinks downward.

"Sa" (歰) is pronounced with the upper radical "zhǐ" (止) reversed [as "lì"] and the rhyme "yīng" (英); the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "not passing through," while the *Shuowén* (說文) states it means "not smooth. It is composed of four "zhǐ" radicals—two upright and two inverted—to form "sa. The text here uses three "zhǐ" radicals to form "shè" (澁), which is an abbreviation. The lower part is pronounced with the "shī" (尸) and "bā" (八) radicals; according to the *Qièyùn* (切韻), it means "sharp" (*lì*). It is formed from the water radical with "gǔ" (骨) as the phonetic component.

Fascicle 15, Volume Fifteen. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Fifteen. "Píchí" (陂池). Regarding "pí" (陂), the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents) states: "A water-enclosure is called a pí. The *Erya* says: "That which is sloping is called a bǎn. Guo's commentary notes: "The ground is not level. "Chí" (池) is pronounced with the initial *l* and final *-i* (liǎn). The *Yùnqiè yīn* (Ciection of Rhymes and Pronunciations) states: "That which holds water is called a chí. Zheng’s sub-commentary on the *Shijing* says: "It is the soaking moisture of the chí waters."
Utpala is here translated as the blue lotus;
padma is here translated as the red lotus;
kumuda is here translated as the crimson lotus.
*Puṇḍarīka* is translated here as "white lotus flower. These four types of flowers have already been fully explained in the eighth fascicle of the preceding section.
*Dào* (蹈) is a derivative of *dǎo* (倒) with the *fǎnqiè* (反切) [phonetic analysis] of *jiàn* (踐); it means to tread upon.

Regarding the *zheng* (zither) and *di* (flute): the upper character for *zheng* is pronounced with the initial *sheng* and the final *fan*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A musical instrument with a drum-like body and strings, like a *zhu*; it originated from the *dase* (great lute) which had twenty-seven strings. Because the people of Qin lacked righteousness, two sons disputed their father’s lute, each taking thirteen strings; thus it was named the *zheng*. The lower character for *di* is pronounced with the initial *tu* and the final *li*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The *di* has seven holes; the common term is 'Qiang flute,' which refers to the three-holed variety. The *Fengsu Tong* states: "*Di* means 'to cleanse' (*di*), signifying that it cleanses depravity and filth while admitting what is elegant and correct. Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han, Qiu Zhong was skilled at making flutes.

Regarding the *konghou*: the upper character is *kong* (empty) and the lower is *hou* (marquis). The *Shiming* states that this was the "靡靡" (*mimi*) music composed by Shi Yan; later it emerged from the empty land between the Sang and the [river], as it was preserved by the Marquis of the state of Kong, and thus it was named accordingly.

The *pípá* (lute) has "zhī" on the upper part and "pú" (pronounced *bā*) on the lower part; it originally originated from the Western Rong and is the name of a Hu (Central Asian) musical instrument. The *Shì míng* states: "Pushing the hand forward is *pí*; drawing the hand back is *pá*. This is named according to the manner of its playing. According to the *Shuōwén*, both characters are composed of the radical "jué" (two jade stones joined), with "bā" as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of "jué" is *jiǎo*.

Regarding *xiāo* (flute): the upper character is pronounced *sūdiào*. The *Erya* states, "The large *xiāo* is called *zhōu*. Guo's commentary notes that it consists of twenty-three tubes arranged side-by-side, each one foot four inches long; the smaller version has sixteen tubes and is one foot two inches long. The *Fengsu Tong* says, "Shun created the *xiāo* to imitate the wings of the phoenix. Regarding *shè* (lute): the lower character is pronounced *suǒcī*. The *Erya* states, "The large *shè* is called *sǎ*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes that it is eight feet one inch long, one foot eight inches wide, and has twenty-seven strings. The *Shiben* states that the Lord Pao-xi first created the *shè*.

The first character, *shùn* (pronounced with the initial *shū* and the final *rùn*), is glossed by Yingyun as "the movement of the eyes. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *zhèn*, while the canonical text (*jīng*) uses *xiùn*; all are interchangeable. The second character, *mò* (pronounced with the final *liù*), refers to the pupil of the eye. The *Shiming* explains it as "silence" (*mò*), meaning that one silently perceives internally.

*Chen-wen* (唇吻): The upper character is pronounced *shí* (倫反); it is also written as *lín* (𠼉) in character dictionaries. The lower character is pronounced *wú-fěn* (無粉反). The *Qieyun* states it means "the mouth's opening. The *Sancang* states it is "the tip of the lips. *Mén-kǔn* (門閫):

The lower character is pronounced *kǔ-běn* (苦本反). The *Qieyun* states it means "the threshold of a door. According to the *Erya*, "a wooden peg is called *zhù*" (橛謂之𨵚). Guo Pu’s commentary identifies this as the door threshold (*mén-kǔn*). Examining the current usage, it refers to the wooden block in the center of the doorway that obstructs the passage.

"Di-xiāng-shàng-tè-jì-fǎn" (遞相上特計反). According to the *Erya*, "Shiyán" (釋言), it says "di" means "dì" (迭). Guo's commentary states: "This refers to alternating. The pronunciation of "dì" is tiánjié-fǎn (田結反). The received text writes this as "㮿" (󱠛), which does not form a valid character.
Continuation of the *Yiqie jing yinyi*, Scroll Two;
Continuation of the *Yiqie jing yinyi*, Scroll Three.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xīlín of Chōngrén Monastery in Yānjīng.
Continuation of the New Translations of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* from the sixteenth fascicle to the fortieth;

the nine fascicles of the newly translated *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*; the one fascicle of the *Pariṇāmanā-cakra Sūtra*; and the one fascicle of the *Daśabala Sūtra*. These four sūtras, totaling thirty-six fascicles, share the same phonetic transcription as this volume.

Volume 16, Fascicle 16. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 16. Potalaka—also transcribed as Putuoluojiā; formerly transcribed as Baotuo Luo. These are all transliterations of the Sanskrit term, differing in their phonetic rendering. It means "Mountain of Small Flower Trees," referring to the fact that this mountain abounds in such trees whose flowers are exceedingly fragrant. This is the solitary and remote mountain on this side of the South Sea, the palace where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara resides.
*Ōng-yü* (蓊鬱): "Ōng" is pronounced as *wū kǒng* (烏孔反). The *Yùpiān* states that *ōngyù* refers to the luxuriant growth of grasses and trees.
*Chún-yuán* (𦟛圓): "Chún" is pronounced as *chǒu róng* (丑容反). The *Ěryǎ* says, "*chún* means even. Guo's commentary explains this as meaning "uniformity. The *Ěryǎ* uses the character *chún*.

The character for *gōng* (bow) is pronounced *jūróng* (居戎反). The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states: "A bow is called *qióng* (穹), meaning it is *qióngqióng* (穹穹然) [arched]. The *Shuowén* (Explaining Characters and Analyzing Forms) says it is a pictographic character. The character for *shì* (arrow) below is also written as *shì* (矢); both are pronounced *shìshì* (式是反). The *Shìběn* (Book of Origins) states that Huang Di’s Yi Mou (*Yímóu*) made arrows.

"Bǎodāng" (寶璫): "Bó" (博) is pronounced with the *bó* rhyme-group; it is a collective name for various precious jewels. It is also written as "Bǎo" (珤), with "yù" (玉) as the semantic component and "fǒu" (缶) as the phonetic component. The lower character "dāng" (當) is pronounced with the *dāng* rhyme-group. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A pierced ear adorned with a pearl. The *Yunying* states: "An ornament for the ear," with "yù" (玉) as the semantic component and "dāng" (當) as the phonetic component.

*Du-lóu* (skull): the upper character is pronounced *tóng* (as in *tónglù*) and the lower is *lèhòu*. The *Pīcāng* states it is the bone of the head; the *Shuōwén* states it is the cranial bone. Both follow the radical "bone" (*gǔ*). The phonetic element is the abbreviated form of *lóu*. In the canonical text, there are variations such as *kuí* or *kuì*, which are vulgar forms and not the correct orthography.

*Hù*: (with the *gǔ* rhyme) the *Erya* states that it means "to rely upon" (*hùshì*). The *Shijing* says, "Without a mother, what is there to rely upon? *Zhānghuáng*: (upper character with the *liáng* rhyme;

lower character with the *guāng* rhyme). The *Qieyun* states it means "fear. The *Kaosheng* states that *zhānghuáng* means "to be terrified. The *Yunying* states it means "sudden haste," or "to be startled and fearful, losing one's composure."

*Jīng-hài* (驚駭): The upper character, *jīng*, is pronounced *jǔ* with the *qīng* rhyme; it means "to be terrified. The lower character, *hài*, is pronounced *hòu-kāi*; the *Qièyùn* states that *hài* also means "to be startled," and the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "composed of the radical 'horse' and the phonetic 'hai'. Sun Xian’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Yu dredged the nine rivers; the North River was particularly difficult to manage, and the masses feared it would not succeed, hence it was named Tuhai (徒駭)."

*Jue* (捔) [with the upper radical *shang* and the lower radical *guo* reversed; sometimes written simply as *jue*]: The *Kaosheng* says it means "to compete. The *Qieyun* says it refers to the game of *gudi* (ram-fighting). The current form is *jue*. The *Shuowen* says it means "to pull from the side and to wrestle" (*ji-jue*). There are editions of the scriptures where it is written as *jue-zhuo*, and others as *jiao*: the latter refers to leveling measures such as pecks and bushels, which does not carry the meaning of wrestling with strength. *Ji* (掎) is pronounced *ju qi*. *Jue* (椓): Also written as *jiao* (斠), it refers to leveling grain measures such as pecks and bushels; neither carries the sense of wrestling with strength. *Ji* (掎) is pronounced *ju qi*.

Volume 17, Fascicle Seventeen: *The New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Seventeen; no phonetic glosses available. Volume 18, Fascicle Eighteen: *The New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Eighteen. **Chuíchǔ (捶楚):** The upper character is pronounced *zhuī* (隹蘂反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To strike with a staff. It is composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 垂 (chuí). Alternatively, it may be written as 箠 (from the bamboo radical), meaning a whip or a riding crop. Or it may be written as 棰 (from the wood radical), meaning a club or mallet. The lower character is pronounced *chuāng* (瘡所反). The *Yunji* states: "Guǎchǔ (榎楚) refers to the *qiū* (楸) tree; it is also a name for the *jīng* (荊) tree. It is composed of the radical 林 (forest) and the phonetic 疋 (pǐ). *Pǐ* is pronounced *shū* (踈); *guǎ* (榎) is pronounced *jiǎ* (賈).

Regarding "kāichǎn" (開闡): the second character is pronounced as chǎnyǎn (昌演). Hàn Kāngbó’s commentary on the *Zhouyī* states that it means "to clarify. The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means "to open. The *Shēnglèi* states it means "to open wide. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the radical "mén" (門) and the phonetic "dān" (單); "dān" is pronounced shàn (善).

The *Jianzeshang jianyan fanwen ziji lüe* (Abridged Collection of Variant Characters for Selecting the Superior and Detecting Deceit) states that "zé" (to select) is written with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "dōng" (東). The *Shuowen jiezi* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) writes it as "dōng" (東), meaning to distinguish; it is composed of "shù" (束) and "bā" (八) below, with the pronunciation "zé" (澤). The *Yunying* (Rhyme Treasury) states that "zé" is also synonymous with "jian" (to pick out); it is written with the radical "hand" and the abbreviated phonetic "zé" (澤).

Regarding "Zhujia" (Master of Agriculture), the *Erya* states that the term "shi" (master) denotes one who presides over; the *Guangya* says it means one who guards. The character is composed of the radical "king" (王) with the phonetic "zhi" (𠬞), where "zhi" is pronounced as "zhujù" (竹句反) and "xià" (下) is pronounced as "jiǎ" (加暇反). Mǎ Róng’s commentary on the *Lúnyǔ* explains that planting the five grains is called "jià" (稼), which refers to the sprouting crops. This deity guards them so that they shall not suffer damage.

Volume 19, Fascicle Nineteenth. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Nineteenth. *Jiàowù* (Awakening). The upper character, *jiào* (教), is from the *Cāngjié Piān*. *Wù* (寤) means awakening; the text of the sūtra uses the vulgar form *wù* (寤). The lower part is pronounced with the *gù* (故) rhyme. The *Kǎoshēng* states: "In awakening, there is something seen and perceived, and one possesses conviction; this is called *wù*. It is composed of the abbreviated form of *mèng* (夢, dream) and the phonetic element *wú* (吾)."

"Hào" (號) means to wail; it is a sobbing cry. The *Erya* states: "Dancing and wailing is *yu* (sacrificial prayer for rain). Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "*Yu* refers to the sacrificial prayer where one utters sighs and entreaties for rain. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "Hù" (唬), with the lower radical "qu" (去) and the phonetic "ji" (急). The *Qieyun* defines it as weeping. The *Kaosheng* explains: "To shed tears without making a sound is called 'qì' (泣); it takes the radical 'water' (水) and the phonetic 'lì' (立)."

*Dào* (稻) and *liáng* (粱): "Tú" (徒) and "hào" (皓) are the phonetic components; the *Yùnyùn* (切韻) states they refer to non-glutinous rice (*gēngdào*). The *Běncǎo* (本草) states that *gēngmǐ* (秔米) primarily benefits the qi and stops vexation and diarrhea, while *dàomǐ* (稻米) primarily warms the interior and causes one to feel much heat. The *Zílín* (字林) states that *gēngdào* is non-sticky, whereas *nuòdào* (糯稻) is sticky. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states that *nuò* is simply *dào*. The lower character is pronounced *liáng*; it is sometimes written as *liáng*. The *Yùnyùn* states it refers to *dàoliáng* (稻粱). The *Guǎngzhì* (廣志) states that there is red *liángmǐ* (粱米) in Liaodong.

*Hǎoxì* (嬉戲): The first character, *hǎo*, is pronounced with the reversed sound [xǔ]; the *Shēnglèi* states it means "beautiful" or "to roam," following the radical *nǚ* (woman) and the phonetic *xǐ*. The second character, *xì*, is pronounced with the reversed sound [xiāngyì]. The *Qièyùn* states it means "to dally" or "to jest. Guō’s commentary on the *Eryā* states it refers to "coquettish play. *Xiè* (謔) is pronounced with the reversed sound [xūnuò].

Fascicle 20, Volume 20 of the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra. *Chunshu* (淳熟): The upper character is pronounced with the initial *shang* and the rhyme *shulun* (時倫); it is corrected to 󱸃. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "clear. The lower character is pronounced with the initial *chang* and the rhyme *liu* (六). The *Kaoseng Zhuan* states it means "to ripen and complete. The *Fangyan* states it means "to soften or rot."

*Jìpàn* (際畔): The upper character *jì* is pronounced with the *zǐ* rhyme and the *lì* tone; according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "edge. The *Yùnyùn* states it means "boundary. The lower character *pàn* is pronounced with the *pú* rhyme and the *bàn* tone; the *Shuōwén* states it means "a field boundary," composed of the radical *tián* (field) and the phonetic *bàn*.

Volume 21, Fascicle 21. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 21. *Chánlǐ* (廛里): The upper character, *chán* (廛), is pronounced with the initial *zhí-lián-fǎn*. The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states that it refers to the vacant space of a marketplace; it also means a residence. The text uses the characters *㕓* and *𫮈*, both of which are vernacular forms. The lower character, *lǐ* (里), is pronounced with the initial *liáng-shǐ-fǎn*. The *Zōulǐ* (周禮) states: "Five households constitute a *línn* (鄰); five *línn* constitute a *lǐ*. The *Fēngsùtōng* (風俗通) states: "*Lǐ* means to stop (*zhǐ*). It refers to fifty households stopping together as one *lǐ*."

Volume 22, Fascicle 22. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 22. *Hun-mèi* (昏寐): The upper character, *hun* (昏), is pronounced with the initial *hū* and the final rhyme *kūn* (呼昆反); the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) dictionary states it means "lack of clarity. The *Zì Lín* (字林) dictionary also gives the pronunciation *hū* and *kūn* (呼困反), meaning "obscurity. In the sūtra text, it is written simply as *hūn* (昬). The *Erya* (爾雅) says: "Hūn means 'to press' (*qiáng*). The *Qièyùn* (切韻) says: "It means 'dusk' (*mù*). It is not used in this [specific] sense here. The lower character, *mèi* (寐), is pronounced *zhì* (致) according to the *Yùpiān* (玉篇), meaning "lying down to sleep. The *Xiaojing* (孝經) says: "Rising early and sleeping late at night. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) states that it is derived from *mèng* (㝱) with a phonetic component.

Regarding "jiǎn" (檢): the upper character is pronounced *yǎn* (儼). The *Erya* states that "jiǎn" means "the same as. The *Shiming* says it is "to restrain" (*jìn*). The *Shuowen* says it is composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "qiān" (*qiānshēng*). The lower character is pronounced *chè* (革, *chùgé fǎn*). It is also written as "cè" (筴). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states that "cè" means "calculation" (*jì*). Lexicons state that "cè" refers to "planning and calculation" (*mò suàn*). The *Shuowen* [also] states it is composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "cì" (*cǐzhì fǎn*). The text here uses "róng" (榮) instead of "sòng" (宋), which is an erroneous character; "sòng" is pronounced *sòng*.

Volume 23, Fascicle 23. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 23. Regarding "xuánfú" (漩澓): the upper character is pronounced as in "qian" (泉) with a retroflex initial; the *Erya* states that "xuánfú" means "to return," which refers to turning back. The lower character is pronounced as "fù" (復); the *Erya*, in its "Shuishu" (釋水) section, says that moving upstream against the current is called "sùhuí" (泝洄), which is precisely "fú" (澓). The *Sancang* (三蒼) states that "fú" means "deep," referring to the places where waters swirl in rivers, seas, and oceans.

*Ku-gǎo* (枯槁): The upper character *ku* (枯) is pronounced with the *kǔ* (苦) radical and *gū* (姑) as the phonetic; the *Qièyùn* states it means "decayed. The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "wood that has dried and died. The lower character *gǎo* (槁) is pronounced with the *kǔ* (苦) radical and *hào* (皓) as the phonetic; the *Qièyùn* states that *gǎo* is also "withered. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the "wood" (*mù*) radical with "high" (*gāo*) as the phonetic.

Regarding "chuán" (boat/raft): the *Fāngyán* states that in Guandong it is called *chuán*, while in Guansi it is called *zhōu*. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "zhou" (boat) and the phonetic "yuán" (abbreviated). "Yuán" is pronounced with the initial *zhuān*. The inscription on lead and tin, as well as the "yuánliú" (following the current), both use this same character. The characters appearing in the scriptures as "chuán" or "huán" are not the original forms. Below, there is also the character "bó" (or "qí"), which is pronounced with the initial *fú* and the final *yuè*. The *Fāngyán* states it means "pǔ"; it refers to lashing bamboo and wood together to float upon a river for the transport of goods. "Pǔ" is pronounced with the initial *pú* and the final *zhù*.

*Yìmò* (瞖瞙): The upper character, *yì* (瞖), is pronounced *yú jì* (於計反); it refers to an eye disease. The lower character, *mò* (瞙), has the phonetic component *mò* (莫). The *Zìtǒng* (字統) states that it means "dimness of vision. Both characters are composed of the radical for "eye" (目) with *mò* (殹) as the phonetic. In the scriptures, this is written as *mó* (膜), meaning the membrane between the skin and the flesh.

"Jewel-cord" (bǎo shéng): "shéng" means to remove flies; the *Shìběn* says it is written as "tè" (spittle), meaning a guiding cord. The *Shàngshū* says, "The cord corrects errors and rectifies deviant intentions. It also says, "Wood follows the cord and becomes straight. The *Shuowén* defines it as a "rope," composed of the radical "silk thread" (mì) with the phonetic element "shéng" (abbreviated from "fēng").

Regarding "feibin" (妃嬪): "fei" (妃) is pronounced *fang* with the rhyme *fei*; Yingyun (*Yunjing*) states it means "to be paired. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says it means "to couple," with the phonetic *pi* (󰁨) having the sound *pu* with the rhyme *bi*. According to the *Mao Shi Zhuan*, "Guan Ge" concerns the virtue of the Queen Mother and Consorts; "fu" (符) has the true sound *zhen*. The *Erya Shiqin* says "bin" (嬪) means "lady" or "wife. The *Liji* states: "While alive they are called father, mother, husband, and wife; when dead, they are called *kao* (考) and *bi* (妣), and *bin*. The *Yao Dian* says: "He sent down his two daughters to Gui Rui to be *bin* to the Yu clan. Kong’s *Zhuan* explains: "He caused them to practice the way of a wife within the Yu clan."

Volume 24, Fascicle 24. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 24. Regarding the term "orphan" (*qióngdú*): the *Book of Documents* states, "Do not oppress the orphaned and the solitary. Kong Anguo says: "Orphaned" (*qióng*) means single; it refers to one who has no second support. "Solitary" (*dú*) means one who has no children. It is also written as the character *qiōng*.

"Gou" (溝) is pronounced *gǒu* (with the radical *kàng* reversed). The *Gōngkǒng Jì* (Record of the Artificers) states: "The space between the *jǐng* (wells) is four feet wide and four feet deep; this is called a *gōu*. Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhōuwǔ* says: "It is the field of two *líng* (neighboring units) of ten *fū* (households), intended for communication with the *chuān* (rivers). The *Shuowén* says: "A water channel; it takes the radical *shuǐ* and the phonetic *gòu*. The second character, "kè" (客), is pronounced *gēng* (with the radical *kàng* reversed). The *Ěryá* says: "A pit (*kāng*) is a void. The *Cāngjié Piān* says: "A pit is a ravine; it means to sink into or a trench. The correct character from ancient times to the present takes the radical *fù* and the phonetic *kàng*. The text uses "kēng" (坑), which is a vulgar form.

*Dui* (堆): On the upper character, it should be pronounced as *léi* (雷) or *kǎo* (考). The *Kǎośēng* says: "It refers to the height of piled earth. The *Shuōwén* says: "A small mound (*fù*). It is composed of the radical 'earth' (*tǔ*) and the phonetic 'zhuī' (*zhuī*). The text of the scripture uses *duī* (塠), which is a vulgar character and incorrect. Below, it is pronounced as *fáng wù* (房務). The *Erya* says: "A large plain is called a *fù*. The *Kǎośēng* says: "It is a type of hill (*qiū*). The *Shìmíng* says: "*Fù* means thick (*hòu*). It is composed of the radical 'dǒu' (*dǒu*), a simplified form of 'earth' (*tǔ*), and the phonetic. The ancient script is written as *dǒu* (𨸏), and the *Dàzhuàn* script as *zhuī* (隹). The text of the scripture uses *fù* (阜) or *bù* (埠), both of which are incorrect.

Regarding "jīng" (荊): the *Qǐèyùn* states it is the name of a tree that can be used for dyeing; it is composed of the radical "grass" (艸) with the phonetic "xíng" (刑). Below, "jì" (紀) has the pronunciation *lì*. The *Kǎoshēng* says it is the name of a sour jujube (*suanzao*) tree. The *Qǐèyùn* says it means "needle" (*zhēn*); it is composed of two "cì" (朿) radicals, where "cì" has the pronunciation *cì*.

The character *xū* (鬚) [is pronounced with the upper radical *xiāng* (相) and the *yù* (俞) reverse-cut; it refers to a small tuft of hair. The lower part is pronounced *ruǐ* (如捶); the *Guǎngyá* states it means "flower," referring to the dots at the tips of the stamens. The *Shuōwén* states that it is formed from three *xīn* (心) radicals to denote *ruǐ*, meaning that what is outside the flower is called the calyx (*é*) and what is inside the flower is called the pistil (*ruǐ*). In the sutras, some versions use three *zhǐ* (止) radicals or the wood radical (*mù*) to form *ruǐ*, but these are all incorrect.]

Scroll 25, Volume 25, *The New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll 25. *Yin-yi* (淫佚): [The character] *yin* is pronounced with the *shang* tone as *yu* (余) and the *zhēn* (針) rhyme; the *Qieyun* states it means "perverse" (*xié*) or "dissolute" (*tàng*). The *Shuowen* states it means "greed" (*tān*). It is composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman) with the phonetic *huán* (㸒). The character *huán* is composed of the radicals *zhuǎo* (爪) and *rén* (壬); its pronunciation is the same as *shàng-xià* (上下) or *yīn-zhì* (寅質), according to the *Qieyun*. [The character] *yi* (佚) means "pleasure" (*yì-lè*). The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radical *rén* (person) with the phonetic *shī* (失).

*Liṅyǔ* (囹圄): The first character is pronounced *dīng* (with the level tone) and the second is pronounced *yǔ* (with the rising tone). It is the name for a prison. According to the *Zhou Li*, prisons first appeared under the Three Kings. The *Shiming* states: "Liṅ" means to lead (*lǐng*) and "yǔ" means to ward off (*yù*); it refers to leading and recording prisoners and warding them off with prohibitions. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Liṅ" is the prison and "yǔ" is the guard; it is a compound character consisting of an external radical and an internal phonetic.

*Bǎngtái* (upper character *bǎng*, pronounced *báimáng*; lower character *tái*, pronounced *chǐchí*). Gu Yewang says it means "to strike. Lexicons say it means "to beat. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "páng" (*shēng*). The lower character is from the *Shuowen*: it means "to strike painfully," composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic element "tái" (*yíshēng*).

*Bǐn* (臏): pronounced *shàng pú rěn fǎn*. The *Dàdài Lǐ* (大戴禮) states: "In human life, one is born with the *bǐn*, and only after that can one walk. The *Shuowén* (說文) says: "The *bǐn* is the knee bone. The *Shàngshū Zhuàn* (尚書傳) says: "For those who break through passes and bridges, scale city walls and moats, or plunder and steal, the punishment is *bǐn*. Gu Yewáng says: "It is a punishment consisting of the amputation of the feet; it is the same as the *chìxíng* (䠊刑) mentioned in the *Lǜxíng* (呂刑). Alternatively, it is written as *yí* (𩪯), where the lower part is pronounced *gǔ dá fǎn*. The *Erya* says: "To cut and tear apart. The *Qièyùn* says: "To skin and slice. It is composed of the radical "knife" (刀) and the phonetic "hài" (害).

*Gōngwéi* (Palace Interior): The upper character is pronounced *jū* (with the phonetic component *róng*, meaning "to oppose"). The *Shìběn* (Book of Origins) states that Yu built palatial chambers. The *Erya* says, "A palace is called a chamber. The *Lǐjì* states, "Based on the conferred name, one establishes the clan; sons each occupy separate palaces. According to antiquity, both the noble and the humble used the term "palace" (*gōng*). From the Qin and Han dynasties onward, it was used exclusively for the residence of the sovereign. [The character] *xià* (lower) is not pronounced *fǎn*. The *Erya* says, "The gates within the palace are called *wéi*. Guo Pu’s commentary states: "This refers to small connecting doors; those that are smaller are called *wéi*."

Regarding the character for "rhinoceros" (xiū): the upper radical is pronounced *xī*. The *Erya* states that the rhinoceros resembles a boar. Guo Pu’s commentary says it resembles a water buffalo, with a pig's head, a large belly, short legs, and three hooves on each foot; it is black in color and has three horns—one on the crown of its head, one on its forehead, and one on its nose. The one on the nose is the "eating-horn" (*shijiao*). It is small and not elongated, and it is fond of eating thorns. There are also those with only a single horn. The lower part of the character is derived from the sound of "ox-tail" (*niuwei*) with a simplified form. The text here uses *chù*, which is an error. The pronunciation of *tuǒ* is *tāguǒ*.

Volume 26, Fascicle 26, New Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Fascicle 26. *Gan* (肝): The *Baihutong* states that it is the essence of wood and resembles wood with leaves. *Wang Shu-he* says that the liver and gallbladder form a functional pair (*fu*), and their condition is manifested in the eyes; thus, when the liver is replete with heat, the eyes become red and dim. *Da* (膽): The *Baihutong* states that the gallbladder is the functional organ (*fu*) of the liver. The *Maijing* states that when the gallbladder is diseased, the spirit cannot maintain its stability. Both characters are composed of the radical "flesh" (*rou*) and the phonetic "gan" (*gan*). The pronunciation of *zhan* (詹) is *zhan*; it is a phono-semantic compound character.

The character for *cháng* (intestines) is pronounced *shàng* with the radical *liáng* (良). The *Shìmíng* (*Explanation of Names*) states: "The intestines and abdomen are the repositories where internal qi flows freely. Below, it is sometimes written as *𦝩*, but the correct form is *󱹪*. The *Báihùtōng* (*Comprehensive Explanation of the White Tiger Classic*) states: "It is the repository of the spleen; its color is black. The *Shuowén* (*Explanations of Words and Texts*) states: "It is the repository of grain. It is composed of the radical *ròu* (flesh) and the component *作* (zuò), forming a pictographic character."

*Huán-pèi*: "Huán" is pronounced with the *shù-guān* (上戶關) reverse-cut; it refers to a jade ring. The *Erya* states: "When the flesh [of the ring] and the hole are equal, it is called a *huán*. Guo’s commentary notes: "This means the circumference and the hole are exactly equal. "Pèi" is pronounced with the *pú-mèi* (下蒲妹) reverse-cut; the rhyme dictionary states it refers to jade pendants. The *Liji* says: "In antiquity, the superior man wore pendants to compare them with his virtue."

"Mother's side" (mǔ xié): "xié" is pronounced as the reversed *mo* (i.e., *huò*). The *Erya* states: "The father is called *kǎo*; the mother is called *bǐ*. The *bǐ* of one's father is called *wángmǔ*. Guo's commentary says: "The character *wáng* is added to honor her. *Cangjie* says the character is composed of the radical *nǚ* (woman) with a dot like rain (*yùdiǎn*), resembling the shape of a woman's breast. The second character, "side" (*xiè*), is pronounced as *xiāng yè*. It is sometimes written as *xiē*, which is the same. The *Shuowen* says it refers to the two sides of the abdomen; it is composed of the radical *ròu* (flesh) and the phonetic *xié*. The sound of *xié* is *yè*; it is composed of three *lì* (strength).

*Chán* (慚) and *kuì* (愧): the former is pronounced *cú hán* (徂含反) and the latter *guǐ wèi* (軌位反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *kuì* is also *chán*. The *Liji* states: "The gentleman does not distress others with what he is capable of, nor does he feel ashamed before others for what he is incapable of. The *Guoya* says: "It means shame. The *Erya* says: "*Kuì* is *chán*. These two characters are mutually explained by one another. The *Shuowen* records them as *kuì* and also as *huìng* (謉) and *jiàn* (聭); both forms are ancient characters.

Volume 27, Fascicle 27. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 27. *Jù* (沮): The upper radical is 慈 (cí) with the reversed stroke; the *Mao Shī Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Book of Poetry) states that *jù* means "to ruin. The *Guǎng Yǎ* (Broad Lexicon) states it means "moist. The *Shuō Wén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) states it is composed of the radical 水 (water) and the phonetic 且 (qiě). The pronunciation of 且 is *zǐ yú* (subradical *yú*), while the lower part is pronounced *huái kuài*. The *Kǎo Shēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states it means "to collapse and crumble. According to the *Shuō Wén*, it is composed of the radical 土 (earth) and the phonetic 褱 (huái); the archaic form is written as 𡎯.

**Fénruò (焚爇):** The upper character, *fēn* (分), is a fanqie pronunciation; it means to burn. The lower character is also written as *ruò* (焫), with the same pronunciation as *ruò* (如雪反). According to the *Yǐngyùn*, it means setting fire to something; it also means to burn. **28. Scroll Twenty-Eight:

The New Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-Eight.** **Yì (翼):** The upper character, *yì* (與職反), is a fanqie pronunciation; it means respectful or to assist. The *Erya* states that "wings" (*yì*) mean respect. The *Lunyu* says, "He advanced with a wing-like gait. Kong’s commentary notes this refers to being upright and cautious. The lower character, *jí* (疾用反), according to the *Yǐngyùn*, means behind or to attend upon. In the sūtra text, it is sometimes written as *yì* (翊); its vulgar usage is also acceptable.

*Yanmao* (延袤): The first character is pronounced *rán* (然) in the upper tone and *hòu* (候) in the fourth tone in the lower part; it means "long" (*yáncháng*) and "broad" (*màoguǎng*). This has already been explained in the seventh fascicle of the preceding scripture.

*Yǔnmìe* (殞滅): The first character is pronounced *wěn* (爲) in the third tone; the *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states that it means "to perish" (*yǔnmù*). The *Erya* says it means "to fall. It is also written as *yǐn* (隕), as in the *Zuozhuan*: "Stars fell like rain. The second character is pronounced *liè* (烈) in the fourth tone; the *Shuowén* writes it as *wēi* (威) and explains: "Fire receives its qi from the month of October (*hài*) and dies in the month of September (*shū*). Therefore, it follows the radical of fire (*huǒ*) and the sign *shū*. Cài Yōng added the water radical to form *miè* (滅)."

*Nièngmì* (佞媚): The *Dingfanyùn* (定反切韻) states it means "flattery" (*chǎn*). The *Lúnyǔ* (論語), in the passage concerning Yong, says, "Yong was benevolent but not sycophantic" (*rén ér bù jì*). Guo’s commentary on the *Ěryá* (爾雅) states, "A sycophant (*níngrén*) is one who appears to be trustworthy. Below, the phonetic is *mì* (祕) with the final *fǎn* (反) as *míng* (明). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "pleasing" or "beautiful. The *Qieyùn* (切韻) states it means "graceful charm. The *Lúnyǔ*, in the passage where Wáng Sūnjiǎ asks, says, "Rather than being sycophantic toward the inner corner [of the room], it is better to be sycophantic toward the stove."

*Qiān* (愆): The upper radical is *qù* (去) with the pinyin *gàn* (乾) as the phonetic; it is also written as three forms: 𮘧, 𠍴, and 󱰺, all of which are identical. The *Erya* states: "To stray (*yì*) is *qiān*; it means transgression. The *Book of Documents* says: "Let one take the former kings as a model, so that one shall forever be without *qiān*. Kong’s commentary explains: "It means transgression. The lower radical is *fēi* (非). The *Zilin* says: "It means to turn one's back on. The *Qieyun* says: "It means to oppose or to resist."

Regarding "qigài" (乞匃): the character *gài* is pronounced with the *ài* rhyme. Gu Yewang states that *gài* also means "to beg. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to seek. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* states that when a person lacks wealth, they "qigài. The *Shuowén* explains it as a compound character formed from "person" (人) and "loss" (亡). It was written in antiquity as two forms, *bāo* (勹) and *jǐ* (几), both pronounced "rén" (人).

The character for *yuán* (猿) has the radical 犬 with the phonetic 袁 (yuan, with the initial *yǔ* and rhyme *yuán* according to the *Erya*, which states: "The *nóu-yuán* is skilled at grasping"). The lower part, *yù* (余救反), refers to the *shānhǎijīng* (Classic of Mountains and Seas), which says: "Mount Gél has many *wèi* (pronounced as above). Guō Pǔ’s commentary states: "It resembles a macaque but is larger, dark blue-black in color, and its tail is four or five feet long, resembling the tail of a otter. It has two prongs on its head; when it rains, it hangs upside down from a tree and uses its tail to plug its nostrils. In the Jiangdong region, it is raised to catch mice. The *Qièyùn* states it is the name of an insect. It is also written as 獑 or 狖; ancient characters include 㹨, which is incorrect.

Xuànfú (袨服): The upper character is pronounced xuánjiàn (玄絹). The *Wénzì jílüè* (Textual Compendium) states it means "sumptuous attire. The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states it means "beautiful clothing. The *Zìshū* (Lexicon of Characters) states that *xuànfú* refers to fresh, bright clothing. It is composed of the radical 衣 (clothing) with 玄 (xuán) as the phonetic.

Volume 29, Fascicle 29. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 29. *Kēn* (慳): The upper radical is *kǔ* (苦); the *qièyùn* (cutting rhyme) states it means "to be stingy. The *Erya* says, "Kēn means firmness. Guo Pu says, "It is like being firmly attached. The lower character is *liáng rèn* (良刃); the *Qièyùn* says it refers to being mean-spirited regarding wealth. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to cherish. Variants such as *lìn* (恡), *lìn* (吝), and *dì* (𠫤) are all vulgar characters.

*Zēng* (繒) and *guàng* (纊): the former is pronounced *jí* (疾) with the retroflex *líng* (綾) as its initial; the latter is pronounced *kǔ* (苦) with the retroflex *bàng* (謗) as its initial. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zēng" refers to silk fabric; "guàng" refers to cotton. The *Xiaoya* says: "The finest kind of *xu* (絮, wadding) is called *guàng*."

*Pòzé* (迫窄): "Pò" is pronounced with the *bó* and *mò* rhymes; it means to press closely upon. Regarding the phonetic component, it implies urgency. In ancient script, it was written as *guī*; below, it is also written as *zè* (迮), pronounced with the *zè* and *bó* rhymes; it means narrowness and also compulsion.

"Dí (洗滌): The first character is pronounced xiàn (先) with the ancient form also written as sǎ (洒). The *Qièyùn* states it means 'to exhaust'; it also refers to bathing and washing, as well as an appearance of solemn reverence. The second character is pronounced tú (徒) with the lè (歷) rhyme. The *Yùpiān* says it means 'to remove'; the *Yùnyīng* says it means 'purity. The *Máoshī* states: 'In the tenth month, dí chǎng (滌場). The commentary says: 'Dí means to sweep.'"

Volume 30, New Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Volume Thirty. "Kāi-pì" (開闢): The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states that it means "to explain" (*jiě*) or "to open" (*zhāng*). The character is composed of the radical "gate" (*mén*) with the phonetic "qián" (*qiān*); the pronunciation of "qián" is as such. The lower part, "fáng-mào" (*fángmào*), according to the *Qièyùn*, means "to open. The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical "gate" with the phonetic "pì" (*bì*). Regarding "opening the four gates," the *Kǒngzǐ Zhuan* (孔傳) says it refers to opening the gates in the four directions. The *Shuōwén* further explains it as being composed of the radical "gate" with the phonetic "pì."

*Yíng* (瑩): The upper radical is *wū* (烏) with the *dìng* (定) tone. Cāngjié (蒼頡) says: "Yíng means to polish. Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* (國語) says: "Chè means clarity. It may also be written as *yíng* (鎣) or *chè* (撤); these two characters are also interchangeable. *Yù* (禦): The upper radical is *yú* (魚) with the *jǔ* (舉) tone. The *Erya* says: "Yù, yǔ, and jìn all mean to prohibit.

The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) says: "It means 'to face'. The *Qièyùn* (切韻) says: "It means 'to confront an enemy. The *Shuowén* (說文) also says it means "to prohibit. It takes the radical *shì* (示) and the phonetic *yù* (御). The lower part is *hú* (胡) with the *gàn* (幹) tone. The *Qièyùn* says: "It means 'to strike against' or 'to resist. It takes the radical *shǒu* (手) and the phonetic *hàn* (旱)."

Volume 31, Scroll 31. *New Flower Adornment Sūtra*, Scroll 31. The characters *a* (pronounced as in "ah-ke"), *la* (pronounced as in "lu-ke"), and *ta* (pronounced as in "da-ke")—these three characters are all Sanskrit terms for the "Secret Gate of Contemplation" (*guānmìmén*), wherein one does not seek the literal meaning of the words.

The character *xián* (咸) is composed of the phonetic *hú* (胡) with the rhyme *yán* (嵒); the *qièyùn* states it means "all" (*jiē*) or "same" (*tóng*). The lower radical *zōng* (宗) has the rhyme *sòng*; the *Shuowen* states it refers to the shuttle that holds the intersecting threads in weaving, being formed from the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *zōng* (宗). The sound of *mì* (糸) is *mi* (覓).

*Dian* (癲): The first character is pronounced *ding* (with the radical *jian* as a phonetic). The *Guangya* states it means "epilepsy" (*diankuang*).
