Regarding the character for *dharmagaṇḍī* (法螺): the lower radical is *luó* (螺), which is the common secular form; its correct form is *luó* (蠃). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "an insect with a shell. The version in the sutra uses the character *lǐ* (𧋠), but both are incorrect forms of the character *luó*.

Regarding *píngtǎn* (平坦): the lower radical is *tàn* (袒). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *tǎn* means "peaceful" (*ān*). The *Guangya* states that it also means "level" (*píng*). The *Lunyu* says, "The gentleman is *tǎntàngtàng*" (坦蕩蕩), which refers to this.

*Xiālè* (陿劣): The first character, *xiá*, is pronounced with the initial *xian* and the final *jiǎ*. Gu Yewang states that it means "constricted" (*pò'ài*) below, while "vast and great" (*guǎngdà*) above. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical *yù* (阝), the enclosure *fāng* (匚), and the phonetic *jiá* (夾). The scriptural text uses *xiá* (狹) with the radical *quǎn* (犬), which refers to training dogs and horses; this is not the intended meaning of the scripture. The second character, *luò* (劣), is pronounced with the initial *liàn* and the final *chuì*. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "weak" (*ruò*) or "having little strength. It is a compound character (*huìyì zì*). The ancient script is written as *hū* (乎) with the radical *yù* (阝), the enclosure *fāng* (匚), and the phonetic *jiá* (夾). The sound of *yù* is *zhuì* (𨸏), the sound of *fāng* is *fāng* (方), and the sound of *jiá* is *tián* (田).

Volume 38, Scroll 38 of the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra. "Puhuan" (霈然): The first character, "Pu" (普), is read as *pǔ* (with the tone of *gài* [蓋] reversed). The second character, "Huan" (霈), is pronounced *huài* (盛, meaning "abundant"; the *Yunyun* [韻韻] states it means "páng-huài" [霶霈]). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "rain" (*yù*) and the phonetic "pei" (*pèi*). The pronunciation of "pei" is the same as above.

Volume 39, Scroll 39. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll 39. "Juhuai" (沮壞): the first character is pronounced as *cí* (慈) with an initial *jǔ* (沮), and the second character is pronounced as *huái* (懷) with an initial *kuì* (瞶). This has already been explained in the twenty-seventh scroll of the previous scripture.

Volume 40, Fascicle 40. *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 40. “*Tánròu* (啗肉): The upper character *tán* (啗) is pronounced with the initial *dú* (徒) and the final *là* (濫), or alternatively as *chàn* (啖). It means to eat or consume; it is also written as *dàn* (噉), pronounced with the initial *dú* (徒) and the final *gǎn* (敢). The lower character *ròu* (肉) is described in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as having the form of flesh and muscle.”

Regarding the character *huì* (卉) in "huìmù" (卉木): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is the general name for all hundred grasses (*bǎicǎo*). It is composed of three *cǎo* (屮), where *cǎo* is pronounced *chūliè* (丑列反). The form of *cǎo* resembles the shape of grass when first sprouting; two *cǎo* combined form *cǎo* (艸), and four *cǎo* form *mǎng* (茻), pronounced *mǎng* (莾). Now, *huì* has been modified from three *cǎo* to thirty strokes.

The character for "zhù" (炷) in "dēng zhù" (燈炷) is a modern form. According to Lu Qian’s *Shìwén* (釋文), Xu Shen’s *Shuōwén* (說文), the *Yùpiān* (玉篇), the *Zílín* (字林), and the *Gǔjīn Zhèngzì* (古今正字), this character is not found anywhere; it is only included within the notes of Sūn Miǎn’s *Guǎngyùn* (廣韻).

The Newly Translated *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Scroll One, Part One; including the Preface to the Sūtra. Regarding the phonetic transmission from India: The sound "Zhú" (竹) accords with the Sanskrit original and is pronounced "Dǔ" (篤). In antiquity it was called Shēndú (身毒), or Xiándòu (賢豆); the new term is Yìndù (印度), all of which are corruptions and shifts. The correct name is *Indrakīla*, which translates as "Moon. The moon has a thousand names, and this is one such appellation. The *Xiyùjì* (Record of the Western Regions) states: "Because the Sun of the Buddha has already set in that land, the births of the Sage (Buddha) have succeeded one another to awaken and benefit sentient beings, like the moon shining upon all; therefore, it is named after the moon."

The name "Shule" (疏勒) is a corruption and abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; its correct form is *Kharoṣṭhī*. This is translated as "Country of the Wicked Nature," because the people of that country are for the most part fierce and unruly. Alternatively, it is said that the country is so named because there is a mountain called *Kharoṣṭhī* there, and the name was established based on that mountain. It is located within the borders of North India.

Gandhāra (the upper character *qián* is pronounced *guán*; formerly transcribed as Jiànduōluó; here translated as "Upholder of the Earth"). In the past, many sages and worthies who had attained the Way resided in this country to maintain its borders, ensuring it was not invaded by other nations. It is also called Gandharva (Xiāngqìluó), meaning that fragrant flowers grow abundantly throughout the kingdom, after which it is named. This country is situated on the northern border of Central India and the southern border of Northern India.

*Kāśmīra* (also called *Kāśyapamīra*; formerly transcribed as *Jibin*, which is an abbreviated corruption) translates as "Who shall enter. This refers to the fact that before this country was established, there was a great dragon lake to which no one dared to approach. Later, an arhat, seeing that the terrain was auspicious and suitable for human habitation, requested from the dragon enough space for one knee. The dragon granted this, and the arhat transformed his body, gradually increasing in size until his knee filled the dragon lake. The dragon, bound by its word, relinquished the land and departed. The arhat then used his supernatural powers to dry up the water completely, whereupon he established a city and walled capital. Everyone said, "If it were not for our holy master, who would have been able to enter? It was because of these words that the name of the country was established. This country is located within the borders of North India.

*Pīzhī* (披緇): The first character, *pī*, is pronounced with the initial *kǐ* (羈) and the final *fǎn* (反). The *Shuowen* states it means "to open" or "to disperse," though it is also written as *pèi* (帔), meaning a shawl or a cloth. It is also written as *bèi* (被), pronounced with the initial *píng* (平) and final *yì* (義), meaning "to wear," "to add," or "clothing. Here, we follow the latter reading. The second character, *zhī* (緇), is pronounced with the final *cè* (側) and *chí* (持). The *Shuowen* states that *zhī* refers to black-colored silk. The *Lunyu* says, "Nied but not zhī" (涅而不緇), with the commentary noting that *niè* (涅) refers to black mud that can dye things black. *Niè* is pronounced with the initial *nú* (奴) and final *jié* (結); it refers to earth baked by the sun combined with water.

*Upādhyāya* (the *u-pa* and *yin* are pronounced with the "u-wo-gu" and "yin-ting-ye-zheng" tones respectively; it is a Sanskrit term formerly transliterated as *yù bō dì yē*, meaning "one who studies closely"). This refers to one who, because a disciple is young, does not leave the teacher but constantly follows them closely to receive and recite the scriptures. It is also translated as "Preceptor" (*qīnjiào*). In countries such as Kucha and Khotan, it was corrupted to *huáshé* or *húshè*; what is called *héshàng* today is neither a Sanskrit term nor a Chinese word, but rather a phonetic corruption from various countries to the west of the Pamirs.

*Móngdī* (蒙鞮): The final *dī* is pronounced as *xi* (奚) with a retroflex *r*-like sound; it is not a standard Sanskrit term and appears to be the name of a monastery in the kingdom of Kaśmīra. Its literal meaning is not detailed. Examining the character *dī*, it belongs to the category of footwear. In the *Bóyǎ*, it is said to mean "to stop.

The *Shuowén* states that it is formed from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "yòu" (*yòu*), with an alternative pronunciation of *yúlíng* (於綾). Here, we do not take that reading; rather, it is pronounced *nǔ* (弩), which in character dictionaries means "resentment" (*èi*). In the *Qièyùn*, it means "anger" (*chēn*), and with the pronunciation *nǔ*, it also denotes the appearance of an angry gaze.

Regarding "jǐn" (僅): the *Qieyun* states it means "able" or "slight. Gu Yewang says it means "merely. The character below is correctly written as "quán" (全); its pronunciation is *jíyuán*. The *Yunyǐng* states it means "complete," and the *Shuowén* states it means "to possess. It is a compound character formed from the semantic union of "gōng" (工) and "jí" (亼). "Jí" (亼) is pronounced *cáirù*; it is a form composed of three elements joined together.

Nālandā, also transcribed as Nà nàlán duō, is the name of a monastery in the Western Regions; in this language, it means "Giving Without Weariness. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that successive emperors built it together as a single monastery, opening its gates to the east to constantly provide for a thousand monks. Since its founding, not a single person has ever committed an offense or harbored suspicion; thus, because giving and offerings within the borders of the Five Indias were never wearied, it was named accordingly. It is located within the region of Central India.
*Liṅliṅ* (the *liṅ* is pronounced with the "lang" and "ding" finals). In the sequence of names herein, one need not seek the literal meaning of the characters.

*Tixī* (the *ti* is pronounced as *di*; it has three pronunciations: *xi*, *fei*, and *yin*). This is an Indian term; in the language of Kucha, it means "Lotus-Vīrya" (Lotus-Diligence), which is the name of a Tripiṭaka Master from that country.

Guo Xin (郭昕) is a personal name; "Xin" (昕) is pronounced as "xu" (許) with the "jin" (斤) radical reversed. Examining the character, it signifies the sun about to rise. The *Shiming* (釋名) states: "Xin means 'joy' (*xin*); it refers to the bright sun about to emerge, at which time all things rejoice."

*Dī* (滴) is pronounced with the *lì* (歷) reverse-cut (*piànqiè*). The *Yùnqù* states it means "water droplets. The *Shuowén* states it means "the edge [of a roof]" (*yá*), composed of the radical for "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic element *dī* (abbreviated). The character below is pronounced with the *jiù* (救) reverse-cut. One should combine *dī* and *lì* to form *liù* (溜). The *Shuowén* states that *liù* is the name of a deity; this is not its usage here. The *Zìshū* states it means "a small stream. It is now written as *liù* (霤). The *Shuowén* states that *liù* is the name of a deity; this is not its usage here.

*Chéng* (pronounced *shàngzhízhēn*, with the final *fǎn* reversed) is a surname. It originally descended from Zhuanxu’s Chongli. During the time of King Xuan of Zhou, Cheng Bo Xiufu entered the service as Grand Marshal (*Dàsīmǎ*) and was enfeoffed at Cheng; subsequently, this became his clan name. The character below (程) is pronounced *wùgèfǎn*. It is a personal name. According to the analysis of the characters, it signifies the tip of a sword’s blade. The *Shuowén* states that it is composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic component "yà" (*è*). The pronunciation of *è* is the same as above.

*Suōzāi* (所齎): The lower radical is *zǔ* (祖) with the phonetic *xī* (西). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states it means "to carry objects while traveling. The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "to send off. The *Qièyùn* (切韻) states it means "to entrust" or "to bequeath. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) with *qí* (齊) as the phonetic. The vulgar form is written as *jī* (賷), which has the same meaning but is not the correct character.

The upper character 鍊 (liàn) is pronounced *láng diàn* (with the second tone on the first syllable), though it is also written as 煉. The *Shuowen jiezi* states that it means "to smelt metal," composed of the radical 金 (*jīn*) and the phonetic 柬 (*jiǎn*, pronounced with the third tone). The *Yun jian* states it means "to smelt metal. According to the *Yinzici*, it is also written as 󱯤. The *Shuowen jiezi* further explains that it is composed of 仌 (*bīng*, meaning ice) and 台 (*tái*, meaning pleasure), with 考 (*kǎo*) as the phonetic. It says: "When ice is heated, it becomes fluid (*yě*); when it encounters cold, it becomes solid. The lower character 冶 (*yě*) is pronounced *yáng zhě* (with the third tone on the first syllable). The *Yun jian* states it means "to smelt metal. The *Shuowen jiezi* states it is composed of 仌 (*bīng*, meaning ice) and 台 (*tái*, meaning pleasure), with 考 (*kǎo*) as the phonetic. It says: "When ice is heated, it becomes fluid (*yě*); when it encounters cold, it becomes solid. (Note: The text repeats the definition for 冶 here, likely due to a textual error in the source).

*Yueyu* (悅豫): The upper character is pronounced *yú xuě* (余雪反). The *Erya* states: "Yueyi" (悅懌) means to be pleased. The *Qieyun* defines it as joy and happiness. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "shuo" (省) with a reduced form. The lower character is pronounced *yáng shù* (羊恕反). The *Erya* states: "Yu" (愉) and "yu" (豫) mean *kaikāng* (愷康), which is happiness; it also says "yu" (豫) means peace and security. The *Yupian* defines it as leisure and ease. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is composed of the radical "elephant" (*xiàng*) and the phonetic "yu" (予).

Volume 2, Second Fascicle. Newly Translated *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Volume Two. *Ka* (珂): Upper radical *ke* (珂), read with the *he* (何) rhyme; according to the *Yùpiān* (玉篇), it belongs to the class of conch shells (*luóshǔ*). Those produced from the sea are as white as snow, and for this reason they were used to adorn the breast of a horse. Lower radical *bó* (博), read with the *gài* (蓋) rhyme; it is also a type of conch shell. The *Ēryá* (爾雅) states: "The *jū* (居) conch lives on land; the *biáo* (𧷼) conch lives in water. Guō's commentary says: "Water and land are different names [for the same genus]. The flesh within the conch is like a *kēdǒu* (蝌蚪—tadpole); it has only a head and a tail. According to the *Shuowén* (說文), the character for *bèi* (貝) depicts its form. In ancient times, the conch was used for trade; therefore, all categories of wealth, goods, buying, and selling are derived from the character for *bèi*. *Biáo* (𧷼) is pronounced *biāo*; *hán* (蜬) is pronounced *hán*.

Regarding the term *bìyù* (jade disc): "Bì" is pronounced as *yì* (必益反). The *Erya* states: "When the circumference (*ròu*) is twice the diameter of the hole (*hǎo*), it is called a *bì*; when the *bì* is six inches in diameter, it is called a *xuán*. Guo's commentary notes: "The 'flesh' (*ròu*) refers to the edge; the 'hole' (*hǎo*) refers to the central aperture. The *Baihūtong* says: "Its exterior is round, resembling Heaven; its interior has a hole, corresponding to Earth. The ruler holds it as a token of sincerity to sacrifice to Heaven. Regarding the term *xià yǔ* (the lower phrase, intended to be reversed): the *Erya* states, "Those made of jade are called *guī* (sacrificial tablets). The *Liji* says, "When holding jade, one does not walk with a hurried gait. The *Shundi* (Annals of Shun) says, "He cultivated the five rites and the five jades. Kong’s commentary notes: "The various lords of the five ranks each held their respective jade. The *Baihūtong* says: "Jade embodies the virtue of the noble person: it is not light when dry, nor heavy when wet. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jade possesses five virtues."

"Ziliang" (資糧): "Zi" (資) is read as *yí* (夷) with a reversed tone; according to the *Yupian*, it means "to assist. Regarding the phonetic component, it is derived from "qu" (取). According to the *Qieyun*, "zi" also refers to wealth and goods. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of "bei" (貝) and the phonetic "ci" (次). "Liang" (糧) is read as *lǚzhāng* (呂張); it is also written as "liáng" (糧). The *Shuowen* says "liang" means "stored grain. The *Qieyun* says it refers to "grain in the granary. The *Erya* says "zhang" (粻) is "liang" (糧). Guo's commentary notes that nowadays in Jiangdong, people commonly call grain "zhang."

CŪ (麤獷): Upper radical *cāng* with *gū* as the reverse-cut (*fǎnqiè*); it means "great" (*dà*). The *Zītǒng* states that the nature of deer is to feed while facing away from one another; because hunters (*yúrén*) harm them, the character is composed of three deer. In common usage, it is abbreviated to *cū*. Its meaning is the same as the following character. Lower radical *gǔ* with *měng* as the reverse-cut; it means "great. The *Zìshū* says it means "fierce" (*měng*). The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical *quǎn* (dog) and the phonetic *guǎng*; it is also pronounced *jù yǐng*.

*Zhe* (上陟列反): The character books state that it refers to the sting of a scorpion (*xié*), a bee, or a wasp (*chài*). In archaic script, it is written as *méng*. *Shāngzhī* (下商隻反): The *Qièyùn* states this refers to an insect that moves its venom. It says there are "stinging poisons" on the ground which must not be touched by their tails. The *Kǎoshēng* states it means to sting or to bite. In archaic script, it is written as *chuò*.

Regarding the character *càn* (磣): the upper radical is *chǔ* (楚) with the phonetic *jǐn* (錦); it is also written as *hěn* (墋). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A mixture of earth, stone, and sand. The text of the sutra uses *càn*, which is incorrect. Regarding the lower part, *lǎ* (剌): the phonetic is *là* (遏). The upper part [of the character] refers to *càn* (磣), while the lower part *lǎ* (剌) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* (切韻) initial *liè*. The *Yun* (韻) states that this character is *lí* (󱍮), meaning "coarse grain" (*tuōsù*, 脫粟)—the husked grain of rice. This character *lǎ* (剌) means "crooked" (*liè*, 戾) and does not carry the meaning of *càn-lǎ* (磣糲).

*Naraka* is a Sanskrit term; it is also called *Naraka*, which translates as "vessel of suffering" or "instrument of suffering. It refers to the instruments used for punishing offenders and is the general name for the hells. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Below this, past twenty thousand [yojanas], is the Avīci hell, equal in depth and breadth to the aforementioned seven *naraka*s. There are eight [additional] *naraka*s, each with sixteen [subsidiary] *utsada*s."

*Tuan* (湍): Pronounced *shàng-tuó-duān*. The *Shuowen* says it means "shallow water flowing over sand. Lexicons say it means "a rapid current" (*lòudà*). Below, *zhí-lí*. The *Yupian* says it means "to gallop or pursue. Lexicons say it means "to race about. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "speed"; it is composed of the radical for "horse" and the phonetic *chí* (abbreviated) with a final *shēng*.

*Lùn* (淪): The upper radical is *lì* (力) with the reversed phonetic *chún* (迍). Lexicons define it as "to sink" or "to submerge. The *Erya* states: "Small waves are called *lùn*. Guo’s commentary says: "This refers to swirling eddies (*yùnlùn*). The lower character is read with the *qièyùn* (rhyme-cutting) pronunciation *nǎi* (乃) and *lì* (曆). The *Qieyun* defines it as "drowning in water. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to drown," taking *shui* (水) as the radical and *ruò* (弱) as the phonetic. The archaic form is written as *luò* (㲻), meaning "a person falling into water."

*Tān* (灘): The *Duanfan* and *Yupian* state it means a river sandbank (*he-tan*). The *Erya* says that when the *Tai-sui* is in the year of *Shen*, it is called *Tun-tan*. The second character, *zhang* (章), with the *yu* (與) radical and the *fan* (反) radical, the *Erya* states that a place in the water where one may dwell is called a *zhou* (洲); a small *zhou* is called a *zhu* (渚); a small *zhu* is called a *zhi* (沚). It is also written as *zhu* (陼) with the same pronunciation; *zhi* (沚) has the pronunciation *zhǐ*.

Volume 3, Scroll 3. New Translation of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Volume 3. Regarding "捫摸" (*mún mó*): the *Mao Shih Zhuan* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry) states that "捫" means to hold; the *Yun Quan* (Dictionary of Rhymes and Explanations) says "捫搎" (*mún sōng*). The lower character, "摸," has the phonetic *mò*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to feel with the hand. According to these sources, "捫搎" and "摸𢱢" are synonymous with "mó suǒ" (to stroke or rub). "搎" is pronounced *sōn*; "𢱢" is pronounced *suǒ*; "挲" is pronounced *suō*.

Regarding "mosquito" (wén-ruì): the upper character *wén* is pronounced as in *wén-zhuāng*. The *Zhuāngzǐ* states that the *jiāomíng* (a tiny insect) nests upon the antennae (*méi*) of mosquitoes. The lower character *ruì* is pronounced as *xù* (with the *shuài* rhyme). Regarding the small mosquito *ruì*, the *Shuōwén* says that the people of Qín call it *ruì*, while the people of Chǔ call it *wén*. The *Tōngsúwén* states that the *yuān* (a small flying insect) transforms into a *ruì*; *yuān* is pronounced as *xiě-yuán*. It is also written with the two characters *mó* and *ruì*.

*Genglang* (𧏙蜋): the first character is pronounced as *shàng* with the rhyme *yang* (上音羊), and the second is pronounced as *lǔ* with the rhyme *zhāng* (下音呂張). The *Erya*, "Explanation of Insects" (*Shichong*), states: "The *qie-geng* is the *genglang*. Guo Pu’s commentary says: "It is a black-shelled insect that eats excrement and soil."

*Cè* (策): The upper radical is *chǔ* (楚) and the phonetic is *gē* (革). The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states it means "plan" (*móu*) or "counsel" (*chóu*). Gù Yěwáng says it is a "horse-whip. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) says: "A *cè* is that which instructs and commands from above, driving and urging those below. The lower character is pronounced *zhì* (制) with the initial *lì*. The *Zìshū* (字書) says it is a "rabbit. The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) says it means "to encourage and stimulate. The *Shuowén* (說文) says it means "strength. It is a compound character formed from the radical *lì* (力) and the phonetic *lì* (厲). The sound of *lì* is as above; it also means "fierce," "to arrange in rows," or "strictly orderly. *Zhì* (制): The upper radical is *zhì* (止) and the phonetic is *zhì* (制). The *Shuowén* says: "To cut off. It is a compound character formed from the radical *zhì* (止) and the phonetic *zhì* (制). The sound of *zhì* is as above; it also means "to control" or "to regulate. The *Lìshì* (禮事) says: "The ruler controls the people through laws; the father controls his children through affection; the elder brother controls his younger brother through righteousness; the husband controls his wife through courtesy; the elder controls the younger through kindness. The *Hánshū* (漢書) says: "The Son of Heaven controls the empire. The *Lìshì* also says: "The ruler controls the people through laws. The *Guǎngyá* says: "To suppress. The *Míngshì* (名事) says: "To control. The *Shìmíng* says: "To stop. The *Dàoxué* (道學) says: "To restrain. The *Wénzi* (文字) says: "To prohibit. The *Jiǎnzǐ* (簡子) says: "To punish. The *Shuōwén* says: "To cut off. The *Shuōwén* also says: "To cut off is to stop. The *Shuōwén* also says: "To stop is to prohibit. The *Shuōwén* also says: "To prohibit is to punish. The character *yùn* (慍) is pronounced with the upper radical *wèn* and the phonetic *fǎn*; the rhyme dictionary states it means "anger. The *Lunyu* says, "When others do not know [him], he does not feel *yùn*. He Yan’s commentary explains that *yùn* means "anger. Generally, when people are unaware of something, a superior person does not become angry (*xià pú bào fǎn*). The *Wujing Yinyi* states that this refers to being intrusive or violent. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as composed of the radicals for "sun" (*rì*) and "together" (*gòng*, pronounced *gǒng*), with the phonetic *bié* for "water" (*shuǐ*). An alternative form is written with the radical for "field" (*tián*) and *gōng*. This latter form significantly deviates from the original meaning of the character.

Scroll Four, Volume Four. Newly Translated *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Scroll Four. "Zhàn" (箭): the upper character is pronounced with the *zǐ* and *jiàn* rhymes (子賤反). Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* states: "Zhùzhàn (竹箭) refers to *xiǎo* (篠, young bamboo). Lexicons state: "Bamboo reaching one *zhàng* in height, with nodes three feet apart, may be made into arrows. The lower character is pronounced with the *wū* rhyme (屋反). The *Erya* says: "A metal tip (*jīn cù*) with trimmed feathers is called a *hòu* (鍭). Guo’s commentary notes: "This is the *pī* (錍) arrow of today. *Xiǎo* is pronounced *sū niǎo* (蘇鳥反); *pī* is pronounced *pǔ xī* (普兮反).

*Míng* (溟): The upper radical is *mò* (莫) with the phonetic *jīng* (經); the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it means "deep. The *Shānhǎi Jīng* (山海經) says the Northern Sea is called *Míng*. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states it is formed from the water radical with *míng* (冥) as the phonetic; the lower part is *pú* (蒲) with *mò* (沒) as the phonetic. The *Yùpiān* (玉篇) calls it *Bóxiè* (渤澥). Dictionaries state that the seawater is *bóbó* (渤渤) in its surging motion.

Regarding "thick membrane" (厚膜): the *Hukou* (胡口) reversed-cut phonetic gloss states it means "heavy" or "broad. The lower character is pronounced as the word "mo" (莫). The *Zi Tong* (字統) states that what is called "membrane" (膜) refers to that which is inside the skin and outside the flesh. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) defines it as "the thin membrane between the flesh"; the character for "thin" (䀭) is pronounced as *gushuai* (古衰).

*Chán* (纏): The upper radical is *chí* (直, with the phonetic *lián* [連] reversed); the gloss says it means "to wind around" or "to bind. The *Shuowen jiezi* says it means "to wrap and constrain," taking *mì* (糸) as the radical and *zhān* (廛) as the phonetic; the lower part is read as *guǎng* (光) and *huǒ* (火) reversed; the gloss says it means "to envelop. The *Shuowen jiezi* says it means "to wrap and bind," taking *yī* (衣) as the radical and *guǒ* (果) as the phonetic. It is vulgarly written as *wèi* (畏), which is a corrupted and abbreviated form of the character.

The seal and its impression are correctly written as 璽 (xǐ). Its name is explained as "seal-trust" (*yìn-xìn*); it is so called because it serves as a basis (*yīn*) for sealing objects and transmitting trust. The character below is pronounced *sī* (with the *shì* rhyme). Cáo Yōng’s *Dúduàn* states: "The seal of the Son of Heaven is made of jade and carved with a tiger; in antiquity, the feudal lords shared its use. The *Yueling* says: "Before the Qin dynasty, the feudal lords and the district magistrates were both called *xǐ*. From this point onward, the Son of Heaven alone used the title *xǐ*, while the feudal lords dared not use it. The *Chuánxǐ pǔ* records: "Prince Yīng of Qin presented the Imperial Succession Seal (*chuánguó xǐ*) to Gāozǔ; it was engraved by Lǐ Sī, and its inscription read: 'Received the mandate from the Heavenly Emperor; may his life be long and prosperous. The pronunciation of 璽 is *chì-zhī* (with the *zhī* rhyme).

*Dian* (癲): the first character is pronounced *ding* (with the *jian* radical). The *Guangya* states it means "madness. The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states it is "the disease of *dian*. The *Shenglei* states it is "the disease of *dian*-wind. It is sometimes written as *dian* (瘨). The lower character is pronounced *xian*. The *Jixun* states it is "the *dian* disease of children. The *Shuowen* states it is "a wind-disease," formed with the radical *na* (疒) and the phonetic *jian* (間). It is also sometimes written as *zhan* (𤺛), which is likewise correct.

The character for "insect" (蟲) is pronounced with the upper radical *zhí gōng* (直躬反). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of three "insects" (虫), and its phonetic is *xǔ guǐ* (許鬼反). Two "insects" combined form the character *gùn* (䖵), pronounced *kūn* (昆). The *Erya* states: "Those with feet are called *chóng* (蟲); those without feet are called *zhài* (豸)," pronounced *wén'ěr* (文爾反). In current vernacular usage, the character *chóng* (虫) is borrowed to represent *chóng* (蟲), with the lower part pronounced *tú wù* (徒沃反). The *Qieyun* defines it as "pain" or "harm. The *Kaosheng* says it means "bitterness. The *Shuowen* explains that the character is formed from *chuò* (屮) with the phonetic *gùn* (虫); *chuò* is pronounced *mǔ liè* (母列反).

Regarding "zhǔzú" (咒詛): it is also written as "zhùchóu" (祝詶), with the phonetic components "shòu" (受) and "fǎn" (反). The *Shuowen jiezi* states that "chóu" (詶) is also "zú" (詛). The lower character, "zè" (側) and "jù" (據), is an archaic form written as "zhǔ" (󱶔). The *Shiming* (釋名) says: "Zhu (祝) belongs to this category; it is the act of attaching good or evil words to one another. "Zu" (詛) means to cause a person's actions to be constrained by their speech. The *Shuowen jiezi* explains it as "from the radical 'yan' (言) and the phonetic 'qie' (且)," with the sound "zī yú" (子余). The version in the Classics uses the radical "kou" (口) and is pronounced "cái yǔ" (才與); this is incorrect.

*Xuànyì* (眩瞖): [The character] *xuàn* is pronounced as *xián* (上玄絹反). Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to delude. The *Cangjie pian* says it refers to "lack of clarity in what is shown. The *Shuowen jiezi* says: "The eyes have no constant master. [The character] *yì* is pronounced as *yú* (於計反). Guo Pu says: "It is an obstruction that covers over. The *Kaosheng* says: "It is the *yì* (film) within the eye. The *Shuowen* says: "It is formed from the radical 目 with the phonetic 殹. Its pronunciation is *yīxí* (音一奚反). In the received text, it is written with the radical 羽 as *yì* (翳), which does not carry the meaning of *xuànyì*.

The upper character 溉 (gài) is pronounced with the initial *k* and the finals *-i* and *-an* (according to the *Yingyun*), meaning "to pour water. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "溉 means to irrigate. Gu Yewang says: "溉 is synonymous with pouring and filling. The lower character 灌 (guàn) is pronounced with the initial *w* and the final *-an*. The *Qieyun* states it means "to soak," and it also means "to pour water. Both characters are phono-semantic compounds (*xing-sheng zi*).

The two characters *hào* (號) and *háo* (嘷) share the same pronunciation, being the reverse of *hú-dāo* (胡刀). Regarding the first character, *hào*, the *Erya* states: "Dancing and *hào* refer to *yú* (sacrificial prayers for rain). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "weeping," which is written identically as *hǔ* (唬). Regarding the second character, *háo*, the *Yupian* defines it as "shouting. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *xiū* (獋), defining it as "the sound of a tiger's rage," and it is also written as *jiǎo* (𤢕).

*Què* (喟): The upper radical is *kùì* (口), the lower is *fǎn* (反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to the sound of a deep sigh or lament. It is also written as *qī* (㕟). The *Erya* states it means "to breathe. It is also pronounced with the initial *kǒu* and the final *guài* (恠). The lower character is read with the *tàndàn* (他旦) cut. The *Yunji* states it means "to sigh. It is also written as *tàn* (嘆), meaning "to grieve."

The upper character *xū* (吁) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* (rhyme-cutting) *kuàng* (況) and *yí* (疑); it is a word expressing wonder or strangeness. The lower character *jī* (嗞) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* *zǐ* (子); the rhyme dictionary states that *jī* refers to the sound of lamentation. The *Erya* writes this as *zī* (咨), stating: "Zē zī, to sigh. Guo’s commentary notes: "People in north of the Yellow River today say 'zē' when sighing"; the phonetic value of *tàn* (歎) is *zē*.

Fifth Scroll, Volume Five. Newly Translated *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Volume Five. "Cètián" (廁填): The first character, "cè" (廁), is pronounced according to the initial "shǐ" (史) and the final rhyme "jiān" (間). It refers to the space between latrines. The second character, "tián" (填), is pronounced according to the initial "táng" (唐) and the final rhyme "xián" (賢); it should be written as the character "tiàn" (瑱). The *Hànshū Xùnzhuàn* (漢書訓纂) states that it refers to pearls and jade used as ornaments for seats. It is also pronounced with the initial "táng" (唐) and the final rhyme "jiàn" (見). The version in the current sutra uses "tián" (填), which is the "tián" meaning to fill or block, and does not carry the sense of an ornamental insertion.

"An instant" (shùn xī): the former character is pronounced *shǎn* (as in *shǎn*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the movement of the eyelashes. The *Kaosheng* states it means "the eyes flickering," referring to the turning of the pupils. It is also written as *zhùn* or *xiàn*, with the same meaning. The latter character is pronounced *jí* (as in *jié*). The *Yaozheng Bingyuan* states: "Ordinary people take a total of 13,300 breaths over the course of a day and night; if there is even a single deviation in one breath, it constitutes illness. In Sanskrit this is called *ānāpāna*; here it is translated as "exhalation and inhalation."

Volume Six, Part Six. *New Translation of the Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, Volume Six. **Jue (覺)**: The upper character is pronounced as in *jiào* (to teach); its correct form is written with the radical for "awakening" (*jiào*). The *Cāngxiè Piān* states it means "arising from sleep. The lower character is pronounced as in *wù* (吾故反). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "being awake and having awareness. *Wù* (寤) is also synonymous with *wù* (晤). In the text of this sūtra, both characters are written with the "cave" radical (*kuàng*) as *wǔ* (窹), which is incorrect. According to the *Shuōwén*, they should be written with the "dream" radical (*mèng*) and the abbreviated form of *wù*.

*Kāi* (upper radical: 可哀反; *kě āi fǎn*). The *Yùnjí* states it means "to open up and create"; the *Shuōwén* defines it as "to initiate," formed with the gate radical (*mén*) and the phonetic *qián*. The variant with the well radical (*jǐng*) is not the standard form; the common usage is incorrect. *Chāng* (lower radical: 昌善反; *chāng shàn fǎn*). The *Yùpiān* also states it means "to open" and "to spread. The *Yùnyīng* explains it as "bright" and "to instruct."

"Jùwù" (遽務): "Jù" (遽) is pronounced *qú* (with the initial *yù* reversed); the *Guóyǔ* commentary states that "jù" means "haste," while the *Yùpiān* states that "jù" means "urgency. The lower character, "wù" (務), is pronounced *máng* (with the initial *yù* reversed). The *Erya* states that "wù" means "exertion"; Guo's commentary explains that "chīmù" (to gallop about) and "shìwù" (affairs and exertion) both refer to striving for oneself.

*Shì* (上吏反): The *Cangjie pian* states that *shì* means "swift" or "rapid. It is composed of the radical "horse" (馬) with the phonetic element "shǐ" (史). The text reads it as *shì* (古穴反), which is the name for a type of horse (*jié tí*) and does not carry the meaning of "speed. The character for "current" (*liú*) below is explained in the *Shuowen jiezi* as being composed of "water" (水) and "lù" (㐬), pronounced *tā hū fǎn*, meaning "to flow. The text reads it as *liú*, which is incorrect. In archaic script, it is also written as *liú* (㳅). *Tí* (騠) is pronounced *zhù xī fǎn*; it refers to a fine horse that runs as soon as it is born from its mother.

Volume Seven, Scroll Seven. Newly Translated *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Scroll Seven. *Nayuta* (the Chinese characters "中羊" [zhōng yáng] are a phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit term; alternatively, it is called *nāyuta*, a numerical designation from the Western Regions). According to the *Huangdi suanjing* (The Yellow Emperor’s Classic of Calculation), there are twenty-three numerical units from ten thousand upward, each having three grades: superior, middle, and inferior. These are: *wan* (10,000), *yi* (100 million), *zhi* (1 billion), *jing* (10 billion), *hai* (100 billion), *zi* (1 trillion), *rang* (10 trillion), *gou* (100 trillion), *jian* (1 quadrillion), *zheng* (10 quadrillion), and *zai* (100 quadrillion). Regarding the lower units, ten tens become the middle unit, and ten hundreds become the superior unit. Ten *yi* (100 million) become one *ji* (1 billion); ten *ji* become one *zhi* (10 billion); ten *zhi* become one *jing* (100 billion). The remaining units may be understood by applying this same principle accordingly. According to the *Huayan jing asengqi pin* (Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapter on the Incalculable) in Huiyuan’s *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings): "One hundred *lakṣa* make one *koṭi*, which corresponds to this 'billion' (*yi*). One *koṭi* times *koṭi* makes one *ayuta*, which corresponds to this 'ten billion' (*zhi*). One *ayuta* times *ayuta* makes one *nayuta*, which corresponds to this 'hundred billion' (*jing*). The rest should be understood by analogy.

*Youisui* (幽邃): The upper character is pronounced *yǒu* (with the radical *qiú* as the phonetic). It means "profound" and "hidden. The *Erya* states: "Profound and deep. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical *shan* (mountain) with *xian* as the phonetic; *xian* has the same pronunciation as above. The *Shuowen* further states that it means "subtle. The lower character is pronounced *suì* (with the radical *si* and *zuì* as the phonetics). The *Shuowen* states that it means "deep and far-reaching. In archaic script, it is also written as *ai* (㥞), with the same pronunciation and meaning.

*Jīxì* (羈繫): The upper character *jū* is pronounced with the *yí* rhyme; the *Shìmíng* (釋名) states that "the *jī* is that which is fastened to the horse's head, and the *mí* is that which is bound to the horse's feet. The lower character, pronounced with the *gǔ yì* rhyme, the *Yùpiān* (玉篇) defines as "binding and fettering," and also "to shut or close."

*Huì* (誨): The first character, *huang* (荒) with the radical *wai* (外), is defined by *Yunying* as "instruction" or "teaching. The *Lunyu* states, "In teaching others, he never grew weary. The second character, *yu* (與), is read as *jiu* (久). The *Lunyu* states, "He was a man who gradually and skillfully guided others. The *Yupian* defines it as "to lead and guide. The *Qieyun* defines it as "comprehensive," with the phonetic *gu xuan* (古泫); *xuan* (泫) is pronounced *hu chen* (胡詃). It also means "to teach. According to the *Shuowen*, it is formed from the radical *yan* (言) and the phonetic component *xiu* (秀).

Scroll 8, Volume 8. Newly Translated *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Scroll 8. *Huī* (暉): Upper radical *xǔ* (許), reversed cut *guī* (歸). The *Qieyun* says it means "light. It is also written as *huī* (輝); both are identical. Lower radical *yú* (余), reversed cut *liù* (六). The *Erya* says it means "bright"; the *Qieyun* says it means "light. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *rì* (日) with the phonetic *hù* (戶).

The first character, 靉 (ài), is pronounced *ài*; the second, 靆 (dài), is pronounced *dài*. The *Guǎngyá* states: "Āidài means 'obscured' (*yìhuì*). The character 薈 (*huì*) has the phonetic reading *wài*. This refers to the flourishing emergence of clouds. The *Tōngsúwén* says: "When clouds cover [the sky], it is called āidài."

"Hai-cu" (駭蹙): "Hai" (駭) is pronounced with the upper radical *xián* (閑) and the suffix *kǎi* (揩). The *Guǎngyá* states: "Hài means to startle. Now, one who is startled must have their mind uplifted; being uplifted is precisely to rise. The *Shuōwén* [explains it] as consisting of the radical *mǎ* (馬) and the phonetic *hài* (亥). "Zì" (蹙) is pronounced with the lower radical *zǐ* (子) and the suffix *liù* (六). The *Qièyùn* states: "Cù means near. The *Shuōwén* states: "It means pressing or urgent," consisting of the radical *qī* (戚) and the phonetic *zú* (足).

Volume Nine, Scroll Nine. Newly Translated *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Volume Nine. *Chen-li* (棽儷): Upper character, pronounced *chì lín* (勅林反). The *Yùpiān* states that it refers to tree branches arranged in pairs. The *Shuowén* states it means trees growing tall and paired, composed of the radical "forest" (*lín*) with the phonetic element "jīn" (*jīn shēng*). Lower character, pronounced *láng jì* (郎計反). The *Zītǒng* states it means a matched pair (*kàng lì*), and also implies grandeur and majesty. The character *chén* (棽) also has the pronunciations *sōng* (松) and *lín* (林); neither of these two pronunciations is accepted here.

*Mahe* (the final character is also written as *hai*, both pronounced like "hu ji") is a Sanskrit term; in its full form, it should be *Maheśvara*, which translates as "Great Sovereign" (*Dazizai*). This refers to the Great Sovereign Heavenly King (*Mahāmaheśvara-deva-rāja*), who is the lord of the Realm of Form (*Rūpadhātu*).

*Tián* (in *cìshàng*) is pronounced *tú nián fǎn*. In the *Yùpiān*, it refers to gold-flower inlays (*jīnhuātián*). The lower character, *chū lì fǎn*, is defined in the *Qièyùn* as "to interpose" (*xiàndià*) and in the *Shuōwén* as "to intersperse" (*zácì*).

The *Shílì jīng* (Sūtra on the Ten Powers), one fascicle: regarding *chàbié* (upper character), according to the *Yùpiān*, its pronunciation is *chū bā fǎn*. However, according to the sūtra, this should be the character *chā* (difference). Thus, the sūtra says: "the various differences in desires, pleasures, and inclinations. The current reading as *chàbié* (distinction) is likely a scribal error resulting from phonetic confusion; I request that those of high learning re-examine the meaning of the sūtra.

*The Sūtra on the Wheel of Dedication*, one fascicle. Regarding "provisions" (*zīliáng*): the upper character, *zī* (pronounced *jíyí fǎn*), according to the *Yùpiān* and *Zhùyuè*, means "wealth and goods. The lower character, *liáng* (pronounced *lǚzhāng fǎn*), is also written as *liáng*. As for "provisions" (*zīliáng*), it refers to the two kinds of provisions—merit and wisdom—which all Mahāsattvas must first cultivate when they intend to proceed toward the two fruits of transformational reliance: Bodhi and Nirvāṇa.

*Wúhǔ* (無怙): The upper character *wú* (無) is pronounced as *fū* (夫) in the ancient and archaic scripts; it resembles the sky’s contraction at the northwest corner. Some texts write it as *jì* (旡), which is not the character *wú*. The lower character *hǔ* (怙) is pronounced as *gǔ* (古). The *Erya* states: "To rely upon (*hù*) means to depend upon. As the *Shijing* says: "Without a father, what is there to rely on? Without a mother, what is there to depend upon?"

"Krodha" (忿恨): The first character, "fen," is pronounced with the phonetic transcription "fèn" (𢾭粉反), meaning anger; it is also pronounced "fèn" (𢾭問反). The second character, "hen," is pronounced with the phonetic transcription "hù gèn" (胡艮反), meaning resentment, grudge, or malice.

The upper character is pronounced *mǎn* (full) and *huǐng* (distant), with the radical *fǎn* (correct). The character *bì* (compare/align) is read as *jiāng* (will/send). The *Shuowen* says it means "two people standing together. The lower part is read as *yáng* (sheep). The *Erya* says it means "to escort. Examining the phonology, *jiāng* also means "great" or "to assist. The *Shuowen* states it is composed of the radicals *shòu* (meat) and *cùn* (inch), with the phonetic component *qiáng* (wall). *Shòu* is pronounced *ròu* (meat) and *qiáng* is pronounced *qiáng* (wall). The version in the scripture uses *luō* (stroke/pull), which is a vulgar character and not the correct form.
