The seventeen fascicles are of the same volume as this continuation of the phonetic commentary. *New Translation of the Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle One (Upper). The *Preface*: The *Mao Commentary on the Book of Poetry* states: “*Huáng* (皇) means great; it means to rectify. The *Erya* states: “*Huáng* means to rectify, to be a king, and to be correct. [The character] is pronounced *yú jǐ* (於紀反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: “It is a particle used when speech is finished. It is composed of the ancient form of the character *yǐ* (已) with the phonetic element *shǐ* (矢). The sound of *sī* (厶) is *yǐ* (以). *New Translation of the Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle One (Upper), together with the Preface. The *Mao Commentary on the Book of Poetry* says: "‘*Huáng*’ (皇) means great; it means to rectify. The *Erya* says: "‘*Huáng*’ means to rectify, to be a king, and to be correct. [The character] is pronounced *yú jǐ* (於紀反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "It is a word used when speech is finished. It is composed of the ancient form of the character *yǐ* (已) with the phonetic element *shǐ* (矢). The sound of *sī* (厶) is *yǐ* (以).

The character *mián* (絡): "On top" it is read as *mí* (彌) with the *biān* (編) auxiliary; its meaning is "fine" (*wēi*) or "to pass through" (*lì*). "Below" the phonetic value is *luò* (洛). According to the *Shuowen*, it means "woven network" (*zhī luò*) or also "gauze" (*luó*).

The character *luó* (羅): "On top" it is read as *lǚ* (魯) with the *jù* (句) auxiliary. The *Erya* states that a bird-catcher's net is called a *luó*. "Below" the phonetic value is *zhào* (教). According to the *Shuowen*, it is a device for catching fish. According to the *Fangyan*, it is a cage or cover. The *Shuowen* maintains that both characters *luó* and *zhào* should be written with the radical *gāng* (岡).

*Yǒng*: The upper character is pronounced *yǐng*. The *Erya* states: "To *yǒng* is to swim. Guo’s commentary says: "To swim submerged at the bottom of the water. The lower character is pronounced *bō*. Regarding the sound: *mò* means to stop; it refers to foam floating on the surface of water. It also means "end" or "tip. These two characters are formed through phonetic-semantic compounding. *Miǎo* is pronounced *wángzhǎo*.

Regarding the Five Beginnings, the *Sānwǔ lìjì* states: "When the manifestations of the vital energy (*qì*) have not yet differentiated, it is called *Tàiyì*. When the primordial energy (*yuánqì*) first begins to sprout, it is called *Tàichū*. The tip of the manifestations of the vital energy is called *Tàishǐ*. When form undergoes transformation and possesses substance, it is called *Tàisù*. When substance and form are fully complete, it is called *Tàijí*. These constitute the Five Beginnings."

*Chè* (枕): On the pillow, it is written with the radical *chán* (列) and the phonetic *fǎn* (反). The *Shuōwén* states: "To remove; to eliminate. Examining its sound, it is *chōu*. The *Shuōwén* further explains: "It means 'to penetrate' (*tōng*). It follows the radical *chì* (彳), the element *pī* (攴), and the phonetic *yù* (育). The lower part is read as *rèn*. The *Yùnquán* states: "A pillow is that which supports the head. It follows the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *yín* (冘). *Yín* has the sound *yín*; *chì* has the sound *chǒu*; *pī* has the sound *pǔshí*. *Chē* (徹): To remove; to take away. The *Shuōwén* states: "To penetrate through. It follows the radical *chì* (彳), the element *pī* (攴), and the phonetic *yù* (育). The lower part is read as *zhīrèn*. The *Yùnquán* states: "A pillow is that which supports the head. It follows the radical *mù* (木) and the phonetic *yín* (冘). *Yín* has the sound *yín*; *chì* has the sound *chǒu*; *pī* has the sound *pǔshí*.

*Ē*: Upper radical *ān* with *gé* as the phonetic (meaning "to block" according to the *Cāngjié piān*; the *Máoshī chuán* says it means "to stop"; the *Shàngshū* says it means "to cut off"). Lower radical *kǒu* with *gòu* as the phonetic (meaning "bandits and rebels" according to the *Kǎoshēng*; the *Yùnquán* says it means "abundant and many"; the *Shuōwén* says it means "violent"; in the *Zìshū*, the character *bǎo* [treasure] takes *pī* [a hand] and *huán* [complete] as its components).
"Manifested upon the stars" (zhù xīngchén shàng):
the "zhù" is pronounced as in *zhāng lú* (反). The *Zhouyi* says: "Among the manifest and luminous forms, none is greater than the sun and moon.
The *Liji* says: "That which is manifest and never ceases is Heaven."
That which is fixed and immovable is "earth" (dì).
It is also said to mean "fixed brilliance," "to stand," and "to accomplish.
In ancient and modern times, the correct character is written with the radical for "grass" (艸) and the phonetic element "shǔ" (署) abbreviated.
The ancient form of the character for "star" (xīng) is written as 曐.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The essence of the myriad things ascends to become the arrayed constellations.
Furthermore, "star" refers to the five planets and their movements through the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*xiù*).

According to the *Qīyào Tiānwén Jīng* (Scripture on the Astronomy of the Seven Luminaries), the three enclosures—the Zǐwēi (Purple Microcosm) and the Tàiwēi (Great Microcosm)—along with the various constellations and their subordinate officials, comprise a total of one thousand four hundred and sixty-four stars that should be employed for divination; "Chén" refers specifically to the Northern Dipper (Běichén).
The *Lunyu* says: "To govern by means of virtue is like the North Star.

"Mian" (緬) is traced back to the *Guoyu* commentary by Jia Gongyan; it means to reflect upon or contemplate. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to fine silk, composed of the radical "silk" (糸) and the phonetic "mian" (面). The character below is pronounced "xu lin"; according to the *Zishu*, it means constant. "Kao" (考) is the phonetic component, meaning to seek or to pursue. The character is a compound of the radicals "hand" (𠂇), "mouth" (口), "gong" (工), and "cun" (寸), conveying its meaning through their combination.

The character above "夫" (fú) is pronounced as *jì* (with the initial *kǎo* sound); it is said that *yí* (𡄻) is a sound of lamentation and sorrow, used here as an exclamation. It is composed of *zhù* (壴) with the character *kǒu* (口) below. The current version in this preface uses *xīn* (心) instead to form *yì* (懿), which is a vulgar usage of the character. The lower "夫" is pronounced *fú*, and "zhù" is pronounced *zhú jù*.

The name of King Prasenajit of Kosala is abbreviated from its Sanskrit; it is properly called Prasenajit Śāta, which translates as "Victorious Army. He was the patron who requested the Buddha to teach on internal and external protection.

*Qū* (pronounced *qù*, with the rhyme of *xià*): The *Shēngyùn* states that it means "sleeve. The *Jíxùn* explains it as "to lift. The *Hànshī* says it means "to remove. The *Shuōwén* defines it as being composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) with the phonetic "remove" (*qù*).

*Nǎi* (pronounced *jīn* [upper tone] and *nú* [modified tone]): This is the archaic form of the character *nǎi*. It is also a particle used for discourse. *Jǐn* (pronounced *jǐng* [lower tone] and *yín*): Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhōulǐ* states that it means "moisture. The *Ěryá* says it refers to "bridges. The *Guǎngyá* also defines it as "ferrying across."

"Red-dyed silk (*ti-you*)" refers to the highest grade. The *Commentary on the Zhou Li* by Zheng Xuan states that it is green-colored silk, while others say it is light red; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as silk of a reddish-yellow color. The "oil" mentioned below refers to silk-oil; in antiquity, colored silk was treated with oil to record matters upon it.

The *Dalu* (Grand Chariot) is pronounced with the retroflex *l* as in "luo" (洛). The *Baixi Tong* (White Tiger General Exposition) states: "It is the Grand Chariot of the Son of Heaven. According to the *Zishu* (Dictionary of Characters), in ancient times it was a simple spoked wheel (*chuilun*), but now it is adorned with magnificent splendor. The *Dai Li* (Great Rites) says: "The ancient chariot and canopy were circular to resemble heaven, with twenty-eight spokes to represent the twenty-eight lunar mansions; the frame was square to resemble earth, with thirty spokes to represent the number of days in a month. Looking up, one observed the celestial phenomena; looking down, one examined the principles of geography. Looking forward, one heard the sounds of the *luan* and *he* bells; looking to the side, one observed the movements of the four seasons. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "That which the Son of Heaven rides is called a *lu*. It is named according to its adornments of gold, jade, and ivory."

The character above is pronounced *zòu* (鄒反) with the phonetic *kǎo* (考); the gloss states it means "to seek" (*qiú*) or "to search for" (*sò*). The character below is pronounced *zhuī* (追反); Jia’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states it means "to connect" (*lián*). The *Qieyun* defines it as "to continue. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *chuè* (叕), which is pronounced *zhìluò* (陟劣反).

*Qiāncháng* (褰裳): The upper character is pronounced *qán* (乾) with the *shēng* (聲) radical *kǎo* (考). The *Erya* states: "If [the water] is deep, one uses a *lì*; if shallow, one *jié*. *Jié* means to lift up one's clothes. Guo’s commentary says it refers to lifting the skirt (*cháng*). *Jié* is pronounced *qù yè* (去謁) in the first instance and *shì yáng* (市羊) in the second. According to the *Zishu*, the upper garment is called *yī* (衣) and the lower garment is called *cháng* (裳).

"Vo zhèn" (沃朕): "Zhèn" (朕) is pronounced *wù* (烏穀反). The *Shàngshū* says: "Qǐ, open your heart and moisten my heart. Jia’s commentary on the *Guóyǔ* states that "vo" means "beautiful"; the *Guǎngyǎ* says "vo" means "clear"; and the *Shuōwén* says "vo" means "to irrigate. Regarding the character "zhèn" below: the *Ěryǎ* says "zhèn" is a term for "I. In antiquity, it was used by both the noble and the humble; it was only from the time of the First Emperor of Qin that it was used exclusively by the Son of Heaven.

"Xi" (襲) in the upper character of "xunli" (尋立) is read as "fan" (反); the *Guoyu* states that "xi" means "to return. Sima Biao’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* says "xi" means "to enter. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says "xi" means "to double-layer. The lower character, "yi" (以), is read as "zhu" (諸); the *Erya* states that "yu" (予) means "me" (我).

Regarding the term *lài* (籟): the "zhī" (之) is pronounced as *luò* (洛) with a retroflex final; the *Guǎngyá* states that the *lài* is a *xiāo* (flute). The larger type has twenty-four tubes, each one foot and four *cùn* long; the smaller type has sixteen tubes, each one foot and two *cùn* long, and it has two bases. The *Shuowén* says it is a three-holed *xiāo*; it is written with the radical for bamboo and the phonetic component *là* (賴).

*Luán* (栾): upper radical *lú*, reversed *huán*. According to the *Lǐjì*, the trees planted at the tombs of the Son of Heaven are pines; those of the feudal lords, cypresses; those of the Great Officers, *luán*; and those of the scholars, willows. The *Shuowén* states that the *luán* tree resembles a *lán* (欄), being composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic component "lan" in abbreviated form (*luán*), with the lower part pronounced *jīnlì*. The commentary on the *Máoshī* says that *jí* (棘) is the sour jujube (*suānzǎo*). Guō’s commentary on the *Ěryǎ* states that *diān jí* (顛棘) has fine leaves and thorns. The *Shuowén* describes it as resembling the jujube, growing in clusters, composed of two "bundles" (*shù*). The *Guǎngyǎ* calls it *zhēn* (箴). The eastern pronunciation is *cì* (㓨).

"Bì" (輔) means to assist. The *Kǒngzhù* on the *Shàngshū* states: "Bì means to support. The *Ěryǎ* says: "Bì means lofty and weighty. The *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn* states: "The Son of Heaven has four neighbors: the Left Assistant (Zuǒfǔ), the Right Assistant (Yòubì), the Front Doubter (Qiányí), and the Rear Supporter (Hòuchéng). The *Guǎngyǎ* states: "Bì means complete. The *Dàdàilǐ* states: "One who is pure and incorruptible, earnest and upright, who corrects errors and remonstrates against depravity—such a person is called a Bì. The *Shuōwén* states: "The character is composed of 弜 (pronounced jù zhī fǎn) and 西 (pronounced tiān niàn fǎn); alternatively, it is written with 攵 as 㢸, or as 󱸳; these characters are all archaic forms."

"Liángbèi" (良賁): "Bèi" (賁) is pronounced as "pǐ yì fǎn" (彼義反); it is a rhyme from the *Yīngwēi* (英微). It is the name of a hexagram. The *Yījīng* (易經) states: "Bèn (Jiànbèi) brings success; for minor matters, there is benefit in having a destination. Liángbèi is the name of a monk who assisted in the translation of this *Rénwáng jīng* (仁王經).
*Cháng Gǔn*: The second character, *gǔn*, is pronounced with the *fǎn* (rhyme) *wěn*.

This is the name of a former Hanlin Academician. *Wò jiàn*: The second character, *jiàn*, is pronounced with the *fǎn* *cái gǎn qī yàn èr fǎn*. The *Shìmíng* states: "A *jiàn* is a writing board (*bǎn*). The *Yùnwěiquán* states: "To use a board for recording documents. The *Shuōwén* states: "*Dú* is a plain board; it takes the radical *mù* (wood) and the phonetic *zhǎn*. The *Jìxùn* states: "One who carves a board to record matters. It is also pronounced with the *fǎn* *qiān*.

Regarding "suì" (邃) in the upper character: although the reading is *zuì* (醉), Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* states that "suì" means "profound. Regarding "zé" (賾) in the lower character: the reading is *chái* (柴) and *gé* (革). Liu Xian’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states that "zé" is a term for what is obscure and profound. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical 頁 with the phonetic element 責; the sound of 頁 is *yí* (夷). The readings in the text as "顊" (*xù*) and "賾" (*zé*) are both incorrect.

*Jiào* (upper tone *jiǎo*) means "to examine" (*kǎo*), as in the *Shēnglüè*. In the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "clear"; in the *Ěryǎ*, it means "straightforward. The *Dàzhuàn* of the *Shàngshū* states: "One examines their intentions to perceive their deeds. The *Tàixuānjīng* says: "The ways of the gentleman and the petty man are clearly distinguished (*jiào rán*). The *Hànshū* says: "It is clearly (*jiào rán*) easy to understand."

The character *suo* (索) [in *gou-suo*] is pronounced with the second tone, reversed from *ge*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to search within a house," composed of the radical *mian* (宀) and the phonetic *suo* (索). The commentary on the sounds states it means "to take" or "to seek. Nowadays, in common usage, the radical *mian* has been dropped; it is written simply as *suo* (索), composed of *shi* (市) and *mi* (糸). The sound of *mian* is pronounced *míxiān*.

*Nie* (躡): When placed above *jin* (金), it is read as *nian* (黏) with a reversed tone. The *Fangyan* says it means "to step upon"; the *Guoyaya* says "to tread"; the *Shuowen* says "to trample. It is composed of the radical "foot" (*zu*) and the phonetic "nie" (*nie*). The pronunciation of *nie* is the same as above.

Regarding "wǎnfǔ" (惋撫): the upper character is pronounced *wū guàn* (烏貫反). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "sighing with regret. The *Guìyuànzhúcóng* (桂菀珠叢) states it means "to sigh in astonishment and store [the emotion] in one's heart. The lower character is pronounced *fāng wǔ* (芳武反). The *Ěryǎ* (爾雅) states: "Fǔ means to cover or to pat."

The *Zhánméng* year—*zhān* pronounced as *rán*—is defined in the *Erya* as the year when the *tàisuì* (the celestial year) is in *yǐ*, and the day is *shí*. According to the *Táng Dì Niánlì* (Chronology of the Tang Emperors), Emperor Dàizōng changed the third year of Guǎngdé, which was *jiǎchén*, to the first year of Yǒngtài; the second year was *yǐshí*, which is precisely the *zhánméng* year. From that time until the present, the fifth year of Tǒnghé, which is *dīnghài*, two hundred and twenty-three years have elapsed.

The *mùjǐn* (hibiscus) flourishes in the second month; the *Ěryá* states that the *jiǎ* is the *mùjǐn*. Guo’s commentary says it resembles a plum tree. Sun Yan’s sub-commentary notes that its flowers are like those of the *shǔkuí*, purple in color, blooming in the morning and withering by evening. This flower reaches its full bloom in the fifth month of summer. The *Preface to the Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā* states: "In the fourth month of summer, this sūtra was translated at the Southern Peach Garden."

Gṛdhrakūṭa, formerly translated as Qisheshuqie Mountain (耆闍崛山), is correctly rendered in Sanskrit as Gṛdhrakūṭa, which means "Vulture Peak" or "Vulture Terrace. This is because vultures frequently dwell upon its peaks, and it resembles a high terrace. It is located beside the city of Rājagṛha and is the place where this sutra was preached. The pronunciation of "gṛ" (姞) is *jǔyǐ* (巨乙反).
Śrāvastī, formerly transcribed as Shewei Guo and correctly as Śrāvastī, means "Good Road" or "Heard Object"; it was the domain governed by King Prasenajit.

The character *jì* (技) is pronounced with the initial *qú* and the final *qǐ*. It signifies ability; the *Jìxùn* states that it means both skill (*jì*) and artistry (*yì*), and also denotes ingenuity. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the element "branch" (*zhī*), or alternatively, it is written with the "person" (*rén*) radical as *jì* (伎), which is a vulgar usage. In the canonical texts, it is written with the "woman" (*nǚ*) radical as *jì* (妓), referring to female musicians; this is not the character for skill or artistry. The final rhyme is *yù* and *jì*. In the *Yùnyùn*, it denotes talent. The *Lúnyǔ* says, "He roamed among the arts" (*yóu yú yì*). Hé’s commentary explains that these are the "six arts" (*liù yì*), namely: ritual (*lǐ*), music (*yuè*), calligraphy (*shū*), mathematics (*shù*), archery (*shè*), and charioteering (*yù*).

"Bhikṣu" is an incorrect rendering of the Sanskrit term; it should be "Bhikṣu," which means "Terrifier of Māras. It possesses five meanings: first, a mendicant; second, one of pure livelihood; third, one of pure precepts; fourth, one who destroys evil; and fifth, [one who has broken through the bonds]. Because it possesses these five meanings, the Sanskrit term is retained without translation.
The five meanings of *bhikṣuṇī* are as previously explained; *nī* is simply the feminine suffix.

*Upāsaka* is an ancient Sanskrit term; its correct form is *upāsaka*. *Upā* means "near," and *saka* means "to serve"; *ka* is the masculine suffix, thus it refers to a "male lay follower" (*upāsaka*). This refers to one who, having received the precepts, draws near to and serves the Triple Gem.

*Upāsikā* is the correct transliteration; *upāsaka* is explained as before, though this is the feminine form of address. *Jambudvīpa* (pronounced with the initial *j* as in "time" and the final *p* as in "fan") is a Sanskrit term; it is the general name for this great earth.

In ancient translations, it was sometimes called *Zhanfu*, *Yanfu*, *Yanjuti*, or *Yanfuli*. The correct transliteration is *Jambū*. The *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra* states that there is a *Jambū* tree growing on the northern edge of this continent, on the southern bank of the Narmadā River, exactly at the center of the continent and facing north toward the water. Beneath this tree, within the water, there is a golden *Jambū* tree; the continent is named after the gold, and the name of the continent is established because of the tree. Therefore, it is called *Jambudvīpa*. The sound of *zhan* is pronounced *zhui* (as in "zhui"), and the sound of *yan* is pronounced *can-lan* (as in "can" and "lan").

*Na-yu-duo*: The middle character is pronounced according to the *zhǔ* rhyme (as in *zhǔ*). In Sanskrit it is sometimes called *nayuta*, a numerical term from the Western Regions; in this land [of China], it is known as "yì" (a unit of counting).

Volume 2, Part 2, New Translation of the *Renwang Huguo Banruo Boluomiduo Jing* (Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for Protecting the State), Volume 2. *Chǒu-xiè* (桎梏): - The upper character (*chǒu*) is pronounced according to the *chì* rhyme (as in *jiǔ*), and the lower character (*xiè*) according to the *hú* rhyme (as in *jiè*). According to the *Yùpiān*, these refer to wooden restraints. They are made by boring holes into wood. That which is worn on the hands is called *chǒu*; that which is worn on the feet is called *xiè*. Both characters are derived from the radical for "wood" (*mù*), with *chǒu* and *jiè* serving as their respective phonetic components.

The upper character of "jiāsuò" (枷鎖) is pronounced with the tone of "jiā" (枷), meaning a neck-shackle; it consists of a wooden block with holes bored through it that is placed upon the neck. It is an implement for imprisoning criminals. The lower character, "shèng" (乘), has the phonetic value of "guǒ" (果); it refers to an iron chain used to bind and tether criminals.

"Jian" (檢) [pronounced *jiǎn* with the initial *yǎn*]. The *Guǎngyǎ* states: "Jian means a box; it also means to enclose. It refers to binding and fastening so that one cannot open or expose it; it also means to examine, referring to the examination and recording of those who are bound. It is composed of the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "qian" (僉).

Mahākāla is a term from the Sanskrit language; *mahā* means "great" and *kāla* means "black. The scripture refers to him as Mahākāla, the Great Black Deity, citing both the Chinese and Sanskrit names together. This deity has the color of a dark blue-black cloud and possesses an immeasurable lifespan. He has eight arms, each holding a different weapon, and he wears a necklace made of pierced skulls. He manifests in a form of great wrath, with the goddess Pṛthivī beneath his feet supporting them with her two hands.

*Chuāng* (瘡): Upper radical *cè* (惻) with the rhyme *zhuāng* (莊); the *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means "wounds and sores" (*chuāngyí*). It is also written as *chuàng* (創). The archaic form is *chǎng* (𭃅). Lower radical *yōu* (憂) with the rhyme *fǎn* (反); the *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) states it refers to the disease of warts. It is also written as *yóu* (肬), which is likewise interchangeable; the archaic form is also *yǒu* (𤴨).

The sun and moon lose their proper courses (shidu). "Du" is pronounced as *gu* in the lower tone; according to Qingcenzi, the sun is the essence of the Great Yang (*taiyang*) and completes one circuit of the heavens in one year, while the moon is the essence of the Great Yin (*taiyin*) and completes one circuit of the heavens in one month. The *Jinpei jing* states that the moon presides over sorrow and calamity, while the sun presides over fortune and virtue; thus, the moon is the "odd number of punishment" (*xingqi*) and the sun is the "odd number of virtue" (*deqi*). They regularly take the winter solstice as the day when the sun is at twenty-one degrees and one-quarter of a degree in the Dipper (*Dou*), the spring equinox as the day it is at fourteen degrees in the Ox (*Niu*), the summer solstice as the day it is at twenty-six degrees in the Eastern Well (*Dongjing*), and the autumn equinox as the day it is at two degrees and one-quarter of a degree in the Horn (*Jiao*). Any deviation from these positions constitutes losing the proper course.

*Bo* (搏) is pronounced *bǔ* (補各反); the *Shuowen* states it means "to strike. *Shi* (蝕) has the phonetic value *shí* (食); the *Shiming* states that when the moon wanes, it is called an eclipse (*shi*), as it gradually erodes away like insects eating the leaves of plants and trees. The *Jiuyao Wuxing Li* (Calendar of the Nine Luminaries and Five Elements) says: "Luo Mo is also named the Eclipse Deity; its head is always hidden and invisible, yet when it encounters the sun or moon, an eclipse occurs. Furthermore, when the sun and moon share the same color, the moon covers the sun and there is a solar eclipse. It is also said that when the sun is directly opposed [to a node] and is as large as the sun, but its light does not shine, this is called 'dark void' (*anxu*); when it coincides with the moon, a lunar eclipse occurs."

A "comet" (huìxīng) is pronounced with the initial *suí* and the final *ruì*; it is a portentous star. The *Erya* states: "The comet is called Chánqīng. Guo Pu’s commentary notes that it is also termed a "Bo-star," because its form is "bo-bo" (blazing or spreading), resembling a broom-sweeping comet; it is alternatively called a "Sǎoxīng" (sweeping star), a "Bóxīng" (bo-star), a "Chánqīng Star," or a "Huìxīng" (comet).

The *Xingzang li* (Calendar of the Movement and Concealment of the Five Planets) concerning Jupiter states: It is the essence of wood; its color is green and its nature is benevolent and compliant. When its movement follows the proper course, it brings blessings; when it moves retrograde or occupies a position of obstruction, it brings calamity. It completes one circuit of the heavens in twelve years. In eighty-three years and seventy-six days, it completes seven such circuits.

Mars is the essence of fire; its color is red and its nature is ritual propriety (*li*). It bears the image of one who upholds the law. When it traverses its path with clarity, the people are at peace and the state is prosperous. If it loses its proper measure and becomes tight and small, there will be military conflict both within and without. Generally, it completes one circuit of the heavens in two years, appearing and vanishing for seven hundred and eighty days. In seventy-nine years, thirty-seven such cycles conclude and forty-two circuits of the heavens are completed.

Venus is the essence of the Great White Jade Star; its color is white and its nature is courageous, bearing the likeness of a general. It completes one circuit of the heavens in one year, being visible for two hundred and forty-four days. At the beginning of the evening, it appears in the west; its motion is somewhat swift, traveling slightly more than one degree per day, until it gradually slows to two hundred and forty-nine degrees, whereupon it halts for eight days. It then moves retrograde for ten days, remains invisible (in the sun's glare) for twelve days at dusk, and subsequently appears in the east at dawn. Generally, it completes five circuits and five degrees in eight years, appearing five times in the evening and five times in the morning.

Mercury is the essence of water; its color is black and its nature is wisdom. It enters and exits the light throughout all four seasons. When it is luminous and moist, the state is prosperous and the people are happy; otherwise, floods or droughts occur. It is always visible during the four seasonal midpoints (*zhòng*), completing one circuit of the heavens in one year. Its distance from the sun is never more than twenty-six degrees, which is why it is often not seen by people. In every thirty-three years, it completes one hundred and four cycles of seventy-four degrees; when it appears in the morning at twenty-six degrees, it should be visible but is not.

Saturn is the essence of earth; its color is yellow and its nature is trustworthiness. It is the symbol of the female ruler. When it follows its proper course, it is bright and brings blessings; when its movement becomes disordered, its color turns red or white, and there will be warfare throughout the world. Its motion is the slowest of all, completing one circuit of the heavens in twenty-nine years and six months (twenty-nine and a half years). It takes three hundred and seventy-eight days for one station of concealment (one *fu*). It completes two circuits of the heavens in fifty-nine years and seventeen months. It first appears in the east at the beginning of this cycle.

"Fànzhǎng" (泛漲): "Fàn" is pronounced with the *fang* rhyme-group (corresponding to the *fan* radical). Guo Yu’s commentary states that "fàn" means to float; the *Mao Shi* Commentary says it is the appearance of flowing. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "fàn" from the "fan" radical. "Zhǎng" is pronounced with the *liàng* rhyme-group (corresponding to the *zhang* radical). The *Kaosheng* explains: when water increases in volume such that the sandy banks collapse and fall into the water, it is called "zhǎng," composed of the "water" radical and the phonetic "zhang. The common pronunciation as an upper tone (*shǎng*) is incorrect.

*Kiáng-yáng* (亢陽): *kǎng* is pronounced with the *shàng* tone and rhymes with *kàng*; it signifies the extreme of sound. According to character dictionaries, it means "high"; according to the *Qièyùn*, it means "drought. The *Yìjīng* says, "The ninth line at the top: the dragon is overreaching (*kànglóng*), there will be regret," which refers to the culmination of the yang.

"Jiangzhu" (降澍) [the first character pronounced as zhù with the "zhū" and "shù" finals reversed]; the *Jixun* (集訓) states: "The rain that falls in its proper season, moistening and nourishing all things so they grow. The text of the scripture uses the character "zhu" (霔), which does not exist in any dictionary; it was created arbitrarily by those who took liberties with the pen.

The character 㮀 (pén) is pronounced with the upper radical *xiá* (嚴) and the phonetic *kǎo* (考), meaning a wooden box; it is also written as 椷. The text of the sūtra uses 凾, which is a vulgar character for 函 (hán). It is named after the Hangu Pass (*Hángù Guān*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it refers to millet or sacrificial grain in a vessel, composed of the radical *míng* (皿) and the phonetic *chéng* (成).

The character for "records" (jí) is composed of the radical "speech" (yán) with the phonetic "jì" (pronounced as lǐ). The *Shìmíng* states: "It means to recognize or record. The lower part, "qín" (pronounced xī), is the phonetic. It refers to registers and official documents. The preface to the *Shàngshū* says: "The creation of written characters and seals replaced the administration of knotted cords; from this, literary records arose. Thus, "wénjí" (literary records) came into being.

The Greatly Powerful Vidyārāja Uṣṇīṣa-cakra Sūtra, Volume One. Regarding the title *Mahābala-uṣṇīṣa-vidyārāja-sūtra*, volume one: as for *Maheśvara*, in the correct Sanskrit it should be *Maheśvara*, which is translated here as "Great Sovereign" (*Dazizai*). He is the Lord of the Realm of Form (*Rūpadhātu*), so called because he attains sovereignty over the trichiliocosm.

*Wei-er* (逶迤): The upper character is pronounced *wei* (as in *wei* for "to act") according to the rhyme scheme; it means "graceful movement. The lower character is pronounced *yi* (as in *yi* for "overflow") according to the rhyme scheme; it means "abundance. The *Hanshu* states that "water curves" (*an wei-er*) refers to the appearance of winding, circuitous, and oblique movement. The lower character is also pronounced *da-lo* (達羅), with the same gloss as above.

*Ucchuṣma* (the "u" and "shu" are pronounced as *chang* and *zhu* respectively; it is a Sanskrit term, though some call it *ucchusama*). This is translated as "Foul Trace. Former translations rendered it as "Impure," which are all erroneous; the new translation renders it as "Defiler of Impurity," a wrathful deity (*krodha*). According to the *Yogatantra*, he manifests his body for the purpose of gathering and transforming sentient beings through two kinds of wheels: first, the Wheel of Command (*ājñā-cakra*), wherein he manifests a majestic and dignified body; second, the Wheel of Wrath (*raudra-cakra*), wherein he manifests an extremely terrifying body. He manifests this fearsome form in order to subdue those sentient beings who are difficult to tame.

"Line" (xiàn): pronounced *shī* with the rhyme *jiǎn* (as in *shījǐan*). The *Zhouli* states: "The Officer of Lines (*xiànrén*) presides over the work of sewing and threading within the royal palace. According to the *Qieyun*, it refers to thread. It is also written as *xiàn*, with the same pronunciation. "Placing" (pīn): pronounced *zhèn* with the rhymes *shéng* and *mǐ* (meaning to stretch a cord to ensure straightness). The vulgar form uses the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) to write it as *pīn*, meaning to arrange or align. The scriptural text uses the radical "wood" (*mù*) to write it as *pīn*; however, *pīn* and *bìng* refer to the name of the *pīn-lǚ* tree, and are not the character for "line-placing" (*xiàn-pīn*).

*Pín-cù* (顰蹙): Upper radical *zhēn* (真) with the *qièyùn* (反切) *fú* (符). It means to knit one's brows; it is also written as *pín* (頻). The *Shuōwén* says it is "sorrow," and also refers to a frown or a smile. In the scriptural text it is written as *pín*, while in the *Qièyùn* it means "number" or "near. This is not its usage here. Lower character: *zǐ-liù* (子六). The *Yùpiān* says it means "to press"; the *Shuōwén* says it means "urgency. It is composed of the radical *qī* (戚) and the phonetic *zú* (足).

Regarding "guān" (key/pivot): The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that a horizontal beam used to hold a gate is called a *guān*. The *Shenglèi* states that a *guān* is that by which something is closed. The *Qieyun* glosses it as a *huīng* (bolt). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "gate" (*mén*) and the phonetic element "jiǎn" (*bàn*). The scriptural text writes it as "guān" with the pronunciation *biàn*. The *Erya* states: "The *guān* is called the *zài*. This does not refer to the meaning of a key-pivot. The *Qieyun* gives the pronunciation for "jiàn" (key) as *qì yǎn*. In character dictionaries, the horizontal bar is called *guān* and the vertical bar is called *jiàn*.

*Zhízhú* (躑躅) is the name of a medicinal herb; *chén* (呈) is pronounced *jǐ* (戟) and *fǎn* (反), and *cì* (次) is pronounced *chóng* (重) and *lù* (錄). The *Bencao* (本草) states it is the *yáng zhízhú* (羊躑躅). Both its leaves and flowers are highly toxic. It is harvested in the third month; the flowers are yellow, though there are also those of five colors. If a sheep mistakenly eats its flowers or leaves, it stumbles (*zhízhú*) and dies, hence the name. According to the *Jīngǔ zhèngzì* (古今正字), "to stumble" means to be unable to move forward. Both characters are written with the "foot" radical (*zú* [足]). In the regions of Zheng and Shu, both sounds are used.

The character for *rāśi* (㲲) is pronounced with the initial *tu* and the rhyme *xie* (according to the *Qieyun*). It refers to white cotton cloth (*pata*), which was highly esteemed in the Western Regions. The scriptural text uses the radical for "silk" (*mi*) to form this character; its vulgar usage is incorrect. Regarding *bān* (瘢):

the upper character is pronounced with the initial *bu* and the rhyme *guan* (according to the *Qieyun*), meaning a scar from a wound; the lower character is pronounced with the initial *hu* and the rhyme *en* (according to the *Qieyun*), meaning a scar. Examining the phonology, a very slight scar is called a *hen* (痕).

*Dunxing* (遁形): Upper character *tu*, lower character *sun*. According to the *Yun*, it means to elude or escape; it refers to remaining hidden and concealed. Examining this, the *Ekākṣarottama-cakravartin-tantra* explains the *anta-dhana* rite as "concealing one's form" (*yinxing*). This is because in that land, heterodox and orthodox beliefs are intermingled and various paths dwell side by side, mutually criticizing one another. Therefore, the Buddha, through his supernatural powers, taught this essential method so that practitioners of *yoga* may attain mastery according to their will and swiftly achieve *siddhi*.

"Guǒ" (裹): The upper character is pronounced with the *xié* rhyme; it refers to an iron plate. Plates made of gold, silver, copper, and so forth are all the same. It is composed of the radical "metal" (金) and the phonetic "yé" (枼). The lower character is pronounced with the *gǔ* rhyme; it means to wrap or to bind. It is composed of the radical "to tear" (坼) and the element "clothing" (衣), with "guǒ" (果) as the phonetic. The scriptural text uses this form "guǒ"; the vulgar usage does not constitute a standard character.

*Caitya* is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is sometimes called *jieti*, sometimes *zhiti*, and should properly be called *zhidi*. This is translated as "accumulation," or "arousing pure faith," or "sacred temple"—all of which are interpretive translations. It refers generally to the construction of tombs, temples, terraces, and pavilions at the sites where the Buddha was cremated, as well as where he walked or preached the Dharma. It is a place where all humans and devas accumulate merit and goodness.

*Zǐkuàng* (紫𨥥): The second character is pronounced *gǔměng* (古猛). It is the name of a medicinal substance. According to the *Bencao* (本草), it originates from the Western Regions (*Xīróng*) and is produced by boiling tree bark and leaves together; it may be used for medicinal purposes. The text uses the two forms *kuàng* (鑛) and *kuàng* (礦); these refer to "the king of metals" (*jīnwáng pǔ*), and are not the character for *zǐkuàng*.

*Chǎo* (稻上初爪反): A phonetic transcription meaning to fry; it is also written as *chāo* (煼) and appears as *chǎo* (炒) in the *Shuowen Jiezi*. It is a vulgar character. Below [the radical]: *tú hào* (徒晧反). The *Bencao* states that *gěngmǐ* (粳米, non-glutinous rice) stops nausea and diarrhea, while *dàomǐ* (稻米, glutinous rice) primarily warms the interior and causes one to feel much heat. According to the *Shuowen*, *nuò* (糯, glutinous rice) is simply *dào* (稻); the character is composed of the radical "grain" (*huó*) with "yǎo" (*yǎo*) as the phonetic.

*Ma* (麻): [The character] *mo* (莫) and *xia* (霞) are the fanqie (phonetic analysis). It refers to ramie (*zhu ma*). The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "To *mao* (𢃷) means to process hemp under a roof; therefore it takes the radical *yǎn* (广). The scripture uses *lin* (林) instead of *ma* (麻); this is a vulgar variant form. *Mao* (𢃷) is pronounced *pu mai* (疋賣). The following [character] *ze* (側) and *jia* (加) are the fanqie. *Ma* (麻) is the phonetic component. Furthermore, *mao* (𢃷) and *san* (糝) share the same sound; they mean dregs. They take *mi* (米) as the semantic component and *shui* (𢃷) as the phonetic component.

*Kǔyáng* (羖羊): "Kǔ" is pronounced as *gū* (with the *shàngshēng* tone). The *Erya* states: "The male is called *yú* (羭) and the female is called *kǔ* (羖). According to the *Qieyun*, it refers to the *kǔlù* (羖䍽) sheep; it is also written as *gǔ* (𦍩), which is the same as the character in the main text. The *Shuowen* explains that *gǔ* (股) means the thigh (*bǐ*), and it is not the character for "goat."

"Xiǎo" (齩): Upper radical 5, *jiǎo* (狡) as phonetic. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To bite; it is formed from the radical 'teeth' with 'jiǎo' as the phonetic. The text of the sutra uses the character "yǎo" (咬) with the mouth radical, pronounced *jiāo*. This refers to the chirping of birds and is not used in this sense here.

The character 齧 (niè): the upper radical is 齒 (chǐ); the phonetic component is 契 (qì) with a slight modification; the sound is that of 考 (kǎo). It means to bite or gnaw. A dictionary states it refers to shallow biting. In the canonical text, it is written as 嚙 (niè) with the radical 口 (kǒu), which is not the original form.

*Tuhui* (虎皮褌): *hu* is pronounced with the *gu* and *hun* rhymes; according to the *Yunji*, it refers to a loincloth (*fūn*). The *Zilin* writes it with the radical for cloth as *niàn* (㡓), while the archaic form is *chún* (裩); both are said to be lower garments. *Mujue* (木橛): *jue* is pronounced with the *qi* and *yue* rhymes.

According to the *Yunji*, it is a wooden peg (*yi*). The *Erya* states: "A *zhi* is called a *yi*. Guo's commentary says it is a "peg" (*jue*). It is also stated that those fixed in the ground are called *kui*; the commentary notes these are door-peg posts. It is also written as *jue*. *Kui* is pronounced *zhēng*.
*Chāi* (拆): In the *Qieyun*, the upper character is read as *chǒu* (丑) with the *gé* (格) final; it means "to destroy. Examining its phonetic, it refers to using the hand to strike or press an object.

The scriptural text uses *zhāi* (拆), which is a vulgar variant form. *Xuánpì* (痃癖): The upper character is also written as *xián* (胘); both are pronounced *hújiān* (胡堅). In the *Qieyun*, it refers to abdominal knots (*dùxuán*). The lower character is pronounced *fāngbì* (芳辟). According to the *Yùpiān*, it is an illness of the abdomen. The *Yàozhèng bìngyuán* states: "From indulging in cold and raw foods, fish, meat, and various fruits, sleeping during the day, and eating at night, the stomach becomes cold and the spleen weak, leading to indigestion. Consequently, these form congealed masses (*zhēnkuài*). When they manifest, they strike the heart and cause the vomiting of sour water."

"Yā" (鴉): The phonetic transcription is "wū jiā" (烏加). In the *Yùnyùn* (韻韻), it is stated that "yā" is another name for "wū" (crow). The *Guǎngyá* (廣雅) says: "Those that are pure black and regurgitate food for their parents are called wū; those that are small and do not regurgitate food for their parents are yā. It is composed of the radical "bird" (鳥) with "yà" (亞) as the phonetic. "Shīzhì" (施智) is the pronunciation of the lower part. In the *Yùpiān* (玉篇), it means "wings" (翅羽). It is also written as "qí" (翄); in ancient texts, it is written as "jì" (翨). According to the *Shuōwén* (說文), it means "the primary feather" (翮), composed of the radical "feather" (羽) with "zhī" (支) as the phonetic.

"Lǔtǔ" (滷土) is pronounced "gǔ" (古). The *Erya* states: "Lǔjīn" (鹺矜) means salty and bitter. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as sandy salt soil, written with the radical for water and the phonetic "lǔ" (鹵). Although the text of the sutra uses the character "lǔ" (鹵) alone, this refers to the name of the imperial ceremonial procession (*lǔbù*) and the musical title (*yè míng*), and does not carry the meaning of "salt soil."

"Snake-skin" (shé): The upper character is pronounced with the *zhē* (遮) and *chā* (切) finals; it refers to a venomous insect. The *Erya* says: "The king of snakes is the python (*mǎng*). The lower character is pronounced with the *tāng* (湯) and *wài* (外) finals, or alternatively with the *shū* (舒) and *ruì* (芮) finals. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "It is the sloughed skin shed by a cicada. The *Guangya* says: "The *fùqīng* (蝮蜻) is the *shé* (蛻). The *fù* (蝮) is pronounced with the *fú* (扶) and *liù* (六) finals; the *huáitáo* (蜟) is pronounced with the *yú* (餘) and *liù* (六) finals. This refers to a cicada that has not yet molted.

*Śveti* (the first character pronounced with the *shī* and *rù* tones, the second pronounced as *jiè*, and the final syllable pronounced as *fǎn*; this is a Sanskrit term; its appearance as *niè* in certain scriptures is an error).

*Hūṃ hūṃ* (the first character pronounced with the *hū* and *gǎn* tones): draw forth the sound from the *nābhi-cakra* (navel wheel) or the ocean of vital energy (*prāṇa-samudra*), joining the lips and sounding it continuously.
*Asvā*: "As" is pronounced with the upper tone (shàng) and "svā" with the *sū-hé* (反) and *wú-kě* (反) tones; this is a Sanskrit term whose literal meaning is not sought.
*Sarpaṇa*: the lower character is originally pronounced *gǔ-zhǎn* (反); it means "brackish soil. To preserve the Sanskrit sound, the borrowed pronunciation is *zhú-gǎn* (反).

*Bhagavān* (薄誐鑁): The upper character *bó* is pronounced with the initial *páng* (反) and the final *wángfàn* (反); it is a term from the Sanskrit language. Formerly it was called *Bhagavat*, or *Pogabàn*; ancient translations rendered it as "World-Honored One" (*Shizun*). Now, because it possesses six meanings, it is generally transliterated as *Bhagavān*. These six are: sovereignty (*īśvara*), brilliance (*tejas*), beauty (*yaśas*), fame (*śrī*), auspiciousness (*bhaga*), and nobility (*prabhutva*).
*Rice husk* (稻穀𥢶): The second character, *huì*, is pronounced as in *kǔ huì*. The *Cāngjié piān* states it means "husk" (*fēng*). *Niǎn* (撚):

The first character, *bǐ*, is pronounced as in *nú diǎn*. The *Qièyùn* defines it as "to pinch or squeeze an object tightly with the fingers," composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic component "rán" (*rán shēng*).

*Lo-ja*: The first character is pronounced *lu* (with the retroflex *g* reversal) and the second is pronounced *zi-luo* (with the retroflex *l* reversal); this is a Sanskrit term, translated here as "King" (*rāja*). The text uses the character "yun" (運), which is an error by those who did not understand the Sanskrit sound.

*Cai-fa*: The first character is pronounced *zuo-zai* (with the *cai* reversal); according to the *Shuowen*, it means "temporary. According to the *Qieyun*, it means "merely. The second character, "fa" (發): according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of "gong" (弓), "shu" (殳), and "bo" (癶). "Bo" (癶) is derived from "zhi" (止), where "zhi" is written as 󱷘 (pronounced *bo*). In clerical script (*lie-shu*), 󱷘 was transformed into 癶. "Shu" (殳) is pronounced *shu*; 󱶢 is pronounced *ta*; and "bo" (癶) is pronounced *bo*.

In the second fascicle of the *Vajraśekhara-tattva-mahātantrarāja-sūtra*, the middle fascicle, the character "拼" (pīn) should be read with the phonetic value of "bǎi méng" (百萠). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is defined as "to draw or pull" (拼撣也). It is formed from the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic element "bing" (并); it is also written as "抨" (pēng), and its ancient form is "󱱈䍬" (pēng). The character "撣" (tán) has the pronunciation "dàn dān" (但丹).

*Dian* (上堂練反): In the *Shu Bao Se*, it is written that *dian* refers to inlaying precious materials to decorate objects; it follows the radical for "metal" (金) and uses "tian" (田) as its phonetic component, though it is also pronounced as "tian. It also refers to floral hair ornaments (*huadian*). *E* (噁烏各反): This is a borrowed pronunciation;
it is a word representing the seed-syllable of the True Word (*mantra*) of the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Regarding "Maṇḍala" (the Chinese transcription is pronounced "mo pan fan"; it is also called "Manṭala" or "Manṭaluo"): this term is translated as "the place where the assembly of all sages gathers," which refers to the present-day ritual altar (*tánchǎng*).

"Xīyì" (心臆): Below "xīn" (心), it should be "lì" (力); the character "yì" (臆) is explained as follows: it refers to the chest and also to the breast; it is composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) and the phonetic "yì" (意, abbreviated).
"Chēn" (詵): "zhē" (遮) and "mǎn" (𤚥); the upper part is pronounced "zhēn" (臻) and the lower part "móu hán" (牟含). This is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term whose literal meaning is not sought.

*Jù huài* (沮壞): "Jù" is pronounced with the initial *ts'iu* and the final *mo*; the *Mao Shih Zhuan* states that "jù" means "huài" (to ruin). The *Guang Ya* states it means "moist. The *Shuowen* takes "shui" (water) as the radical and "qie" as the phonetic; "qie" is pronounced *ts'iu-yü*. "Huài" is pronounced *huai-huan*. The *Kaosheng* states it means "to collapse and crumble. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to fail"; it takes "tu" (earth) as the radical and "huai" as the phonetic; "huan" is pronounced *wu-guai*. The archaic form is written as *𡎯*.

The character *chōu* (搊) is pronounced with the initial *zhōu* (󱶛) and the final *shēng* (聲); it means to hook with the fingers. The version in the *sūtra* as *tì* (󱳱) or *zhì* (󱹉) is not the original character. The character below, *zhí* (直) and *zhì* (炙), according to the *Qièyùn*, means to shake (*zhèn*) or to throw (*tóu*); its archaic form is written as *zhì* (擿). According to this, "hooking and throwing" (*chōuzhì*) refers to manipulating the *vajra* with the right hand.

The character 幖 (biāo) is pronounced with the initial *bū* and the final rhyme *yáo*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A banner; it is placed upon the head, composed of the radical 巾 and the phonetic 票. In the sutra text, it is written as 手 (hand), meaning to brandish or raise up; it also refers to the tip of a tree. Below, the character 尺 (chì) is the phonetic. According to the *Qieyun*, it means a banner (*fān*). A dictionary states it means a "standardized insignia" (*jīngbiǎo*). The *Bóyá* writes it as 󲐜, which is identical to the sutra text. It is written here with the radical 心 (heart/mind), which is a slight error.

The character above is pronounced with the *wo-ge* (我各) reverse; the *Zishu* (字書) states it refers to the upper part of the throat. The *Shuowen* (說文) defines it as the palate (*jiǎn*), also written as *è* (腭) or *yù* (齶).

*Shahu*: The upper character is pronounced with the *jiāfǎn* (reversed-cut) rhyme; it belongs to the category of *juàn* (silk). Examining its phonetics, it resembles *juàn* but is lighter. The lower character is pronounced with the *húgǔ* rhyme. The *Yùpiān* states that it is *luóhú* (gauze); it resembles *luó* (gauze) but is lighter.
*Sao* (upper radical *su*, reversed; lower radical *ku*, reversed) refers to the characters in the mantra for which no Chinese gloss is sought.
*Yandang* (upper radical *yu*, *jian*; lower radical *tu*, *lang*) is a Sanskrit term; this is translated as "unguent" (*vilepana*).

The *Vajrabhairava-paramahṛdaya-vidyārāja-sūtra*, one fascicle. Regarding the character for *gǔ* (蠱) at the beginning: the commentary by Gu Zheng on the *Zhouli* states that *gǔ* refers to a pestilential object that harms people; the *Zishu* states it is a parasite within the abdomen; the *Erya* states that *gǔ* is also *zhì* (𧒓); examining its phonetic, it is a *mèi* (魅) spirit; and the *Wenzi Dianshuo* explains that it is composed of the radicals "insect" (虫) and "vessel" (皿).

Regarding the "zǎoguàn" (澡罐): the first character is pronounced with the "zǎo" (澡) radical and the "lǎo" (老) rhyme; the second character is pronounced with the "guān" (官) radical and the "huàn" (喚) rhyme.

According to this, the *zǎoguàn* is a copper vessel (*tóngpǐng*). Regarding the "tiáo" (絛) below it: in the *Qièyùn*, it refers to the lacing of boots (*xuētiáo*); in dictionaries, *tiáo* also means a cord. The *Zílín* writes it as "tāo" (縚).

*Huǎn* (搵): Lower tone, *wēn* (溫) and *kùn* (困) rhyme with it. *Qièyùn* says it means "internal things" or "within water. *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to brace" or "to support. It is formed from the radical *shǒu* (hand) with the phonetic *wūn*. *Càn* (鑱): Upper tone, *shì* (士) and *xián* (銜) rhyme with it. *Qièyùn* says it means "sharp.

The *Fāngyán* says that people of Wu call the iron of a plowshare *càn*. The lower tone is *yuán* (圓) and *jué* (厥). *Qièyùn* says it is a battle-axe (*yuè*). In the *Shàngshū*, it says "The King held the yellow axe in his left hand. The *Zílín* says an axe is a jade axe. The *Shuōwén* says it is formed from the radical *jīn* (metal) with the phonetic *yuè*. The sound of *yuè* is the same as above. The character *yuè* is formed from *guǐ* (󱳙) and *gē* (戈); the sound of *guǐ* is *jué*, and the sound of *gē* is *guò*.

*Fǔshuò* (upper radical *fǔ*, lower *shuò*; phonetic transcription *shuāngjiǎo*): According to the *Qièyùn*, this refers to the battle-axe (*fùyè*). The *Zhōushū* states, "Shennong managed the axes and hatchets. Below, the character is correctly written as *shuò*, with the pronunciation *shuāngjiǎo*. According to the *Tōngsùwén*, a spear eighteen feet long is called a *shuò*.

The "three sweets" (sāntika) are so named because their phonetic transcriptions and rhymes are superior, signifying beauty and sweetness. The *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakra-varti-tantra* states that the three sweets refer to ghee (*sarpis*), milk (*kṣīra*), and curd (*dadhi*); these are precisely what is esteemed in the Western Regions.

The character *jì* (機) is pronounced *jū* (居) in the upper radical and *chǔ* (除旅反) in the lower; the *Fāngyán* states that *zhù* (杼) refers to a weaving implement, while the *Shuowén* defines *zhù* as "that which holds the woof. Both characters are composed of the radical *mù* (木) with *jǐ* (几) and *yǔ* (予) as phonetic components.

The Secret Dharma of the Acala-dūta Dhāraṇī, one fascicle. Regarding the character for "beast" (獸): in the *Qiūjiù* (下舒救) phonetic glosses, it means to guard (*shǒu*). The *Guóyǔ* (國語) states that three beasts make a herd. The *Zìlín* (字林) states that those with two feet are called birds (*qín*), while those with four feet are called beasts (*shòu*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "dog" (犬) and the phonetic "xiù" (嘼), where the sound of "xiù" is pronounced as *chǐujiù* (丑救反). The text of the scripture uses the character "shòu" (狩), which refers to hunting in winter; this is not its usage here.

"Lóngjiū" (龍湫): "Lóng" is pronounced with the *zhòng* (鍾) and *fǎnqiè* (反切) [of *zhōng*]; it means "prince" (*jūn*) according to the *Yùnyùn* (切韻). The *Lìjì* (禮記) states that the tortoise, dragon, qilin, and phoenix are the four auspicious omens (*sìshuì*). The *Yì* (易) says, "Clouds follow the dragon. The *Lúnhéng* (論衡) states, "The dragon is also a domestic animal (*chù*); if it were not a domestic animal, how could it be captured? "Xià" (下) is pronounced with the *yóu* (由) and *fǎnqiè* [of *yǒu*]. It is the name of a water deity. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲), *jiū* (湫) means "to gather" (*jù*); it refers to water that does not flow.

Regarding "犢牸" (*dú zì*): the first character, "犢," is pronounced with the initial *tú* and the final *mù*. The *Erya* states: "Its offspring is a calf. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "People of Qingzhou today call a calf '𤘽' (pronounced *huǒ kǒu*). The second character, "牸," is pronounced with the initial *jí* and the final *lì*. In the *Qieyun*, it is defined as a female ox; it follows the radical for "ox" and takes its phonetic from "字" (*zì*), which also means "to love" or "to nourish."
"Bǐjiǎo" (篦攪) on the upper line: "fǎn kǎo" (反考). It refers to a bamboo comb (*zhúbǐ*). On the lower line, it is read as "gǔ qiǎo" (古巧). The *Qièyùn* states that it means to move with the hand;

it takes the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "jué" (*jué*). "Zhǐbò" (指擘) on the lower line: "bǔ gé" (補革). The *Sāncāng* says that "bò" refers to the thumb. Master Lù’s *Shìwén* says that the thumbs of both hands are collectively called "bò. When the present sutra says "as large as a finger-bò," it means its shape and size are like that of a thumb.

Regarding the term *jiàn* (sword hilt): according to the *Shìmíng*, it means "to restrain" (*jiǎn*), as it serves to prevent and restrain irregularities. The *Guǎngyá* lists more than ten names for swords, such as Lóngquán, Tài'ē, Gānjiāng, Mòyé, Duànsuǐ, Shéyú, and Yǐcháng; these are all alternative designations for the sword. The character below is pronounced *bì* (as in *bìjià*). According to the *Qièyùn*, it refers to the hilt of a knife or sword. The text of the scripture uses the character *bǎ*, which the *Shuōwén* defines as a decoration for horse reins; this is not its usage here. There is also a variant written with the metal radical as *jiàn*, which is entirely incorrect.

*Hsi-hou*: The first character is pronounced with the *hu* rhyme and the *mài* final; the second character is pronounced with the *hu* rhyme and the *kòu* final. Regarding the sound of *hsi-hou*, it means "vague" or "indistinct. As the *Shijing* says: "I see this *hsi-hou* [encounter].

*Pǔbiàn Zhìzàng Bānrěbōluómìduō Xīnjīng* (The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom, the Treasury of Universal Knowledge). One fascicle. *Língjiù*: The second character is pronounced with the *jí* rhyme and the *xiù* final. According to this, *Língjiù* is the name of a mountain in the Western Regions; some call it *Jiùfēng* (Vulture Peak) and others *Jiùtái* (Vulture Terrace), as has already been explained above.

The character *zong* (總) in the first syllable is pronounced with the *qie* (反切) *zuǒ kǒng*; it means "to gather," "all," "entirely," or "universally. The *Zishu* (字書) states that *zong* means "to assemble the multitude. The character *chi* (持) in the second syllable is pronounced with the *qie* *zhí zhī*; it means "to hold" or "to grasp. According to the Sanskrit term *dhāraṇī*, this is translated here as "total retention" (*zongchi*). This refers to the retention of texts, meanings, mantras, and patience.
