Regarding the character "pù" (瀑) in "pùliú" (瀑流): it is pronounced with the initial *pó* according to the *Qièyùn*. It means torrential rain; the *Cāngjié jiěgǔ* states it refers to water surging upward. The *Shuōwén* defines it as being composed of the radical "water" (氵) and the phonetic "bào" (暴). Regarding the character "xià" (下) in "xiàliú" (下流): the *Shuōwén* defines it as being composed of the radical "water" (氵) and the phonetic "lù" (㐬), which is pronounced *tā hū* (他忽反). "Lù" (㐬) is written in an inverted manner like the character "yōu" (㜽); "yōu" (㜽) is an archaic form of the character "zǐ" (子).

*Song* (竦): The first character is pronounced *xi* with the *gong* rhyme. The *Erya* states: "To *song* means to be afraid. The *Qieyun* states: "It means reverence. Gu Yewang says: "It means to rise up; it also means to leap. The *Guoyu* states: "To *song* the good and suppress the evil. The second character is also written as *shu* (豎), which is the same; it is pronounced *zhu* (with the *yu* sound being *yi-zhu*). The *Yupian* states: "It means to stand upright; it also refers to a servant who has not yet undergone the capping ceremony (*guan*)."

*Feibang* (誹謗) [the first character pronounced with the upper radical *fei* and the lower *pu* with the *lang* rhyme; the *Dadai Li* states: "The pillars for slander and the drums for remonstrance were established"]. Ying Shao’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states: "The wooden boards at the side of bridges are for recording errors and faults in governance. Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuozhuan* states: "Slander means to curse others with words. According to the *Shuowen*, these two characters explain each other; they follow the radical for speech (*yan*) and are both form-sound characters (*xing-sheng*).

*Quái kuài*: The upper character *kuǐ* (魁) is pronounced with the *kǔ* rhyme-group (*guī*). Kong’s commentary on the *Shūjìng* states that it means "leader" (*shuài*); the *Guǎngyá* says it means "master" (*zhǔ*); Zheng’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says it means "head" (*shǒu*); and the *Shījì* says it means "mighty" (*zhuàng dà*). It is composed of the radical *dǒu* (斗) and the phonetic *guǐ* (鬼). The lower character *kuài* (膾) is pronounced with the *wài* rhyme-group. The *Guǎngyá* says it means "to mince" (*gē*). According to this, *quái kuài* refers to the leaders who slaughter and execute the violent and wicked; it is composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and the phonetic *huì* (會).

"Lóng-xià" (聾瞎): "Lóng" (聾) is pronounced with the initial *l-*, rhyming with *dōng* (東), according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*. It means "the ears do not communicate," composed of the radical "ear" (*ér*) and the phonetic "long" (*lóng*). In the canonical text it is written as "lí" (𠯓), which does not form a valid character. "Xià" (瞎) is pronounced with the final *-p-*, rhyming with *hū* (呼). A dictionary states it means "the eyes do not see objects. It is also said to mean "one eye lacks a pupil. It is composed of the radical "eye" (*mù*) and the phonetic "hài" (害) in abbreviated form. (Note: The term "liǎo" [了] in the original text appears to be a scribal error for "lí" [𠯓], a variant form of "lóng" [聾].)

*Wǔ* (upper radical): pronounced *yú* (formed by the *wǔ* and *cìe* [consonants]). It means the neck cannot extend. According to the *Yùpiān*, it refers to a *huǐ* (a type of snake). Sūnxiāngzi says that the Duke of Zhou had a hunched back (*pèi wǔ*). The lower character is also written as *dàn* or *à*; neither is the original form. The pronunciation is *wǔ yǎ*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that it refers to being unable to speak. The *Shuōwén* explains it as composed of the *nà* (sickness) radical with *yà* as the phonetic component; the *nà* radical is pronounced *nǚ è*.

Regarding the characters for *móu* (mosquito) and *méng* (gadfly): the *Wénzìtǒng* states that *móu* refers to a flying insect that bites humans. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *wén*, because it emerges at dusk (*hūn*); thus it is composed of the radical *guǔn* (phonetic value *kūn*) with the abbreviated form of *hūn* as its phonetic. The character in the canonical text uses *wén*; this is a vulgar variant. Regarding *méng*, the *Shēnglèi* states that it is a gadfly larger than a common fly. The *Shuōwén* also defines it as a flying insect that bites humans, composed of the radical *guǔn* with *wáng* as its phonetic. The character in the canonical text written as *jiào* is incorrect.

The character for *fei* (蛾) is pronounced with the upper radical *fu* (甫) and the non-cutting rhyme *fei* (非); it means "to fly. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is a pictographic character representing the form of a bird flying upward. In the original text of the sutra, there is also the character *fei* (蜚), pronounced *fei* (費), meaning a stinking insect; its lower part is pronounced *wu-he* (五何). The *Daidai Li* states that among insects that eat mulberry leaves, some possess silk and transform their forms to fly as moths (*ei*). According to the *Shuowen*, this character is formed from the radical "insect" (*chong*) and the phonetic component "I" (*wo*).

*Lūyǐ* (螻蟻): the first character is pronounced *lè* (with the rhyme *hòu*) and is also written as *yǐ*; the second character is pronounced *yǐ* (with the rhymes *qí* and *kǎi*). The *Xiaoya* states: "The larger ones are *bífú*, which are also large ants; the smaller ones are ant-larvae. Both the *Shuowen* and the *Erya* write it with the radical *qǐ* as *yǐ*. In the Classics, it is written as *yì* according to its meaning, while *yǐ* is a vulgar character. Nowadays, the common people generally call them *lūyǐ*. One tradition says that the larger are called *lū* and the smaller are called *yǐzǐ* (ant-larvae).

*Lín* (上力尋反; *lìxún*): According to the *Qièyùn*, this refers to the disease of urinary obstruction. Regarding its medicinal indications and etiology, there are five types of *lín*: cold, exhaustion, qi, blood, and food. The *Yùpiān* states that *lín* means difficulty urinating; it is composed of the radical *zhé* (sickness) and the phonetic *lín*. In the canonical texts, it is written with the water radical as *lín* (淋), meaning to drench with water, but this is not the usage here. *Lì* (下力至反; *lìzhì*): According to the *Qièyùn*, this refers to the disease of diarrhea. Gu Yewang says it is dysentery. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical *zhé* (sickness) and the phonetic *chà*; the radical *zhé* is pronounced *nǚ'ài* (*nuò*).

Regarding the character for *hizhì* (痔): "zhí" is pronounced with the *liǎn* (上直里反) tone. The *Yùpiān* states it is a disease of the posterior parts; the *Jìxùn* states it is a disease of the lower body; and the *Shuōwén* states it is a disease of the rear. It is composed of the radical *nà* (疒, pronounced *nǚ è*) and the phonetic element *zhì* (峙, abbreviated). The radical *nà* is pronounced *nǚ è*.

The character for "lòu" (瘻) is pronounced with the *lu* and *hóu* rhymes; it refers to a chronic sore or ulcer. The *Jíxùn* states that it is a sore that does not heal after a long time. The lower radical is pronounced *chǔliáng*. The *Lǐjì* says, "If one has a sore on the head, one should wash [the hair]. In the *Shuōwén*, both characters are composed of the "sickness" radical (*zhé*) and the phonetic component *lóu*; *cāng* serves as the phonetic indicator. The radical *zhé* is pronounced *nǚ'ài*.

*Bì* (髀): The upper part of the thigh. In ancient texts it is also written as *pǐ* (䠋). According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the outer part of the thigh. It is also pronounced *fāng'ěr* (方爾); according to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic element "bēi" (卑). In the scriptural text, it is written with the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) as *yì* (䏶), which is a vulgar character. Below [the character] is *xíngdìng* (刑定). The *Yupian* states that it is the large bone at the front of the calf. The *Shuowen* states it is the shinbone (*zhàng*). *Zhàng* (胻) is pronounced *xìng* (幸); *zhì* (䠊) is pronounced *féi* (肥).

*Luèli* (瘰癧): The first character is pronounced with the initial *láng* and the final *guǒ*. The *Zìshū* states it is a disease of knotted sinews (*jīnjié*). Both characters are written with the radical *nà* (疒).

The second character is formed with *lì* (歷) as the phonetic component, with the radical omitted. *Jièxiǎn* (疥癬): The first character is pronounced with the initial *jiē* and the final *ài*. The *Zhōulǐ* states that in the summer there is the disease of nourishing scabies (*yǎngjièzhījí*). The *Jixùn* states it is a wind-sore (*fēngchuāng*). The *Wénzìjílüè* writes it with the radical *chóng* (虫) as *jiè*. The *Shuowén* states it means "to scratch" (*sāo*). It is formed with *jiè* (介) as the phonetic component. The second character is pronounced with the initial *xiān* and the final *jiǎn*. The *Jixùn* states *xiǎn* means "to move" (*xǐ*), referring to its creeping and shifting nature. The *Shuowén* states it is a dry sore (*qiányáng*). It is formed with *xiān* (鮮) as the phonetic component. *Sāo*: Pronounced *sǎo* (with the tone of *dāo*). *Ài*: Pronounced *yīng* (with the tone of *jiè*). *Yáng*: Pronounced *yáng*.

*Bào* (薄教反; *báo*)—according to the *Shuowen*, this character is written with the radical 皮 (*pi*) and means a pustule or a sore that develops on the face; it is also written as 皰, and in the vernacular as 䩅. *Lài* (下來大反; *lài*)—the *Guangya* states it means "wound"; the *Cangjie pian* states it means "pain. The *Shuowen* correctly writes it as 癘, meaning a malignant disease; it is composed of the radical 疒 (*nuǎi*) and the phonetic component 厲 (*lì*; *lái dà fǎn*), where 疒 has the pronunciation *nǚ è fǎn*.

*Udumbara* (the "tu-han" in the original is a phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit; the old translation was *youtan*, while the correct form is *wutanbapuo*). This refers to the auspicious, rare, and wondrous celestial flower. This flower does not exist in the world except when a Tathāgata descends to be born and a Golden Wheel-turning King appears; through the power of their great merit and virtue, this flower is caused to manifest.

The character *zhì* (制) is pronounced with the initial *dǐng* (丁) and the final *-fǎn* (反). Some say it is *caitya*, while others say it was formerly called *zhītí* (支提); these are all corruptions of the Sanskrit sound, though in reality they refer to the same thing. The old *Yīnyì* (音義) translates it as "temple" (*miào*), referring to terms such as "monastery" (*sì*) and "stupa-temple" (*támìāo*).

*Niē* (top radical *ni*, with the phonetic *nú dī*): According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "niē" means to smear; it refers to the mixing of soil and water. *Ní* is its pronunciation. The text of the sutra uses "ní," which is a name for water. The *Mao Shi Shu* states that "Ni" was originally a small town in Zhongwei, not a term used in the classics. The *Yunji* defines it as pressing with the hand; it also means to press down (*nà*). It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "niè" (abbreviated).

"Inserting an arrow" (chā jiàn): "chā" is a *bǔqiè* (rhyme-gloss) for "chù"; it means to enter. It is also written as "chā," but neither is according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*. According to the *Shuowen*, it is formed with the radical "hand" (shǒu) and the phonetic "zhā" (zhā). The pronunciation of "zhā" is the same as above; it refers to thrusting a spearhead (gān) into something. The character below is pronounced "jiān" (xian4); it is a vulgar form. The correct form is "zhā" (zhā), which is originally the name of a bamboo species. It resembles reeds and grows in clusters; it can be used for the shafts of arrows, and thus the arrow itself is named after it. It is formed with the radical "bamboo" (zhú) and the phonetic "qián. The pronunciation of "gǎo" (the shaft) is "gān-dàn" (gan4 dan4).

In the middle fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-vistara-pariṣad-susthitaguhyadhāraṇī-sūtra*, the section on "Exorcism" (*yàn-dǎo*): The upper character, 厭 (*yàn*), is pronounced with the "yan" rhyme; it means to "attach" or "perform. According to the *Zìshū*, it refers to a *mèi* (demon). The lower character, 禱 (*dǎo*), is pronounced with the "lǎo" rhyme. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "To seek blessings is called *dǎo*; this refers to praying to Heaven, Earth, and the Altars of Soil and Grain. Bao Xian’s commentary on the *Lunyu* states: "It refers to entreating the spirits and deities. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "To report matters and seek blessings; it follows the radical for 'divinity' (*shì*) and takes the abbreviated form of 'longevity' (*shòu*) as its phonetic component. The pronunciation of 燾 (*tào*) is like that of "peach" (*táo*).

To roll [the thread] is called *shànguǎn* (上貫) in the ancient ritual terminology; in the vernacular dialect it is called *xù* (續), meaning "to continue. Gu Yewang states that it refers to being joined together in succession. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) with the phonetic element "rán" (*rán*). In the *Qieyun*, it is read as *shìzhēng* (市征). The *Yunji* (韻集) states it means "completion" (*bì*) or "accomplishment" (*jiù*). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "wǔ" (*wù*) with the phonetic element "dīng" (*dīng*).

The characters for *fú* (輻) and *wǎng* (輞) above are read as *liù fǎn* (six tones). In character dictionaries, *fú* refers to the spokes of a wheel; the *Dàodé jīng* (Classic of the Way and Its Power) states: "Thirty spokes converge upon a single hub, yet it is the absence of the hub that performs its function. In the following section, *wǎng* is transcribed with two reversed initial consonants (*liǎng fǎn*). According to the *Yùn* (Rhymes), it refers to the rim of a wheel. In the *Shuōwén*, both characters are composed of the radical "car" (*chē*) with "fú" and "wǎng" (in abbreviated form) as their phonetic components.

*Jià* (upper character: *máo*; rhyme: *wǔ biāo fǎn*). According to the *Qièyùn*, it refers to field seedlings; the *Shēng* states they have not yet flowered. The *Shuowén* says: "From *cǎo* (grass) above *tián* (field). The lower character is read as *gǔ yà fǎn*. The *Shī* says: "Causing the people to *jià* (plant) and *sè* (harvest). The *Shū* says: "Planting is called *jià*; gathering is called *sè*. The *Shuowén* [explains] it as being from *huò* (grain) with *jià* (marry) abbreviated as the phonetic.

Volume 3, Part 2. *The Great Jewel Extensive Pavilion Well-Abiding Secret Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, Volume 2. **Dān (耽嗜)**: Also written as *dàn* (妉) with the same pronunciation; according to the *Erya*, it means "excessive pleasure. According to the *Qieyun*, it means "excessive indulgence. The lower radical is pronounced *chánglì* (常利). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the character *shì* (嗜) also has the variant *tán* (𩝙), which is formed with the "ear" radical (*ěr*). The term *shèngshè* (聖攝) is transcribed as *āryasaṃgraha*. The term *shèngyǎn* (聖演) is transcribed as *āryadeśanā*. The term *shèngshuō* (聖說) is transcribed as *āryabhāṣita*. The term *shèngjiè* (聖戒) is transcribed as *āryaśīla*. The term *shèngjìn* (聖進) is transcribed as *āryavīrya*. The term *shèngniàn* (聖念) is transcribed as *āryasmṛti*. The term *shèngding* (聖定) is transcribed as *āryasamādhi*. The term *shènghuì* (聖慧) is transcribed as *āryaprajñā*. The term *shèngde* (聖得) is transcribed as *āryalābha*. The term *shèngshì* (聖事) is transcribed as *āryakārya*. The term *shèngyì* (聖意) is transcribed as *āryābhiprāya*. The term *shèngli* (聖力) is transcribed as *āryabala*. The term *shèngdé* (聖德) is transcribed as *āryaguṇa*. The term *shèngmèng* (聖命) is transcribed as *āryājñā*. The term *shèngyǔ* (聖語) is transcribed as *āryavāk*. The term *shèngzǔ* (聖祖) is transcribed as *āryapitāmaha*. The term *shèngfù* (聖父) is transcribed as *āryapitṛ*. The term *shèngmǔ* (聖母) is transcribed as *āryamātṛ*. The term *sh

Regarding "huán" (rings and bracelets): it is also written as "huán" (pronounced with the *guān* rhyme). Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that it means "revolving" (*xuán*) or "governing" (*tǒng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "When the thickness of the metal (*ròu*) and the diameter of the hole (*hǎo*) are equal, it is called a *huán*. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* explains: "The 'flesh' (*ròu*) refers to the edge; the 'hole' (*hǎo*) refers to the aperture. This means the edge and the aperture are proportionally equal. The lower radical is "chuān" (pronounced with the *liàn* rhyme). The *Donggong Jiushi* states: "A *chuàn* is an ornament for the arm. According to the *Jin gu zheng zi*, this character follows the "metal" radical and uses "chuān" as its phonetic component.

*Xuān* (諠): The common form is written as *xuān* (喧), while the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *huān* (讙). All three forms share the same pronunciation, with the rhyme *huán* (況袁反). In the *Yunying*, it refers to the sound of clamorous speech; in character dictionaries, *xuān* is also synonymous with *huān*. *Nào* (下): Pronounced *nújiào* (奴教反). According to the *Qieyun*, it means "not quiet. Examining its phonetic component, it signifies a vulgar clamor; it is composed of the radical "person" (*ren*) inside a marketplace (*shi*). It is also written as *nào* (鬧), while the common form *nà* (𡗚) is a simplified version.

*Pú* (蒲北反) and *fù* (又作仆同) mean to fall prostrate on the ground; the *Erya* states: "To stumble and fall. Guo's commentary says: "To trip, falter, and collapse. According to the *Qieyun*, *pú* means to die or to fall forward; its pronunciation is *zhù lì* (竹利反), which is identical in both sound and meaning to *zhì* (躓).

The character 󱳪 (zhā) is pronounced with the initial *chí* and the final *gē* (rev). The *Kǎo Shēng* states that 󱳪 also means "to open. Lexicons define it as "to tear. The correct orthography for both ancient and modern times is 捇 (*chì*), which takes the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 赤 (chì); it is also written as 𣂔. The text of the scripture uses 搩, which is incorrect. If one follows the form with the radical 石 (stone), it is 磔 (*zhā*, pronounced *zhāng gē*), which also means "to open."

*The Dhāraṇī for Adorning the Bodhimanda*, one fascicle. Vārāṇasī (the "n" sound of Vārāṇasī is pronounced *ning* with the *gui* tone; it is the name of a country in the Sanskrit language, also called Vārāṇasī; ancient scriptures refer to it as the kingdom of Pārāyana).

*Yojana* (the initial *yǎn* pronounced with the *zhū* rhyme, followed by the sound *shàn*; it is a Sanskrit term, sometimes called *yu shé nà*, and formerly translated as *yóu xún*, both of which are corruptions and abbreviations). The correct term is *yojana*, which refers to the distance a royal army could travel in one day during the era of the ancient sage-kings. In various sūtras and śāstras, the measurements of *li* (Chinese miles) are stated differently: some say forty *li*, some thirty *li*, and others only sixteen *li*. This is likely because the pace of the sage-kings' travels varied—whether they were slow or swift—or because different units such as the *cubit* (*zhǒu*) or ancient *chǐ* (inches) were employed; despite these differences in perspective, it ultimately refers to the daily marching distance of a king’s army. According to the *Xiyùjì* (Records of the Western Regions), thirty *li* is established as the standard. This was determined after Master Xuánzàng personally investigated distances and compiled this travelogue, which he presented to Emperor Tàizōng; his account is therefore unerring.

Regarding the character for *bhūrja* (樺皮), the *Hùmà Fǎn Wénzì Jílüè* states that it is the name of a tree found on mountains; its wood is suitable for making candles because it contains red and white resinous veins. In the five regions of India, there was originally no paper or silk; instead, they used strips of *pātra* (貝多) leaves, *tāla* (多羅) leaves, or fine white *bhūrja* bark to write upon Buddhist scriptures (*vaṃśa*), much like the ancient Chinese use of bamboo slips. The character is derived from the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "huā" (華).

The character *táng* (樘) in "wheel-pole" (*lún-táng*) is pronounced with the *zé* and *gēng* finals; dictionaries state that *táng* means a pillar, and it is also written as *zhàng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* also says it is a pillar, formed from the radical "wood" (*mù*) and the phonetic "hall" (*táng*). The wheel-pole is precisely the pillar or shaft on top of a stupa that supports the dew-dish (*lùpán*). The *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* states: "Eight types of people are permitted to erect stupas: from the Tathāgata down to the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). From the eight dew-dishes upward, these are all Buddha-stupas; from the Wheel-Turning King downward, only one dew-dish is installed. One must not prostrate before those seen below the level of the Wheel-Turning King, as they are not holy stupas."

"Jūn" (均) in "Jūntíng" (均亭): the upper character is pronounced *jūn* (反切: 居勻反), meaning "even" or "level" according to the dictionaries; the lower character is pronounced *dīng* (反切: 特丁反). The phonetic component of "tíng" (亭) is also "level. Today, a "tíngzǐ" (亭子, pavilion) takes its name because it is level and even on all four sides. The character "jūn" (均) is composed of "tǔ" (土, earth) as the semantic radical and "yún" (勻, even) as the phonetic. The character "tíng" (亭) is composed of "gāo" (高, high) and the abbreviated form of "dīng" (丁) as the phonetic. The character "jīng" (經, warp-thread/measuring line) is written with "jīn" (金, metal) and refers to thirty *jīn* (斤) in weight. The character "tíng" (亭) is written with "rén" (人, person) and refers to "stopping" (*tíng*) or "resting. These are not the same as the "jūntíng" (均亭) used for the four corners of a painting altar.

*The Chapter on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into the Alphabet*, one fascicle. This is the *Siddham* (Sanskrit script) version; it cannot be translated or explained [as it stands]. *The Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-spoken Samantabhadra-dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle. Regarding the character *cái* (纔): when heard above, it is pronounced as *zài* (在), with the rhyme of *cái* (裁). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "briefly" or "momentarily. The *Dōngguān Hàn jì* says it means "scarcely" or "not long. The pronunciation of *chán* (毚) is *shì xián* (士咸).

*Mōmèn* (摩捫): The first character, *mó*, is pronounced with the initial *mo* and the final rhyme *pó* (according to the *Yùpiān*, it means to rub or stroke with the hand; the character *suō* [in *sō*] is pronounced with the initial *sō* and the final rhyme *kā*). The second character, *mǎng*, is pronounced with the initial *mó*. According to the *Shuōwén*, *mèn* means to caress or hold; the *Shēnglèi* states that *mèn* is also synonymous with *mō* (to feel or grope). Both characters are radical 64 (hand) and have *má* and *mén* as their phonetic components.

The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī for Eliminating All Diseases, Spoken by the Buddha. One fascicle. Regarding *tanyin* (痰癊): the upper character, *tan*, is pronounced with the level tone of *dàn* (淡). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states it refers to a disease of water in the diaphragm (*gé*). The *Shuowén* (說文) explains it as composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *yán* (炎). The lower character, *yìn* (癊), is pronounced with the departing tone of *yì* (邑). The *Zílín* (字林) writes this as *dǐng* (𤷜), stating it is a disease of thin water in the heart. The *Yùnquán* (韻詮) states that *yìn* is also *tán*; these two characters are mutually explained. It is composed of the radical *nà* and the phonetic *yīn* (陰). The version of the scripture that uses the grass radical (*cǎo*) to form *yìn* (蔭) is incorrect.
Regarding "hemorrhoids" (zhìbìng): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a disease of the posterior [body]. This was already explained in the middle of the first fascicle of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*.

Regarding "malaria" (sòu): the *Kao Sheng* states it is a disease where qi strikes the throat; the *Cangjie Pian* states it is a disease of alternating cold and heat. The *Wenzi Dian* explains that it takes the radical "sickness" (疒) and the phonetic "sou" (欶), with the pronunciation of "sou" being as above. The scriptural text uses the character "sòu" (嗽) with the mouth radical, which is incorrect. Below, "shāi" (痁): according to the *Qieyun*, it is a chronic fever. The character dictionary states it takes the radical "sickness" (疒) and the phonetic "nüe" (虐). The scriptural text uses the single character "nüe" (虐), which means tyranny, severity, or cruelty, and does not carry the meaning of chronic fever. The pronunciation of "he" (苛) is hé; the pronunciation of "ku" (酷) is kū; the pronunciation of "shāi" (痁) is shīliánfǎn.

The Liturgical Text for the Veneration and Repentance of the Thirty-five Buddhas, one fascicle. The Dhāraṇī Sūtra Capable of Eliminating All Eye Diseases, one fascicle. Regarding the character *yìmó* (翳膜): In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it states that *yì* (翳) refers to a film over the eye; it is formed from the radical "eye" (*mù*) with *ēi* (殹) as the phonetic component. The text of this sūtra uses the character *yì* (翳) with the "feather" (*yǔ*) radical, which is not the same as the word for eye disease. Regarding the character *mó* (膜): The dictionary *Zishu* defines it as lack of clarity in vision. The *Shiming* explains it as a "curtain" (*mù*), like a screen or partition. The *Wenziji lüe* (Abridged Collection of Characters) forms it with the "eye" radical as *mí* (瞙). The text of this sūtra uses the character *mó* (膜) with the "moon" (*yuè*) radical, referring to the fascia between the skin and the flesh.

Regarding "eye-vein" (mòu): the *Shìmíng* explains the name as "eye-limit," meaning that there is a limit to seeing objects; it is composed of the radical "eye" (目) and the phonetic "limit" (限). Below, "mò" (莫獲反) refers to blood vessels. The *Shìmíng* states that "vein" (mài) means "curtain" (mù), referring to how they form a network curtain over the body. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) and the phonetic "piě" (派省); the form used in the scriptures as "mài" is a vulgar character.

*The Maṇḍala Sūtra of the Eight Great Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle, including the *Praise of the Maṇḍala*. "Maṇḍala" (the upper character pronounced guàn) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; it is also called *maṇḍalaka* or *maṇḍara*, all of which refer to the same thing. In Chinese, it is translated as "the assembly of the many sages," which refers to the present ritual altar (*maṇḍala*).

The term *típó* (拓鉢): the upper character is pronounced with the *tuó* rhyme and the *gè* reversed; it refers to holding an object in the hand. The lower character is pronounced with the *běi* and *mò* rhymes; in lexicographical works, it is sometimes written as *jū*. It is synonymous with an *yú* vessel (a basin). The *Biography of Tancheng* states that when Tancheng burned incense and recited incantations over his bowl, blue lotus flowers appeared in an instant. The *Record of the Western Regions* states that the Buddha’s bowl is located in the kingdom of Gandhāva.

The character *míng* (冥) is pronounced either *mò jīng fǎn* or *mò dìng fǎn*. In the *Erya*, it means "darkness"; in the *Qieyun*, it means "gloom" or "night. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that since the moon begins to darken from the sixteenth day, the character is composed of "six" (*liù*) and "day" (*rì*), with the phonetic component *mìng* (pronounced *mò xiān fǎn*). It also takes the form of a covering. The character *jīng* (經), when written with the water radical as *míng* (溟), denotes the appearance of a fine drizzle or refers to the "Ming Sea," but it does not mean "darkness. Furthermore, there is a variant written with the roof radical and the "all" (*jù*) radical as *míng* (𡨋), which is not the original character. The roof radical (*mián*) is pronounced *mò xiān fǎn*.

*The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Parṇaśavarī Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle. Regarding "zhù" (祝): In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written as "chóu" (詶) and is also "zhù" (詛). Today it is written as "zhòu" (咒), which is a vulgar character. The lower radical is "zè" (側), with the phonetic "jù" (據); in ancient texts it was written as "zhì" (󱶔). The *Shiming* states: "It belongs to the category of 'zhù' (祝), because good or evil words are attached (*shǔ*) to one another. "Zhù" (詛) means to obstruct; it refers to causing a person to be constrained by their speech. In the scriptural text, the character is written with the radical "mouth" (口) as "jǔ" (咀), pronounced "cáiyǔ" (才與); this means "to chew," and is not the intended meaning of the scripture.

The *yuè* (battle-axe): the upper part is round (*jué fǎn*) and the lower part is square (*jǔ fǎn*). The *Zìlín* states that the *yuè* is a jade axe. The *Shūjìng Mùshì* says, "The King held a yellow *yuè* in his left hand. Kǒng’s *Chuān* explains: "The *yuè* is an axe adorned with yellow; holding the *yuè* in the left hand signifies having no intent to execute. According to the *Shuowén*, it is composed of the radical 金 (*jīn*) and the phonetic 戉 (*yùè*), with the pronunciation of 戉 being the same as above. It is also composed of the radical 戈 (*guō*) and the phonetic 󱳙 (*jué*), with the pronunciation of 󱳙 being *jué*.

*Tà* (the radical *tà*, pronounced with the initial *tú* and the final *hé* according to the *Qièyùn*; it means to kick). Gu Yewang says it means to tread upon. The *Zílín* says it means to step on. The scriptural text uses *tà* written with the radical *tà* (from *tà*), which is also interchangeable; its pronunciation is the same as above. It takes the radical *wǔ* (water), not *shuǐ* (water); *wǔ* is an archaic variant character.

The character above is *juān* (pronounced with the initial *q* and final *-an*, rhyming with *zǐquán*); it means to bore or to carve. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means to split wood. It is also said that *zhuó* (琢) means to chisel metal or stone. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (金, metal) and the phonetic *juàn* (雋). The sound of *juàn* is *cúyuǎn*. [Note: Some write it with the radical *zhuī* (隹, bird), but this is not the original character. The character *gōng* (弓, bow) contains the element *wò* (臥, lying down). [End of entry].

"Powdered" (fěn): [the character] is pronounced as *fāng* (with the rhyme *wěn*) and refers to powdered rice. The *Bowu zhi* states that Zhou burned lead to produce *húfěn* (calamine powder). "To press" (xià): [the character] is pronounced as *nú* (with the rhyme *jié*). According to the *Zishu*, it means to press down with the hand; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "niè" (*niè*), the pronunciation of which is the same as above.

The *Vaiśravaṇa-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle. "Vaiśravaṇa" is a Sanskrit term; it is also called Vaiśrāvaṇa or Vaiśramaṇa. This is translated as "Universal Renown" (*Pǔwén*) or "Much-Hearing" (*Duōwén*), because this king is most wealthy, his treasures appear spontaneously, and many people have heard of him. He presides over yakṣas and rākṣasas. "Yakṣa" is translated as "Injurer," meaning they are able to harm people.
* Cintāmaṇi (alternatively transcribed as *Cintāmaṇi*); both are Sanskrit terms differing only in prosodic weight. This is translated as "Wish-fulfilling Jewel" (*yìrúizhū*).

The Ritual Method for the Mantra of Hārītī: One fascicle. *Hārītī* is a Sanskrit term; alternatively, it is pronounced as *Hālītī*, with the first character borrowed from the sound of *kě* (with the tone mark) and the second from *dǐngyǐ*. This is translated as "Joy" (*huānxǐ*), or alternatively as "Heavenly Mother" (*tiānmǔ*).

*Duàn* (斷): In the *Shuǎngyùn*, it is read with the initial *tú* and the final *guǎn*. It means "to sever. According to the *Shuowén*, it means "to cut. It is a compound character formed from *jīn* (a hatchet) and *jǐ* (the ancient form of *jué*). The character *jì* (繼, to continue) also contains this radical. In the canonical text, it is written as *duàn*; the abbreviated form is sometimes used, which is the common vulgar usage. *Xù* (續): Read with the initials *xú* and *lǚ*. It means "to draw out a thread. In the *Qieyun*, it means "precedent" or "lineage. According to the *Zìshū*, it means "to continue. It also refers to the "thread of a cocoon. It is formed from the radical *mì* (silk thread) and the phonetic *zhù* (abbreviated).

*Gān cuì* (甘脃): the second character is pronounced *xuàn suì* (下詮歲反). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means "fragile" (*cuìruò*); according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "pliant" (*nuǎn*); according to the *Shuōwén*, it means "flesh that is soft and easily broken. It is composed of the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) and the phonetic element "abbreviated *jué*" (*jiě shěng*). The archaic form is written as *shē* (膬), which is identical in meaning. The text here uses *huī* (危) instead of *cuì* (脆), which is incorrect.

*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra for Delivering the Hungry Ghosts with Flaming Mouths*, one fascicle. **Zhēn (針):** The upper radical is *zhí* (職) with the phonetic *lín* (林). It is also written as *zhēn* (鍼). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A needle for sewing clothes. The *Guǎnzǐ* says: "A woman is only fully considered a woman after she possesses one needle, one blade, and one awl. The lower part is read as *róng* (容). The *Qieyun* states: "The edge of a sword; it also means sharp. It is composed of the radical *jīn* (金) and the phonetic *fēng* (夆).

*Kùjiè* (枯䩌): The upper character, read as *kǔgū* (苦姑) according to the *Qièyùn*, means decayed; it takes the radical *běn* (本) and the phonetic *gǔ* (古). The lower character, read as *jíxiāo* (即消), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states means the facial skin has become parched black; it is a compound character formed from the semantic element *miàn* (面) and the phonetic *jiāo* (焦). In the scriptural text, it is written as *jué* (燋) with the *huǒ* (火) radical, which refers to the scorching of an object by fire.

The Heart Recitation Method of the Lotus Family of the *Vajraśekhara*, one fascicle. Regarding the character *hù* (戶): according to the sub-entry for *chū* (樞), Zhu Changzhu’s commentary on the *Erya* states that it refers to the pivot of a door or gate. Han Kangbo states that the pivot is the mechanism that governs movement. The *Guangya* says it is the "root" (*ben*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as being composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic "qū" (區); the pronunciation of *qū* is *qi jū* (豈俱反), meaning a boundary or enclosure (*yù*).

*Zuòqiè* (左笡): *qiè* is pronounced with the *jià* and *yè* finals. The *Pīcāng* states it means "to thrust upward against. It is composed of the radical "bamboo" (*zhú*) and the phonetic "qiè" (*qiè*). *Chèkāi* (掣開): *chè* is pronounced with the *chāng* and *shì* finals.

The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to pull and release. The *Erya* says, "to drag and pull. Guo’s commentary states this refers to "dragging along the ground. *Yè* is pronounced with the *yú* and *shì* finals; *tā* is pronounced with the *tā* final. These two characters are sometimes colloquially pronounced with the entering tone.
*Chōu*: Pronounced *chòu* (with the *zōu* rhyme). It refers to the sound produced by hooking with the fingers. The reading in the canonical text as *zhǎo* is a vulgar character and incorrect.
*Hàn*: Pronounced *hàn* (with the *gǎn* rhyme). According to the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to shake. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to sway," derived from the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "gǎn."

*The Ritual for the Recitation of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes according to the Vajraśekhara Yoga*, one fascicle. "Chen" (沈): To sink. According to the *Zhilin* (直林) and the *Qieyun* (切韻), it means to submerge. In the *Zishu* (字書), it is classified as a voiced consonant (*duó*) and also means "below. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字) states that it is formed from the radical "water" (水) and the phonetic "yin" (冘). The sound of "yin" is *yín*. The text of this scripture uses "chén" (沉), which is not correct; the standard form is "nì" (溺). The archaic form is "niè" (㲻), which is the same. According to the *Shuowen*, "nì" (溺) also means to submerge; it is formed from the radical "person" (人) and the element "submerged in water" (沒在水). *The Ritual for the Recitation of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes according to the Vajraśekhara Yoga*, one fascicle. [End] [Note: The original text contains a commentary on the characters "chén" (沈) and "nì" (溺), explaining their meanings, pronunciations, and etymologies.]
*Chè* (掣): Upper radical *chāng-liè* (昌列反), meaning to pull; also pronounced *chāng-shì* (昌世反), as previously explained. Lower radical *pǔ-bó* (普伯反), meaning to stroke with the hand.

*Chuī-jī* (捶擊): Upper character *zhī-lěi* (之累反); the *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it also means to strike. Lower character *gǔ-lì* (古歷反); according to the *Qièyùn*, it means to beat. The *Shuōwén* explains it as being composed of the hand radical and the phonetic *chèn* (𣪠).

The character *he* (賀) is pronounced with the lower radical *san* (糝), the phonetic being *shèng* (乘) and *gǎn* (感). In the Classics it is written as *sàn* (糝). This is a mantra phrase; one does not seek its literal meaning.

The character *gǔ* (谷) is pronounced with the upper radical *gǔ* (古) and *wū* (屋). In the *Qièyùn*, it means "mountain valley," and also "to nourish. Laozi says, "The valley-spirit does not die; this is the Mysterious Female (*xuánpìn*). It is also pronounced with the lower radical *yù* (欲), the phonetic being *xǔ* (許) and *liǎng* (兩). In the canonical texts, writing it with a single dot as *jiù* or with the radical *bǔ* (卜) as *jiù* are both erroneous transcriptions.

*Biàn* (upper radical *shēn*, lower *dī*, pinyin: biàn; also read as *chuí*): A whip for striking horses; it is also a term for a riding crop. The lower character is pronounced *tā* (pinyin: tā). The *Shàngshū* says, "He was whipped to record [the offense]. The *Lǐjì* says, "When King Cheng committed an error, the Duke of Zhou then whipped Bóqīn. The *Shuowén* states that it is composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) with *dá* as its phonetic component.

"Kā" (in the term *kā-chu*, where "kā" is a reverse-cut [rhyme] for *kǔ*) means to pinch an object with the fingernails according to the *Qieyun*. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "xuàn" (*xuàn* being pronounced *xiàn*). The text of the sutra uses the character "tāo" (composed of "yǎo"), which is pronounced *tāo* (with the second tone). This is not the usage intended in the sutra. "Yǎo" is pronounced *yǎo* (with the third tone).

*The Ritual for the Recitation of the Five Secret Practices of Vajrasattva in the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara*, one fascicle. "Jiè" (藉): The upper character is pronounced with the ancient *yǎ* (雅) and *qiè* (切) rhymes; it also means "to borrow. The lower character is pronounced with the *cí* (慈) and *yè* (夜) rhymes. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "jiè" (藉) refers to using orchids or grasses to cover the ground for sacrifices; it is composed of the radical "grass" (艹) and the phonetic "jiè" (藉), with the pronunciation *qíng* (情) and *yì* (亦). It is incorrect for the text to use the character "jí" (籍) with the "bamboo" (竹) radical.

The character *diào* (調) is pronounced with the initial *d-*, the final *-u*, and the departing tone (*tú liáo fǎn*). The *Jìxùn* states that it means "to harmonize" (*hé*) and also "to dally with" (*tiáonòng*). The character *zhì* (擲) is pronounced with the initial *zh-*, the final *-i*, and the departing tone (*zhí zhī fǎn*); its archaic form is written as *zhì* (擿). It means "to shake" (*zhèn*). According to the *Shuōwén*, it means "to throw" (*tóuzhì*). It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "Zhèng" (*zhèng shēng*).

*Zhì* (胯): [Radical] 竹 (zhú), [Phonetic] 吏 (lì). According to the *Yùpiān*, it means "to rest" or "to place"; according to the *Shuōwén*, it is composed of the radical 四 (sì) with the phonetic 直 (zhí); the sound of 四 is *zhuǐ*. Below is 苦化 (kǔ huà). It refers to the waist and hips. According to the *Qièyùn*, it refers to the space between the two thighs; it is composed of the radical 肉 (ròu) with the phonetic 夸 (kuā); the sound of 夸 is *kǔ huā*.

The Secret Recitation Ritual of Vajrarāja Bodhisattva, one fascicle. [Regarding the character "pín" (顰)]: The upper part is the radical *shǔ* (尨), read as *zhēn* (真) or *fǎn* (反); the lower part is *mò* (莫) and *bì* (丕). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to the hair above the eyes, resembling the shape of eyebrows. The *Yupian* states it means to listen with knit brows. The text of this scripture uses the character *pín* (嚬) with the mouth radical (*kǒu*), meaning to smile; it is not the character for "knit brows" (*pínmiéi*). The characters *méi* (眉) and *pín* (顰) have both been used interchangeably for a long time, as is commonly transmitted in the world today.

*Fēi* (upper radical *fǔ*, lower *wēi*; according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to the color of silk; the lower part is also written as *qún* [two forms with the same pronunciation]; according to the *Zilin*, it is clothing; the *Shiming* states that what is above is called *qún* and what is below is called *shāng*; it follows the radical for clothing and takes *jūn* as its phonetic).

"Lian-si" (藕絲) refers to the fibers of the lotus root; the *Erya* states: "The plant is called hé-fúqú; its fruit is lián, and its root is liǎn. The character below (絲) is pronounced xī-zī; the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as that which is produced by silkworms, composed of two "sì" radicals, where "sì" is pronounced mì.

*Binbin* (繽紛): The first character, *bǐn*, has the phonetic gloss *shàng pǐ bīn fǎn*; the rhyme dictionary states it means "abundant. The second character, *bīn*, has the phonetic gloss *xià fǔ wén fǎn*; the rhyme dictionary states it means "great" and describes a state of being numerous. It also refers to the state of being "fēnyún" (紛紜), meaning chaotic or disordered.

The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin King, one fascicle. “Piǎng” (竝): The *Shuowen* states it means standing side by side; the *Qieyun* defines it as a comparison. It is composed of two “lì” (立) radicals; the current scripture uses this as a vulgar character. “Xià” (下): Pronounced *shūzhǔ*. The *Yupian* defines it as a young child who has not yet undergone the capping ceremony; the *Qieyun* defines it as standing. The *Shuowen* writes it as “dòu” (豆); the scriptural text uses “lì” (立), which is a vulgar usage. “Tóng” (童): The *Yupian* defines it as a small child; the *Qieyun* defines it as standing. The *Shuowen* writes it as “dòu” (豆); the scriptural text uses “lì” (立), which is a vulgar usage.

Regarding the character above [the radical for] "net" (網), its two readings are *wǎng* and *jiǎng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The Lord Baoxi tied nets to fish; it takes the radical 糸 (silk) and uses 罔 as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of 罔 is as stated above. It is also written as 网 or 罟, which represent the form of an interlaced knot. The character below [the radical for] "wood" (木) has the reading *qì* (or *jī*). The *Erya* says: "A stake is called a *yì*. Guo Pu’s commentary states: "It is a wedge. It is also written as 橜 or 樴. The pronunciation of 樴 is *tè*, and that of 杙 is *yángshì*. It takes the radical 木 and 弋 as the phonetic component.

The character for *mài* (wheat/barley) [is pronounced with the initial] *kǎo* (the sound of *kǎo*). It refers to the awns of grain; it is also said to mean rice that has not yet been husked. *Kuǎn* is also a valid variant. The character for *mài* below is a vulgar form of *mài*. According to the *Baihūtong*, wheat (*mài*) is metal; it grows when metal is dominant and dies when fire is dominant. It has been written as *mài* since ancient times.

*Yè-ài*: The upper character *yè* is pronounced as *yǐ-luò* (乙劣); the *Shuowen* defines it as "upward-moving qi. The lower character *ài* is pronounced as *yī-xī* (伊昔); the *Yunjí* states it means "the throat. The *Erya* writes it with the character *yì* (齸) from the "Teeth" radical; Kuo Pu’s commentary notes that in Jiangdong, the throat is called *yì*. In the *Hanshu*, when Emperor Xuan died, the Prince of Yi arrived at the capital and did not weep beneath the city walls, saying, "My throat (*ài*) is in pain."

*Kài* (咳): The upper character is pronounced *kǎi* (苦槩反); the *Shuowen* states it means "to cough" (*qìngkài*), composed of the radical *qiàn* (欠) with the phonetic *hài* (亥). The lower character is pronounced *zòu* (蘇奏反); it refers to a lung ailment. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒, pronounced *nǚ è*) with the phonetic *sòu* (欶, the pronunciation of which is the same as above). In the scriptural text, it is written as *kǒu* (口) followed by *shòu* (嗽), forming *kǒushòu*; both forms are not the original characters.

The Method for Reciting the Dharma of the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, one fascicle. *Fan-cu*: Upper radical is *fu* (pronounced with the *yuan* tone), lower is *bun* (pronounced with the *qieyun* tone). It means "to cover," derived from the phonetic *chang*. The character *you* is pronounced as *shou* or *han*. The lower part is *yu* (pronounced *yù*). It means "to approach. The method of the seal is to contract the upper joints of the middle fingers of both hands into the shape of a jewel. According to the *Shuowen*, it is derived from *qi* and *zu* as phonetics. In some versions of the scripture, it is written as *cu* (from *jiu*), which is the original character.

The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī, one fascicle. Regarding the character *píng* (絣): the *Shūzìshū* (字書) states it means to stretch out black cords (*zhèn hēishéng*). The *Jixùn* (集訓) states it means to stretch or pull (*pīngtán*). It may also be written with the hand radical as *pīn*, which is likewise acceptable. The *Zìgào* (字誥) records it as *bǐng* (󱱈), an archaic form. The pronunciation of *tán* (撣) is the same as *tán* (彈).

The character 庳 (pí) [is read as pí, with the phonetic component 皮 (pí) and the radical 厂 (hàn)]. In the *Zhou Li*, "庳" means short; Gu Yewang says it means low or humble. It is composed of 厂 (hàn, pronounced hā-dàn) and 卑 (bēi) as its phonetic. 厂 (hàn) is pronounced hā-dàn.

"㧙" (left index finger): pronounced *pián* (as in *míè*) with a *kǎo* sound; it means "to twist" (*yǎo*). Pronounced *yāo* (as in *jiǎo*) with a *yǎo* sound; it refers to the method of forming a seal with the fingers as handles.

"為鞘" (*wéi qiào*): pronounced *xiào* (as in *yào*) with a *kǎo* sound; the commentary states it is the sheath for a sword or blade. It is derived from "革" (*gé*, leather) with the phonetic component "肖" (*xiào*); alternatively, written as "韒" with the radical "韋" (*wéi*), this is also acceptable.

"Coiled above" (pán): the rhyme is *bàn* (伴僈). The *Guǎngyá* states that "pán" means "to coil. The *Fānyǔ* states that when a dragon has not yet ascended to heaven and remains coiled within its lair, it is called a "coiled dragon" (*pánlóng*). According to the *Shuowén*, the character is composed of "insect" (虫) and "fán" (番) as the phonetic; "fán" is pronounced as above, and "màn" (僈) is pronounced *mǔguān*.

The Method for Reciting the Name of Akṣobhya Tathāgata, one fascicle. *Maṃjughoṣa* (莽莫枳): the first character is pronounced as *mǎng* (with the initial *mǎng* following the *bǎng* rhyme) and the second as *jī* (following the *jīng* rhyme). Some say it is *mòjì* (莫計), others say *mòjī* (莫鷄); these are all transliterations of the Sanskrit, indicating a repetition in the scripture. It is the name of the Mother of the Vajra Family.

*He yi*: The upper character is pronounced *hu* (with the *gē* and *qièyùn* tones); it means "red," and also "brilliant and flourishing. It is composed of two *chì* characters. The lower character is pronounced *yáng yì*; according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "great. Thus, *he yì* describes the appearance of being grand and flourishing. The scriptural text uses the character with the "fire" radical (*huǒ*)—written as *hè*—which is incorrect.

The *Sūtra of the Most Victorious and Peerless Great Majestic Virtue Golden Wheel Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Blazing Radiance Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle. *Chì* (熾): The sound of the character *kǎo* (考). It means "blazing" (*chì*) and also "abundant. According to the *Shuowen*, it refers to fierce fire; according to the *Zishu*, it refers to bright light. It is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "shěng" (省), with the final rhyme being *chéngzhèng* (承政). In the *Yunji*, it means "long"; the *Fangyan* says it means "vast and great"; the *Shuowen* also says it means "much. It is composed of the radical "vessel" (*míng*) and the phonetic "chéng" (成).

Regarding "Rāhu" (羅睺): the character "hù" (胡) is pronounced with the *diào* (釣) tone. According to the *Fāngyán* (方言), it means "one glance. Here, "Lóuhòu" (羅睺) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit; alternatively, it is called "Luòhù" (攞護), which translates as "obscuration of darkness. It is able to obstruct the light of the sun and moon, and is thus the planet of darkness (*tamas*).

*Ketu* is a Sanskrit term, also transliterated as *Kītu* or *Kidu*, which in Chinese means "eclipse-extender"; it is also a dark luminary. According to the records, Rāhu and Ketu are constantly hidden and do not appear; when they encounter the paths of the sun and moon, an eclipse occurs. They are also called the two luminaries, Jian and Zui. (The character for "eclipse," *shi*, is pronounced like "food.")

Regarding "comet" (*huìbèi*): the first character is pronounced *xú* (as in *xù*) and the second is pronounced *pómù* (as in *mù*). The *Erya* states: "The comet star is called *chānqiāng*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "A comet is also called *bèi*; this refers to its appearance being *bèibèi*, resembling a broom-sweeping brush. Li Chunfeng says: "Whatever [constellation] a comet or *bèi* star strikes is invariably ominous. *Chān* is pronounced *chúxián* and *qiāng* is pronounced *chǔgēng*.

The *Secret Instructions on the Five Planets* concerning Venus states: "Venus is the quintessence of metal in the western quarter; it is also named Chang-geng. It is one hundred li in diameter, white in color, and luminous. Its appearance is like that of a general; it moves according to its orbit, appearing and disappearing at the proper times. When a general achieves merit, Venus conjoins with Mars; when there is warfare, it moves for one year to complete one circuit of the heavens, never exceeding fifty degrees from the sun."

Mars is also called *Hinghuo* (the Luminous Confuser); it is the essence of fire from the south and is also known as the Star of Punishment. Its diameter is seventy *li*, its color is red and luminous, and its orbit completes one revolution through the heavens in two years; wherever it halts or transgresses, all such positions are ominous.

The Star of the Pacifier (Zhèn-xīng) is the quintessence of Earth at the center; it is also called Dì-hóu (Earth Marquis). Its diameter is fifty *lǐ*. It is yellow in color and moves slowly, completing one circuit of the heavens in twenty-nine years. Regarding the character for "star" (*xīng*): according to the *Shuōwén*, it is written as *xíng* from the radical *jīng* (crystal), meaning "the quintessence of all things. The archaic form is written as *chén*, which is a pictograph. The pronunciation of *jīng* is "qīng"; it also refers to radiant light.

Regarding *fen-nü* (忿怒): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it also means "to be angry," composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "fen" (*fen*), with an alternative pronunciation of *fū-wèn*. The *Yupian* defines it as "resentment" (*èi*), and the *Qieyun* defines it as "wrathful anger," also pronounced *nǔ*. Examining the iconography of wrathful deities (*krodha*), the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-sūtra* states that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest their bodies based on two kinds of wheels (*cakra*), resulting in different manifestations: first, the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), which manifests the True Body (*dharmakāya*), as this body is obtained through the fruition of the vows and practices cultivated; second, the Wheel of Command (*ājñā-cakra*), which manifests the Wrathful Body (*krodhakāya*), because it appears with fierce majesty arising from great compassion.

*Śatru* (pronounced *śat-lu*, with the second syllable following the *du-hu* rhyme and the third following the *li-gu* rhyme; alternatively spelled *sṭo-lu*, both being Sanskrit terms with varying weights), here translated as "enemy," refers to one who acts as an adversary and brings harm to all wholesome dharmas.

*Yàn* (厭) and *dǎo* (禱): The upper character is read as *yàn* or *yán* (the latter being a variant). In dictionaries it is written as *yàn* (󰚏), meaning "to exorcise" (*yànráng*). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "sorcery" (*yànmèi*) or "to attach. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *yàn* (猒), explaining it as "a dog with meat on its tongue. The lower character is read as *dù hào* (都皓). In the *Qìnyùn*, it means "to request. Dictionaries state it refers to "praying to the celestial deities. The *Lúnyǔ* says, "He requested [permission] from the deities above and below."

Regarding "zhù" (呪詛): the upper character is also written as "zhù" (祝) or "chóu" (詶), with the same pronunciation as "shòu" (受). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "chóu" is also "zhù. The lower character is pronounced "zè jù" (側據); its ancient form is "zhā" (樝). The *Shiming* explains it as "belonging to the category of 'zhù' (祝)," meaning to attach good or evil words to one another. "Zhù" (詛) means to cause a person's actions to be constrained by their words. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "qù" (且), where "qù" is pronounced "zǐ yú" (子余). In the classics, it is written with the radical "mouth" (口) as "jǔ" (咀), pronounced "cái yǔ" (才與), meaning to chew; this is not the usage intended here.
