The forty-one fascicles of the *Sūtra* share the same phonetic commentary as this fascicle. Regarding the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā Prajñāpāramitā Recitation Rite* (*Renwang banruo boluomi niansong yigui*), one fascicle:

in the "Zi" (子) section of the *Xùyīn* (Continued Phonetics), "zuǎn" (纂) is transcribed with the upper radical "guǎn" (管) and the phonetic "yì" (集). The *Erya*, "Shigu" (釋詁), states: "Zuǎn means to succeed. The *Shuowen* states: "From 'mì' (糸) and 'suàn' (算) as the phonetic; 'suàn' is pronounced *sūguǎn*. The scriptural text uses "mò" (莫) to form "zuǎn," which does not constitute a valid character. The lower part is the fanqie "láng" (郎). In the *Yùnyīn* (韻英), it is "lì" (歷). The *Erya* says: "Lì means enumeration. The *Shuowen* states: "From 'zhǐ' (止) and 'lì' (厤) as the phonetic; 'lì' is pronounced as above. The scriptural text uses "lì" (曆); this is the character for "calendar" (*lìrì*) and is not the "zuǎnlì" (纂歷) [of the title].

*Nai* (迺): *pi* (辟) and *shang* (上) are the two characters for its phonetic analysis; it is a word used in the *Qieyun*. The *Erya* states: "Reing" (*reng nai*). Guo Pu’s commentary says: "Nai" (*nai*) is simply "nai" (*nai*). The *Shiwen* says it is an ancient form of the character "nai" (*nai*). Below, *bi* (必) and *yi* (益) are the two characters for its phonetic analysis; it means "command" (*ming*). Regarding the sound, it means "to summon. In the *Qieyun*, it means "to eliminate."

"Liáng-bèn (良賁): The second character, bèn, has the phonetic value *pǐ* (彼) with the rhyme *yì* (義). The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states that 'bèn' means 'subtlety' (*wēi*) and is also the name of a hexagram. The *Yì* says: 'Bèn: success; small advantage; it is beneficial to have a destination. Upon examination, Liáng-bèn is the name of the śramaṇa who assisted in the translation of the *Renwang jīng*."

Regarding "Chánggǔn" (常袞): the character "gǔn" (袞) is pronounced as "wěn" (穩) with a retroflex final. The *Líjì* (Book of Rites), *Yùzǎo* (Jade Robes) chapter, states: "The Son of Heaven wears the *lónggǔn* (dragon robe) for sacrifices. Zheng Xuan’s commentary notes: "The *gǔn* is so called because dragons are painted upon the upper garment. Now, "Chánggǔn" refers to the name of the Hanlin Academician Rùn-wén.

The Ritual for Recitation of the Yoga Lotus Family, one fascicle. *Hūsu* (戶樞): Following the *Erya*, it says "the pivot is called the *wéi*" (*guǒ pǔ zhù yún mén fēi shū jī*). According to the *Guǎyá*, the pivot is the base; it refers to the place where the door leaf turns. The *Shuowén* states that it is composed of the radical for wood with the phonetic *qū*.

"Zhù è" (拄腭): "Xià" (下) is pronounced as "wǒ gè fǎn" (我各反). It refers to the upper palate within the mouth. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is the "river above the mouth. It is written with the character "gǔ" (谷), where the phonetic component is pronounced as "qiáng lüè fǎn" (強略反). The strokes above the mouth are drawn in eight layers to resemble the shape of the palate.

*Bìkāi* (擘開): The first character is pronounced with the *shàngshēng* (上聲) tone *líng* (夌). The *Guǎngyá* states that it means "to divide"; the *Shuōwén* states it means "to wave" or "also to open," composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 辟 (bì).

*Liansuǒ* (聯鎖): The first character is pronounced with the *shàngshēng* (上聲) tone *zhǎn* (鱣). The *Shēnglèi* states that it means "uninterrupted"; the *Shuōwén* states it means "to connect," composed of the radical 耳 (ear)—as the ear is connected to the cheek—and the radical 糸 (silk), forming a compound character meaning "to connect without interruption. The second character is pronounced with the *sùguǒ* (蘇果) rhyme. Lexicons state it refers to "fishing hooks and chains linked together."

*The Ritual for Subduing Māras in the Yoga of Vajraśekhara*, one fascicle. Regarding the character "chui" (鍬): it is pronounced with the lower radical as *qiè* (七消反). It is also written as "chui" (鍫), while the standard form is "zhui" (鐰). In archaic script, it was written as "zhi" (󱷛). The *Erya* states: "The character 'zhi' (󱷛) is called 'wei' (疀). Guo's commentary notes: "'Chui' (鍬) and 'chua' (鍤) are the same characters. The *Fangyan* states: "In the regions of Zhao and Wei, 'chua' (鍤) is called 'chui' (鍬); in Jiangdong, it is called 'pie' (鐅); in Ba and Shu, it is called 'chua' (鍤). These are all regional and vernacular variations of the name. The pronunciation of "pie" (鐅) is *piànmiè* (片蔑反); the pronunciation of "chua" (鍤) is *chā* (插).

*Dunju* (蹲踞): the first character is pronounced *cún* (存); the second is pronounced *jū* (居) with the alternative reading *yù* (御). It refers to the sound of a fox crouching. According to the *Shiming* (釋名), *dùn* means "to preserve" (*cún*); it refers to preserving one's posterior by not sitting directly upon the mat. *Jù* (踞) means "squatting like a winnowing basket" (*jīqí*). The *Lǐjì* (禮記) states: "One must not squat like a winnowing basket. *Jī* (箕) is pronounced *jī* (基).

*Quēlú* (屈蔞): The first character is read as *jūn* (律反) and the second as *lì* (力句反). It resembles white *méo* grass and grows as a creeping vine; it is now commonly called "long-life grass" (*chángmìng cǎo*). *Dùn* (㪻): The first character is read as *jū* (居怨反).

It refers to a vessel for scooping up things; it is also said to mean "bailing out water. It is composed of the radical *dòu* (斗) with the phonetic *luán* (䜌). *Luán* is pronounced *liàn* (戀), and *dùn* is pronounced *yǐzhǎo* (以沼反). This is the character for "scooping" (*duìndùn*, 㪻).

The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of Avalokiteśvara Tārā, in one fascicle. *Ācārya*—the Sanskrit term pronounced "Zhongyin shi cha fan" (阿闍梨中音士遮反)—is also called *Ācāri*, correctly rendered as *Ācārya*. This is translated as "Personal Teacher" (*qīnjiào*), meaning one who is able to personally instruct other students.

Regarding "nābhi" (navel): the upper character is *zú* (臍), with the phonetic gloss *xú xī*; according to the *Qièyùn*, it means "navel. The lower character is *yāo* (腰), with the phonetic gloss *yǐ xiāo*; according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "waist and spine. The upper character is written as *zì* (𦝫). Regarding "two *kōng*" (二空):

according to the *Yogācāra-vidyādhara-vidhi*, when performing various mudrās, one uses the five wheels (*pañca-cakra*) and the ten *pāramitās*. The five wheels refer to earth, water, fire, wind, and space. [The instruction] for the two hands to each take the little finger as the head and proceed in order along the wheels means that "joining the two *kōng*" refers to joining and extending the two thumbs upright. The version of the sūtra that reads "two *qiāng*" (二腔)—with the phonetic gloss *kǔ jiāng*—is actually the character for "sheep carcass" (羊腔); this is a scribal error that greatly deviates from the meaning of the sūtra.

The Ritual for the Recitation of Avalokiteśvara Amoghapāśa Bodhisattva, one fascicle. Regarding "Tiger" (虎): In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it says: "A lord among mountain beasts. The *Huainanzi* says: "When the tiger roars, the valley wind arises. It is composed of the radical "person" (人) with the phonetic "hū" (虍). The sound of "hū" is pronounced as "hǔ". Because its claws resemble those of a human, it takes the radical "person"; alternatively, it is written as 虓. [Note: The character 虓 contains the taboo name of the Emperor and does not form a standard character; another variant is 𧆞, which is a vulgar transformation and not the correct form. Regarding "Wolf" (狼): The lower part is pronounced as "lǎng". In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it says: "Resembles a dog; it has white cheeks and a pointed head. The *Erya* says: "The female wolf is called a lán; its offspring are called xià. The sound of "xià" is pronounced as "húdí".

*Jiā* (pronounced *gǔyá* in the ancient dialect): The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states that *jiā* means "to add" (*jiā*), referring to a wooden device placed upon the neck. That which is on the hands is called *zhì*, that on the feet is called *gù*, and that on the neck is called *jiā*; these constitute the five types of wooden restraints for criminals. *Xià* (pronounced *suǒguǒ*): According to the *Qièyùn*, this refers to an iron chain, meaning a linked series of rings.
The character *zhǐ* (指) with the phonetic *nǎn* (𢅎) [reading *xià* (下), ancient pronunciation *gǔ liǎo fǎn*] has already been explained above.

Regarding "Amṛtakuṇḍalī Bodhisattva’s Ritual for Offerings and Recitation" (*Gānlùjūntálu Púsà gòngyǎng niànshòu yí*), one fascicle: the character *xǐ* (洗) [with the phonetic *xiān lǐ fǎn*, also written as *sǎ* (洒)] means to wash, cleanse, scrub, or scour; the lower part [the radical *lì* (厶)] is pronounced *tú lì fǎn*. According to the *Qièyùn*, it means purity or the removal of filth; it also means to rinse away or purify.

The upper radical of *jiù* (咎) is pronounced *qián* (乾) and is also written as *qiān* (愆); the *Erya* writes it as *qiān* (諐). The *Shiyanyan* states: "To stray and *qiān* are transgressions. The lower part is pronounced *qí* (其). The *Yunji* states: "It means transgression (*guò*) and calamity (*zāi*). The *Erya* states: "*Jiù* means emaciated illness. The *Shuowen* states: "People differ from one another. It follows the radical for 'person' (*rén*) and the character *gè* (各). The versions in the scriptures use *huì* (𠧨), but both *jiù* (咎) and *huì* (𠧨) are not the original characters.

*Jing*: (with the initial *lǎng* and final *dīng*) refers to a golden bell; its phonetic approximation is similar to a *zhōng* (bronze bell) but smaller. *Xià*: (with the initial *tú* and final *luò*) refers to the large bell used today. In the *Zuozhuan*, it says: "The golden bells and bronze tongues vibrate as an extension of civil culture. It is also said that the *duó* (bell) of the Upper Army Commandant was used to stop bandits.

The character for *jià* (駕) is pronounced *yǎ* (訝) according to ancient phonetics; it means to mount or ride. The *Shijing* says, "I shall mount my carriage" (*jià wǒ qí jù*, where *jù* is pronounced *xū* [戌] and *jù* [倨]). The *Qieyun* states it is "to drive. The *Shiben* says, "Hanging the yoke on the ox and mounting to drive the horse. The *Zhouli* mentions the "five types of driving": sounding the *huán* and *luán* bells, following the bends of water, stopping at markers, dancing at crossroads, and assisting in the pursuit of game. The *Shuowen* explains it as consisting of the radical "horse" and "you-you," which is a compound character representing the hands. The text of the scripture uses the character *yù* (御), meaning to attend upon or to employ; it is not the character for "driving."

*Ucchuṣma* is a Sanskrit term, also known as *Ucchuṣma*; the old translation was "Vajra of Foul Traces" (*Huiji Jingang*), which is erroneous and appears to disparage the holy one. The new translation is "Wrathful Deity Who Removes Impurities. This refers to manifesting a body of majestic wrath through vajra-wisdom in order to subdue sentient beings who are difficult to tame and are defiled by evil.

*Àodàn* (傲誕): The first character is pronounced with the *wǔdǎo* (五倒) reverse-cut; it means arrogance (*màn*) and haughtiness (*jù*). The *Kǎoshēng* says it means to hold oneself in high esteem. The *Erya* says it means jesting (*xiè*). The second character is pronounced with the *túdàn* (徒旦) reverse-cut; the *Zìshū* says it means great (*dà*). The *Qièyùn* says it means trust (*xìn*). Gu Yewang says it means to deceive (*qī*). It is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic "extend" (*yán*). *Xiè* (謔) is pronounced *xiāngxuè*.

"Chou-hui" (臭穢): "Chou" (臭) is pronounced with the upper radical *ch'ih* and the *ch'iu* rhyme; it is a general term for all odors. The *Kao-sheng* states that it means "foul stench. According to the *Shuo-wen*, the character is composed of the "dog" radical and two "zi" (自) radicals—the latter being the nose—forming a compound ideograph. Its archaic form was written as 殠, while the vulgar form is 臰. The text of the scriptures uses the character 𭊴 with the "mouth" radical, but this character does not exist [in standard usage].

The Ritual for Paying Homage and Repentance to the Thirty-Seven Honored Ones, one fascicle. The term *miào* (妙) refers to the archaic character for *fǎ* (法); nowadays the character *fǎ* is commonly used. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "law" (*fǎ*); according to the *Changyun*, it means "constant" (*cháng*) or also "number" (*shù*).

*The Eulogy on the Dharmakāya by the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva: A Liturgy for Paying Homage to the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. Regarding the character *zhì* (只) in the title: in the *Xùzì* (序字), it is pronounced as *yù* (宇). In the *Yǔzhòu* (宇宙), it is pronounced as *yù* (宇); the *Jìhuìnxún* (集訓) states it means "the world" (*huán yù*). According to the *Qièyùn*, it means "great" or "border"; it is composed of the radical *mián* (宀, pronounced *mò xiān*) and the phonetic *yú* (于). *The Eulogy on the Dharmakāya by the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva: A Liturgy for Paying Homage to the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. Regarding the character *zhì* (只) in the title: in the *Xùzì* (序字), it is pronounced as *yù* (宇). In the *Yǔzhòu* (宇宙), it is pronounced as *yù* (宇); the *Jìhuìnxún* (集訓) states it means "the world" (*huán yù*). According to the *Qièyùn*, it means "great" or "border"; it is composed of the radical *mián* (宀, pronounced *mò xiān*) and the phonetic *yú* (于).

Wòdàng (沃盪): The first character, wù, is pronounced with the initial *ʔ* (烏酷反). The *Yùnchuán* states that it means "to pour"; the *Shēnglèi* states that it means "to drench from above with water. The second character, xià, is pronounced with the final *-lǎng* (徒朗反). The *Qièyùn* defines it as "to wash away" (*dí-dàng*) and also "to shake or move. It is composed of the radical *míng* (皿, vessel) and the phonetic *tāng* (湯).

*Du-bu dharani-mukha*, one fascicle. "Ping" (絣) refers to the northern reading *meng* (萠) with the rhyme *zhen* (振) and the radical *heisheng* (黑繩). It is derived from the radical for "silk" (*si*) and the phonetic *bing* (并). Although the script uses the hand radical, the pronunciation is *ping* (普耕), meaning to stretch or pull; it is not used in this context.
*Soma* is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Wondrous Arm" (*Miaobi*).

*Vajrāyus-tārā-dhāraṇī-japa-vidhi* (The Ritual for Reciting the Vajrāyus Dhāraṇī), one fascicle. *Maheśvara* is an ancient Sanskrit term; its correct form is *Mahesvara*, which is translated as "Great Sovereign" (*Daizai*), the Lord of the Heaven of Form (*Rūpadhātu*).

"Yun" (搵) is pronounced with the first character as "wu" (烏) and the second as "kun" (困), following the *Qieyun* rhyme dictionary; it means to press down. According to the *Fangyan*, it refers to thrusting an object into water; the pronunciation of "nu" (抐) is "nu" (奴) and "kun" (困). The second character, "su" (蘇), is the plant *Perilla*. According to the scriptures, the character for "yun su" (搵蘇) should be read as "su" (酥); according to the *Qieyun*, "su" (酥) refers to milk and curd.

The character *zhì* (擲) is pronounced with the upper radical *zhí* (直) and the rhyming component *zhì* (炙); the *Yùnyùn* (韻) states it means "to throw," "to shake," or "to cast. In archaic script, it is written as *zhì* (擿).

In the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, "The Gate of Contemplation on the Forty-two Characters for Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Dafangguang fo huayan jing rufa jie sishier zi guanmen*), one fascicle, the text itself provides explanations for forty-two Sanskrit characters; for the remainder, there are no available phonetic transcriptions or glosses.

The Ritual Manual for the Contemplative Practice of the Heart Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, in one fascicle. Regarding the term *shenpei* (身帔): the *Kaosheng* (考聲) states it refers to a head-cloth (*jinpei*); the *Qieyun* (切韻) states it is a garment (*yipei*). The *Shuowen* (說文) states it is composed of the radical *jin* (巾) with the phonetic *pi* (丕), or pronounced *pi* (披), meaning a shawl (*chandan*); it does not refer to the ceremonial sash (*xiapei*) worn by women.

*Qīnghú* (light gauze): "Hú" is pronounced with the *gǔ* rhyme (hù). The *Yùnchuán* states that *gǔ* resembles *luó* (gauze) but is finer. The *Qièyùn* states it is *luóhú* (gauze). It is formed from the radical *mì* (silk thread) and the phonetic *gǔ*;

the sound of *gǔ* is like *gǔ*. *Jiāoféng* (interlaced seams): "Féng" is pronounced with the *fú yòng* rhyme. The *Erya* says: "Yù" refers to the seams of a lamb-skin robe (*láoyóu*). The *Shuowén* says: "It means the stitching of a garment. It is formed from the radical *mì* and the phonetic *féng*; the sound of *yù* is like *yù*, and the sound of *zhì* (stitching) is like *zài*; *féng* is also pronounced as *féng*.

The Great Sage Mañjuśrī’s Sūtra on the Meritorious Adornments of the Buddha-field, Scroll One, Part One. [Regarding the character] *mén* (門): below the radical for "gate," the phonetic component is *kǔ* (苦). The *Shēnglèi* (Sound Categories) states: "*Kǔn* (閫) is the threshold. The *Jízhù* (Collected Annotations) states: it refers to the wooden bar that limits the door. Gù Yěwáng states: it is the door-sill. The *Shuōwén* (Explanations of Characters) states: it is the door-sill; it is composed of the radical for "gate" with *kùn* (困) as the phonetic.

*Śaṅkha*: the first character is pronounced *shīliáng* (失良) and the second *qiāngshē* (羌奢); it is a term from the Sanskrit language, or alternatively written as *xiǎngkā* (餉佉), with the first character pronounced *shīliàng* (失量). This translates as "conch," specifically the ritual conch used for blowing; it is commonly written with the character for "snail" (*luó*).

*Chéng* (澄): Upper radical *zhǐ* (直), level tone; rhyme *líng* (陵); it means clear water. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "settled and stable. The *Shuōwén* says it means "congealed. It is also written as the character *zhēng* (徵). Lower radical *suī* (雖), departing tone; according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "to look deeply. Lexicons state it means "moist and lustrous. It is formed with the radical *mù* (目) and the phonetic *zuì* (醉) in abbreviated form. To write it as *chǎo* (󱷀) is a vulgar character.
*Śamatha* is a Sanskrit term; its Chinese translation is "stopping the mind" (*zhǐxīn*) or "tranquility" (*jìjìng*), which refers to meditative concentration (*dìng*).

Regarding the character *pīhuàn* (披擐): the upper radical *pī* (披) is pronounced as *bèi* (被), and the dictionary states it means "to add"; the phonetic examination identifies it as "clothing. The lower part *huàn* (擐) is pronounced as *huàn* (患); the *Guìyuàn Zhūcóng* (桂苑珠叢) states that it means "to pierce the body through with armor," and the *Wǔjīng Yīnyì* (五經音義) also gives the pronunciation *gǔhuàn* (古患).

The upper character of "謦欬" (qǐngkài) is pronounced with the initial *l* (cold fan); the *Shuowen* states that "謦" is also "欬" (coughing). The lower character is pronounced with the initial *k* (ku dài fan); the *Shuowen* says it means "reversal of qi" (upward-moving breath), and it is also "瘶" (a type of cough). There are also those who write it as "謦," with the phonetic *kǒng* (kǒu dìng fan), meaning a musical instrument; or as "咳," with the phonetic *hái* (hú lái fan), meaning the coughing of an infant. None of these are used here. "瘶" is pronounced *sōu* (sū zòu fan).

"Biàn mèn" (遍捫): "mèn" is pronounced as *mo* with a *ben* rhyme (莫奔反). The *Shēnglèi* states that it means "to touch"; the *Jixùn* states it means "to stroke. The *Shuowén* explains it as "to hold or support," composed of the radical 手 (hand) and the phonetic 門 (mén). "Xiǎn bì" (險詖): "xiǎn" is pronounced as *xiāng jiǎn* (香撿反).

The *Shuowén* states it means "obstacles and difficulties," composed of the radical 阜 (hill/mound) and the phonetic 僉 (qiān). "Bì" is pronounced as *bǐ yì* (彼義反). The *Qièyùn* states it means "sycophancy"; the *Shuowén* states it means "treacherous and perverse," composed of the radical 言 (speech) and the phonetic 彼 (pǐ) in abbreviated form.

The character 麤 (cū) [meaning "coarse" or "wild"] has the upper radical 倉 (cāng) and the phonetic 穌 (sū); it is the correct form. The common variant 鹿 (lù) is incorrect. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states that "麤" means "sparse" (*chūsū*). The *Guǎngyá* states it means "vile. The *Shuowén* states it is composed of three "deer" (*lù*) with the phonetic 虢 (guō) below, read as *měng*. The *Jixùn* states: "Like a dog, it is wild and evil, and cannot be approached; therefore, it follows the 'dog' radical. Some editions of the sutra write this as the character 礦 (*kuàng*), which is incorrect.

In the middle fascicle of the *Mahāsthavira Mañjuśrī Buddha-vadha-guṇa-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, the term "diànshì" (鈿飾) appears. The *Shàngtáng Liànfǎ Yùnjí* (上堂練反韻集) states that it means to inlay precious materials such as lutes to adorn objects; the lower character is pronounced "shēng" (織) with the fanqie "zhì" (織). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "cosmetic adornment. The *Wénzìdiǎn* (文字典) explains that its refined form is "xiūshì" (修飾), and that the correct orthography follows the character "jīn" (巾) with the phonetic "sì" (飤), the pronunciation being similar [to "diàn"].

*Zhunsheng* (準繩): "Shang" (上) is pronounced as *yun* (允) in fanqie; it means measurement and standard. "Pingzhun" (平準) is the same. "Xia" (下) is pronounced as *shiling* (食陵); according to the *Yupian*, it means to seek, and according to the *Zishu*, it means straight. The *Book of Documents* says, "Wood follows the line and becomes straight. The *Shiben* says that Chui invented the level and the line.

The characters for *xīyí* (熙怡) are "xu" (虛) on top and "hà" (下) below; they are the opposite of their homophones. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *xīyí* means harmony and joy. The *Erya* states it means being pleased and submissive. The *Fangyan* states it means delight. In the scriptures, it is sometimes written as *xī* (嬉), which is incorrect.

Volume 3, Part 2: *The Sūtra on the Meritorious Adornments of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-Killing*. Volume 2. *Sumeru*—formerly transliterated as *Xumi* or *Miliu*—is a corruption of the Sanskrit term; the correct form is now given as *Sumeru*, which translates as "Wondrously High" (*Miaogao*). This refers to what the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* describes as the four tiers of the Wondrously High Mountain. Furthermore, it is said that there are one thousand [worlds] each for the desire-realm heavens and the Brahma-worlds of *Sumeru*; this is an instance where the Chinese and Sanskrit names are presented interchangeably.

*Yojana* was formerly translated as *youxun* or *yushena*; it has no direct semantic equivalent, but is translated as "one journey," specifically the distance a royal army of ancient sage-kings could travel in one day. This has already been explained in detail in the previous *Mahā-māyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra*.

The upper character 疲 (pí) is pronounced *pí* (with the phonetic *gǔ*); according to the *Guoyu*, it means "fatigue," and the *Guangya*, "weariness. It is composed of the radical 疒 (*zhé*) with 皮 (*pí*) as its phonetic; the lower character 厭 (*yàn*) has the pronunciation *yàn*. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "satiety" and also "weariness. The text states: "It is formed from 犬 (*quán*) and 甘肉 (*gān ròu*), meaning 'a dog's satiety for meat. In current vernacular usage, it has been transformed into the character 厭, which is used interchangeably."

*Māgadha* is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is also called *Makata*, *Makati*, or *Moketi*, all of which refer to the same place. This is translated as "Free from Harm," meaning that the laws of this country do not employ corporal punishment or execution; those who commit crimes punishable by death are merely sent to the *śmaśāna* (the Cold Forest). It is also called "The Great Body Country," signifying that among the five regions of India, this country is the largest and governs over all other nations. Furthermore, it is called "Pervasive Wisdom," meaning that wise and intelligent people are found throughout the entire kingdom. These names are all established according to their respective meanings.

*Ekabāha*: "Bāha" is the lower tone; it is a Sanskrit term translated here as *chuí* (also written as *chuán*, both pronounced with the same initial *shì* and rhyme *yuán*). It refers to a granary or storage bin. *Mahāsukha-vajrasattva-sādhana-vidhi*: *Mahāsukha-vajrasattva-sādhana-vidhi*, one fascicle.

"Place upon the hip" (*zhì kuà shàng*): "Kuà" is pronounced with the *zhú* and *lì* rhymes; it means to rest or place. The *Shuowén* states it means "to entrust. It is formed from the radical *wǎng* with the phonetic *zhí*; the lower part is read as *kāihuà*. Regarding the sound, it refers to the space between the two thighs. Some write it as "crossing over" (*kuà yè*), but that is not its usage here.

"Zuòlüè" (側捩) is a *fǎnqiè* (phonetic transcription) for "zì" (側) and "liè" (綀). The character "zì" means "beside. The character "liè" (下綀) is transcribed as "jié" (結); the *Yùpiān* states it means "to twist" (*āoliè*). It is composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "lì" (戾), with "lì" having the same pronunciation as above. The *Shuōwén* writes it as "lì" (戾), meaning "a dog under a door. The scriptural text uses the character "lì" (綟) with the radical "silk" (糸); according to the *Guǎngyùn*, this refers to a small knot in hemp. It does not mean "twisting the fingers to form a mudrā."
"Bending the bow" (wān gōng): the *Wǔguān Fǎnyùn Jí* states that this refers to the curved posture of drawing a bow; it has already been explained previously. "Konghou" (kōng hóu):
the upper character is pronounced *kōng* and the lower *hóu*; it is the name of a musical instrument; its explanation has already been completed previously.

The Ritual Manual for the Accomplishment of the Yoga of the King of the Lotus Sutra, one fascicle. "Yoga" is a Sanskrit term; it is sometimes transcribed as *yūqi* or *yǔxié*, both of which are erroneous. It is translated here as "correspondence" (*xiāngying*). According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are four kinds of correspondence: correspondence of vehicle, correspondence of object, correspondence of practice, and correspondence of fruit.

The character *jì* (記) in the phrase "listing below" (*jiǎng xià fāng liè*) refers to the division of rhymes based on phonetic oppositions (*fǎn qiè yùn fēn*). To "examine the sounds" (*kǎo shēng*) means to decide or determine them. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written with the radical "speech" (*yán*) as *xiè*; this is also the same as the text of the sutra. However, the *Pīcāng* states that when written with the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) as *biè*, it means planting seeds densely or transplanting; it is not the character for "recording" (*jì*).
*Śamatha* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "calming" (*zhi*).

*Vipaśyanā* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "contemplation" (*guan*). It should be understood that calming and contemplation are simply two names for concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*), as already explained in the previous *New Pronunciation and Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The character for *zhōu* (洲) is pronounced *zhōu* (上音州); the character for *zhǔ* (渚) is pronounced *zhǎng yǔ* (下章與反). The *Erya* states: "That which can be inhabited within the water is called a *zhōu*; a small *zhōu* is a *zhǔ*; a small *zhǔ* is a *zhǐ*. The *Shijing* says: "Upon an island in the Yellow River. The *Fangyan* states: "*Zhōu* means a sandbank (*tān*)," with the pronunciation *tā dān* (灘音他丹反). *Zhǐ* (沚) is pronounced *zhǐ* (止). *Zhǔ* (渚) is sometimes written as *zhǔ* (陼).

*Qiàn*: upper radical *jiàn* (反), the *Shuowen* states it means "to lack" (*shǎo*). Lower radical *hù* (𪛏), pronounced *jié* (𪛏) with the *yán* (陷) rhyme; the *Yupian* says it means "to enter," and the *Qieyun* says it means "to collapse and sink" (*huìmò*) or "to fall. The *Shuowen* states that *zuò* (作) refers to *zào* (臽), a small pit; it is composed of the character for "person" (*rén*) inside the character for "mortar" (*jiù*), pronounced *jiù*.

Regarding "diàn" (墊) in the *Shàngshū* [Book of Documents], which reads "the common people were mired in darkness and submerged" (*xià mín hūn diàn*), the *Kǒng Zhuàn* (Confucius’s Commentary) states: "This means the people of the world were bewildered and submerged. The *Yùpiān* (Jade Lexicon) states: "Diàn means 'below'. The character *mù* (瞀) has the phonetic reading *wù*.

The character 雜 (zá) is formed by combining the phonetic 徂 (cú) with the rhyming indicator 合 (hé). The *Yùnyùn* states it means "to gather" or "to pierce. The *Zílín* states it means "multitude. The lower radical 楚 (chǔ) has the rhyme indicator 洽 (qià). The character 刺 (cì) means "to enter"; it takes the hand radical as its semantic component and 臿 (chā) as its phonetic. The pronunciation of 臿 is the same as above. To write it as 𢰔 or 插 is not the original form of the character.

The character for *zì* (cow) [is pronounced] *jí* with the *lì* radical; it refers to a mother cow in the *Yěwáng* lexicon. The *Fāngyán* states that a female ox is called *zì* and a male is called *tè*, while their offspring are called *dú*. All these characters are formed from the "ox" radical (*niú*) combined with semantic and phonetic components.

"Kān-cuì" (甘脃): "Gān" means sweet; it also means to taste. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "holding one [thing] in the mouth. "Cuì" (下) has the phonetic value of *qī zuì* (七醉反); the *Yupian* states it means weak. The *Kaosheng* says it means tender. The correct character for the current usage follows "ròu" (肉) and takes "jué shěng" (絕省) as its phonetic component, signifying that the flesh is firm yet easily broken. In the scriptures, the character is often written with "wēi" (危), which is a vulgar form.

**Mèng (㝱寐):** The upper character is pronounced *mò* (莫弄反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to be awake while asleep," composed of the radical *mián* (宀) and the element *qiáng* (爿), with *mèng* (夢) as the phonetic. According to the *Zhouli*, one divines the good or bad fortune of the six types of dreams by means of the sun, moon, and stars: first, the dream of the upright; second, the dream of the distorted; third, the dream of thought; fourth, the dream of realization; fifth, the dream of joy; and sixth, the dream of fear. The lower character is pronounced *mì* (蜜二反). It means to lie down or to rest, composed of a simplified form of *mèng* (㝱) and the phonetic *wèi* (未). Although the classical text uses the single character *mèng* (夢), its common usage is also correct.
*Lo-dhi-ra*: This is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; in Chinese it is translated as "blood" (*xue*).
[The character] *que* (却) is used here as the correct orthography for the upward-toned character.

The Ritual for the Recitation of Vajrasattva in the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara, one fascicle. The character "Meng" (懵) is pronounced with the *mo* and *weng* finals; it represents the sound of the Sanskrit syllable, not its literal meaning. The character "Weng" (亘) is pronounced with the *gu* and *deng* finals.

*Jie* (睫): The upper radical is *jié* (即葉反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to the eyelashes (*mùbàngmáo*). The *Shiming* states that "jie" means "to insert" (*chā*), referring to what is inserted into the eye socket; it is also said to be the hair on the face above the eyes, formed from the radical *mù* with the phonetic *jié* (abbreviated) as the suffix. The lower character is *rú* (如均反), also written as *xiùn*. The *Qieyun* defines it as the movement of the eyelids, formed from the radical *mù* with the phonetic *rùn* as the suffix.

*Nie* (to bite or gnaw) is pronounced *jié* (結) with the initial *rén* (研). The *Lǐjì* (*Book of Rites*) states: "Do not gnaw on bones. The *Shuowén* (*Explanations of Simple and Compound Characters*) says: "Nǐè" (齧) means to bite; it is composed of the radical for teeth (*chí*) and the phonetic *bié* (㓞), which is pronounced *kǒu xià* (口黠). The text of the scripture uses *niè* (嚙), which is incorrect.

Vārāṇasī (the "vā" sound is pronounced like *fa* or alternatively as *póluǎnísī*; also called *póluónà*). This is the name of a kingdom in the Western Regions according to the Sanskrit language. Regarding the upper character *léi* (雷): it is pronounced with the *lú* rhyme reversed (meaning *luò*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as *léi*. The *Yi Zhuan* states: "Heaven’s thunder is *wúwàng*. The *Lunheng* says: "It is the agitation of the qi of yin and yang. Regarding the lower character *táng* (堂): it is pronounced with the *liàn* rhyme reversed.

The *Shuowen* defines it as: "The radiance of the agitation of yin and yang; it follows the radical for rain (*yù*) and the phonetic *shēn* (𠠤). Vārāṇasī is the name of a country in the Western Regions according to the Sanskrit language. Regarding the upper character *léi* (雷): it is pronounced with the *lú* rhyme reversed (meaning *luò*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* records it as *léi*. The *Yi Zhuan* states: "Heaven’s thunder is *wúwàng*. The *Lunheng* says: "It is the agitation of the qi of yin and yang. Regarding the lower character *táng* (堂): it is pronounced with the *liàn* rhyme reversed. The *Yupian* states: "It is a flash of lightning. The *Shiming* says: "Lightning is *shàn* (𣧠); it means that having suddenly appeared, it then vanishes. The *Shuowen* defines it as: "The radiance of the agitation of yin and yang; it follows the radical for rain (*yù*) and the phonetic *shēn* (𠠤)."

Regarding the character *pīlì* (霹靂): the upper radical is pronounced *pǐ* (覷反) and the lower is *líng* (靈反). A dictionary states that *pīlì* refers to a great thunderbolt striking an object. The *Lunheng* says it is the sound produced when heaven and earth act as a furnace and yin and yang act as the gases, striking against one another. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the "rain" radical (*yù*) and the phonetic component *bìlì*. Although the original scriptures contain two variant forms written with the "stone" radical as *pǐlè* (礔礰), these are vulgar usages and not the original characters.

*Móng* (蚊): The upper radical is *wù* (勿) and the phonetic is *fén* (汾). The *Fāngyán* (方言) states that in the state of Qín, the term for a small fly that bites humans was called *móng*. The *Shuōwén* writes it as *wén* (蟁); the Wú dialect pronounces it as *mín*; the canonical text writes it as *wén* (蚉), which is a vulgar character. The lower radical is pronounced *mò gēng* (莫耕). The *Shēnglèi* (聲類) states it belongs to the category of *móng* and *ruì* (small flies). It resembles a fly but is larger; the *Shuōwén* says it metamorphoses among grasses and flowers in mountains and marshes. It is also found on the bodies of deer. The large variety is called *móng*, while the small variety is called *qí* (齧), pronounced *zàn* (蹔).

The upper character "huáng" (皇) in "locust" (蝗) is a phonetic component; it refers to the flying locust. The *Erya* states: "That which eats the heart of the seedling is called míng; that which eats the leaves is called yì; that which eats the joints is called zéi; and that which eats the roots is called móu. These are all different names for the same insect. The lower character is the standard form "chóng" (蟲). The *Erya* states: "Those with legs are called chóng; those without legs are called zhài."

"Hàn-lào" (旱澇): "Hàn" (旱) is pronounced with the initial *hú* and the final *kǎo*; "lào" (澇) is pronounced with the initials *gē* and *gè*. The *Qièyùn* states that it means "scarcity of rain. The *Shuowen* explains it as composed of the radicals "sun" (日) and "shield" (干), with the lower part pronounced *láo*. The *Yupian* states it refers to "floodwaters," while the *Qièyùn* defines it as "to soak" or "to linger"; it may also be written as "lǎo" (潦). It also has the pronunciation *lǎo*, meaning "stagnant water," but this is not the usage intended here.

Regarding the "axe" (yuèfǔ): the upper part is pronounced *yuán* (as in *yuán*) and the lower part is pronounced *jǔ* (as in *jǔ*). The *Shàngshū* states: "The King’s left [hand] held a yellow axe. Confucius’s commentary notes: "It was decorated with yellow; it takes the radical 'gold' (*jīn*) and the phonetic 'guì' (*guì*); the pronunciation of 'guì' is as above. It is written as *wù* (戊), which is incorrect. The character is composed of the radical 'spear' (*gē*) and the phonetic 'jué' (*jué*). The pronunciation of 'jué' is as above. To write it as *wù* is erroneous.

*Pí* (on the ground): *fáng* (房) and *yì* (益) are the fanqie pronunciation. The *Zílín* states: "To *pí* is to stroke or strike. The *Erya* states: "*Pí* is to stroke the heart. Guo's commentary says: "This refers to beating one's breast. *Jīng'è* (startled and shocked): *wǔ* (五) and *gè* (各) are the fanqie pronunciation.

The *Yùnjí* states: "Also, *è* is to be startled. The *Shuowén* takes *xīn* (心) as the radical and *è* (咢) as the phonetic; the sound of *è* is the same as above. The *Shuowén* states that the correct form is the character *ǎi* (㖾).

*Tiao* (弔, 切韻; *tiao*, *yue*): To leap over. According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of the radical "to run" (*zou*) and the phonetic element "zhao. In the scriptural texts, it is written with the radical "foot" (*zu*) as *tiao* or *tiao*; both are vulgar characters. Below, *mo* (伯, 反): *Shenglei* states it means "to cross over. *Qieyun* states it means "to stride across. According to the *Shuowen*, it means "to mount a horse," composed of the radical "horse" (*ma*) and the phonetic element "mo."

The Sūtra of the Ritual for the Accomplishment of the Holy Krodhavajrakumāra Caṇḍa, Volume One (Part I). Regarding the character *bó* (縛) [in the title]: The *Fuyue Wang* (符籰王) reads it with the tone of *kǎo* (考), meaning "to bind. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to bind" (*shù*, 束), composed of the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *pó* (搏) in abbreviated form. The text here uses the character *zhuān* (專) to represent *bó*; this is a scribal error in the transmission. Below, it is read as *bù* (簿) [with the tone *jué* (角)]. The *Yunjí* (韻集) states it means "to pull against" (*xiāng bō*, 相𢷏). It is sometimes written as *pò* (撲) with the sound *pǔ* (普) and the tone *bǔ* (卜); this is not the character for "pulling against."

Regarding the character for "dry" (乾): the ancient pronunciation was *qian* (as indicated by the "han-fan" notation); its original phonetic value was *qian*, but it is now borrowed to serve as the character for "dry" (*gan*) in contrast to "moist. In archaic script, it was written with the "water" radical (*shui*) as *gan* (with the lower part pronounced *suo-dao-fan*). The *Yupian* states it means "to dry with fire," while the *Qieyun* states that "gan" also means "arid."
*Soma* (the character *su* is pronounced with an upper tone; it is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term, here translated as "Wondrous Arm").

*Qiūdǐn* (the first syllable is pronounced as *qiū*, the second as *yǐn*; this is the name of an insect according to the *Qieyun*). The latter is also written as *yǐn*. The *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) section of the *Book of Rites* states: "In the first month of summer, the earthworms emerge. The *Erya* states: "The *qianlin* [earthworm]. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "In Jiangdong, they are called 'cold earthworms' (*hanlin*). The pronunciation of *qian* is *qiāng yǐn fǎn*.

“Niǎo” (尿): Below the character for “niú” (牛), it is pronounced with the initial *n* and the final *-ào* (弔反). The *Kǎośēng* (考聲) states it means “to be immersed. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states it is formed from the radical “water” (水) and the phonetic “shěng” (󱷲省).

The current scriptural text uses the character “niào” (尿), which is a vulgar form used interchangeably [with the former]. “Bó” (髆): The upper part is pronounced with the initial *bó* (愽) and the final *-āng* (傭). It refers to the hip or thigh. The *Shuōwén* states it means “the shoulder blade” (肩髆) and is formed from the radical “bone” (骨) and the phonetic “zhuān” (專). The scriptural text uses the character “pó” (膊) with the radical “flesh” (肉), pronounced *pǔ bó* (普博反), meaning “dried meat”; this does not accord with the meaning of the scripture. “Yōng” (傭): The lower part is pronounced *chǒu lóng* (丑龍反). Zheng’s commentary on the *Mao Shī* (毛詩) states it means “evenness” (滽均). The *Shuōwén* states it means “straightness” (均直) and is formed from the radical “person” (人) and the phonetic “yōng” (庸). Some versions use the character “zhōng” (𦟛), a vulgar form that is also commonly accepted.

*Bèng* (to flee in haste): *shàng* (upper radical) is *běi* (北) with the *zhèng* (諍) reversal; the *Yùnjí* (韻集) states it means "to disperse"; the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to escape"; the *Shuōwén* (說文) states it is formed from *zǒu* (走) with *cāo* (𧻓) below, where *cāo* has the phonetic value *qīluàn* (七亂); the *Zílín* (字林) states it means "to flee and hide"; the *Qièyùn* (切韻) also states it means "to punish. The *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents) says, "He banished the Sanmiao to Sanwei. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to conceal"; it is a compound character (*huìyì zì*) formed from a rat inside a hole.

Volume Two: The Middle Volume of the *Āryakrodhavajrakumārasādhana-vidhi-sūtra*. Regarding the character 𦝫 (tāo): it is also used for a waist-band (*yāo*). According to the *Xiàozìlín*, it means "to weave with silk like a cord. It is composed of the radical 糸 (silk) and the abbreviated form of 條 (tiáo) as the phonetic element. The *Zītǒng* writes it as 縚; this is also used interchangeably with 縚, which is also pronounced *táodào*.

*Uṇḍura*. According to the *Yùn jí* (Rhyme Collection), "uṇ" (pronounced with the *kùn* rhyme) means to press an object into water; "nǔ" (pronounced *nèn*) is its phonetic component. "Lú" (rhyme *lí gǔ*) and "lā" (rhyme *lí zhà*)—the three characters *lú-dì-lā* are Sanskrit terms translated here as "blood."

Regarding "to ruin" (*jù huài*): the *Zuǒ Zhuan* states that "to ruin" (*jù*) also means "to destroy. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "qū" (pronounced *zǐ yú*). The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "to collapse" or "to crumble. The *Jīngǔzhèngzì* states that "to be destroyed by oneself" is called *huài*, composed of the radical "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "huái" (pronounced *huái*; meaning "to contain"). The *Shuowen* explains that the character "huái" is composed of the radical "clothing" (*yī*) and the phonetic "tán" (pronounced *tán hé*). The upper part of "tán" consists of "crossed eyes" (*héng mù*) and the lower part consists of "water" (*shuǐ*; pronounced *bié*). The text here uses "huài," which was erroneously written by scribes during transcription.

The character for *yuán* (黿) has the upper radical *yuán* (元); the *Shuowen* states it is a type of turtle. The lower part is read as *dáhé* (達河); the *Shuowen* states it is an aquatic creature shaped like a lizard (*chì*) and measuring five or six feet. It is composed of the phonetic *dàn* (單) with the radical *mǎng* (猛) and the phonetic *nà* (那). This is a character formed by combining a semantic and a phonetic component.

The characters for *guī* (tortoise) and *biè* (turtle) are as follows: Regarding *guī*: The character for "ghost" (*guǐ*) is read as *fǎn* (the opposite). The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "Guī means 'old' (*jiù*). It is that which has an outer shell and inner flesh; it follows the form of the *tuó* (a mythical serpent-like creature). The head of the tortoise resembles the *tuó*. This is the nature of Heaven and Earth. Broad-shouldered [tortoises] have no males; they belong to the class of turtles. The character for 'male' (*xióng*) uses the *tuó* as its image, representing the shape of the four legs, head, and tail. Regarding *biè*: It is read as *bī miè fǎn* (the *bī* and *miè* sounds reversed). The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "A water-dwelling crustacean. It takes the character *mǐn* (toad) as its radical and *biè* as its phonetic. There are those who write it with the fish radical as *bié*, but this is incorrect.

The character *jìn* (噤) is pronounced *qú yǐn* (上渠飲反). The *Zītǒng* states that it means the mouth is closed due to cold. The *Shuowén* explains it as consisting of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic "jin" (*jìn*). Some write it as *yù* (䫴), which is pronounced *nú è* (怒而) and means grinding one's teeth in anger; this is not the character for *jìn* (噤).

"Bhūrja" (樺皮) is the name of a tree; its bark can be used as a candle because it contains red and white fibers. The fine white fibers are suitable for writing on Buddhist scriptures (*vaṃśa-pustaka*). Since that land lacks paper, they mostly use *pattā-leaf* (貝多葉) or *tāla-leaf* (多羅葉), or else write characters upon *bhūrja-bark*.

Regarding "man-teng" (creeper): the *Wuyan Fanyun Ji* states it is a melon vine; the *Tudeng* (of the *Qieyun*) states it is a *liu-teng* herb; the *Kaosheng* states it is a *tengluo* (climbing vine).

Volume 3, Part 2: The Ritual Manual for the Accomplishment of the Holy Krodhavajrakumāra, Part 2. Regarding the term *xiè* (齧): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is derived from the character for "tooth" (*chǐ*) with the phonetic *nuò* (㓞). Its pronunciation is *kē* (口黠反). The text here uses *niè* (嚙), which is incorrect.

*Qū* (upper radical *qǐ*, *jù* reversed; the *Kǎośēng* says it means to run away, and also to pursue). The *Shī* says: "Neither galloping nor driving. The *Shuōwén* says: "From the radical *mǎ* (horse) and the phonetic *qū*. The text reads *qū*; this is a vulgar character. *Bì* (lower radical *bì*, *rèn* reversed): The *Qièyùn* says it means to expel (*bìn*). The *Jixùn* says it means to abandon. The *Shuōwén* says: "From the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *bīn*."

The character 𥳋 (top part) is pronounced *tān* (as in *tān-fǎn*); the *Yùnjí* states it refers to the head of grain. It is also pronounced *hàn* (as in *hàn-fǎn*), meaning "to attach. It is composed of the radical 竹 (*zhú*) and the phonetic 參 (*cān*).

The character 脚鋜 (bottom part): the lower radical is read as *shìjiǎo* (as in *shìjiǎo-fǎn*). Gù Yěwáng states it means "an iron shackle for the feet. The *Yùnlüè* states it means "a foot-iron. It is composed of the radical 金 (*jīn*) and the phonetic 浞 (*zhuó*, written here in abbreviated form). The scriptural text writes it as 鎙; this is a vulgar variant, sometimes also pronounced *shuò*, which belongs to the category of spears (*gē*) and is not used here. The pronunciation of 浞 is the same as above.

Regarding the character below "arrowhead" (箭鏃), it is pronounced as *mù* (木) with a retroflex final. The *Erya* states: "A metal-pointed arrow with trimmed feathers is called a *hòu*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "This refers to the *pī* arrows used today. *Hòu* is pronounced *hóu*; *pī* is pronounced *pī*.

The Ritual for the Recitation of the Greatly Efficacious and Accomplished King Yamāntaka, the Holy Wrathful King. One fascicle. Regarding the character for *shuò* (槊) in the seal-script: the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to make a spear. The *Tongsu Wenzhang* says that a *máo* (矛) measuring one *zhàng* and eight *chǐ* in length is called a *shuò*. The script in the sutra uses the character with the metal radical (*zī*, 鎙), which is not the common usage. [The phonetic] below is *yú* (於). The *Yunjí* says it refers to a "seal" (*fuyìn*). The *Shìmíng* says: "A seal (*yìn*) is 'trust' (*xìn*). It is 'because' (*yīn'). When an object is sealed, it is because one is entrusting trust to it. It is composed of the radicals for "claw" (*zhuǎo*) and "node" (*jié*). In ancient script, it was written as *bó* (󱰑). The sound of *jié* is *jiē* (節).

The day of the planet荧惑 (Yinghuo) is the same as the day of Mars (火星). The *Five Planets’ Secret Instructions on Mutual Communication* states: "Yinghuo is the essence of fire from the south; it is also called the Star of Punishment (罰星). Its diameter is seventy li, its color is red and luminous, and its movement takes two years to complete one circuit of the heavens. This has already been fully explained in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (仁王經).
*She-dǒ-lú*, or as it is also called *shuài-dǒ-lú*, or *shè-duō-lú*, are all phonetic corruptions of a Sanskrit term;

this is translated here as "banner" (*yùnjia*). From the *Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa-rāja-sūtra*, Chapter on the Golden-Winged Bird King, Volume One: "Bāozhì" (the first character is pronounced with the initial *bì* and rhyme *yáo*; according to the *Kǎoshēng*, *biāo* means "to raise up," or it may be written with the radical for wood as *biāo*; the scriptural character is *biāo* with the radical for hand, which is a vulgar form). The second character, *chāngzhì*, is pronounced with the final *zhì*. According to the *Zìshū*, *chì* refers to a banner atop a standard; it is composed of the radical for cloth and the phonetic element *zhì*.

*Zàn* (upper character) is pronounced *jiān* (with the rhyme of *xiàn*); the *Shuowen* states it is written with *zàn* and means to sprinkle or soil. *Sǎ* (lower character) is pronounced *shā yǎ*; it also means to scatter and sprinkle, sharing the same definition as the character *zàn*. *Rìyǐ* (upper character) has the pronunciation *yì*;

(lower character) has the pronunciation *yǐ*. Gu Yewang says it is the "thousand-bead" plant. The *Bencao* says that *yìcí* is temperate in nature and primarily treats the rigidity of tendons and bones where they cannot be extended or bent. Furthermore, the two characters for *yìqì* (beneficial qi) both follow the radical for grass; *yì* takes *yǐ* as its phonetic.

*Yíng* (upper character pronounced *yī*, lower character pronounced *ráo*). The *Mao Shi Zhuan* states that it means "to extend. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to gather and bind," composed of the radical *mì* (silk) with the phonetic *yíng* (abbreviated). *Rào* means "to entwine," composed of the radical *mì* with the phonetic *yáo*.

The *Five-Syllable Dhāraṇī Stotra*, one fascicle. *Sǒnglì* (竦慄): "Sǒng" (竦) is pronounced with the initial *xī* and the final *gǒng*. According to the *Erya*, "sǒng" means fear. The *Shijing* says: "Not trembling, not sǒng. "Lì" (慄) is pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final *zhì*. Regarding its sound, it refers to quivering with fear. The *Shijing* says: "Trembling and anxious. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) and the phonetic "piào" (*piao*).

*Tìqì* (weeping): "Tà" (上) is pronounced *tāi* with the *lǐ* rhyme; the *Yùnjí* states it refers to tears from the eyes. In ancient and modern standard characters, it is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the phonetic "dì" (*dì*). "Qì" (下) is pronounced *jí*; the *Qièyùn* defines it as wailing. The *Jíxùn* explains that to shed tears silently is called *qì*.

*Qi* (泚): The *shàng* tone is *shàn*, and the *lǐ* tone is *fǎn*. This is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term. According to the characters, it describes the appearance of water that is deep and clear.

In the *Amoghapāśa-mahābhiṣeka-prabhāsa-mantra-sūtra* (一卷), it is stated: "The *Amoghapāśa-mahābhiṣeka-prabhāsa-mantra-sūtra* in one fascicle. Regarding *shé* (虵): the *shàng* tone is *shè*, and the *zhē* tone is *fǎn*. The *Mao Shi* says: "Only the *huǐ* (蜥蜴) and the *shé* (蛇). The *Zhou Yi* says: "The *shé* belongs to the category of *zhài* (creeping creatures). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is written with the radical *tuó* (它); *tuó* is pronounced *tú hé fǎn*, and the following character is *xǔ yè fǎn*. It is the name of a venomous insect.
*Mitara* (the *ra* is pronounced with the *da* and *ke* reversed; it is a Sanskrit term meaning "corpse of a dead person").
*Vajraśekhara Trailokyavijaya Mañjuśrī Five-Syllable Mantra Supreme Aspect*, one fascicle; no phonetic glosses available.

The Ritual for the Recitation of Vajrapāṇi-Ālokiteśvara-Mahācaṇḍa-rāja, in one fascicle. Regarding the character *suǎn* (痠): The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states that it means "aching pain. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "bone pain. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states it is composed of the radical *nà* (疒) and the phonetic *suǎn* (酸, abbreviated). Regarding the character *chǔ* (憷): The *Yīnpǔ* (音譜) states it means "pain. Gù Yěwáng (顧野王) states it means "sharpness of heart" (*xīnlì*). It is composed of the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *chǔ* (楚). Its pronunciation is also *chū* (初) with the departing tone. In the canonical texts, it is sometimes written simply as *chǔ*; this refers to "Jingchu" (荊楚). It is also the name of a province, but it is not the original character [for the meaning of pain].

Fúróng (芙蓉): the upper character is pronounced fáng (防) and the lower yúfēng (餘封). It refers to the lotus. The *Erya* states: "Hé (荷) is fúqú (芙渠). Guo's commentary notes that it is also called fúróng; in Jiangdong, it is called hé. The *Commentary on the Mao Shih* states: "That which has not yet opened is called fúróng; that which has already opened is called hǎndàn."

*Bhagavat*: the first syllable is pronounced with a departing tone (rising tone), and the second is a transcription of the vernacular Sanskrit; formerly it was called *Bāgavā*, or *Bójiǎfàn* (薄伽梵), or also *Bójiǎbàn* (薄伽伴); all of these are corruptions. This is translated as "World-Honored One" (*Shìzūn*), which is a collective name for six meanings.

*Śakti*: the first character is pronounced *shuó* (with the initial *sh-*) and the second is pronounced *dǐ* (with the initial *d-*); this is a Sanskrit term, which here means "spear. The scripture states that one "grasps a *śakti* in the hand," referring to the spear or lance held by the King of Wrathful Power (*Krodharāja*). Regarding the second character *dǐ*, some versions of the scripture read it with the initial *zhǐ*; however, this is not the original Sanskrit pronunciation.

*Vajra*. (The first *vajra* is pronounced with an aspirated *r*, and the two *vajra*s are pronounced as a single combined sound. In the original Sanskrit, it is correctly called *vajra*; formerly it was transliterated as *vaja-ra* or *bajra*. This translates as "Diamond" (*jīngāng*). According to the sutras, "holding the *vajra*" refers to the *vajra* held by the Honored One Acala (Unmoving).

The Ritual for the Recitation of the Lotus Family for the Accomplishment of the Great Compassion of Avalokiteśvara, in one fascicle. *Kang-pi* (糠粃): The upper character, *kang*, is pronounced with the *ku* and *gang* finals; it is also written as *kang*. The *Yunlüe* states that it refers to the husks of rice. The lower character, *pi*, is pronounced with the *bu* and *ji* finals; it is also written as *bi*. Gu Yewang states that it refers to grain that has not ripened. The *Guoyu* states: "An army should have no *bang-kang* (unripe grain). Both characters share the same radical, *禾* (grain).

Regarding the character *jí* (棘): the upper part is pronounced *jì* (力反) and the *Yùnjí* states it is the name of a small jujube tree; the lower part is also written as *cì* (㓨), pronounced *qī cì fǎn*. The *Erya* states: "Cào (茦) is *cì* (刺). Guo Pu’s commentary says: "It refers to the needle-like thorns of grasses. The pronunciation of *cào* is *chū gé fǎn*. The *Fāngyán* states: "Any grass or wood that pricks a person is called *cì*."

The character for *zhàng* (脹) is pronounced with the upper radical *zhī* (知) and *liàng* (亮) as the phonetic; the *Kǎośēng* (*Kǎoshēng*) states it means "full. In the *Qièyùn*, it means "swelling at the elbow," composed of the radical *ròu* (肉) and the abbreviated form of *zhāng* (張) as the phonetic; the lower part is pronounced *sū lái* (蘇來). The *Shuōwén* defines *sāi* (腮) as the jaw; *hàn* (頷) is pronounced *hú gǎn* (胡感). Lexicons state it refers to the cheek. The version in the scripture uses *sāi* (腮), which is a vulgar character.

Regarding "跣足" (xiǎn zú): the *Jíxùn* states that it means the feet are in direct contact with the ground; it is composed of the radical "foot" (足) with "xiān" as the phonetic component. The character below is "jí yù" (即玉). The *Erya* says it refers to the toes; it is composed of "kǒu" (口) and "zhǐ" (止). The form used in the scriptures is "zú" (足); this was altered by scribes through cursive writing and is incorrect.

One should step down with the foot; the *Shuowen* states that this character denotes the appearance of walking while placing the foot upon the ground, composed of the radical "foot" (足) and the phonetic "da" (沓), with the pronunciation of "da" being the same as above. It is also written as "ta" (蹋); the *Qieyun* states it means to kick or tread upon. According to the sutra, it should be the character "ta" (蹋); however, when written as "ta" (踏), the pronunciation is also "tada" (他荅反).

*Ji-pèi*: The upper character is pronounced *wū huī* (烏恢反); the *Shuowen* states it is an ornament of five-colored silk, formed with the radical *mì* (糸) and the phonetic *wēi* (畏). The lower character is pronounced *pú mèi* (蒲妹反); the *Yunying* states it refers to jade pendants (*yùpèi*). The *Liji* says: "The superior man of antiquity necessarily used jade pendants to compare his virtue [with them]."

Regarding "xiāng-ruí" (香緌): the upper character is pronounced *xǔ* (許) with the *liáng* (良) rhyme. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "fragrant aroma" (*xiāngfēn*). Its correct form is from the radical *shǔ* (黍); its variants *jìn* (𪏽) or *xiāng* (薌) refer to the fragrance of grain. The text’s use of the radical *cǎo* (草) to form *yú* (萫) is not the original character; the lower part is pronounced *rú* (儒) with the *jiā* (佳) rhyme. The *Yupian* states it refers to the tassels of a crown. The *Erya* says, "huī-ruí" (褘緌). Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "It is a fragrant tassel. It is so named because the interlaced sash is fastened to the body. It belongs to the radical *mì* (糸) with the phonetic *wěi* (委). The text’s use of *ruí* (蕤) is actually the name of a medicinal herb, *weirui* (葳蕤). Furthermore, *ruibin* (蕤賓) is the name of the *lüguǎn* (律管) for the fifth month. According to the scripture, [the Bodhisattva] adorns the body of the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara with *jù* (䋿), *dài* (𤧑), *xiāng* (香), and *ruí* (緌). To use the characters *yú* (萫) and *ruí* (蕤) greatly deviates from the intent of the scripture.

The character 𣱦 (fen) has "fu" as its upper radical and "yun" as its lower radical. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "fen-yun" refers to auspicious vapors; it is also written as "fen-yuan" (qi). Both characters are composed of the radical "qi" (the phonetic for "qi") with "fen" and "yun" as their respective phonetic components. The pronunciation of "qi" is that of "qi" (breath/vapor).

"Huàn jiǎ" (to don armor). The character "huàn" is pronounced with the *shàngshēng* (rising tone) and is glossed as "guàn" (to pierce) in the *Zílín*. Both the phonetic transcription and the gloss in the *Shìwén* are identical. According to the *Wǔjīng Zìyàng*, the pronunciation is "gǔ huàn" (ancient reading: guàn). The subsequent character "jiǎ" (armor) may also be written as "jiǎ" with the radical "jīn" (metal), forming "jià," which is also acceptable.

*Guān-zì-zài Rú-yì-lún Yú-jia* (The Yoga of Avalokiteśvara’s Wish-Fulfilling Wheel), one fascicle. Regarding "xián" (閒): The *Shànggǔ Yùnjí* (Ancient Pronunciation Collection) states it means a mountain stream or ravine. The *Erya* says: "A valley where mountains flank water is called a *jiàn* (澗). It is also written as "jiàn" (澗); this vulgar usage is also acceptable. Regarding "gǔ" (古): The *Pǔmíng* (Jade Lexicon) states it refers to a mountain valley. The *Erya* says: "Water flowing into a gully is called a *gǔ* (谷). Furthermore, "gǔ" (谷) means to nourish. As the *Laozi* says: "The spirit of the valley does not die; this is the Mysterious Female."

Regarding "nǔxíng" (naked form): the upper character is pronounced *huā* (with the *wǎ* rhyme) to avoid vulgar taboos, hence this pronunciation. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, its original pronunciation was *lángguǒ*; Gu Yewang states that "nǔ" means to remove clothes and expose the body, derived from the radical for "clothing" (*yī*) with the phonetic component *guǒ*. The scriptural text uses the character *shēn* (body) to form *nuǒ* (also written as *lě*), both of which are vernacular usages. There are also scriptures where it is written with the radical for "divinity" (*shì*) as *luàn*, pronounced *guàn*; this fails to convey the meaning of the character and is an error in transcription.

The Ritual for the Contemplative Recitation and Practice of the Bodhisattva’s Prajñāpāramitā, one fascicle. *Che-ji* (掣擊): The *Yunquan* states that "che" (掣) means to pull; the *Zishu* states it means to draw. It is also pronounced with the initial *chāng* and final *zhì*. "Ji" (擊) has the ancient reading *gǔ-lì*. The *Quanyun* defines it as striking or hitting. The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "kei" (𣪠); the sound of "kei" is *qì*.

The Ritual Manual for the Practice of Samantabhadra from the *Vajraśekhara Tāvatṃsaka-vaśavartin-lalita-vistara-parivarta*, one fascicle. "Lotus root" (*lián gēn*): This refers to the "five mouths" (*wǔ kǒu*) of the lotus fiber (*lián sī*). The *Erya* states: "The *fúqú* has the lotus root (*ǒu*) as its root. Guo's commentary says: "It is also called *fúróng*; in Jiangdong it is called *hé*."

*Kiǎo*: In ancient times, the pronunciation was *xiá* (according to the *Yīnpǔ*, it means armor or mail). The *Wǔjīng Wénzì* records it as written simply as *jiǎ* (armor), meaning "military armor. Below, it is also written with the two forms *tiáo* and *tāo*, meaning "cotton or silk rope," and is also pronounced *tādào*.

*Mālīkīdevatāpuṣpamālya-sūtra*. *Mālīkīdevatāpuṣpamālya-sūtra*, one fascicle. "Finger" (zhǐ): In the *Shàngzhí* (upper volume), it is pronounced with the rhyme of *chì* (雉). The *Yùnlüè* (Rhyme Compendium) states it means a finger; it also means to point (*zhǐhuī*) or to dismiss (*chì*). The lower character is pronounced with the rhyme of *gǔqiǎo* (古巧). The *Yùpiān* (Jade Chapter) says it means the movement of a hand. The *Shuōwén* (Explanations of Words and Texts) states it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "jué" (*jué*).

*Suōhè* (馺𩣯): The second character is pronounced with the *sū* and *hé* rhymes; it is a term from the Sanskrit language. According to the dictionary, *suōhè* describes the appearance of a horse galloping swiftly. *Hùshù* (槲樹): The first character is pronounced with the *hú* and *gǔ* rhymes;

it is the name of a tree. Examining its phonetics, its leaves resemble those of the pine but are finer. The *Erya* states: "The *cùpòxīn* (樕撲心)"; Guo’s commentary notes that *hù* and *cù* are alternative names for this tree, with the phonetic component *hú*. The text of the scripture uses the character *gǔ* (穀), which is also used interchangeably.

The Essential Method for Recitation of the Golden Wheel Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, one fascicle; The Ritual for the Altar of the Painted Image of the Great Peacock Vidyārājñī, one fascicle; The Yoga Vajraśekhara Explanation of the Chapter on the Alphabet, one fascicle. The three scriptures listed above have no phonetic transcriptions or glosses available.

The Dharma of the Great Sage Deity, the Twin-bodied Vināyaka, in one fascicle. Regarding "Vināyaka," formerly it was transliterated as "Pināyaka," both of which are incorrect Sanskrit forms. It should be pronounced *Vaineyaka* (the first syllable *vai* is pronounced as *wei*, the second *na* as *ya*, and the third *ka* as *ca*). This means "Obstructing Deity" (*zàng'ài shén*); it refers to one who manifests with a human body and an elephant head, capable of obstructing all superior undertakings.

*Tóng* (copper): Upper radical *tú* (徒), reversed *hóng* (紅). The *Yùnyùn* (Rhyme Dictionary) states it is the first grade of metal. The *Shānhǎijīng* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states that on Mount Nǚlín, the southern slopes abound in red copper. The *Shuōwén* (Explanations of Characters) states it is "red metal," composed of the radical *jīn* (metal) with *tóng* (same) as its phonetic component; the lower part is read as *shìruò* (市若). The *Yùnlüè* (Concise Rhyme Dictionary) states it refers to cups and ladles, composed of the radical *mù* (wood) with *sháo* (勺) as its phonetic component; *sháo* has the pronunciation *zhé* (斫).

*Jūn* (㪻): Upper radical *yóu* (油), upper phonetic *jū* (居) with the variant *yuàn* (怨); the character dictionary states that *lù* (欥) means to scoop up things, following the radical *dǒu* (斗) and the phonetic *luán* (䜌). The pronunciation of *lù* (欥) is *yǐzhǎo* (以沼). It also means to scoop. *Lúbò* (蘿蔔):

Upper phonetic *luó* (羅), lower phonetic *pú* (蒲) with the variant *běi* (北); this is a vulgar character. The *Erya* (爾雅) calls it *lúbó* (蘆菔). Guo Pu’s commentary states: "The *lúbó* belongs to the category of *wúqīng* (蕪菁). It has purple flowers, large leaves, and a root that can be eaten. The *Bencao* (本草) states: "Its nature is cold and sharp; it can remove noxious vapors from the five viscera (*wǔzàng*). Consuming it makes one white and clean. Furthermore, it counteracts the toxicity of flour. If one has overeaten, it may be eaten raw."

*Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle; *The Vajraśekhara Yoga of the Supreme Three Secrets of Trailokyavijaya*, one fascicle; and according to the catalog, *The Mahāyāna Treatise on Dependent Origination*, one fascicle. These three scriptures above all lack phonetic transcriptions or glosses.
