*Continuation of the Pronunciation of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, twenty fascicles.
The above, from the first to the twentieth fascicle, are identical to this volume in their continuation of the pronunciation.

Volume One, Part One: The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School. Volume One. *Lai-huang* (痿黃): *Lai* (痿) is pronounced with the *zhui* (隹) radical; it refers to the disease of dampness (*shibing*). The *Jixun* (集訓) states it means "the feet cannot reach [the ground]. The *Shiming* (釋名) says it is "withering" (*weiyi*); like the leaves of grass and trees that wither and die upon the earth. It is formed with the *na* (疒) radical and the phonetic *wei* (委). The lower character *hu* (胡) has the pronunciation *guang* (光). The *Erya* (爾雅) calls it the "disease of *xuan-huang*" (玄黃). Guo’s commentary states: "*Xuan-huang*" is a general term for human diseases; those who explain it as a disease of horses have lost its true meaning.

Regarding the term *jiàocuì* (憔顇): the upper character is pronounced *qiáo* (齊遙反) and the lower is *suì* (情遂反). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that *jiàocuì* means emaciated and wretched. The *Cāngjiépiān* (蒼頡篇) writes it as *qiáocuì* (憔悴), explaining it as sorrow and anxiety. The *Máoshī* (毛詩) uses the "speech" radical (*yán*) to write it as *qiáosuì* (譙誶). Bān Gù uses the "sickness" radical (*nà*) to write it as *chāocuì* (癄瘁). Emperor Wǔ’s *Lìfùrén Fù* (李夫人賦) uses the "woman" radical (*nǚ*) to write it as *tiāocuì* (嫶𡝵). The *Zuǒzhuan* uses the "grass" radical (*cǎo*) to write it as *jiāocuì* (蕉萃). Since there is no single standard form across these various texts, the current scriptural text mostly uses *jiàocuì*.

Regarding the character *yǔ* (蘡薁): the first radical is pronounced *yì* or *yíng*; the second is pronounced *yú* or *liù*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that it is the name of a plant that can be eaten, resembling the grape (*pútú*) but smaller, with black berries. The *Shuōwén* states that both characters are composed of the "grass" (*cǎo*) radical, with *yīng* and *ào* serving as their phonetic components respectively.

Regarding *bīngzhū* (椶櫚): the upper character is pronounced *hóng* (red) with the *fǎn* (rhyme) *guǎn*, and the lower character is pronounced *lì* (force) with the *fǎn* *jū*. The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states that it is the name of a type of tree. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states: "The *bīngzhū* tree has leaves but no branches; both characters are derived from the radical 'wood' (*mù*), with *zhū* (㚇) serving as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of *bīng* is *bìng*.

Regarding the *nārikela* (yēzǐ): the *Yùnjí* states that "nārikela" is the name for a fruit-bearing tree; its leaves are similar on both the front and back surfaces. It grows in Jiaozhi and on islands in the sea. Its large fruits can be made into vessels. It belongs to the "wood" radical and is pronounced with the sound "yé."

*Chāngpú* (菖蒲): the first character is pronounced *shàng* (上) with the *qiǎo* (巧) rhyme group followed by *chí* (尺) and *liáng* (良) as the initial; the second character is pronounced *xià* (下) with *bó* (薄) and *hú* (胡) as the initials. According to the *Qièyùn*, *chāngpú* is the name of a herb resembling orchid (*lán*) that can be used to make mats. The *Běncǎo* states that *chāngpú* is a medicinal name; its roots are harvested in the eighth month, and those with one hundred nodes are considered superior. *Lán* (蘭) is pronounced *liáng* (良) with *rèn* (刃) as the initial.

*Miàn* (麥): The upper radical is *mǎng* (猛); the *Shuowen* states it is the husk of wheat. The *Fangyan* says it is what is now called "barley" (*dàmài*). The lower radical is *zhí* (職). This character does not appear in the *Zishu*. The *Xin Zilin* states that *yì* (󱆄) is the awn of wheat. Examining the character *mài* (麥), it has been written with the *zōu* (夂) radical since ancient times. The *Baihūtong* states: "Wheat is metal (*jīn*). It grows when metal is dominant and dies when fire is dominant. *Míng* (𪍿) takes *kuàng* (礦) as its abbreviated phonetic; *yì* (󱆄) takes *yì* (弋) as its phonetic complement. The pronunciation of *jiǔ* (久) is *suī* (雖).

"Hang-tun" (the first character read as *k'ang* in the ancient pronunciation and the second as *tu-lun*; this is a vulgar character, the correct form being *t'un*) refers to a large fish in the rivers and seas. Its shape resembles that of a *shu* (a type of water-demon), hence it is so named. When wind and waves are about to arise, this fish first emerges upon the surface of the water; its appearing and disappearing in an instant indicates that a storm is coming.

*Jiāo* (鮫): Ancient pronunciation *xiáo*. The *Shuowen* states it is the name of a sea fish; its skin has patterns that can be used to ornament knives and swords. It is composed of the radical "fish" (*yú*) and the phonetic "jiāo" (交). The lower character *yǔ* (語) has the ancient pronunciation *jū*. The *Shuowen* states it is an aquatic creature. It is composed of the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and the element *zào* (𧢲), forming *zhǎo* (鰍). The *Erya* says: "The intestines of a fish are called *yǐ* (乙); the tail of a fish is called *bǐng* (丙). Guo’s commentary states: "Both resemble characters from the seal script, and they were named accordingly."

*Chuāng* (瘡): The upper radical is *chǔ* (楚, with the *liáng* [良] rhyme). In ancient texts it is written as *chuàng* (創) or *chēng* (𭃅), meaning "to break with a blade. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "A *chuāng* is a wound (*shāng*)," meaning that the body has sustained a breakage or injury. The *Lǐjì* (禮記) says: "If there is a *chuāng* on the head, one washes the hair. The lower character is pronounced *jiè* (介). It is also written as *jiè* (疥). The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "a scab" (*sào*). It is composed of the *nà* (疒) radical and the phonetic *jiè*. Writing it as *jiè* (疥) is likewise correct.
*Śāla* (the first character pronounced as *shā* with the second character having the sound *nǚ lín*): a name for a fruit tree in the Sanskrit language.
*Sāvitra* (the first character pronounced as *sū dāo*): in the Sanskrit language, this means a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*).

*Ding* (橜): Pronounced *ding* (丁) with the final rhyme *-deng*; the sound is derived from *ding* (丁), meaning to nail or fasten wood. The lower character is pronounced *qi* (其) with the final rhyme *-yue* (月); the *Yunlüe* (韻略) states it means a wooden stake (*yi*). The *Erya* (爾雅) says: "That which is in the ground is called an *nie* (臬). Guo Pu’s commentary states: "This refers to the gate-stake (*men-que*). It is also written as the character *jue* (橛).

*Ōu* (逆): Upper radical *wū* with the phonetic *kǒu*; the rhyme is *tù*. It means to vomit; it is also written as *òu* with the same meaning. The *Shílì Běncǎo* states that pig gallbladder stops dry vomiting (*qián-òu*). *Yì* (上): Upper radical *yáng* with the phonetic *shì*;

the rhyme is *shì*. The *Erya* says: "The *mó* is called *yì*. Guō's commentary states: "It is the same as *què* (a wooden peg). It is also written as *yí*, with the same definition. The *Fāngyán* notes that in the north, people call a *què* a *mó*. The pronunciation of *mó* is *chí*.

*Jia* (家): The character is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* and rhyme *yá*. The *Erya* states: "The space between the window and the door is called *yi*; that which is inside it is called *jia*. The *Shuowen* explains: "*Jia* means 'dwelling' (*jū*). The character consists of *mián* (莫仙反) above and a simplified form of *jiā* (豭, 古牙反) as the phonetic component. *Mián* (莫仙反) denotes the appearance of a deep chamber; *jiā* (音古牙反, 下即移反) denotes 'wealth' according to the *Shuowen*, or 'property,' composed of the radical *bèi* (貝) and the phonetic *cǐ* (此)."

*Upādhyāya* (the first syllable pronounced as *shàng-ān-gǔ* or alternatively as *yù-pō-dì-yē*; these are variations in the weight of the Sanskrit vowels) translates into Chinese as "One Who Is Recited Near" (*jìn-sòng*). This is because, as a disciple is young, they do not leave the teacher but constantly follows and stays near them to receive and recite [the teachings]. *Upādhyāya* is also translated as "Intimate Instructor" (*qīn-jào*). The older translation "One Who Knows Offenses and Knows Non-offenses" (*zhī-zuì zhī-wú-zuì*) is termed *Huánshàng*. Alternatively, it is called *Héshá*, which are corruptions and phonetic shifts occurring in countries such as Khotan; these are not the elegant terminology of India itself.

The upper character "gē" (割) means to split; the *Erya* states it means "to tear asunder. The *Yunjí* says it means "to flay" and also "to cut off. The lower part is pronounced *bànglǐ* (傍禮); this is a vulgar form. The correct character is "qī" (䯗), which means the thigh; it is composed of the radical "bone" (骨) with the phonetic "bǐ" (坒). The sound of "bǐ" is like that of "bǐ" (比).

*Jì* (famine). In ancient script, it was written as 𩚮 and also as 饑; they share the same pronunciation, *jǐ zhì* (the latter being pronounced *jìn*). The *Erya* states: "When the grains do not ripen, it is called *jì*. Guo's commentary says: "The five grains do not come to fruition. It further states: "When the vegetables do not ripen, it is called *jìn*. The commentary notes: "All grasses and herbs that can be eaten are collectively termed *shū* (vegetables). The *Guliang Zhuan* of the *Chunqiu* states: "When two grains fail to reach a full harvest, it is called *jì*; when three grains fail to reach a full harvest, it is called *jìn*; when five grains fail to reach a full harvest, it is called a *zāi* (calamity). [The character for] *zāi* is the standard form of the character *zāi*.

*Wēng* (剜): The upper character is pronounced with the *wǔ* rhyme of *huán*. The *Pīcāng* states that *wēn* is synonymous with *guā* (to cut). The meaning is the same in the *Guǎngyá*. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to gouge" (*tiāo*), composed of the radical *dāo* (knife) and the phonetic *yín* (𡖅, pinyin: yán). The character *wēn* used in the scripture is a vulgar form.

Volume 2, Part 2, *Mūla-bhaiṣajya-vastu*, Volume 2. *Kalandaka* (the latter syllable pronounced as *jiāngqiē*; formerly transcribed as *Jiālántuó* or *Jiālántuójiā*, both being corruptions of the Sanskrit term). The original term is *Kalandaka*, which means "bird with a beautiful voice. This refers to a large bamboo grove on the outskirts of Rājagṛha where this bird frequently dwells; thus, it was named after the bird.

*Huàn* (痔): The upper character is pronounced with the *hú* rhyme-group and the *guàn* final; it is an onomatopoeic term for illness. The *Jìxùn* states it means "sorrow. The *Qièyùn* defines it as "bitterness" or "evil. The *Shuōwén* explains it as "composed of the radical *xīn* (heart) and the phonetic *huàn*; the sound of *huàn* is *gǔ huàn*. The lower character is pronounced *zhí lǐ*. The *Qièyùn* defines it as "the disease of leakage. The *Kǎoshēng* states it is "a disease of the posterior. The *Shuōwén* explains it as "composed of the radical *nà* (sickness) and the abbreviated phonetic *zhì*; the sound of *nà* is *nǚ è*. *Li* (裏): The *Qièyùn* defines it as "the disease of leakage. The *Kǎoshēng* states it is "a disease of the rear. The *Shuōwén* explains it as "composed of the radical *nà* (sickness) and the abbreviated phonetic *zhì*; the sound of *nà* is *nǚ è*."

Vaiśālī (the "Śā" in the original text is pronounced as *pú* with a reversed *jì*; in Sanskrit it is also called Vaiśālī; formerly translated as Vye-ye-li or Pi-ye-li, all of which are corruptions and abbreviations). This is translated as "City of Vast Purity" (*Guǎngyánchéng*), so named because this city was the largest, most expansive, and most magnificent within the borders of Central India.
Vārāṇasī (also pronounced Póluónàisī; formerly transcribed as Póluónài) is a name for a country in the Western Regions, derived from the Sanskrit language.
*Tṛṇa* (transcribed as Dímiáo) is also the name of a country in the Western Regions; because that country produces this grass in great abundance, it was named after it.

The first character, *chū* (樗), is pronounced with the initial *chǔ* (丑) and the final *jū* (居); the *Erya* states that it is the mountain *chū* (*kǎo shānchū*). The second character, *pú* (蒱), is pronounced with the initial *bó* (薄) and the final *hú* (胡); the *Erya* says it is the *yángpú* (楊蒱) or willow; Guo’s commentary notes that it can be used for making arrows. According to the *Bowuzhi*, the two characters *chūpú* refer to a game of dice; it records that when Laozi entered the Hu lands, he created the game of *chūpú*.

*Yán* (鉛) [upper radical: 金, phonetic: 專, zhuan]. In the *Yùpiān*, it is said that lead is a blue metal; the *Shàngshū* states that Qīngzhōu contributed lead as tribute. The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of the radical 金 and the phonetic 專. The text here reads *líng* (鈴), which is a vulgar character; its lower part is pronounced *xiān* (先) with the *qì* (戚) rhyme, and it is also a type of lead. The *Ěryá* says, "Tin is called *yǎn* (鈏). Guò Pǔ’s commentary states it is white tin (*báilà*). The *Shuōwén* says it is between *láng* (鋃) and *xī* (錫), composed of the radical 金 and the phonetic 易. The pronunciation of *yǎn* (鈏) is *yìrěn* (弋忍).

"Jiāncuò" (間錯): "jiān" is read as *shànggǔ xiàn* (上古莧) in the *Erya*, which states that "jiān" means "alternation. In the *Yupian*, it is *jiān* with the *qièyùn* (rhyme category) *cì*; in the *Yunji*, it means "to alternate," "to separate," or "to intermingle. Regarding "cuò," the *Kaosheng* states that east and west constitute "jiāo" (crossing), while up and down constitute "cuò" (intermingling). The character in the legal texts is written with the "silk" radical (*miè*) as *fán* (𦅘), which is identical to *guī* (橺). In the *Qièyùn*, this is categorized as *jūn* (桾), but it does not carry the meaning of "jiāncuò" (intermingling).

The elder sister-in-law (sǎo) was surprised that Sū Hào had reacted in such a way. The *Erya*, "Explanation of Kinship" (*Shiqin*), states: "The wife of one's elder brother is called sǎo; the wife of one's younger brother is called fù. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is formed from the radical for woman and the phonetic element *sǒu*; it is also written as sǎo, which is an archaic form, while the form used in legal statutes (*lüwén*)—written with the radical for woman and the phonetic element *gèng*—is a vulgar character. The second character, *guài* (古壞反), according to the *Yunji*, means "strange"; it is also written as the character *guài*.

"Huāng-hù" (恍惚): the first character is pronounced with the initial *hǔ* and the final rhyme *huǎng*; the second is pronounced with the initial *hū* and the final rhyme *gǔ*. The *Zìlín* states that it means "the mind is not clear. The *Lǎozǐ* says, "Vague and indistinct, yet within it there is something. Both characters are written with the radical for "heart" (*xīn*); the latter is pronounced *guāng* or *hù*, and is sometimes written as *hù*.

Volume 3, Part 3: The Fundamental Medicine Section (Mūlavyākaraṇa-bhaiṣajyavastu), Volume Three. *Uddāna* (the Sanskrit term is pronounced with the initial *u* as in "wu" [in the sense of "upper"] and the second syllable as "tu" [in the sense of "ke"]—this translates into Chinese as "Collection" (*saṃgraha*), "Compendium," "Summary," or alternatively "Footprints" (*padapāda*), or "Uddāna"; these are all translations according to their respective meanings and refer to the verses (*gāthā*).

*Kuáng-lì* (獷戾): The upper character is pronounced *měng* (猛) with an ancient reading; dictionaries define it as "evil. Gu Yewang states that it refers to a dog that cannot be relied upon. The lower character is pronounced *lì* (計) with an initial *l-*. The *Erya* defines it as "crime," while the *Qieyun* defines it as "contrariety. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "crookedness. The character is composed of the radical "dog" (*quán*) with the element "door" (*hù*) below it. Both characters share the "dog" radical. In legal texts, the character *kǔ* (穬) is formed with the "grain" (*huó*) radical; this refers to the grain *fū* (𦬆) and is not the same as *kuáng-lì*.

*Luó* (羅): In the *Shànglǔ* (上魯), it is pronounced with the rhyme *hé* (何). The *Yùnlüè* (韻略) states it means "net. The *Shī* (詩) says, "I have encountered these hundred nets" (*féng cǐ bǎi luó*). The *Ěryǎ* (爾雅) states, "The bird-catcher's net is called *luó*. It is also written as *luó* (羅) with the phonetic *qí liàng* (其亮). The *Shuōwén* (說文) defines it as "an implement for catching beasts," composed of the radical *gōng* (弓) and the abbreviated phonetic *liàng* (諒).

*Vihāra*: the sound *ha* may be pronounced as *he*; it is a phonetic shift from the Sanskrit term, which is translated here as "temple" (*si*). Alternatively, it is called *saṃghārāma*, which is translated as "monastic garden. The Vinaya states that constructing five hundred *vihāras* refers to building five hundred temples.

Regarding the term for "ship" (shànghuǐ): according to local dialects, it is called *chuán* in the Gōngdōng region and *zhōu* in the Guānxī region. The *Shuowén* states that it is composed of the radical "boat" (*zhōu*) and the phonetic element "yuán" (abbreviated) with the sound *yuán* (homophonous with *zhuān*). The "yuán" in "along the road" (*yánlù*) and the "xián" in "lead" (*qiānxī*) are both modeled after this. In the legal statutes (*lǜwén*), the characters used as "guān" (official) are written as *chuán* or *huán*; these are all vulgar forms. The character pronounced *mò* (as in *mòjiǎn*) refers to a large ship; it is composed of the radical "boat" and the phonetic element "bái. The *Qièyùn Hǎizhōng* states: "A large ship; composed of the radical 'boat' and the phonetic element 'bái'."

*Yī cuō* (the first character pronounced *cuō*, the second *guó*): Dictionaries state that this means to grasp an object with the hand. The *Suàn jīng* (Mathematical Classic) states that sixty-four grains of millet make one *guī* (a small measure), and four *guī* make one *cuō*. It follows the radical for "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic *zuì*; it is also pronounced *zāng guó*, meaning to grasp with the hand.

"San" (sǔ hàn fǎn): According to the *Guǎng yùn*, it means "an umbrella. Lu Shi’s edition reads "sàn" (chù qià fǎn). The *Shuōwén* defines it as "to stab a person," composed of the radical "hand" and the phonetic "zhā" (chā; the same pronunciation as above), meaning "to thrust the hand into a person's mouth. The *Lǜwén* (Vinaya Text) writes it as "chā" or "chā," both of which are erroneous transcriptions.

Scroll Four, Volume Four: *Mūlavyākaraṇa-vastu* (Fundamental Matters of Medicine), Scroll Four. Regarding the character for "earth" (*tǔ*): The *Shàngshū* says, "On this earth, one sows and reaps. The *Shuowén* says, "Earth is 'to emit' (*tù*); it can emit and give birth to the myriad things. It is composed of two [horizontal strokes], which represent the number of earth; the radical *jiǔ* (〓) symbolizes things emerging from within the earth. The ancient reading is *gǔběn* (古本); the following characters are also written as *jī* (㯓) or *fèi* (㒆). Regarding the character for "bed" (*tà*) (pronounced *tǔhé*): The *Zìshū* says, "A bed or couch. It is composed of the radical *mù* (wood) and the phonetic *yǎng* (󱫕). The sound of *yǎng* is the same as above.

*Běi* (陂) is pronounced *pǐ* (宜反). The *Shàngshū* states: "A marsh dammed up is called *bēi*. The *Éryá* says: "That which is a dammed marsh is called *bēi*. Guo's commentary notes: "The terrain is not level. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical *huò* (𨸏) with the phonetic *pí* (皮). The lower character is pronounced *hù* (吳反). The *Qièyùn* defines it as "rivers and lakes. The *Guǎngyá* states: "*Hú* (湖) is also a pond," composed of the radical *shuǐ* (水) with the phonetic *hú* (胡).

The character *táo* (逃) [with the phonetic *tú* and *dāo*] is explained in the *Jíxùn* as "to perish" and "to depart. The *Shuowén* defines it as "to flee" (*cuàn*). The *Qièyùn* defines it as "to run away and avoid," composed of the radical *chuò* (辵, *chǐu lüè*) and the phonetic *zhào*. It is also written as the character *cáo* (󱶅). The character *pí* (避) [with the phonetic *yì*] means "to hide," "to avoid," "to depart," or "to turn back. In the *Xiaojing*, the commentary on "Zengzi avoids his seat" states: "It means to rise to answer."

The country of Tianzhu (India) is pronounced "Zhu" as in "Duduo"; it is also called Shendu, Xiandou, or Yindu, all of which are corruptions. The correct name is *Indraka*, which means "Moon. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that because sentient beings wander incessantly in saṃsāra through the long night of ignorance without any presiding authority, it is like the moon that succeeds the sun once it has vanished; since the sages and worthies of that land follow one another's tracks to guide ordinary people and benefit all things, just as the moon shines upon all, it is named for the moon.

Magadha—also transcribed as Mojieti or Mojieti—are all phonetic corruptions of the Sanskrit term. Since ancient times, translators have established names according to their meaning: some call it "The Unreachable," signifying that enemy nations cannot invade its borders; others call it "Pervasive Wisdom," meaning that wise and intelligent people abound throughout the kingdom; and others say "Free from Harm," meaning that the laws of the land do not employ execution, and those who commit capital offenses are merely sent to the Cold Forest (Śītavana).

*Dào* (稻): The upper character is pronounced with the *tú* and *hào* rhymes (*tù hào*). According to the *Qièyùn*, it refers to *gēngdào* (non-glutinous rice). The *Lǐjì* states that "exquisite rice is called *shū*"; the *Běncǎo* states that "glutinous rice (*jīngmǐ*) primarily benefits the vital energy (*qì*) and stops vexation and diarrhea, while non-glutinous rice (*dàomǐ*) primarily warms the interior and causes one to feel much heat. This clearly shows they are two distinct substances. The *Shuōwén* says that in the state of Pèi, rice is called *nuò*. The *Zílín* says that *dàomǐ* is glutinous (*nián*), whereas *gēngmǐ* is not glutinous. The lower character, *gǔ* (古), is pronounced with the *àn* rhyme (*gǔ àn*). The *Zìshū* says it refers to the stem or trunk.

Scroll Five, Volume V: *Mūlavyavahāra* (Fundamental Medical Matters). Scroll Five. "Tuojié" (拓頰): The upper character, "tuó" (拓), is pronounced with the initial *th-* (as in *tālò*). In the *Jílüè* (集略), it is said that this refers to using the hand to press against an object; the lower character, "jié" (頰), according to the *Qièyùn*, refers to the cheek. According to the commentary, "tuójié" has the same meaning as "zhīyí" (搘頤—propping one's chin). "Jié" (頰) is an archaic form (*zìwén*), also written as "jí" (𩠣), which is an ancient character.

"Mén" (門) [pronounced with the initial *mǒ* and the final *bié*]: The *Erya* states that the main gate is called the *yingmén*. Gu Yewang says: "That which is at the hall or room is called a *hù* (door); that which is at the city walls or moats is called a *mén* (gate). The *Shuowen* explains it as being composed of two doors (*hù*) forming a gate; the lower character is "kǔn" (苦本反). The *Shuowen* further explains it as the threshold of a gate, formed from the radical "mén" with the phonetic element "kùn" (困).

*Utpala* (the "wēn-gǔ" in the title is a reversed transcription; formerly transcribed as *òu bō luó*, *yōu bō luó*, or *wū bō luó*—all are variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation). This means "blue lotus. Its flowers are blue in color, its petals are narrow and long, and its fragrance is perceived from afar. It is rarely found among humans; it exists only in the great Anavatapta Lake.

*Kumuda*—in Sanskrit, it is also called *kumuda* or *kumudā*; in Chinese, it means "red lotus. Its color is a deep crimson and it is extremely fragrant. It is not found among ordinary humans, but rather emerges from the great dragon ponds.

*Puṇḍarīka* is a corruption or abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; it is also called *puṇḍarīka* or *puṇḍarīka*. This translates as "white lotus. Its flowers are like snow or silver, their brilliance dazzling the eyes, and they are exceedingly fragrant and abundant. They mostly grow in that pond, and they do not exist among humans. The sound *ṭi* (in *puṇḍarīka*) is pronounced with the *nu-ya* rhyme.

"Lóng-ǎ" (聾瘂): The upper character "lóng" (聾) is pronounced with the *dōng* rhyme (祿東反). The *Zuozhuan* states: "When the ears do not hear the harmony of the five musical notes, it is called 'lóng'. Du Yu’s commentary explains that "lóng" means "obscured. The *Cangjie pian* says it refers to the ears not hearing. The *Shuowen jiezi* defines it as consisting of the radical "ear" (耳) and the phonetic "long" (龍). The lower character "ǎ" (瘂) is pronounced with the *jia* rhyme (賈反). The *Kaoseng shengyun* states that it refers to being unable to speak. Regarding the correct orthography of past and present, "yǎn" (瘖) is used; it consists of the radical "sickness" (疒) and the phonetic "ya" (亞). The radical "sickness" is pronounced with the *nü-ai* rhyme (女厄反). In legal texts, it is written with the radical "mouth" (口) as "a" (啞), pronounced *ai*. The *Zhouyi* says: "Laughing and speaking, 'a-a'. This is not the same character as "lóng-ǎ."

*Chou-xie* (桎梏). The upper character is pronounced *jiu* (久) with the departing tone; the lower character is pronounced *jie* (戒) with the entering tone. The *Yupian* states that these are "shackles" (*zhiguo*). The *Kaosheng* says they are used to restrain criminals. Those worn on the hands are called *chou* (杻), and those worn on the feet are called *xie* (械); both follow the radical for wood and take *chou* and *jie* as their phonetic components.

*Liḷīci*: "Li" (㚲) is pronounced with the *gu* (古) and *tu* (吐) finals reversed; in Sanskrit it is traditionally called *Licchavi*, also rendered as *Lichavi*, which means "noble clan," specifically referring to the sons of princes or grandsons of kings.

The character *gǎo* (稿) [with the phonetic components "old" and "cut"] refers to the stalks of grain; it also refers to the "draft" (*gǎoběn*) of a text, meaning a preliminary or rough version. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It means grass (*cǎo*). It is formed with 'grass' as the semantic component and 'gǎo' as the phonetic component. The pronunciation of *gǎo* is as stated above.

Regarding the term *chělù* (車輅): the upper character is pronounced *jiǔ* (魚反) and the lower is *luògù* (洛故反). The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "That which the Son of Heaven rides is called a *chělù*. The *Dàdài Lǐ* (大戴禮) says: "The ancient *chělù* had a circular canopy to resemble heaven and a square chassis to resemble earth; its twenty-eight spokes resembled the twenty-eight lunar mansions, and its thirty radial lines resembled the number of days in a month. Looking upward, one observed the celestial phenomena (*wénwén*); looking downward, one examined the terrestrial principles (*dìlǐ*). One listened forward to the sounds of the *luán* and *huó* bells, and looked sideways at the movement of the four seasons."
*Maṇava* is a term from the Sanskrit language; alternatively, it is called *manava*, which means "youth" (*routong* 儒童), referring to one who practices the Noble Path.

On the banks of the Gaṅgā River—formerly called the "Ganges" (the *qiang* 弶 in the original text is a phonetic error)—it should properly be called the *Gaṅgā* (pronounced like *jing* 殑 followed by *ga* 伽, with the initial *g* sounding like that of a fish). This is the name of a river in the Western Regions. This river originally flows from the southern side of Lake Anavatapta (the "Pool Without Heat"); because its sands are most fine, they are used as a metaphor.

Ācārya—formerly transliterated as *āsheli* or *āzali*—is a phonetic shift of the Sanskrit term. It is translated here as "Right Practice" (*zhengxing*) or "Model of Conduct" (*guifan*), meaning one who teaches and instructs others in wholesome dharmas so that they may understand the proper model of conduct.

Regarding the character *hè* (翮): the upper radical is also written as *qì* (翄), with the phonetic *shīzhì* (施智). The *Ji xùn* (集訓) states it means "the wing of a bird. The lower part has the phonetic *húgé* (胡革). The *Yù piān* (玉篇) states it means "bird feathers. The *Erya* (爾雅) states that the base of a feather is called *hè*. Guō Pǔ’s commentary says it refers to "bird feathers. It is formed from the radicals *yǔ* (羽), *zhī* (支), and *lì* (鬲), all serving as phonetic components.

Volume Six, Part Six: The Root Vinaya on Medicines, Volume Six. Regarding "fú-mán" (福鞔): "Mán" (鞔) is read as *huán* (桓) with a level tone; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to cover. According to the Vinaya text, it says: "With hands adorned by a hundred blessings and marked with ten thousand characters. This refers to what is described in various sutras and vinayas as "hands with webs and palms adorned by a hundred blessings. In the Vinaya text, the character is written with the "chariot" radical (*chē*) as "mǎn" (輓), pronounced *wǎn*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines this as "to pull a chariot. This is highly inconsistent with the intent of the Vinaya.

*Cōng* (聰): The upper radical is *cāng* with the *hóng* rhyme. The *Shuowen* writes it as *cōng*. The *Shangshu* says, "Listening is called *cōng*. Kong’s Commentary states, "The ears are clear and discerning. The *Shuowen* says, "To observe; composed of the radical 'ear' and the phonetic 'hù'. The sound of *hù* is the same as above. The character *hù* is composed of the radical 'heart' and the phonetic *hù*, whose sound is *chǔjiāng*. The *Lüwen* writes it as *sōng*, which is a vulgar form. The lower part is *yuè* with the *huì* rhyme. The *Hongfan* says, "*Ruì* (睿) is made into *shèng* (聖). Zheng’s Commentary on the *Liji* says, "The refinement of thought. The *Guoyaya* says, "Wisdom. The correct character for ancient and modern usage is *shēnmíng* (深明). It is composed of the radicals 'cán', 'mù', and the abbreviated form of 'gǔ'. The sound of *cán* is *zàn*. The *Lüwen* writes it as *nǎn*, which does not form a valid character.

*Jì* (pronounced *qǔ qǐ*): This is a rhyming compound meaning "artistic skill" (*yìnéng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhī. In literary texts, it is written as *jì*. The lower character, *yù jì*: according to the *Kaosheng*, it means "talent" (*cái*); according to the *Qieyun*, it means "ability" (*néng*); the *Guangya* states it means "constant" (*cháng*). The *Lunyu* says, "He dallied with the arts" (*yóu yú yì*).

*Tiěshǎo* (iron spear). The "shǎo" is pronounced with the *jié* (結) and *fǎn* (反) finals. The *Shuowén* states that it means "black metal," composed of the radical "metal" (*jīn*) and the phonetic "shǎo. In the *Lǜwén*, it is written as "tiě" (a vulgar character). Below, "shuāngchì" (雙捉) is the pronunciation. The *Bóyá* states it is a weapon; the *Yùnquán* states it is a long spear. It is a compound character formed from the radical "spear" (*máo*) and the phonetic "xiào. In the *Lǜwén*, it is sometimes written as "shuò" (another vulgar character).

The character *pùlì* (𥬰立) is pronounced *chùgé* (楚革). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *zhé* (𠕋), stating that it refers to "divine mandates" (*fúmìng*), meaning the symbolic credentials and instructional mandates bestowed upon one to confer the imperial throne; its form resembles that of stacked bamboo slips or tablets. The *Lüwen* (Text on the Rites) writes it as *shùqū* (束驅), meaning "to bind and drive. The *Shuowen* states this refers to a "whip for horses," and is not the character *pùlì*.

*Śaṅkha* (the first character pronounced as *shì* or *liàng*; in Sanskrit it is sometimes written as *śaṅkha*, two characters). This is translated here as "conch" (*luó*), which refers to the ritual conch shell blown today.

*Hèhè* (the first character pronounced as *hū* or *gé*; the *Yùnjí* states it means "bright" or "abundant"; the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "to emit"). The *Shī* says, "Majestic is Grand Minister Sīyǐn. The *Ěryā* says, "Majestic and swift. Guō’s commentary states this refers to an appearance of abundance and rapidity. The legal texts write it with the radical for fire as *hè* (火), meaning the color red; this is not the meaning of *hèhè*.

*Upāsaka* (the *u-po-so-jiā* [鄔波索迦] is a transliteration of the Sanskrit; the old translation "youposai" [優婆塞] is erroneous) means "male lay follower" (*upāsaka*), which is one of the seven classes of followers (*saptanikāya*).

The character for "parrot" (鸚鵡) has the upper radical *wu* (烏) with the phonetic *geng* (耕) as an alternative reading, while the lower part is pronounced *wu* (武); it is sometimes written as 䳇. The *Shanhaijing* states: "On Mount Huang there is a bird with green feathers and a red beak; it has a human tongue and can speak like a person; it is named 'parrot' (*yingwu*). Both characters are *xing-sheng* (phonetic-semantic) compounds formed from the radical *bird* (鳥) combined with *ying* (嬰) and *wu* (武).

The "evil *chī*" (惡鴟) is pronounced *zhī* in the *Yǐnlǜ Yǔyì*; the *Yǐnyá* calls it the "strange *chī*" (*guàichī*). Guō’s commentary states that this is the *chīxiū*. Nowadays in Jiangdong, people generally call strange birds by this name, or refer to them as *xiāochī*. The commentary notes that this is the same as the *tǔxiāo*. It is sometimes written as *𩿍*, which is a vulgar character; the form *dī* found in legal texts is incorrect.

*Nièshā* (搦殺): The character *niè* (上女陌反) is explained in the *Zītǒng* as "to seize and grasp," formed with the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic element "nuò" (溺) in abbreviated form; it is also pronounced *nǚjiǎo* (女角反). According to the *Qièyùn*, it means "to hold. The character *suǒ* (下所八反) is explained in the *Erya* as "to cut, stab, and kill. To write it as *shā* (煞) is a vulgar character.

*Tà* (pronounced with the initial *jū* and *yuē* in the colloquial, and the rhyme of *shǒu*). It means to step upon. The *Shìmíng* states: "It is called *tà* because when sitting, one's feet are behind. The lower radical is *tú* (with the initial *hé*). The *Kǎoshēng* states: "To place [the foot] on the ground while walking. It is also written as *tà*. The *Zìlín* states: "To kick."

Volume Seven, Part One of the *Mūla-bhaiṣajya-vastu*, Volume Seven. "Qing-lü" (青輅): "Qing" (青) is the color of the East; the *Record of Mount Luofu* states that both "male-qing" and "female-qing" are names for types of wood. Here, we do not adopt the reading with the "zhu" (下) tone. The *Shiming* (*Explanations of Names*) states: "The white carriage (*bai-lü*) ridden by the Son of Heaven is named according to its adornments with gold, jade, ivory, and so forth. This was already explained previously in the fifth volume.

*Huái yū* (懷迂): The upper radical is *hù* (戶) and the phonetic component is *guāi* (乖). The *Erya* states that *huái* means "to come" (*lái*). The *Qieyun* defines it as "peaceful" (*ān*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "composed of the radical 'heart' (*xīn*) and the phonetic 'huái' (*shēng*)," with the pronunciation of *huái* being the same as *shàng xià wáng jù* (上下王俱反). Gu Yewang states that *yū* means "great" (*dà*) and "distant" (*yuǎn*). The *Yunjí* also says it means "distant. According to these sources, *huáiyū* refers to thinking of and welcoming those who are far away, specifically the worthy (*xián*).

"Quǔjiàn" (曲磵): "Quǔ" (曲) is pronounced with the *yù* (玉) and *wǎn* (宛) rhymes, meaning winding; "jiàn" (磵) is pronounced with the *gǔ* (古) and *ān* (安) rhymes, or is written as "jiàn" (㵎). The *Erya* states: "A mountain with water on both sides is called a jiàn. Gu Yewang says it refers to a hundred streams.

*Guan* (罐): The ancient reading is *guǎn*. The *Jixùn* states that it is a vessel for drawing water, derived from the radical *fǒu* (缶) with the phonetic *huàn* (雚). *Fǒu* is pronounced *fāngjiǔ*; *huàn* is pronounced *guàn*. The lower character [of the next entry] is read as *gǔxìng*. The *Yùpiān* states it is a rope for drawing water. The *Shuowén* states it is a well-rope for drawing water, derived from the radical *mì* (糸) with the phonetic *gēng* (更). *Mì* is pronounced *mò*. *Gěng* (綆): Derived from the radical *mì* (糸) with the phonetic *gēng* (更). *Mì* is pronounced *mò*. "Bō" (簸): Above is the character *huǒ* (火), read as *fǎn* (反). The *Shuowen* defines it as "to sift. It is composed of the radical *jī* (箕) and the phonetic *pǒ* (跛) in abbreviated form; it is also pronounced *bù gè* (布箇). This refers to the winnowing fan used today. *Fēng* (𦅘):

Above is *shàng* (上), below is *gǔ xiàn* (古莧), read as *fǎn* (反). It should be written with the character *jiān* (間). This has already been explained in detail in the second fascicle of the preceding [text] of the Vinaya.

*Fu* (孚) means to be trusted by those above and not to turn back. The *Shijing* says, "The myriad states act in trust. In the *Yupian*, *fu* means sincerity and also joy. The *Shuowen* says that a bird's *fu* refers to the egg; it is composed of the radicals for "claw" (*zhuo*) and "child" (*zi*), representing its form. The lower part is read as *fu* (符) with the *yun* (rhyme) *yu* (遇). The *Qieyun* says it means to entrust and also to adhere. It is formed from "to give" (*fu*) with "self" (*zi*) as the phonetic component. It signifies the mutual reliance and attachment of sounds.

*Zhuǎ* (爪): On the upper radical, *zú* (卒) with the tone *suǐ* (髓). The *Guǎngyá* says it is the "beak" (*mí*) of the mouth; dictionaries say it is the "bill. According to the *Shuowén*, this [radical] is based on the phonetic *shù* (束); it is also written as two forms: *zuǐ* (觜) and *wěi* (𠲿). *Shù* (束) is pronounced *qiān sì* (千四) or *zhòng huī wèi* (衆暉衛). Below, it is read as *zé jiǎo* (側絞). The *Qièyùn* states it is the "claw" or "spur," and also refers to the hand-claw. The *Shuowén* says: "To turn the hand over is called a 'claw' (*zhǎo*); it represents the shape of three fingers. It is also written as the character *yòu* (又).

*Poṣadha* (the first character pronounced as *bǎo* with the *máo* tone, and the second as *shā* with the *zǎo* tone) is a term from the Sanskrit language; the old translation "Bùsà" is a corruption and abbreviation. This means "Prolonged Purity," referring to the recitation of the precepts on the fifteenth day to increase pure karma.

Volume Eight, Part One of the *Mūla-bhaiṣajya-vastu*, Volume Eight. *Jiāoliáo* (鷦鷯): The upper character, *jiāo* (鷦), is pronounced as *xiāo* (霄) with the *qiǎo* (巧) radical; the *Erya* states it is the "táo-chóng" (挑蟲) bird, and Guo’s commentary identifies it as the "táo-què" (桃雀). In common parlance, it is called the "qiǎofù" (巧婦). The lower character, *liáo* (鷯), is pronounced as *luòxiāo* (洛簫); the *Qieyun* states that the *jiāoliáo* is a small bird. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that both characters are written with the "bird" radical (*niǎo*) and that both *jiāo* and *láo* are phono-semantic compounds.

The term "Brahman" is not the correct Sanskrit; it should be *brahmacārin*, which is translated as "pure conduct" (*jingxing*) or "Brahma-conduct" (*fanxing*). It is traditionally transmitted that they claim to have been born from the mouth of Brahmā; thus, they take only the name "Brahma. Regarding their worldly occupations, they transmit and study the four Vedas, and for the most part possess broad knowledge and maintain pure integrity. Among them, those who are intelligent and highly accomplished often serve as teachers to emperors and kings.

*Kṣatriya* (the first character is pronounced *shàng* [shang] with an initial retroflex, also a Sanskrit term; translated here as "Lord of the Fields") refers to the noble lineage of royal clans from ancient times. They study the four Vedas, possess vast learning and a powerful memory, and are characterized by benevolence, forbearance, and great compassion. Among them, those who possess virtuous integrity and superior merit are established as kings by the multitude.

*Vaiśya* is also a Sanskrit term; *vai* is pronounced with the *gui* (ㄍㄨㄟˋ) tone, or it is called *vṛṣala*, which is translated here as "Lord of the Fields. Although they possess great merit and abundant treasures, they cannot penetrate the classical texts or engage in the commerce of accumulation. When granted fiefs and estates, they mostly serve as elders (*śreṣṭhin*) to honorably govern the borders of the kingdom and provide relief for the poor.

*Śūdra* is also an incorrect rendering of the Sanskrit term; it should be *śaudra*. It has many names, and its single essential meaning is translated as "the mixed multitude" (*saṃkīrṇa*). Alternatively, it refers to those whose occupations involve extensive labor in fields, sowing, planting, and livestock management; or those skilled in various crafts and arts; or those who engage in fishing, hunting, and trapping; or those who perform manual labor for hire. Among the four castes, this is the lowest.

The character for *shēng* (nephew) is pronounced "wài" in the first tone and "shēng" in the fourth tone. The *Shìqīn* (Explanations of Kinship) states: "The father of one's wife is called the *wàijiù* (maternal uncle); the mother of one's wife is called the *wàigū* (maternal aunt). Guo’s commentary says: "One whom I call 'uncle,' I [the nephew] am called by him 'nephew' (*shēng*). It further states: "The son of a paternal aunt is a nephew; the son of a maternal uncle is a nephew. Guo’s commentary says: "Nephew (*shēng*) is synonymous with 'born' (*shēng*')."

The upper character is *wáng* (亡分反) with the variant *móu* (俗); it is also written as *móu* (蚉), while the correct form is *méng* (蟁). The *Shuowen* states that it is a biting flying insect; the character is derived from a simplified form of *hūn* (昬), because it emerges during the dusk. The lower character is *yǐ* (牛倚反); the *Shuowen* writes it as *yì* (螘) or *bīchù* (蚍𧉈). The *Erya* states: "The *bīchù* is the large ant; the small ones are *yì*. It is derived from *chóng* (虫) and the phonetic *qǐ* (豈). The current form *yǐ* (蟻) is a vulgar character.

*Āgama* (pronounced *āgumagui*, with the *gui* reversed, or alternatively *āhanmo*, or *āxiang*)—all are Sanskrit terms differing in their phonetic weight. This is translated as "Treasury" (*zàng*) or "Tradition" (*chuán*), meaning the Buddha’s secret treasury transmitted through successive generations; it may also be rendered as "Teaching" (*jiào*), referring to the four types of *āgamas*: the *Dīrgha*, *Madhyama*, *Ekottara*, and *Saṃyukta*.

The character *xīyí* (熙怡): the upper radical is *xū* (虛) with the phonetic *jī* (飢). The *Zītǒng* (字統) states it means "harmony" (*héhé*). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "beauty" (*měi*). It is formed from the radical *huǒ* (灬), which is pronounced *biyáo*, and the phonetic *yí* (󱷥). *Huǒ* is pronounced *bìyáo*. *Yīn* (巸) has the same pronunciation; the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "joyful delight" (*xǐyuè*), while the *Shuōwén* states it means "harmony" (*hé*). It is formed from the radical *xīn* (心) and the phonetic *tái* (台). *Tái* is pronounced *yí*. This is seen in the *Ěryǎ*. Furthermore, in ancient script, *yǐ* (以) is used as the character *tái*.

Regarding the character for *bànglǐ* (篣籬), the *Bùguāng* (步光) glossary reads "fān" (反). The *Zìlín* (字林) states it is a *bàngjī* (蒡箕); it resembles a winnowing fan but is smaller, made of bamboo. It is classified under the "bamboo" radical with the phonetic component "páng" (旁), which shares the same pronunciation. The characters for "shàngxià" (上下) are pronounced "lí" (離). The *Yùnlüè* (韻略) states that *yèlǐ* (笟籬) is used; the character for *yè* (笟) is pronounced "zèjiào" (側教).

*Kuāng* (筐) and *jī* (箕): "Kuāng" is pronounced with the initial *wáng* (上聲); the *Yùpiān* states it is a type of basket. The *Chūnqiū chuán* says it is a vessel used for *kuāng*, *jǔ*, *qí*, and *fǔ*. The *Fāngyán* states that those which are round are called *kuāng* and those which are square are called *jǔ*; "jǔ" is pronounced with the initials *jū xǔ* (居許反). "Qí" (錡) is pronounced with the initials *yú yǐ* (魚倚反), and the following character is pronounced with the initials *jū zhī* (居之反). The *Shìběn* states that Shàokāng invented the *jī* and *zhào* (篲).

Scroll Nine, Volume Nine: The Fundamental Medicinal Matters (Mūla-bhaiṣajya-vastu), Scroll Nine. *Huàn jiǎ* (to don armor). In ancient times, it was pronounced *guàn*. The *Zhuō zhuan* states that *huàn* means "to thread through. The *Guìyuàn zhūcóng* says: "To thread one's body through clothing and armor is called *huàn*; 'yī' (clothing) has the departing tone, meaning 'to put on. Its original pronunciation is *hú guàn*. The *Shuowén* explains it as being composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "huáng" (*huáng*). The character for "armor" (*jiǎ*) is sometimes written as "jiè" (*jiè*), which is incorrect.

*Shìshù* (柿子): [The characters are pronounced] *chú lǐ* (鋤里) according to the *Yùn* (韻). It is the name of a fruit tree. The *Běncǎo* (本草) states: "Dried persimmon (*qiánshì*) strengthens the intestines and stomach, builds the spleen, and consumes residual blood. Furthermore, red persimmon (*hóngshì*) supplements the qi and continues the channels. Moreover, pickled persimmon (*liànshì*) astringes the lower burner, builds the spleen, and can transform dark freckles on the face; it is extremely beneficial if taken for a long time. [The character] *liàn* (醂) is pronounced *lì gǎn* (力感).

Regarding the term *wéi* (帷): the *Shìmíng* (釋名) states that it means "to surround" (*wéi*), referring to its function of enclosing oneself as a screen. The *Shuowén* (說文) explains it as "that which is at the side is called a *wéi*; it is composed of the radical *mǐn* (巾) and the phonetic *zhuī* (隹). The reading for the character below is *mó* (摩). Gù Yěwáng states that "that which covers above is called a *mò* (幕). The *Shuowén*'s phonetics and definitions are the same; it is composed of the radical *mǐn* (巾) and the phonetic *mò* (莫).

Regarding "jālāvanaddha" (網鞔): the character *mó* (鞔) is pronounced with the lower radical *muán* (桓反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, *mó* means "to cover. In this context, *jālāvanaddha* refers to the mark of the Tathāgata’s hands and feet being connected like those of a king of geese, without any gaps. The Vinaya texts write it as *wǎng* (輞), meaning "wheel-rim," which is incorrect; they also write it as *màn* (縵) with the pronunciation *mò pàn fǎn*, both of these characters are erroneous.

The character *qǐ* (器皿): Qūlì (丘利) reversed; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "vessel" (*míng*). It is composed of *jí* (㗊) and *quán* (犬); *jí* signifies "many mouths," with the phonetic *zhī* (戢). It resembles the shape of a vessel. *Dà* (大) is pronounced *yǒng* (永) with the *wǔ* (武) rhyme. According to the *Yupian*, it is a general term for vessels. The *Shuowen* also presents it as *píng* (竝), which represents the shape of a container for holding things.

The character for "monkey" (獼) is pronounced with the upper radical *zhèng* (正) as the female sound (read as *cí* [雌], following the *yīqiè yùn* system where this refers to the male-female distinction); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "female" (*pǐn*) is called *cí*, derived from the radical *zhuī* (隹) with the phonetic *cǐ* (此). Next is the character for "monkey" (*mí*), pronounced *wǔyī* (武移); Gu Yewang states that "mí" is simply another name for the monkey.

Volume Ten, Part One of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*. **Analysis:** The character 析 (*xī*) means to divide, to cut, to apportion, or to distribute. Regarding its phonetic value, it is analyzed as follows: according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to separate. It is composed of the radical 八 (eight) and the element 刀 (knife), representing the form of splitting. The lower part is pronounced *xiān* (as in *qī*). The *Erya* states: "Between Xi-mu and Han-zhin lies the region of the Northern Dipper. According to the *Shuowen*, [the character 破] means to split wood; it is composed of the radical 斤 (axe), signifying that an axe can split wood—a word formed through associative meaning.

To act as an enemy (*chóu*). [The rhyme is] *xià* (下) with the *shì* (市) reverse-cut; it means resentment or a match. Examining its phonetics, it refers to an adversary. The *Shuowen* says: "It is like a *zhòu* (雔). It is composed of the radical 'speech' (*yán*) and the phonetic component *zhòu*. The pronunciation of *zhòu* is the same as above."
*Vilandi*: The first character is pronounced *bu* (with the *mi* rhyme) and the second is *ding-li*.

The Sanskrit etymology is not fully established for its correspondence. *Saṃghāṭī*: In the Sanskrit language, it was formerly called *saṃghārī* and also *saṃghāci*; this is translated as "double-layered" (*hezhòng*), meaning that it is cut and joined together to form a double layer. This one robe must necessarily be made by cutting [the cloth] into pieces. As for the other two robes, they may or may not be cut. According to the Dharmaguptaka, Sarvāstivāda, and many other schools, they are generally not cut; however, according to the Mahīśāsaka and Mahāsāṃghika schools, they are cut. If they are not cut, one simply attaches the corners [of the patches]; this is based on the explanation of Master Xuanying.

Regarding "gǔ" (轂) and "wǎng" (輞): the ancient pronunciation of "gǔ" was *lù* (鹿). The *Kǎo Shēng* (考聲) states it refers to the hub of a wheel; the *Shuōwén* (說文) states it means the solid core of a chariot. The *Shī* (詩) says, "Patterned rugs and long hubs," with the character following "chē" (車) and the phonetic element being "jiàn" (𣪊). The character "wǎng" (輞), which follows "liǎng" (兩) and "fǎn" (反), takes "chē" (車) as its radical and "wǎng" (罔) as its phonetic; it appears as "jìng" (𨊾) in the *Lǜwén* (律文), though this is a vulgar usage of the character.

The character *wēn* (溫) is pronounced with the upper radical *wū* (烏) and the phonetic *kūn* (昆); the *Qièyùn* states it means "harmony" (*hé*) or "goodness" (*shàn*). The *Yùpiān* says it means "excellent" (*liáng*), and the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "gentle and warm" (*róuwēn*). The lower part is pronounced *guǎn* (管). The *Shuōwén* says it refers to "boiling water" (*tāngshí*). It is also written as *nuǎn* (暖), *huǎn* (煖), or *niǎn* (㬉)—these three forms all mean "warmth. The legal texts (*lǜwén*) use the character *sūn* (燸), but this character cannot be found [in standard dictionaries].

Volume 11, Fascicle 11. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle 11. Regarding "grass hut" (*cáo ān*): it is also written as "twenty" (*èng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "hundred herbs" (*bǎihuì*) is composed of the radical *chǔ* (pronounced *chǔ liè fǎn*), which represents the shape of grasses and trees when first sprouting; it consists of two *chǔ* radicals and takes *zǎo* as its phonetic component. Below, "hut" (*ān*) is pronounced *niǎo hán fǎn*. The *Yunying* states that an "hut" (*ān lú*) is a dwelling. The *Yupian* also says it is a dwelling, composed of the radical *guǎng* with *yǎn* as its phonetic component.

*Tān* (灘) and *zhǔ* (渚): The *Erya* states that when the Tai-sui is in the year of Shen, it is called *Tun-tan*. The *Yupian* says it refers to a riverbank (*he-tan*). The *Fangyan* states that in Jiangdong, a mound of sand in the water is called *tan*; in the north of the Yellow River, it is called *tan* (pronounced *zhang yu* [章與]). The *Erya* states that a place in the water where one may dwell is called a *zhou* (洲); a small *zhou* is called a *zhǔ* (渚), which is also written as *zhu* (陼). *Tun* (涒) is pronounced *ta kun* (他昆).

"Āo" (撈): The *Shanglù* (上魯) commentary states it is pronounced *dāo* (刀反). The *Yùpiān* (*Yùpiān* 云) says it means "to take. The *Zílín* (*Zílín* 云) says it means "to reach out and grasp for an object"; it is composed of the radical "hand" (手) with the phonetic "láo" (勞). In the *Lǜwén* (律文), it is written as "lào" (澇) with the pronunciation *lángdào* (郎到反); this does not carry the meaning of "to fish out. The character below, "chǐ" (尺), has the *fǎnqiè* (反切) *lǜ* (律). It means "to advance" or "to go far. The *Shuōwén* (*Shuōwén* 云) states that the character "chū" (出) is derived from the ancient form of "chū," which resembles the shape of something emerging in four directions. In the *Lǜwén*, it is written as "chū" (出) with two mountains (二山); this is a scribal error.

Regarding "xuánguō" (漩濄): the upper character is pronounced *xuan* (with the *quǎn* and *fǎn* tones). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "a swirling pool in water," formed with the radical for water and the phonetic element *xuan*. In legal texts, it is written simply as *xuan*, meaning "to turn" or "successively completed"; this is not its usage here. The lower character is pronounced *he* (烏和反). The *Zilin* states it refers to a place where water turns back; the *Shuowen* says it is formed with the radical for water and the phonetic element *guo*. In legal texts, it is written as *wo* (音戈), which is a name for a type of water and does not carry the meaning of "swirling."

The character for *xiā má* (toad): the first radical is *hú* (胡) with the phonetic *jiā* (加); the second radical is *mò* (莫) with the phonetic *jiā* (加). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is an aquatic insect. In the records of the Jin dynasty, Emperor Hui, while in Huālín Garden, heard the sound of a toad and asked his attendants, "Does that which cries belong to the official or to the private? In the standard orthography of past and present, it belongs to the category of *wā* (frog/toad), written as 蛙, following the radical for insects (*虫*) and taking *duàn* (叚) in abbreviated form as the phonetic. Below this, there is also the form 蟆, following the radical for insects (*虫*) and taking *mò* (莫) as the phonetic.

In the context of marriage, the *Erya* states that those on the wife’s side are called *hun-xiongdi* (marriage brothers), while those on the groom’s side are called *yin-xiongdi* (affinity brothers). The *Liji* says: "When taking a wife, the wife is yin; because she enters at the time of dusk (*hun*), it is called *hun*. The *Kaoseng* says it means "ritual" (*yi*). The *Shiming* says it means "the substance" (*ti*), referring to knowing the general principles of things. The *Zhouli* speaks of the five rituals: *ji*, *xiu*, *bin*, *jun*, and *jia*. The *Lunyu* says: "Without learning the ritual (*li*), there is no way to stand. In ancient texts, this character is written as *li*.

Volume 12, Fascicle 12, *Mūla-bhaiṣajya-vastu*. Fascicle 12. Regarding "kṛśa" (black and emaciated): the *Qieyun* provides the phonetic analysis as "xià suǒ" (下所). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "kṛśa" means "emaciated" (*zhòu*). The *Erya* states that "qú" means "leanness" (*jí*). Guo Pu’s commentary notes that the people of Qi call being thin "qú," pronounced "qú," though it is also written as "quó" (癯). "Kṛśa" is also written as "shòu" (瘦).

Fù (腹): The upper radical is 方 (fāng) and the phonetic component is 反 (fǎn). It refers to the abdomen and heart. The *Erya* states: "Zhúfù (竺腹) means thick. Gu Yewang says: "The spleen constitutes the abdomen, which serves to contain what is heavy; it is also one of the five viscera. It is formed with the radical 肉 (meat) and the phonetic 复 (fù). The pronunciation of 复 is fù; the lower character is pronounced zhū liàng (猪亮). In the *Qieyun*, it means distension and fullness. In the *Zuozhuan*, it means pain. In dictionaries, it is written as 痮, with the same pronunciation.

*Chuān huì* (瘡殨): "Chū" is pronounced with the *liáng* rhyme-cut; it refers to wounds or sores (*chuāngyí*). In archaic script it was written as *chuàng*. The *Shìmíng* states: "A sore (*chuāng*) is an injury," meaning that the body has sustained a wound. The *Lǐjì* says: "If there is a sore on the head, one washes [it]. "Xià" is pronounced with the *hù* rhyme-cut. The *Jíxùn* states: "It means the flesh is putrefied. According to this, *chuān huì* is precisely the putrefaction of the flesh, which is *huàn nòu*. "Nòu" is pronounced with the *nú dōng* rhyme-cut. The *Lǜwén* (Legal Texts) writes it as *huì*, and the *Yùpiān* defines it as "scattered and disordered," but this is not the meaning of *chuān huì*.

*Shè* (澀): Upper radical 7, *lún* (倫) as the phonetic component; it also refers to cracked skin. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means the fine hair on the skin has stood up, formed from the radical "skin" (*pí*) with "qūn" (*qūn*, same pronunciation) as the phonetic. The lower part, *sè* (色), is pronounced *lì* (立); according to lexicographical works, it means obstructed and impassable. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is formed from four instances of "stop" (*zhǐ*)—two upright and two inverted—and is written as *shè* (歰) or *sè* (濇), with the same pronunciation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as not being smooth.

*Kang* (䧫) [pronounced *hú* with the *dào* tone, also written as *háo*]: The *Shuowen* states it refers to city moats; dictionaries state that *huáng* is the same as *háo*. In legal texts, it is written with the "earth" radical as *háo*. The vulgar form without the "water" radical is *huáng*, while the form with the "water" radical is *háo*. Below: *gēng* [pronounced *gēng*]. The *Qieyun* states it is a ditch (*quàn*). The *Erya* states it is a hollow (*xū*); Guo’s commentary states it is a trench (*quàn*). In legal texts, it is written as *ní-kēng*; both are errors resulting from vulgar transmission.

Fàn (upper radical 孚, pinyin fú, jian-yan fan; rhyme ying): "Extensive" or "abundant. *Yùpiān* says it means "overflowing"; *Qièyùn* says it means "floating," and it is also written as fàn. Zhìliàng fan (lower radical 氵, pinyin zhì): *Kǎoshēng* says it means "a great flood filling [the land]. It is composed of the radical water (氵) with the phonetic element zhāng.

*Zòu* (pronounced *zàng hòu fǎn*, with the phonetic component *kǎo*): a gathering or assembly. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "the confluence of waters," taking *zòu* as its phonetic component. Below, *cí yǔ fǎn*: according to the *Qieyun*, it means "to assemble. It takes *kǎo* as its phonetic component; "multitude" is its meaning. The character 𠕋 (zhì) is pronounced *chū* with the initial *gē* (革) according to the *Shuowen*. The *Shuowen* states: "Earthly tablets (*tǔ zhì*) are auspicious mandates (*fúmìng*"; it refers to the auspicious credentials and instructional mandates of the supreme sages bestowed upon the imperial throne, having the form of bamboo slips (*jiǎn zhì*) joined together by stringing holes through them. Nowadays, some write it with the radical 竹 (bamboo), as 𠕋. Regarding the character 立 (lì) below: the *Qieyun* states it means "to dwell" (*zhù*) or "to accomplish" (*chéng*), and also "to stand. The character 𠕋 (zhì) is pronounced *chū* with the initial *gē* (革) according to the *Shuowen*. The *Shuowen* states: "Earthly tablets (*tǔ zhì*) are auspicious mandates (*fúmìng*"; it refers to the auspicious credentials and instructional mandates of the supreme sages bestowed upon the imperial throne, having the form of bamboo slips (*jiǎn zhì*) joined together by stringing holes through them. Nowadays, some write it with the radical 竹 (bamboo), as 𠕋. Regarding the character 立 (lì) below: the *Qieyun* states it means "to dwell" (*zhù*) or "to accomplish" (*chéng*), and also "to stand."

*Keng-k'en* (耕墾): "Keng" is pronounced *piang* (並) with a reversed final; according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "plow. The *Zhōushū* states: "In the time of Shennong, Heaven rained down grain; Shennong tilled and sowed it. The *Shuowén* explains that it is composed of the radical *lèi* (耒), which resembles the shape of a plow. *Lèi* is pronounced *lúduì* (盧對) with a reversed final; the *Shuowén* defines it as "a curved piece of wood. The *Shìběn* says: "Shennong invented the *lèi*. *Xià* (下) is pronounced *kānghèn* (康佷); the *Yùpiān* says it means "to cultivate fields. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to till. The *Qièyùn* says it means "strength. It is composed of the radical *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *zūn* (貇); *zūn* has the same pronunciation as above.

*Jambūnada-suvarṇa* (the gold of the Jambu River). *Jambū* is a Sanskrit term; "gold" is the Chinese translation (*tángyán*). Formerly, the Sanskrit was called *Yān-fú-tí* or *Yān-fú-lì*, which are corruptions; the correct transcription is *Lán-móu*. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-śāstra* states: "There is a *jambū* tree growing on the northern edge of this continent, on the southern bank of the Narmadā River. Beneath the water at the base of this tree, there is *jambū* gold. Its ancient name is *Yān-fú-tán-jīn* (Jambūnada-gold). The pronunciation of *lán* is like that of *sǎn* or *lǎn*.

Volume 13, Part 13 of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*. Regarding the character for "finger" (zhǐ): the upper part is read as *zhì* (as in *zhǐzhì*, meaning "to point with the finger") according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "zhǐ. The lower part is read as *tā* (as in *tālì*, meaning "to push aside") according to the *Yupian*; in the *Qieyun*, it means "to move. According to the Vinaya, it refers to picking or poking with a finger; it is composed of the radical "hand" and the phonetic "shí. In ancient texts, it was also pronounced *zhì* or *zhānggē* (as in *zhānggē*), but these are not adopted here; we follow only the first reading.

Regarding the term *niàn* (撚): the *Shàngdiǎn fānyán* states it means "to spin" (*niànxù*); the *Cāngjié piān* states it means "to twist thread. It is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "rán" (*ránshēng*). Below, it is also written as *xiàn* (線), while the vulgar form is *yán* (綖). Its pronunciation is *sìjiàn* (私箭反). The *Shuōwén* states it means "thread" (*lǚxiàn*). The *Zhou Lǐ* states: "The *Xiàn-rén* (Director of Thread) presides over the sewing and threading affairs of the royal palace; he employs female attendants (*nǚyù*) for this service."

*Gen* (root/stump): In ancient times, it was read as *hen*. The *Yun* states it means "a root-rampart" (*gen-hu*). The *Erya* says "the celestial root is the *hu*. Guo’s commentary notes: "The horns (*jiao*) are originally tied below to the *di*; it is like a tree having roots. *Xia* (below): read as *cai*. The *Shuowen* defines it as "to plant," composed of the radical "wood" (*mu*) and the phonetic element "ze" (*cai*) in abbreviated form. It appears as *zhang* in poetic prosody; this vulgar character lacks textual authority.

The character for "dry" (乾) is pronounced *gǎn* (with the ancient reading *hán*). Its original form is written as [the character for] "heaven" (*yǔ*) with the phonetic component "heart" (*qián*). It is borrowed to mean "dryness" (as opposed to moisture). The second character, "moisture" (溼), is pronounced *shī* (with the ancient reading *sū lǎo*). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to dry by fire. It is composed of the radical "fire" (*huǒ*) and the phonetic "zaó" (*sāo*), where *sāo* is pronounced like *zào*.

The character 𦁛 (top part) is pronounced with the initial *tu* and rhyme *xiè*; the *Qièyùn* records it as 㲲 (*dié*), meaning white cotton cloth. The lower part, 蕠 (*ní*, *jū*), is a name for a plant according to the *Yùpiān*. The *Yùnjí* states it is *wùmá* (coarse hemp); it follows the radical for grass (*cǎo*), and its phonetic component is 絮 (*xù*), with the same pronunciation as above.

Volume 14, Fascicle 14, *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle 14, Part 1: Sacrificial Offerings (*jìcí*). [The character] *zǐ* (子) is pronounced as in *lìfǎn* (例反); it means to examine the sounds and offer sacrifices. According to the *Yùpiān*, it means to sacrifice. The *Erya* states: "The *dì* (禘) is the great sacrifice. Guo's commentary says: "A great sacrifice once every five years. The *Shuowen* says: "It is composed of 'hand' (*shǒu*) holding 'meat' (*ròu') to display it for sacrifice. Furthermore, *jí* (即) is 'hand' and *yuè* (月) is 'meat. The lower part is pronounced as in *sīzīfǎn* (似茲反). The *Erya* states: "The spring sacrifice is called *cí* (祠). Guo Pu’s commentary says: "'Cí' means to eat (*shí*); its pronunciation is like that of *jùn sì* (餕飤)."

*Khadira* (the first character pronounced *qiān* with the *è* tone; a Western Indian name for a type of wood that has no direct equivalent in this land, though it is similar to the *kǔliàn* [mimosa] wood here, being so hard and rigid that it can be used for stakes and nails). What was formerly called *khadira* wood is this very same species.

"Jiǎo" (攪) [is pronounced qiǎo in reverse]. The *Mao Shī Zhuàn* says it means "to disturb. Lexicons say it means "to agitate. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to move," composed of the radical "hand" (手) and the phonetic "jiǎo" (攪), with the final rhyme being zhílí (直离). The *Guǎngyá* says it refers to a pond or pool; it further states that stagnant water is called a "chí" (池).

Huái (懷): Upper radical 戶 (hù), with the phonetic 乖 (guāi) as the classifier; it means "peaceful" or "to stop. According to the *Yùpiān*, it means "harmony" or "sentiment. Regarding its pronunciation, the *Kǎoshēng* states it means "to embrace," composed of the radical 心 (xīn) and the phonetic 褱 (huái); the latter is pronounced with the rhyme 汝鴆反 (rǔzhèn fǎn). The *Kǎoshēng* further states it refers to "the body being pregnant. The *Shuōwén* states it means "pregnancy," composed of the radical 女 (nǚ) and the phonetic 壬 (rén); it is also pronounced with the rhyme 如林反 (rúlín fǎn), with the same definition.

*Luǎn yǔ* (輦輿): The upper character is pronounced *lì* with the *zhǎn* rhyme. The *Shuowen* states: "A carriage drawn by men. It refers to the form of a person pulling it from the front; the radical *㚘* (pronounced *bàn*) signifies two men. In ancient times, high officials (*qīng dàfū*) also rode in such vehicles. Since the Qin and Han dynasties, the Son of Heaven has used them. The *Yupian* states: "That which the Son of Heaven and the Empress ride in is called a *luǎn*. Regarding the lower character, according to my research, it is pronounced *yú* with the *jù* and *yǔ* rhymes. The *Shuowen* states: "A carriage body. The *Yupian* says: "A multitude of carriages" or "to lift. Another definition: "A carriage without wheels is called a *yǔ*. This is a compound character formed from the radicals *chē* and *yú*. In Buddhist scriptures (*lüwén*), it is written as *yù* (轝), which is incorrect.

Regarding "left armpit" (zuò yàxià): the *Yìfǎn Yùpiān* states that "yè" means the armpit (*gē*) and also refers to the area beneath the ribs. It is also pronounced *yì*, composed of the radical "flesh" (肉) and the phonetic "yè" (省). Volume 15, Fascicle 15: *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*. Regarding "gentle speech" (*rú yǔ*): the *Zhù Fǎnqiè Yùn* defines it as "direct. The *Shuōwén Jiězì* defines it as "gentle" (*róu*).

The *Lǐjì*, in the "Wén Àigōng" chapter, asks Confucius about the conduct of a scholar (*rú*); this character is composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "xū" (需), with the final rhyme being *yǔ* (舉). The *Shuōwén* further explains that speaking directly is called "discourse" (*lùn*), while debating and challenging is called "speech" (*yǔ*), composed of the radical "speech" (言) and the phonetic "wú" (吾). According to the Vinaya text, "gentle speech" (*xúxú rúyǔ*) refers to speech that is harmonious and soft. To write this as the character "nèi" (濡)—which is the name of a river—is incorrect for the term "gentle speech. It should be written as "rú."

*Yueyu* (悅豫): The first character, *yue*, is pronounced with the *shang* tone and the *yu* rhyme (as noted in the *Yùpiān*, it means "joy"; according to the *Ěryǎ*, it means "to be pleased and submit"). The *Xiàojīng* states, "If one respects a single person, then all people under heaven will be pleased. The *Shuowén* explains it as "composed of the radical 'heart' (*xīn*) and the phonetic 'shuō' (abbreviated). The second character, *yu*, is pronounced with the *xià* tone and the *rú* rhyme; the *Yùnjí* says it means "completeness" or "priority. According to the *Ěryǎ*, *yu* means "joy. The *Shàngshū* records, "The King had an illness and was not *yu*. Kong’s Commentary explains: "In the year following the conquest of Zhou, King Wu fell ill and was not joyful or at ease."

Vaiśravaṇa (the upper character pronounced *pù* with the *jì* tone, and the lower character pronounced *ní* with the *jiā* tone; this is the Sanskrit term, formerly translated as Pishamen). This is translated here as "Much-Hearing" (*Duōwén*). He is the Northern Heavenly King who presides over the yakṣas, and he is the most wealthy and affluent.

The upper character *shé* (舌) is pronounced with the initials *sh- and finals *-lieh* (烈反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "That which is in the mouth for speaking; it is composed of the radical *qian* (千) and the character *kou* (口), with *kou* also serving as the phonetic. The lower character *shì* (舓) is pronounced with the initials *sh- and finals *-zhi* (紙反). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The tongue taking food; it is composed of the radical *she* (舌) and the phonetic *yi* (易). It may also be written as *lì* (𦧇) or *shì* (䑛), both of which are vulgar forms. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as *qí* (蚔), with the pronunciation *qi* (岐); this is not an erroneous transcription of the character.

In terms of its usage, it refers to speech that contains rhymes through the method of *fanqie* (phonetic analysis), as well as playful banter. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It means 'speech. It is composed of the radical 'yan' (speech) and the phonetic element 'yan' (sound); the latter is pronounced *hu kuai*. The *Yupian* states: "It means conversation. The *Shuowen Jiezi* further states: "It means to assemble virtuous words. As the *Shijing* says, "Be careful in the speech you utter," it is a compound character (*huiyi*) formed from the radicals "yan" (speech) and "she" (tongue).

*Varga* (the first character pronounced *pú-mò*, the second *qí-jǔ*; a Sanskrit term; alternatively called *vargu*), translated as "collection" (*jù*), refers to the various distinctions of chapters, sections, and categories. It is synonymous with the term *khandhaka* found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Volume 16, Fascicle 16, *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle 16. Regarding the character for "painting" (*huà*): it is pronounced with the *hú* rhyme (as in *hù*). The *Erya* states: "To paint forms. The *Shiming* states: "Painting is 'hanging' (*guà*); it is to hang the five colors upon an object. The *Shuowen* states: "It is composed of *yù* and the four boundaries of *tián*; *yù* is that by which one paints; the first [radical] is earth. In the Vinaya text, it is written as 畫, which is a vulgar form. Below, it is read with the *rǎng* rhyme (as in *rǎng*). The *Shuowen* states: "A wall (*yuán*); composed of *sè* and the phonetic *piàn*. In the Vinaya text, it is written as 㮈 or 㮆; neither is the original character.

The character 跌 (dié) is also pronounced with the tone of 腳 (jué), which is the reverse of 居約 (jūyuè). The *Jìxùn* states it means "hands and feet. The *Shìmíng* says "foot" (*jiǎo*) is derived from "to retreat" (*què*), because when sitting, one's feet are behind. The lower radical is read as *tújié*. The *Qièyùn* defines it as "stumbling" (*diètī*). The *Yùnquán* says it means "to err" (*chādiè*). The *Guǎngyá* says it refers to "having a lapse in walking. According to the *Shuōwén*, it is a compound character formed by combining "foot" (*zú*) and "error" (*shī*), conveying the meaning through its constituent parts.

*Yáo-yàng*: the first character is pronounced *shàng yú zhāo fǎn* (upper tone, with initial *yú* and final *-zhāo*), and the second is pronounced *xià yú liàng fǎn* (lower tone, with initial *yú* and final *-liàng*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "to move. The *Erya* states: "That which is called *fúyáo* is termed *yàn*. *Yàn* is pronounced *bì yáo fǎn*. Guo’s commentary says: "A violent wind that rises from below. *Yáng* means the wind carries objects aloft; it is composed of the radical "wind" (*fēng*) and the phonetic "yì," though it is also pronounced *yáng*.

*Yíng*: with the second tone, *líng* (余陵反); according to the *Yùpiān*, it is the name of an insect. The *Shījīng* says, "The green fly buzzes about" (*yíngyíng qīngyíng*). The *Shuōwén* says it is formed from the radical "insect" (*chóng*) and the phonetic component *mǐng* (黽); *mǐng* is pronounced *měng*. The character below, *qīyǔ* (七予反), refers to the maggots produced by flies. According to the *Kǎoshēng*, it refers to maggots within meat. The *Shuōwén* forms this character with the radical "flesh" (*ròu*) as *dǎn* (膽); the *Lǜwén* writes it as *qū* (蛆), which is a vulgar form.

*Nuǒ* (upper radical *hú*, *guǒ* rhyme): The phonetic gloss says it means to strip off clothes and expose the flesh. Its original pronunciation is *láng* (*guǒ* rhyme). It is also written as *luò* or *nǎo*; these two forms are identical. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical *yī* (clothing) and the phonetic *guǒ*. In the *Lüwen*, the character is written with the radical *shì* (deity), which is an error. The lower part is read as *luò* (*gù* rhyme). The *Qieyun* states it means to be exposed or leaked; it means to be spoiled or to leak. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *lù* (dew) means moist luster; it is composed of the radical *yǔ* (rain) and the phonetic *lù*.

Volume 17, Fascicle Seventeen: Root Medicinal Matters, Fascicle Seventeen. *Jiang* (降): In the *Erya*, it is said that *jiang* means "to descend"; in the *Yupian*, it means "to return"; according to the phonetic analysis, it means "to fall. The *Shangshu* says, "He sent down two daughters to the Guirei [confluence]. *Xia* (下): Pronounced *tu-zan*. In the *Qieyun*, it is said that *dan* (誕) means "great" and "trustworthy. In the *Yupian*, it means "to deceive. The *Guoye* says it means "to give birth. The *Shuowen* says it is formed with the radical for "speech" and the phonetic "yan," and is also written as *zhan* (這).

"Huǎng" (恍) [with the pinyin *huǎng*]: The *Yùpiān* states it means "vague and indistinct" (*huǎnghū*). The *Lǎozǐ* says, "Vaguely and indistinctly, yet within it there is something. The Imperial Commentary states: "The 'something' refers to the Dao above. Because it proceeds from existence back to non-existence and returns to the Ultimate Dao, it is said that 'within it there is something. Regarding the phonology: "Huǎng" means the mind is confused and obscured. It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "guāng" (*guāng*). The lower part, "mò xī," has the pinyin *mò xī*. The *Qièyùn* states it means "erroneous"; the *Shuowén* states it means "deluded. It is composed of the radical "chuò" (*chuò*, sound *chǒu lüè*) and the phonetic "mǐ" (*mǐ*). "Chuò" is a variant form of "辶" (*chuò*). *Note: The original text contains a mixture of classical Chinese characters, phonetic annotations, and lexicographical definitions. The translation above preserves the technical nature of the source while rendering it into accessible English.*

Aniruddha (the final syllable pronounced with the *dāng wèi* tone; a Sanskrit term) is also called Anuruddha (formerly transcribed as Anarulu; correctly Aniruddha). This means "Non-extinction" (*amṛta*), which is the name of an Arhat, specifically referring to the one foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

Volume 18, Fascicle 18, *Mūla-bhaiṣajya-vastu*. Fascicle 18. Regarding "bending the bow" (*wān gōng*): the *Yùnjí* states that "bending" refers to the curved posture of drawing a bow; the *Shuowén* states it is composed of the radical "bow" (*gōng*) and the phonetic "luán" (read as *jūróng*). The *Qièyùn* states it means "bow and arrow. The *Shìmíng* states that "bow" is "qióng," meaning that when it is drawn, it is arched and vaulted (*qióngqióng*). The *Shìběn* states that Huí, a minister of the Yellow Emperor, invented the bow. The *Shuowén* states it imitates the shape of a bow.

*Chùtūn* (𧘂突): The upper character is pronounced with the *chǐ* and *róng* rhymes; it means "to face" or "to encounter. Regarding its phonetic component (*kǎo*), it signifies movement or the Way, and it also refers to an intersection. The *Yùpiān* states it also means "to push" or "to shove" (*tú*). The lower character is pronounced with the *dú* and *gǔ* rhymes; the *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to deceive," while the *Yùnyīng* says it means "to strike. The *Shuōwén* says it refers to a dog attempting to emerge from a den.

"Dance" (wǔ): "without a master" (wú zhǔ). It is a rhyme for *gēnwǔ* (singing and dancing). The *Zuozhuan* states: "Dancing is that by which the eight musical tones are regulated and the eight winds are set in motion. The *Erya* states: "Wǔ is the same as *yú* (praying for rain). According to the *Shuowen*, it is composed of *chuǎn* (crossed feet) with *wú* (to lack) as the phonetic. The ritual texts write it as *wǔ* (from *rén*) [which is incorrect].
