Volume 19, Fascicle 19, *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle 19. *Ān* (知諳): Upper character, *zhì*; the phonetic component is *chí* (陟). It means to be aware or cognizant. Regarding its pronunciation, it denotes clarity and understanding. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) with the phonetic component "arrow" (*shǐ*). Lower character, *hán* (含); the phonetic component is *wū* (烏). The *Yupian* states it means trust or confidence. The *Yunying* states it means to remember. It is composed of the radical "speech" (*yán*) with the phonetic component "sound" (*yīnshēng*).

*Chí* (篲): The upper radical is *zhí* (之, the opposite of *zhì*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to grasp and hold," composed of the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *sì*. The lower radical is *qiú suì* (囚歲). The *Erya*, in the "Explanation of Herbs" (*Shicao*), states: "The *wangchui* (王篲) is the *jian* (葥). Guo's commentary says: "It resembles *li* (藜); its wood can be used to make brooms. In Jiangdong, it is called the "falling broom" (*luozhou*). Guo Pu’s preface to the *Sancai Tuji* says: "I repeatedly swept the path with the broom. It is also written as *huì* (彗), which is likewise acceptable. In legal texts, it is written as *zào* (㨹) with the hand radical; this is incorrect.

The character 𨏦 (shāng) is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *rèn*. The *Yùpiān* states it is the sound of a carriage; the *Kǎoshēng* states it means the rolling of a carriage. It is also written as 躙, meaning to trample underfoot. The *Gōngjīn zhèngzì* states that it is composed of the radical 車 and the phonetic 閵; the pronunciation of 閵 is the same as above, with the *qièyùn* reading *shīliáng*. The *Qièyùn* defines it as damage or pain. It is sometimes written as 慯.

The *Chuan* (舶) [is pronounced with the initial] *chang* and the *yuan* reversed; the *Yunyun* says it means "to pass through. The *Yunjí* says it means "to pierce or break. The *Yupian* says it means "to leak. The lower character is pronounced *bai*; the *Kaosheng* says it refers to a large ship on the great ocean, composed of the radical for "boat" (*zhou*) and the phonetic *bai*.

Regarding the character "mu" (木) in the term *mokujō* (木槍): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "mu" means "to cover," referring to how plants cover the earth as they grow; it is written with the radical "grass" (艹) below and resembles roots below and branches above. The lower component is pronounced *shiyang* (七羊反). The *Zilin* states that *qiang* (槍) refers to a spear (*shaosuo*), composed of the radical "wood" (木) and the phonetic "cang" (倉).

Volume 20, Fascicle 20: *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*. "Vāsi" (皤私)—the initial character is pronounced as *pó* (蒲波反); the correct transcription is *vāsīṣṭha*, a term from the Sanskrit language, which means "superior" or "most excellent."

The character *zǐ* (觜) is pronounced *shàng jí wěi fǎn* (上即委反). The *Bēicāng* (埤倉) records it as *mí* (𭪿), and the *Shuōwén* (說文) agrees that it refers to the beak of a bird. In legal texts (*lǜwén*), it is written with the radical for "mouth" (*kǒu*) as *zuǐ* (嘴); this character does not exist in standard dictionaries. The lower part is pronounced *duō guān fǎn* (多官反). The *Yùn* (韻) states it is *xù* (緒). It means "correct. Examining its phonetic component, it means "direct. The *Shuōwén* says it means "beginning. It is composed of the radical *lì* (立) and the phonetic *duān* (耑). *Duān* has the same pronunciation as above; it is said to resemble an object newly born that has not yet raised its head, sharing the same meaning as the character *qǐ* (豈). It does not take the radical for "mountain" (*shān*).

*Jiǎo* (絞): The ancient phonetic transcription is *qiǎo*. The *Kǎoshēng* states that it means "to bind. The *Erya* says, "*Jiǎo* is binding. Guo’s commentary notes that it refers to twisting and binding with ropes and cords. The second character, *jū* (居), has the phonetic transcription *yǐng*. The *Shuowen* states that *xiàng* (項) is the neck; it is composed of the radical *xié* (頁) and the phonetic *jīng* (巠).

The character for "to sell" (稱) is also pronounced *píng* (with the rhyme category *chù líng*) according to the *Shuowen*. It is explained as "to appraise" (*quán*) or "to lift up" (*jǔ*). It is also pronounced *chāng yùn*. It signifies knowing the weight [of goods]. It is composed of the radical *huò* (grain) and the phonetic *chén* (which is pronounced the same as *shàng xià mò xiè*). The *Qieyun* states it means "to sell at a loss. The *Kaosheng* states it means "to sell goods. It is composed of the radical *shì* (scholar) and the phonetic *mǎi* (buy).

The *Zílín* says it means "lineage" (*yìn*). The *Shuōwén* says it is formed from the radical *yóu* with the phonetic *yuè*; *yuè* has the sound *shàngbào* for the upper part and *zuòmù* for the lower part. The *Yùnquán* says it refers to the clan (*zōngzú*). The *Eryā* says: "The father’s paternal uncles and their descendants are called *zú*; the father’s paternal great-grandfather and his female descendants are called *zú*. Furthermore, it says: 'Siblings of the same surname who are children of cousins are called *qīn* (relatives). Guo Pu’s note says: 'Among relatives of the same surname, there is no mourning dress (*fú*')."

*Keng-hui* (糠穢): The upper character, *keng*, is pronounced with the *gāng* rhyme. The *Yùpiān* states it refers to the husk of rice; it is also written as *kāng* and has the same meaning. The *Shuowén* says it is the skin of grain, formed from the radical for "grain" (*huó*) and the phonetic *kāng*. The lower character, *yì*, is pronounced with the *fèi* rhyme. The *Qièyùn* states it means "vile"; dictionaries define it as "mixed filth. Gù Yěwáng says it means "impure. It is also written as *huì*, and both pronunciations and glosses are identical.

Regarding "jiāng" (疆), the pronunciation is *liáng* (良) with the final *-ǎi* (反); the *Erya* states: "Jiāngjiè means boundary, defense, enclosure, and fringe. Guo's commentary notes: "The boundaries of fields, borders, perimeters, and defensive outposts are all on the outer fringes. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jiāng is composed of the radical 'earth' and the phonetic 'qiáng' (彊). As for "jiè" (界), it is composed of the radical 'field' and the element 'jiè' (介), representing the shape of dividing a boundary. In legal texts, it is written as "qiáng" (彊), which is not the correct form of the character "qiáng" (強).

The character *yǎn* (黶子) is pronounced with the upper radical *shàng* (上) and the phonetic *yàn* (厭). The *Yùn yùn* (切韻) states it refers to black moles on the face. Regarding "chuāngpào" (瘡疱): the *Liángfǎn Yùpiān* states it refers to sores or wounds (*chuāngyí*). The *Lìjì* states, "If there is a sore on the head, one washes [the hair]. In archaic texts it is written as "chuāng" (創). In the *Qièyùn*, it is written as "biào" (皰), defined as a facial sore; the *Shuōwén* correctly defines it as "pào" (皰), meaning the skin has risen up. Guo's commentary notes: "Zeng" (曾) means "repeated" (*chóng*). It further states: "The son of a *zengsun* is called a *xuansun* (玄孫); the son of a *xuansun* is called a *laisun* (來孫); the son of a *laisun* is called a *kunsun* (晜孫); the son of a *kunsun* is called a *rengsun* (仍孫); and the son of a *rengsun* is called a *yunsun* (雲孫). Regarding "kun" (晜), it is an archaic form of the character "kun" (昆). Guo's commentary notes: "Kun" (晜) means "subsequent."

"Bǎi xī" (百䡬): The lower character is pronounced with the *mo* and *bàn* rhymes. According to the text, "Bǎi xī" is the name of the king who was the ancestral predecessor of Śākyamuni. Regarding "yù" (餘壻), it is also written as "yì" (𦕓) or "qǐng" (聟);

these are both vernacular characters pronounced with the *sū* and *jì* rhymes. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "the husband of a woman. The *Erya*, in the section on "Explaining Relatives," says: "The husband of a daughter is called *xì*; the parents of a wife and the parents of the *xì* are mutually called *hūn yīn* (marriage relations); two *xì* are called *yà*. Guo's commentary notes: "In Jiangdong, those of the same school are called *liáo xì* (colleague-husbands)."

Volume 2, Part 2: The Fundamental Matter of Schism in the Sangha, Section Two. Regarding "naked-footed" (跣足): the upper character *sǎo* (蘇典反) has the sound of *kǎo*; "walking on foot" (*tú zǎo*) means that the feet touch the ground. The lower character "foot" (*jiǎo*) was already fully explained in the preceding section on the *Mūla-bhaiṣajya-vastu*.

*Bēnchí* (奔馳). The *Wénzì jílüè* (Textual Collection and Abridgment) states that "bēn" means to startle; the *Shuowén* (Explanations of Characters and Words) records it as "to run. The *Erya* (Classic of Terms and Explanations) says, "The great carriage is called *bēn*," with Guo’s commentary noting this refers to the place where people walk, step, and run. Below, *zhílí* (直离) is the phonetic transcription. The *Qièyùn* (Phonetic Guide) says it means to pursue; the *Zishū* (Dictionary of Characters) says it means to gallop. The *Shuowén* explains the character as being composed of "mǎ" (horse) and the abbreviated form of "chí" (pool) as its phonetic component.

Regarding "to slander" (誹謗): the *Fǎnwén* (Explanations of Characters) states that "誹" is also "謗. It is pronounced with the initial *fāng* and the final *wēi* (誹亦謗也，又音方微反). The lower character is pronounced *bù* and *kuàng* (下補曠反). The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states it means "to defame" (謗毀也). It is composed of the radical "speech" (言) on the left and "非" (*fēi*) as the phonetic component on the right.

Pūraṇa (formerly transcribed as Púlánà, which is an error; the correct form should be Pūraṇa Kāśyapa)—*pūraṇa* means "full," and *Kāśyapa* is the clan name meaning "tortoise. This is the name of a non-Buddhist teacher who propounded the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).

Makkhali Gosāla—formerly called Mōgālī; the full name is Makkhali Gosāla. "Makkhali" is his clan name, and "Gosāla" is his mother's name. He is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who maintains that suffering and pleasure do not arise from causes, but occur spontaneously.

Śāṃśitiya (formerly translated as Śāṇakāyana) is fully called Śāṃśitiyapilāndīputra; Śāṃśitiya means "Equal Victory," while Pilāndī is the name of his mother. This refers to those non-Buddhist practitioners who do not require cultivation, who for eighty thousand great kalpas naturally undergo birth and death like the spinning of a ball of thread.

Amata—formerly transcribed as Ajita-keśakambala; *Ajita* means "Unconquerable," *Keśa* means "hair," and *Kambala* means "garment. This non-Buddhist practitioner wears garments made of human hair and subjects himself to the austerity of being scorched by five fires.

Kṛṣṇa Kātyāyana—formerly called Kalakūṭa, which means "Black-Necked"—is a member of the Kātyāyana clan. This non-Buddhist teacher responds according to the person: if someone asks whether existence exists, he answers that it does; if asked whether non-existence exists, he answers that it does.

Nigaṇṭha (formerly transcribed as Nìqiánduó; *nirgrantha* means "without ties," which is the general name for this class of non-Buddhist practitioners). Jñātiputra (here *jñāti* means "kinsman" or "friend"; *putra* refers to his mother's name). This school maintains that suffering has no fixed cause, yet it must necessarily be endured; they hold that only non-orthodox paths can sever it.

Regarding "gēngdū" (跟趺): according to the *Gǔhén* (古痕) method of phonetic analysis, it is defined as the back of the heel. According to the *Wúfǎn* (無反), the character below refers to the foot; the *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states that "jiǎodū" (脚趺) refers to the top of the foot. Furthermore, the *Shuōwén* (說文) records that it may also be written with the radical "fù" (付) as "fū" (跗).

Volume Three, Part Three: The Fundamental Matter of Schism in the Saṃgha. Volume Three. Māṇava. The Blessed One said: "Māṇava" was formerly translated as "Mānaba," which means "Young Sage" (Rutong Xian).
*Veda*: The "shang" (上) in *Bìtuózhòu shàng* (薜陀咒上) is pronounced *pú* (蒲) with the *jì* (計) tone; it is a term from the Sanskrit language. Formerly it was called *Wéiyuē* (韋陁) or *Fèiyuē* (吠陁);

here it is translated as "Clarification" (*Míng*), meaning "Mantra of Clarification. *Vaiśālī*: Formerly called *Wéiyélí* (維耶離) or *Píyélí* (毘耶離); the correct transliteration is *Chuǐshèlí* (吹舍釐). It is translated as "Extensive Splendor" (*Guǎngyán*). It is located south of the Ganges River in Central India.

"Hōng" (轟) is pronounced *shàng hū* (上呼) with the retroflex *hóng* (宏) as the final; the *Shuowen jiezi* states it is the sound of a multitude of chariots, the character being composed of three "chariots" (*chē*).

"Pǐ" (圮) is pronounced *shàng píng bǐ* (上平鄙) with the retroflex *pǐ* (圮); the *Zishu* states it means "to overturn," and "pǐ" also means "to destroy. The *Yunlüe* states it means "the collapse of a bank. The *Shangshu* states, "He issued mandates and destroyed his clans. The *Shuowen* states it is formed from "earth" (*tǔ*) and the phonetic "yǐ" (*yǐ shēng*), with the final *qièyùn* rhyme being *wǔ gān* (五肝). The *Erya* states that "repeated banks" (*chóng yá àn*) refers to two banks that are layered.

"Bèi lǚ" (背僂): The *Bǔmèi* (補妹) rhyme-cut states it refers to the spine; the *Erya* (爾雅) states "tǎibèi" (鮐背) signifies longevity. Guo's commentary notes that one whose back skin is like that of a *tái* (鮐) fish is like an elder. "Xià" (下): *Lìzhǔ* (力主) rhyme-cut; the *Zishū* (字書) states "yǒulǚ" (傴僂) means physical infirmity. The *Qieyun* (切韻) states "lǚ" (僂) means to be bent. The *Yùpiān* (玉篇) states it means to walk with a stoop. It is composed of the radical "person" (人) and the phonetic "lǚ" (縷) in abbreviated form. "Tái" (鮐) has the sound *tái*.

*Shòu jí* (瘦瘠): The upper character is pronounced *jiù* (救) and the lower is pronounced *qín xī* (秦昔). According to the *Qièyùn*, it means emaciated or impaired by illness. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Emaciated and gaunt. The *Erya* states: "Gaunt (*qú*), thin, and emaciated. Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "The people of Qi call the emaciated *qú yóu*. The pronunciation of *yóu* is *qú*. The *Shuowen* writes this as *dǎn* (𤸃).

Scroll 4, Volume IV, Root Matter on Schism in the Sangha, Scroll IV. *Ti-chui* (洟唾): The upper character *ti* (洟) is pronounced with the initial *th-* and the final *-k* (according to the *Qieyun*, it means nasal mucus). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is "nasal fluid," written with the radical for water (*shui*) and the phonetic *yi*. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as *di* (涕), pronounced with the initial *th-* and the final *-l-* (according to the *Shuowen*, it means eye-fluid, which does not carry the meaning of nasal mucus here). The lower character *chui* (唾) is pronounced with the initial *t-* and the final *-wo-* (according to the *Shuowen*, it means oral fluid). The *Liji* says, "In declining food, one does not spit. The *Shuowen* states it is written with the radical for mouth (*kou*) and the abbreviated phonetic *duo*.

Regarding "flattery" (chǎnyǔ): the character above is *chǒu* (with the phonetic *yàn*) and the dictionary states it means "deceptive speech. It is formed with the radical "speech" (*yán*) and the phonetic *xiàn*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is written as *chèn* with the character *yán*, meaning "sycophancy. The character below is *yú* (with the phonetic *jǔ*). The *Qieyun* says it refers to "talk"; the *Shuowen Jiezi* says it refers to "discourse," formed with the radical "speech" and the phonetic *wú*.

"Pānqiū" (攀鞦): the first character is read as *pǔ* with the *bān* rhyme; the *Shuowen* states it means "to pull. The *Qieyun* states it means "to long for," composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic "fán" (*fén*). The second character is read as *chī* with the *yóu* rhyme. The *Yunying* states it refers to the "leather rein of a carriage," composed of the radical "metal" (*gé*) and the phonetic "qiū" (*qiū*). It is also written as 鞧, 緧, or 䋺; these three forms are identical in pronunciation and definition.

"Kǐng-yè" (哽噎): the first character is pronounced as xiàngǔ (杏) and the second as wūjié (烏結). It means the obstruction of breath. The *Yùpiān* states that it is like a bone stuck in the throat. The term "yàn" (咽) used in the legal texts is pronounced as wùjiàn (烏見) or yān (煙), which does not carry the meaning of "kǐng-yè."

*Xūxī* (歔欷): The first character is read as *xiǔ* (朽) with the phonetic *jū* (居), and the second is read as *xù* (許) with the phonetic *jì* (既). It denotes a sound of grief. The *Yùnlüè* (韻略) states it means weeping. Gu Yewang says it is the lingering sound of sobbing. The *Shuowén* (說文) states that both characters follow the radical *qiàn* (欠) and have the sounds *xū* (虛) and *xī* (希); the second character is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

The character *zǎn* (攢) is pronounced with an initial *jiǔ* (九) and a final *shàng* (上) tone; the *Kǎo shēng* (考聲) states it means "growing in clusters. The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states it means "to join together. The *Shuōwén* (說文) states its correct form is written with the radical *zàn* (贊). The lower part, *qī hé* (七何), is the character *hé* (何); the *Zílín* (字林) states it means "to rub an object with the hand to make it tight. Both characters take the radical *shǒu* (手).

The character 𢗅 (jù) is pronounced with the upper radical *mò* (莫) and the lower radical *láng* (郎). The *Qieyun* states that it means "to fear" (*xī*). The *Shuowen* writes it as 忙 (*máng*). The *Yupian* states it means "haste. Dictionaries state it also means "trembling with fear" and "distress. It is formed from the radical 辵 (*chuō*) and the phonetic 豦 (*qū*), which has the pronunciation *jù*. The common variant is written with the radical 辵 and the phonetic 丑略 (*chǔlüè*), while the sound of 豦 remains *jù*.

*La-zhé*: Upper radical 手 (shǒu), phonetic 藍荅反 (lán dá fǎn); the *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states it means "to break. It is the standard character for "to destroy" (*cuī*) throughout ancient and modern times, composed of the radical 手 and the phonetic 立 (lì). The *Shuōwén Jiězì* writes it as 󱶍 (pinyin: zhé; yùpian: zhé shè fǎn). The *Yùpiān* states it also means "to break," while the *Zílín* states it refers to "folding clothes."

*Tièjǐ* (鐵𭪿): The upper character *tiè* is pronounced with the *jié* (結) tone. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "black metal. The *Shenyijing* (Scripture on Divine Marvels) says: "In the south there is a beast called Chietie (齧鐵), as large as a water buffalo; its dung can be used to make weapons. The lower character is also written as *zǐ* (觜); the *Zilizang* (Forest of Characters) states it means "the beak of a bird. It is not the character *huò* (唃) found in the Vinaya texts.

On top of the bellows (fēngdài), there is also the character 㰆, which is homophonous with 蒲拜反 (púbàifǎn). The *Shuowen* defines it as "a bag made of leather. The *Kaosheng* says it is "an implement for blowing fire. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as 排 (pái), which refers to the name of a wooden structure at the stern of a boat; this is not its usage here. Below it is the character 耐 (nài) with the phonetic value *dùnài*. The *Shuowen* writes it as 帒 (dài), defining it as "a pouch for holding objects."

*Jūn* (upper character *qīlún* [反]; *shuōwén* says: "The skin cracks and rises in fine lines"). It is also written as *jūn*, which is the same. In the *Lǜwén*, it is written with the radical *zú* (foot) as *qūn*; *shuōwén* says this means "to retreat," which is not its usage here. The lower character is *zhīlǒng* [反]. *Shuōwén* says it means "sickness. *Shìmíng* says: "It is called *zhòng* because heat is concentrated (*zhōng*) therein. It is composed of the radical *ròu* (flesh) and the phonetic *chóng* (heavy).

Regarding the character for *kōng* (箜篌): the first radical is pronounced *kǔ* (苦) with the tone *fǎn* (反), and the second radical is *hú* (胡) with the tone *gōu* (鉤). The *Zìyuàn* (字苑) states that the *kōnghóu* was originally a music of the Hu (barbarians). The *Hànshū* (漢書) records that Emperor Ling enjoyed Hu-style clothing and thus had the *hu kōnghóu* (Hu lute) created. The *Shìběn* (世本) states it was the "Mímí" (靡靡) melody composed by Shíyán (師延). It is named after the lord of the state of Kōng (空) located above the [mountain] *Zhēng* (𠿒).

Fascicle Five. The Fifth Volume of the *Mūlasaṃghabheda-vastu*. The character *dàn* (黕): in the *Shàngdūgǎn-fǎn Zìshū*, it means dregs or impurities; in the *Zílín*, it means black. The lower radical *suōlì-fǎn*: the *Qièyùn* states it means complexion, and also refers to a beautiful luster.

Regarding "Miaochi" (妙翅): the *Shishi* (施智) commentary reverses this, stating that according to the *Shuowen* (說文), it refers to bird feathers; it is also written as "chi" (翄). Now, Miaochi is the Golden-Winged Bird (*garuḍa*). The old Sanskrit transcription was *kalola*, while the correct form is *garuḍa*. This is translated as "Golden-Winged" (*jīnchì*) or "Exquisite-Winged" (*miaochì*). This bird possesses the four modes of birth—womb, egg, and so forth—and is able to devour dragons born by those same four modes, as has already been explained above.

"Konghe (恐嚇)"—the *shang* rhyme is *qiu* and the *long* rhyme is *zong*; the *Yunyun* states it means "to startle. The *Erya* states it means "to fear. It is composed of the radical "heart" (*xin*) with the phonetic "gong" (*gong*, pronounced *gǒng*). The *Huge* (呼格) rhyme for the character below is *he*. The *Yupian* states it means "to roar in anger. The *Zishu* states it is the sound of shouting in anger; it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kou*) with the phonetic "he" (*he*).

*Xiāo-ái* (囂埃): The "xiāo" is pronounced as *xǔ jiāo* (許嬌反). The *Yùnyīng* (韻英) states it means clamor; the *Shuowén* (說文) states it means sound. It refers to breath emerging from the head. It is composed of *jí* (㗊, pronounced *zhí*) and *yè* (頁, the head). *Jí* is pronounced *zhí*; *qì* (气) is pronounced *qì*. The character below, *wū kāi* (烏開反), is explained in the *Shuowén* as fine dust. It is composed of *tǔ* (土) and the phonetic *yǐ* (矣).

The term *xūn hú* (獯狐) should, according to the Vinaya texts, be written as two characters: *xūn* (𪇑, pronounced *xūn*) and *hú* (鶘, pronounced *hú*). The *Jìxùn* (集訓) states: "The *xūn hú* is a strange bird; its shape resembles that of the earth-owl (*tǔxiāo*), it hides by day and emerges at night, and it delights in eating snakes and rats. The current character *xūn* (獯) is actually a variant name for the Xiongnu people, known as *Xūnyù*. The character *hú* (狐) refers to the beast ridden by ghosts. The subsequent passage in the Vinaya text states: "Or [the head] is made like that of a wild fox (*yěhú*). This is correct.

The character 斤 (jīn) is pronounced *jǔ* (with the initial *xìn*) in the upper part; the *Shuowen* states it means "to hew wood" and depicts the shape of an axe. In the *Qieyun*, it is sixteen *liang*. The lower part, 斫 (zhé), is pronounced *jué*; the *Jixun* states it means "to pare," and the *Shuowen* notes that "hewing" (*zhǔ*) is also "to hew" (*zhé*), following the radical 斤 with the phonetic 𠁁. In lexicographical works it is written as 斵, with the same pronunciation and meaning; alternative forms such as 𣃆 or 𧯞 are both not the original characters.

*Menmo* (upper character *men*, pinyin *mò*; lower character *mo*, pinyin *mó*): According to the *Zishu*, it means to stroke or caress. The *Kaosheng* states: "To *mo*, *men*, and *mo* is to stroke and caress; it follows the radical for 'hand' and takes 'men' as its phonetic. The lower character *mo* has the pinyin *mó*. The *Yunying* states: "To *mosha* (stroke/gently rub) is also to stroke and caress."

*Yojana* (formerly transliterated as *youyan*, *youxun*, or *yushena*; it is a phonetic shift from the Sanskrit term) has no direct equivalent in Chinese. It is said to be sixteen *li* or forty *li*, representing the distance a royal army could travel in one day according to ancient sages.

Volume Six, Part Six: The Fundamental Matter of Schism in the Sangha, Volume Six. *Jiyan* (囈言): The first character, *ji*, is pronounced with the initial *yú* (魚) and the final *jì* (祭). It is also written as *zhuì* (䆿). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Sleep-talking; it means to startle while speaking. It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) and the phonetic *yì* (藝). It is also written as *zhuì* (䆿), composed of the radical *xiǎn* (省) and the phonetic *niè* (臬). The character *niè* is pronounced with the initial *yú* (魚) and the final *jié* (結). The subsequent character, *yán* (言), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It is composed of the radical *kǒu* (口) and the phonetic *xīn* (辛). The pronunciation of *xīn* is *xīn* (𠍴).

Volume Seven, Part Seven: The Fundamental Matter of Schism in the Sangha, Volume Seven. Regarding "Jici" (祭祠): the upper character is pronounced with the initial *zǐ* and the final *lì* (as per the *Yùnyǔ*). It means to offer sacrifices (*xiǎng*) or to perform ancestral rites (*sì*). The *Erya* states: "The sacrifice to Heaven is called *fánchái* (burning wood). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the character is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the element "meat" (*ròu*), signifying holding meat to present it. The lower character is pronounced *cí*. The *Erya* states: "The spring sacrifice is called *cí*. Guo's commentary notes: "*Cí* is like eating; its pronunciation is *sì*."

The character for *xiǎn* (浣) in the first syllable is interchangeable with *huàn* (澣); its pronunciation is *húguǎn* (胡管反). Lexicons state that it means "to wash. The second syllable, *zhuó* (濯), has the phonetic transcription *zhíjué* (直覺反). The *Qieyun* states that *zhuó* also means "to wash. The *Liji* (Book of Rites) says, "Wash clothes and rinse caps before attending court. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains that it is composed of the radical "water" (*shui*) and the phonetic component "gàn" (*gan*).

*Upādhyāya*: [The first syllable] *u-pa* is pronounced with three tones (the first being *wu-gu*, the second *tang-he*). In Sanskrit, this is translated as "personal teacher" (*qīnjiào*); the old transliteration "Heshang" is erroneous. This has already been explained previously.

The term for the hub (*gǔ*) is pronounced with the *chún* (迍) and *fǎnqiè* (反切) [of the *Yùnyùn*]. The *Zhōu lǐ* states that the spokes (*líng*) are square to represent the earth; the cover represents heaven, while the wheel is circular to represent the sun and moon. The character below is pronounced *wū* (屋). The *Yùpiān* identifies it as the hub of a chariot. The *Shī jīng* says, "Patterned rugs and long hubs," and the *Lǎozi* says, "Thirty spokes converge in a single hub."

Uruvilvā is a corruption and abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; its full form is Uruvilvākāśyapa. *Uruvilvā* means "wood-apple tree" (*feronia limonia*), so named because there was a wood-apple tree on his chest that resembled the fruit of the wood-apple tree. *Kāśyapa* means "Drinking Light," which is his clan name (*gotra*).

Volume 8, Fascicle 8, Root Matter on Schism in the Sangha, Fascicle 8. Regarding "washing and rinsing" (zǎoshòu): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "zǎo" means to wash. The *Liji* says, "The Confucian has one who washes the body and bathes in virtue. The *Chenyán* states it means to prostrate; the *Sūqīn* provides the fanqie as "sùjìng" (lower tone). The *Yùn* states it means to rinse the mouth. In the *Jìnshū*, Sūn Chǔ said to Wáng Wǔzǐ, "The reason for 'rinsing stone' is to sharpen one's teeth. The legal text (*lǜwén*) uses the character "zǎo" (藻), which refers to the aquatic plants *píng* and *zǎo* forming patterns when intertwined; this does not carry the meaning of "washing and rinsing."

Regarding "jǐngwù" (警寤): the upper character *jǐng* (警) is pronounced *jū yǐng* (居影); the *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states it means "to be on guard" (*jǐngjiè* 警戒). The *Shuōwén* (說文) states it means "to awaken" (*wù* 寤). Lexicons state it means "to observe and perceive" (*juéchá* 覺察). The *Lǐjì* (禮記) says, "When about to ascend to the hall, one's voice should be raised"; Zheng’s commentary explains this as meaning "to alert those within. The lower character *wù* (寤) is pronounced *fàng wǒ* (放吾); the *Shuōwén* states it means "awakening" (*wùjué* 寤覺), being composed of the abbreviated form of *mǎo* (艸) with *wǔ* (吾) as the phonetic. In legal texts (*lǜwén*), it is written as *jīng* (驚), which the *Shuōwén* defines as "a runaway horse. It is also written as *wù* (窹), which the *Shuōwén* defines as "what the people of Chu call a hearth. Neither of these is the character for "alerting and awakening" (*jǐngwù*).

Regarding "Wei" (未) as explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi*: it means "flavor" (*wei*). Among the Five Elements, wood reaches its maturity in Wei; its form represents overlapping leaves. Wood possesses flavor. The character is pronounced "zhi" (支) for the upper radical and "chang-shu" (常恕) for the phonetic component. The *Changyun* states it means "dawn"; the *Kaosheng* states it means "clarity. The *Shuowen* further explains that it refers to the morning when the sun has not yet risen, composed of the "sun" radical with "shu" (署) as the phonetic.

*Yu* (to drive) is pronounced *shang* (with the *niu* radical reversed); the *Shuowen* states it means "to harness. The *Zhouli* mentions the "five types of driving" (*wuyù*), namely: sounding the *huánluán* bells; following the bends of water; passing through a marshy area; stopping the dance at a crossroads; and pursuing game on the left side of the road. The *Shiben* states that Haisi harnessed oxen, Xiang Wang rode them, and Han Ai invented the art of driving. *Xià* (mare) is pronounced *pí* (with the *rěn* radical reversed). The *Erya* calls it *pǐnchě*; Guo’s commentary notes it is a "grass-mare," with *chě* pronounced *shè*.

Regarding "chariot" (*chēlù*): the upper character is pronounced *jiǔ* (with the rhyme *yú*), as the *Shī* says, "the light chariot with the tinkling bells on its bit. The lower character is pronounced *gù* (with the rhyme *luò*). According to the *Zhōu Lǐ*, there are five types of chariots (*wǔ lù*) named according to their ornamentation; this is the Great Chariot (*Dà lù*) ridden by the Son of Heaven. The preface to the *Wén xuǎn* states that the rough-spoked wheel (*chuī lún*) was the beginning of the Great Chariot.

*Upāsaka* (the *u* sound is pronounced like *wu*; the *so* sound is pronounced like *su*; the *ka* sound is pronounced like *jiang* [qieyun: *kha*]; it is a Sanskrit term; the old translation "youposai" is erroneous). This means "male lay follower," referring to a white-robed person who observes the ten precepts of wholesome conduct.

The character *bì* (襞) has the initial *bi* (必益反) for the upper radical and the final *tié* (徒叶反) for the lower radical. Dictionaries state that *bìlüè* (襞掠) means to fold or layer garments; both radicals are the "clothing" (*yī*) radical with *pì* (辟) as the phonetic component. In ritual texts, the lower character is written as *zhí* (𢮕), pronounced *jiǎo* (󰪑), meaning to measure objects; it does not carry the meaning of *bìtié* (襞褺).

The character 鞭 (biān) is pronounced with the upper radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *dī* (lower part of 低). Its gloss says it is a "horse-whip. Lexicons state it is a "biting whip" (*mǎcè*). The lower part is pronounced *tā* (he tā fǎn); lexicons state it means "to strike. The *Shàngshū* says, "He struck him to record [the offense]. The *Lǐjì* says, "When King Cheng committed an error, he then struck Bóqī. It follows the hand radical with the phonetic *dá*. In legal texts, it is written as 韃 (*dà*) following the metal radical (*cónggē*), which is not the correct form.

*Āidài* (upper tone *ài*, lower tone *dài*). The *Pīcāng* states: "Āidài" describes the appearance of clouds arising in dense, luxuriant masses. The *Qièyùn* says it is the appearance of clouds; the *Tōngsùwén* states that clouds covering the sun are called *āidài*. *Huì* is pronounced with the initial *wū* and the final *wài*.

*Feifei* (霏霏): The rhyme dictionary states that *fenfei* (雰霏) describes the falling of snow; it is composed of the radical "rain" (*yǔ*) and the phonetic "fei" (*fēi*). The pronunciation of *fēn* is *fǔwén* (撫文). Volume Nine, Part Nine:

*Gēnběn pòsēng shì* (根本破僧事), Volume Nine. *Dìhài* (躓害): The upper character, *zhì* (躓), is pronounced *zhèlì* (陟利). The *Shuowén* states it means "obstruction. The *Zishū* states it means "to stumble. It is composed of the radical "foot" (*zú*) and the phonetic "zhì" (*zhì*). The lower character, *hài* (害), is pronounced *hù'ài* (戶艾). The *Shuowén* states it means "injury. It is composed of the radical "roof" (*mián*—meaning "house") and the phonetic "fēng" (*fēng*—meaning "speech"). Injury arises from within the house. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as *hài*; this is a vernacular form with the phonetic *jiè* (介).

"Kuài" (怪) is pronounced with the ancient initials *huài* and *fǎn*. The *Lunyu* states, "The Master did not speak of strange things (*guài*)," and Wang Su’s commentary explains it as "strange anomalies. The text of the Vinaya also uses the character "guài," which is likewise acceptable. In the *Yunjian*, it means "to be startled"; it is composed of the radical "heart" (*xīn*) and the phonetic "è" (*è*). The pronunciation of "è" is the same as above.

"Wa-li" (瓦礫): "Wa" is pronounced as in "wu-gua-fan. The *Erya* states: "A ceramic vessel is called a *deng*. The *Gukao Shi* states: "The Lord of Kunwu was the first to produce ceramics. "Li" (礫) is pronounced as in "lang-ji-fan. The *Zilin* defines it as sand and gravel. The *Shiming* states: "Li refers to small pebbles. The term appears in the Vinaya texts as "li-pi-shi" (礰石), which is a phonetic transcription and does not carry the meaning of "ceramic debris."

*Jiǎng* (牖): The upper character is *chū* (楚) with the two reversed; the *Shìmíng* (*Explanations of Names*) states that *jiǎng* means "clear hearing" (*cōng*), referring to the clarity of perception when looking outward from within. The *Shuōwén* (*Explanations of Characters*) states that what is in a house is called *jiǎng*; the lower part is read as *jiǔ* (久). The *Shuōwén* further explains it as piercing a wall and using wood to form a lattice. The *Lǐjì* (*Book of Rites*) states: "The Confucian scholar has a door of wild grass and a window of jar-rim. The *Shuōwén* explains this [character for *huò* (甕)] as being composed of *piàn* (片) and the phonetic *fǔ* (甫).

Volume Ten, Part One of the *Mūlasaṃghabheda-vastu*. "Quǎn" (捲): According to the *Yùpiān*, it means "without rolls" or "without vigor. It is the force of rolling. The *Qièyùn* defines it as "folding the hand. The *Guǎngyá* states that "quánquán" (拳拳) means "anxious concern. The lower character (捲): In the *Qièyùn*, it is read as *dǔtǐng* (都挺反), meaning "to strike. In the Qin pronunciation, it is *dégěng* (得耿反). The *Shuōwén* explains it as "striking with a staff. It is also pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

*Zì* (牸): Pronounced *shí* (上疾吏反) according to the *Qièyùn*. It refers to a female ox (*niú bǐn*). According to the *Yùpiān*, it means a mother cow. Pronounced *xià shì hài fǎn*. The *Erya* states that the *chái* (豺) has "dog-like feet. Guo's commentary notes that its legs resemble those of a dog. The *Liji* says, "The *chái* then sacrifices to the beasts. It is composed of the radical *zhài* (豸) and the phonetic *cái* (才). The character *zhài* (豸) is pronounced *wén ěr fǎn*.

*Naraka* (pronounced with the retroflex *ṇa*, or alternatively *Nalaka*; these are different transliterations of the Sanskrit term) means "instrument of suffering" or "implement of suffering. This refers to the instruments used for undergoing suffering, specifically the collective name for the eight cold and eight hot great hells, including the Avīci Hell.

"Hai" (pronounced with the initial *h* and the final rhyme *lai-fan*): the *Fangyan* states that the people of Chu called laughter "hai" (with the final rhyme *si-miao-fan*). The *Liji* says, "One does not laugh while holding the ropes [of the coffin], nor does one laugh when facing a funeral. The *Shuowen* explains it as "joyful laughter," stating that it is composed of the radical for "dog" (*quan*) and the character for "bamboo" (*zhu*), implying that one laughs only after finding pleasure. There are also two other forms, *ji* and *li*, but neither is correct.

*Qiú* (upper character pronounced *yue*, lower character pronounced *yu*). The *Erya* states: "A *ti* is called a *yi*. Guo's commentary says: "It is a stake (*qiue*) driven into the ground; that which is on the ground is called a *nie*. Guo's commentary further states: "This refers to the gate-stake (*men-qiue*). It is also written as *que*. *Ti* is pronounced *te*; *nie* is pronounced *yu-lie*.

*Bèng* (pronounced *běng*, with the first character read as *běng* and the second as *zhèng* according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, meaning "to scatter") is written as *bèng* or *fēi*. The *Qieyun* states it means "congealed blood. The *Shiming* says it is *huì*; this refers to flowing and spreading filth. *Huì* is pronounced *huā* (with the second tone). It is the sound of water.

*Pá* (上蒲巴反) means to scratch; it is also written as *bǎ* (下古獲反). The *Yùpiān* states that it refers to the palm or the ear. The *Yīnpǔ* states that it means to strike with the hand; it is composed of the radical "hand" (*shǒu*) and the phonetic element "guó" (*guó shēng*).

"Fire ascends" (huǒ shàng): "shàng" is pronounced as *hū* with the *guǒ* rhyme. The *Shāngshū* says, "Fire and the sun blaze upward. The *Shìběn* says, "Suìrén [the Sage] drilled wood to produce fire. "Xià" (below) is pronounced as *lì* with the *xiǎo* rhyme. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to roast. The *Kǎoshēng* says it means "to press with fire. It follows the radical for "roasting" (*zhì*) and takes *liáo* as its phonetic component. In the *Lǜwén*, it is written as "liào" following the fire radical, which is also acceptable. *Liáo* is pronounced *liáo*; *suì* is pronounced *suì*.

*Bhagavān* (pronounced *bójiàn*, with the second syllable reversed as *bójiǎn* according to the Sanskrit; alternatively transcribed as *Bhagavat*; formerly translated as "World-Honored One" because he is revered by both the mundane and supramundane worlds). The six meanings have already been explained previously; this is the tenth among the ten titles [of the Buddha].

*Tathāgata* (呾他揭多)—the initial syllable is pronounced with the "dang ge" (當割) tone; in the old Sanskrit transcription it was called *Tadāgata* or *Tadāgada*, which is translated as "Tathāgata. This is the first of the ten titles.

"Pānghuài" (霶霈): the first character is pronounced with the *pǔ* rhyme and the *láng* final; the second is pronounced with the *pǔ* rhyme and the *gài* final. The *Qièyùn* states that "pānghuài" refers to heavy rain. Lexicons describe it as the appearance of torrential rain. Both characters are composed of the "rain" radical (*yù*) and are phono-semantic compounds. The term appears in the Vinaya texts as "pāngpèi" (滂沛), which describes the appearance of flowing water and does not carry the meaning of heavy rain.
*Sahā* (索訶): The first character is pronounced as *sū* (蘇各反) and the second as *hā* (呵). In Sanskrit, it was formerly called *Sapō*; this is translated as the "Endurance World" (*Kṣānti-loka*).

*Xù* (旭): The first character is pronounced as *xǔ* (許玉反). The *Qièyùn* states it means "early morning. The *Shuowén* states it refers to the appearance of the sun at dawn, or "clarity," composed of the radical for "sun" and the phonetic element *jiǔ*. The second character is pronounced as *shí* (時掌反). The *Shuowén* states it means "to ascend. In ancient script, it is written as the character for "up" (*shàng*), and it also has the two pronunciations *shàng* and *tóng* (同). It is the same as the above.

*Cháo xī* (morning sun): "shè" is the reversed *qièyùn* (phonetic analysis); it means dawn. The *Erya* states: "cháo-dàn" (morning) means early. The *Laozi* says: "A whirlwind does not last the whole morning. *Xià* is pronounced with the *qièyùn* *xǔ jī*; it refers to sunlight. It is composed of the radical "sun" (*rì*) and the phonetic component "xī" (*xī*).

"Pínjǔ" (貧窶): The upper character, "pín" (貧), is pronounced with the initial *k* (符巾反); according to the *Zìshū* (字書), it means "extreme poverty" or "destitution. Its archaic form is written as "qióng" (窮). The lower character, "jǔ" (窶), is pronounced with the initial *q* (其矩反); according to the *Qièyùn* (切韻), it means "poor and lacking propriety. The *Erya* (爾雅) states, "Jǔ means poverty," and Guo's commentary explains this as "being poor and lowly."

Regarding the character *yàng* (樣): The *Guǎngyǎ* states it means a mallet (*chuí*). Lexicons cite the *Guǎngyǎ* as using the character *zhui* (椎). The *Lǎozǐ* says, "The mallet-wheel chariot" (*zhūilún chē*).

Regarding *shéngquān* (繩棬): the *Yùnpǐn* defines it as a rope; it also means straight. The *Shàngshū* says, "Wood follows the line and becomes straight" (*mù cóng shéng zé zhèng*). The *Yùnpǐn* states it is a vessel shaped like a dipper made by bending bamboo. According to this, *shéngquān* refers to using a rope to form a ring-like shape (*quān*) for the purpose of tying objects. In the legal texts (*lǜwén*), it is written as *bì* (𢃩), which is identical to *kùn* (憒); it means slight confusion or distress.

Regarding the characters *huan* (貆) and *he* (貈): the first is pronounced *hu-guan* (呼官反) and the second *xia-ge* (下各反). The *Erya* states that the young of the *he* is called *huan*. The *Tianzi Zhuan* records that when the Son of Heaven was hunting at Lake Qi, he captured a black *he* to sacrifice to the Lord of the River. In legal texts, the characters *huan* (獾) and *mo* (狢) are used; their pronunciations are identical, and these vernacular characters are also used interchangeably.

"Kui" (匱乏) means "to seek higher positions. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is pronounced with the rhyme of "jie" (竭); according to the *Qieyun*, it also means "lack. The lower character, "fa" (乏), is pronounced with the rhyme of "fang fa" (房法). The *Shuowen* states that it means "poverty" and also "lack. The *Zuo Zhuan* says that turning a "zheng" (正) upside down forms "fa" (乏); the character does not derive from [the character] "zhi" (之).

*Kǎnglì* (伉儷): The first character is pronounced *kǔ* with the *làng* rhyme; the second is pronounced *láng* with the *jì* rhyme. Lexicons state it means "equal" (*děng*) and also "rival" (*dí*). Gu Yewang says, "Unable to protect one's *kǎnglì*" refers to this.

*Shū guī shàng shì zhú fǎn qiè yùn*: *Shū* means "sudden" (*shūhù*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "swift. It is composed of *quán* (dog) and *yóu*; it refers to a dog running swiftly. In the *Lüwen*, it is written as *shū*. The *Erya* says: "*Shū shū huì huì* [describes] departing from calamity and poison; it is also a dark-blue silk. This does not carry the meaning of "swift. Below, *jǔ wéi fǎn qiè yùn* says: "To return; to reach; also, to be tranquil and still."

Volume Eleven, Part One: The Fundamental Matter of Schism in the Sangha, Volume Eleven. Regarding the term *yòu-yù* (猶豫): the upper character, *yòu*, is pronounced with the *zhōu* radical and the *rén* rhyme; the lower character, *yù*, is pronounced with the *yáng* radical and the *jiǎ* rhyme. The *Zìshū* (Dictionary of Characters) states it means "first" or "to prepare. The *Kǎoshēng* (Investigation of Sounds) states that *yòu-yù* refers to being indecisive. The *Erya* states that *yòu* is like the *jǐ* (a species of deer). Master Lù’s *Shìwén* (Explanatory Text) states: "In Longxi, the young dog is called *yòu*; when walking, the *yù* goes ahead of the person."

Regarding "wùchǎn" (erroneous/contrary): the upper character is pronounced *gù* (as in *gùfàn*). The *Yùnyùn* states it means "error. The *Shuōwén* uses the character "wù" (悞) with the same meaning. The lower character is pronounced *chānyuǎn*. The *Shuōwén* states it means "to deviate" and also "to err. It is said to mean "lying opposite one another. It is composed of "xī" (夕) and "ruò" (若), with the phonetic "wǎ" (瓦). The radical "jǐng" (井) has the phonetic "zhéjià" (陟駕). The form used in the Vinaya texts as "chǎn" (舛) is not the original character.

The character *zú* (卒) in the phrase *zú suì* (卒歲) has the pronunciation *shàng zǐ yù fǎn*. The *Shuōwén* says it means "to finish"; the *Qièyùn* says it means "exhausted" or "already. The character is composed of *qiú* (求) and one stroke. The *Lǜwén* (律文) writes it as *zhū* (𣨛). The *Erya* says: "*zhū*, *cúlò* (徂落), *yì* (殪), *xī* (𣦸)"—the meanings here differ from "to finish the year. The character *suì* (歲) in the phrase *zú suì* has the pronunciation *xià xiāng yì fǎn*. The *Erya* says: "In summer it is called *suì*. Guo’s commentary states: "This takes the movement of the planet Jupiter (*Suìxīng*) through one station [as its basis]. The *Shuōwén* says it is composed of two *zhǐ* (止) and the phonetic *xū* (戌), written as *wǎn* (𣥗).

*Xunming* (殉命): Upper character, *cí* with the rhyme *rùn* (according to the *Guǎngyùn*, it means to accompany a living person to their burial; it also means to seek). Gu Yewang says: "To exert one's strength to follow in death. It is called *xùn* because the person follows the object [of sacrifice] in death. Lower character, *méi* with the rhyme *bìng*. The *Qièyùn* says: "To employ; to instruct and guide. The *Yùpiān* says: "To trust. The *Shuōwén* states that it is composed of the radical "mouth" (*kǒu*) and the phonetic component "jí" (*jí*).

"Qiān yī" (to lift the garment): "qù" and "gàn" are the reversed pronunciations. Ye Wang states that in Qi and Lu, "shě" (to abandon/drop) is called "qiān. The *Liji* says, "In the heat, do not lift your skirt (*mǔ qiān shāng*). Zheng’s commentary states, "It refers to lifting the hem (*qiū*). "Xià yú jī" is the reversed pronunciation. The *Shiben* states that Huangdi’s minister Hu Cao, whose surname was Hu, created clothing; what is above is called "yī" (upper garment), and what is below is called "shāng" (lower garment).

The character 𡍩 (chǎng) is pronounced with the upper part *chǒu* (the same as in *gélǚ*) and the lower part *chì* (as in *chìliàng* or *chìliǎng*). It is commonly written as 坼 (*chè*). According to the *Qièyùn*, it means to split; it also means to break or destroy. The character below is pronounced *chì* (as in *chìliàng* or *chìliǎng*). The *Zìpǔ* states that the character 車 (*chē*) is from the *Zílín*, which says it means an open shed. It is composed of the radical 广 (*guǎng*, pronounced *yǎn*) and the phonetic 敞 (*chǎng*). The sound of 广 is *yǎn*.

Regarding "cǎo shàn" (草苫): the character *shàn* is pronounced with the initial *zhān* and final *-ièr*. The *Erya* states, "The white canopy is called *shàn*. Guo’s commentary notes that it is a canopy made of white rushes (*bai mao*). Today, in Jiangdong, it is called *gài*, pronounced with the initial *hú* and final *-là*.

Volume 12, Fascicle 12: *Mūlasaṃghabheda*. Fascicle 12. Regarding "yúchéng" (踰城): the phonetic gloss states it means to transcend (*yù*) or to pass over. Gu Yewang says: "There is none who transcends my village. It is also written as "yú" (逾) with the same meaning. The lower radical is "shìzhēng" (市征). Cui Bao’s *Gǔjīn Zhù* (Notes on Ancient and Modern Times) states: "Chéng" (城) means "to contain" (*shèng*). It is that which contains the people and things received. The *Shuowén* says: "That by which the people are contained; it takes 'tǔ' (earth) as the semantic component and 'chéng' (cheng) as the phonetic component."

*Néng* (niece/nephew): the first character is pronounced as *shàng wǔ huì fǎn* (the upper part is read as *wǔ huì*) and the second has the phonetic value of *shēng*. The *Erya* states: "The son of one's paternal aunt is called *néng*; the son of one's maternal uncle is also called *néng*; one says that he whom I call 'uncle,' I call my *néng*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes this character as *biān*, with the same definition as in the *Erya*.

*Kuī* (上, qù guī fǎn): The *Yùpiān* defines it as "a slight glance. The *Shuōwén* states that it is formed with the radical "cave" (*xué*) and the phonetic component "guī. Lexicons also write it as *kuī*, which is identical. The *Qièyùn* defines it as "to spy. The *Yùpiān* further states it refers to the "credentials of a duke or marquis" or "to watch/spy. It is also pronounced *chì yàn fǎn*.

The character for *guō* (瓦鍋) is pronounced with the initial *wǔ* and the final *guǎ* (五寡反); it is also written as *fánxiàng* (凡像). Its shape is like that of a tile (*wǎ*). The lower part is pronounced *gǔ* and *huó* (古和反). Dictionaries state it is an iron vessel; the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as *yǒu* (󱷖), stating it is a cauldron (*fǔ*) with legs and a spout made of clay. It is also written as *wō* (堝), and the *Qieyun* states it is a "sweet cauldron" (*gānwō*). Today it is written as *guō*, though some say it is a warming vessel.

*Upādhyāya*: The first character, *ū* (pronounced with the *gǔ* tone), and the second, *dài* (pronounced with the *hè* tone), are Sanskrit terms; here they are translated as "Preceptor" (*qīnjiào*). This has already been explained previously. *Tiáozhí*:

The first character, *tiáo* (pronounced with the *yáo* tone), the *Cāngjié piān* states means "leaping," while the *Guǎngyǎ* states means "bounding. The second character, *zhí* (pronounced with the *zhì* tone), refers to leaping one's body toward the ground. Both characters for *tiáozhí* are composed of the "foot" radical (*zú*) and the phonetic component *zhào*. *Zhèng* [the commentator] states that these are both sounds.

Volume 13, Fascicle 13: *Mūla-saṃghabheda-vastu*. Fascicle 13. "Ūnā" (癰瘡): The first character is pronounced as *yōng* (容) with an initial *shang* (上), or alternatively as *yōng* (癰). According to the *Yùn yùn*, it refers to a carbuncle (*piḍaka*) or a malignant ulcer (*gaṇḍa*). The second character is pronounced as *chǔ liáng* (楚良). According to the *Yù piān*, it means a wound or sore (*vraṇa*). In archaic script, it was written as *chuàng* (創). The *Lìjì* states: "If there is a wound on the head, one washes it."

*Kang-mi* (秔米): The phonetic gloss reads *gǔ xíng fǎn*. The *Shìwén* states it is "rice. The *Běncǎo* says that when boiled to make dry rice for eating, it stops diarrhea. Furthermore, *jīng* (粳) is a vulgar character; its lower radical is *mò lǐ fǎn*. The *Shìwén* defines it as "the grain of the *kǔ* (穬) millet," depicting the shape of the rice grain.

Regarding the character *mi* (written below with the phonetic *wu*): the rhyme dictionary states it means "to bring the mouths together. Lexicons state it is formed from the radical *qian* with the sound *wu*. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as *wu* (from the radical *kou*), meaning the sound of lamentation such as "Alas! (*wuhū*); it does not carry the meaning of "sucking" (*mīzà*).

Volume 14, Fascicle 14. *Mūlasaṃghabheda-vastu*, Fascicle 14. *Caṇḍāla*. (The first character is pronounced "shang" with the tone mark on "zhu"; the Sanskrit term is *caṇḍāla*, which is translated as "one who kills. This refers generally to those of the caste engaged in slaughter and butchery. It is also called "Fierce and Blazing Evil Karma. According to the laws of the Western Regions, such persons must carry a distinctive emblem when they travel, either shaking a bell or carrying a bamboo staff for splitting heads; otherwise, the king shall punish them.)
*Māṇava* is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it means "Scholar-Child" (*Routong*) or "Sage. Regarding the character *chuáng* (bed):

the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is composed of the radical *mu* (wood) and the phonetic *qiáng* (sound of *qiáng*, with the lower part pronounced as *gǔhuáng*). Lexicons define it as a "longitudinal beam," referring to a horizontal wooden member. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as *guāng*, which refers to the name of the *huāngláng* tree; today, this character *guāng* is also commonly used for the bed-frame.

Regarding "Ōu" (歐): the upper radical is "Ōu" (謳), pronounced *kǒu* (口反). The *Kǎoshēng* states that "Ōu" refers to the desire to vomit; dictionaries state it is a disease of the stomach; the *Shuōwén* states it means "to vomit," composed of the radical "quàn" (欠) with the phonetic "qū" (區). In prosodic texts, it is written as "Ōu" (漚), pronounced *āhóu* (烏侯反) or also *yúhóu* (於侯反), meaning long-term soaking, which is not the meaning of "Ōu. The lower character is read as *bǐchūn* (彼春反). It means "to transform. According to the *Qièyùn*, it means "to penetrate. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "wén" (文) with the phonetic "luán" (䜌).

Fascicle 15, Volume Fifteen: *Mūla-saṃghabheda-vastu*. Regarding the term "hūlú" (鵂鶹): The *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds) states it is a strange bird. The *Jìxùn* (Collection of Explanations) states that the hūlú is the same as the *jiéhú* (𪇑鶘), a malevolent bird. The *Erya* states: "The *è* (鵅) and the *jìqī* (鵋䳢). Guo’s commentary notes: "In the Jiangdong region today, the hūlú is called the *jìqī*. - *È*: sound *gé*. - *Jì*: sound *jì*. - *Qī*: sound *qī*. This bird hides during the day and flies at night; both "hūlú" and "jiéhú" are names derived from its cry. Its shape is like that of a horned eagle (*jīngyīng*), dark blue-black in color, and it is fond of eating snakes and mice.

Regarding the character *zhai* (摘): the commentary on the *Shangzhe* (上陟) rhyme group states that its sound is *zhé* (陟革反) and means "to pick up things with the hand. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文) records it as *ti* (揥), meaning "to take. The *Lüwen* (律文) records it as *zhi* (擿). It is also pronounced *tā* (他曆反) with the second tone, *qī* (七庾反); the *Qieyun* (切韻) classifies it as "to gather" (*shōu*) or "to seek" (*mì*). It is composed of the radicals for "ear" (*ěr*) and "hand" (*yòu*; note that *yòu* is the hand itself). The *Lüwen* records it as *qu* (取), which is a vulgar character.

*Yīgè* (衣裓): The first character is pronounced *gǔ* (古) with the final rhyme *dé* (得); it refers to the front lapel of a garment. It is also said to refer to the large sash worn by women. *Chóuchú* (躊躇):

The first character is pronounced *zhòu liú* (紂流) and the second has the phonetic *chú* (除). The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) states that "to *chóuchú*" means the mind is not resolved and one does not proceed immediately. The *Hànshī wàizhuàn* (韓詩外傳) states that "*chóuchú*" is synonymous with *páihuái* (俳佪), meaning to hesitate and not advance. The *Guǎngyǎ* (廣雅) states it means *yóuyù* (猶豫). Both characters are written with the radical for feet (*zú*) and take *shòu* (壽) as their phonetic.

The term *fuma* (駙馬) refers to the title of an official; it is derived from the character *fu* (副), meaning "to assist" or "vice. Emperor Kuangwen stated that during the reign of King Mu of Zhou, there was a man who could train horses well, and the king gave him his daughter in marriage. Because he attended to the horses near the Son of Heaven, he was called a *fuma*. According to the *Hanshu*, Jin Midi was skilled at managing imperial horses, and thus this official title originated.

"Hun-gou" (婚媾): "Hun" (婚) is pronounced with the initial *h* and the final *-un* (呼昆反). The *Li* (禮) states that the wife is the Yin (the female principle); because the taking of a wife occurs at twilight (*hun*), it is called "hun. The *Erya* (爾雅) states that the party of the wife is called "hun," while the party of the groom is called "yin" (姻). "Gou" (媾) has the ancient pronunciation *hou* (古侯反). The *Zishu* (字書) states that a repeated marriage is called "gou."

Volume 16, Fascicle 16: *Mūlasaṃghabheda-vastu*, Fascicle 16. "Ūru" (thigh): In the *Fǎnyùn* (Dictionary of Pronunciations), it is glossed as "the thigh. The *Shuōwén* states it is composed of the radical "bone" (*gǔ*) and the phonetic "bēi. It is also written as "yī" (䯗) and is interchangeable. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as "pì" (䏶), which is incorrect. Below this, the *Shuōwén* uses the character for "flesh" (*ròu*) to represent the form of muscle and sinew; the current variant form uses the character "ròu" (肉).

"Bǎolù" (寶輅): "Bó" is pronounced with the *bó* of *bóqièyùn* (博切韻); it means precious, auspicious, or also *jiān* (賝). The *Lìjì* (禮記) states: "The earth does not conceal its treasures. In archaic script, it is written as *bǎo* (珤), composed of the radical "jade" (玉) and the phonetic "fǒu" (缶). The lower character "luò" (洛) has the pronunciation *gù* (故). This refers to the *Dàlù* (大輅) or Grand Carriage. According to the five types of carriages, they are named according to their ornamentation; that which is adorned with precious gems is called the *Bǎolù*.

"Eye-twitching" (mùrǔn): the upper character is read as qí (with the *lù* rhyme). The *Yùpiān* states: "Li [the trigram] represents the eye; the eye is the refined essence of the vital breath (*qì*). The *Shuōwén* says it "images the shape of the eye. In archaic script it is written as 󱵜. The lower character is read as lún (with the *rén* rhyme). According to the *Kǎośēng*, it means the eyelid moves. It is also written as 眴; the *Lǜ* text uses 𥌎, pronounced rúyuán, meaning the skin of the eye hangs down, which does not carry the meaning of twitching.

The quail (*chún*)—the "shang" in its name is pronounced *cháng*; the *Zílín* states it is the *yóuchún*. The *Huáihánzǐ* says that the shrimp-mole (*xiāmā*) transforms into a quail. The *Éryā* states: "Among birds whose male and female cannot be distinguished, if the right wing covers the left, it is male."

Volume 17, Fascicle Seventeen: *Mūlasaṃghabhedavastu*, Fascicle Seventeen. The character 鞌 (ān) [is pronounced with the upper radical 鳥寒反 (niǎo hán fǎn) and the phonetic 韻 (yùn); it means a saddle. It is sometimes written as 鞍 (ān), but this is a vulgar form and not the correct character]. The lower part [of the character] is pronounced 兵媚反 (bīng mèi fǎn). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to a horse’s saddle. The *Shijing* says, “Six saddles like silk. [The character is formed from 糸 (silk) and 韋 (flexible leather), forming 韋; this represents the shape of the object. The forms made with 口 (mouth) and 亡 (to lose) to create 轡 (rein) or 韁 (bridle) are both incorrect.]

Regarding the character *chou* (欶): the upper radical is *jiao* (角); dictionaries state it means "to suck with the mouth," though it is also written as *sou* (嗽). In the Vinaya texts it is written as *si* (嗍), which is incorrect. The lower part is read as *yu* (於) or *rong* (容); the *Qieyun* states it refers to "abscesses, jaundice, or sores. In the Vinaya texts it is written as *tou* (㿈), which is a vulgar character.

"Xūjiē (吁嗟): 'xū' is a word expressing doubt or wonder; it is composed of the radical 口 (mouth) with the phonetic 于 (yú), and according to the rhyme rules, its pronunciation is *xiǔjū* (朽居反), meaning to blow or exhale. It is not the character 吁. Below [the character], 子 (zǐ) is the *xié* (邪) initial. The *Yùnyùn* states that it is a word for sighing or lamenting."

Vaiśravaṇa (the first character pronounced with the initial *pu* and the final *ji*; the second character pronounced with the initials *ni* and *jia*)—in the old Sanskrit transcription, this was called Piśāmen—is here translated as "Much-Hearing" (*Bahuśruta*), which is the name of the Northern Heavenly King.

Volume 18, Fascicle 18: *Mūlasaṃghabheda-vastu*. Fascicle 18. Regarding "Jinmào" (金㡌): the lower character is pronounced according to the *Mòbào* (莫報) fanqie method. In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is written as "yù" (曰). The *Yunji* states that it refers to a small head-cloth worn by the Man tribes; it is also written as "fù" (覆), both meaning "to cover. It is used [in this sense].
*Gēnhuán* (脚跟下): This is a *gǔhén* (古痕) phonetic transcription; it refers to the heel at the back of the foot. *Tiàozhí* (跳躑):
The first character is read as *tíngyáo* (亭遙) and the second as *chéngyì* (呈亦); this was already explained and annotated in the twelfth fascicle above.

"Yeguan" (野干) is *śṛgāla* in Sanskrit, which here is translated as "wild jackal. According to the *Qinghuang* (青黃), it is yellowish-green in color and resembles a dog; it travels in packs and howls at night with a voice like that of a wolf. Guo's commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states that the wild jackal can climb trees. The *Guangya* says it nests in precarious cliffs and tall trees. Its pronunciation is also *yegan* (夜干), which distinguishes it from the fox (*hú*). The *Chan jing* (禪經) mentions seeing both a wild fox and a wild jackal, clarifying that they are two distinct creatures. The *Vinaya* texts render it as *hàn* (犴), pronounced *àn* or *é-hán*; the *Shuowen* defines it as a dog of the Hu lands, but this is not the character for the wild jackal.

*Qiān* (牽): "Pāo" (抛) and "shàng" (上) are the *kǔjiān* (苦堅) reverse-cut rhymes; it means to lead or to pull. The *Kǎoshēng* (考聲) says it means to advance. The *Shuōwén* (說文) says it is formed from the radical *mìng* (冖) with the phonetic *xián* (玄); *mìng* is pronounced *kuíyíng* (葵營). To write it as *qiān* (牽) is incorrect. Below, *pǐ* (疋) and *mào* (皃) are the rhymes; the *Zìshū* (字書) says a *pāochē* (抛車) is a device for flying bricks and stones. It is also pronounced *pǔbāo* (普包), but that is not accepted here.

The character 楩 (pián) is annotated as "fén-lián" (a compound of 房 and 連); the commentary states it refers to a type of grain. The *Erya* says: "Lún (棆) is wú-chí (without blemish). Guo's commentary notes: "It belongs to the pián family and resembles the yùzhāng (cinnamomum camphora). The *Shìwén* also gives the pronunciation "bì-shàn" (婢善), while the character 棆 is pronounced "lún" (倫). Both are identical.

"Rèntāi" (妊胎): The first character, "rèn," has the phonetic value of *zhèn* (朕) or *yù* (又) with the final *lín* (林). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to conceive. The *Qieyun* defines it as "the body conceiving," following the female radical with the third tone (*shēng*). The monastic texts write it as "yìnn" (姙), which is a vulgar form. The second character, "tāi" (胎), has the phonetic value of *tāng* (湯) with the final *lái* (來). The *Kaosheng* states it refers to the "pāochái" (胞胎) or the womb during gestation. The *Erya* states, "Tāi is the beginning [of life]. Guo's commentary notes: "The *peitai* (肧胎) is that which is not yet fully formed; it is also the very beginning of things."

Volume 19, Fascicle 19: *Mūla-bhikṣu-saṃghabheda-vastu*. Fascicle 19. **Zhòngguǒ (重裹)**: The upper character, *zhòng* (重), is pronounced with the *chù* (切) rhyme *róng* (容). The *Qièyùn* states it means "double-layered. The *Kǎoshēng* states it means "repeated layers. The lower character, *guǒ* (裹), is pronounced with the *chù* (切) rhyme *huǒ* (火). The *Qièyùn* states it means "to wrap. The *Shēnglèi* states it means "to bind, to tie, and to fasten. It is composed of the radical *yī* (衣, "clothing") and the phonetic *guǒ* (果).

Regarding *xié* (shoes): the first character is pronounced with the *xǔ* and *yú* rhymes. The *Shìmíng* states: "The *xié* was originally a foreign garment favored by King Wǔlíng of Zhào; it takes the radical *gē* (leather) and the phonetic *huá*. It may also be written as *xuē*, which is likewise correct. Regarding *hùjiā* (sandals/slipper-like footwear): the *Qièyùn* states: "The *xié* (sandals) belong to the category of *lǚ* (footwear); it takes the radical *gē* (leather) and the phonetic *jié* (abbreviated). It is now written as *xié* and is used interchangeably. The pronunciation of *jié* is the same as *xié*, while the rhyme of *huá* is *gǔxié*.

The character *níng* (獰): the upper radical is *gēng* (庚); the *Qièyùn* states it means "ferocious. It is sometimes written as *níng* (㹾), and the *Kǎoshēng* states it refers to a person's unwholesome disposition. The lower part is *wù* (各) with the radical *zhèng* (正), meaning "evil"; there is also the reading *wù* (故), but this is not accepted here.

The character 鵮 (kǎo) is pronounced with the initial *k* and the final *-uǎn* (as indicated by the "Kǔxián" rhyme). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "a bird pecking at things. It is also written as 㪠. In the Vinaya texts, it appears as 呫 (chā), pronounced with the initial *t* and the final *-kuāng* (as indicated by the "Tākuāng" rhyme), meaning "to taste"; however, when pronounced with the initial *r* and the final *-shè* (as indicated by the "Érshè" rhyme), it does not carry the meaning of "pecking. The lower radical is 竹 (zhú). The *Qieyun* states that it means "a bird pecking at things. The *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as being composed of the radical 口 (mouth) and the phonetic component 豖 (chū); the character 豖 has the initial *ch* and the final *-yù*. The characters 琢 (zhuó) and 𣵡 (luò) both derive from this.

*Kiáng* (弶): Upper radical *qíng* (其亮反), rhyme *yīng* (英); the commentary states it is a device for catching animals, composed of the radical "bow" (*gōng*) with the phonetic element *jīng* (*jìng*). Lower radical *chù* (楚革反); the *Qièyùn* states it is a village fence. The *Shuowen* states it is hard wood, composed of the radical "wood" (*mù*) with the phonetic element *cè* (*cè*), the pronunciation of which is as above.

Volume 20, Fascicle 20: *Mūlasaṃghabheda-vastu*. Fascicle 20. Regarding the term "dǒusò" (抖擻): the upper character is pronounced with the radical *shǒu* (hand) and the phonetic *dǒu*; the lower character is pronounced with the radical *shǒu* and the phonetic *sòu*. The *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds) states that "dǒu" means to lift up, and "sòu" also means to shake; both characters take the radical *shǒu* and the phonetic *dǒu*. The text of the Vinaya uses the character "shù" (捒), which is not the original character.

"Old cat" (lǎomāo): "xià" is a reverse-phonetic compound (fǎnqiè) for "mò. It is the name of a beast that eats rats; according to the *Fāngyán*, it resembles a tiger but is small, and people raise it to catch mice.

"Póu" (on the ground): "póu" is a reverse-phonetic compound for "báo," with the *Zílín* giving the pronunciation "shǒu. It means to scoop up with the hands. The *Lǜwén* (Vinaya Texts) writes this as "bàng" (*bōng*). The *Shuōwén* states that it resembles a gourd (*hù*) and can be used as a drinking vessel; it is not the character "póu" (to scoop).
*Sūtra* (Skt.; formerly transcribed as *xiūduluó* or *sùdànlán*) is translated as "sūtra" (scripture).
*Vinaya* (also transcribed as *bìnàiyé*, *bíànyè*, or *pínàiyé*—all variations of the Sanskrit term) means "the treasury of discipline," which is the Vinaya (the monastic code).
*Abhidharma* was formerly called *Abhituan*; this is a corruption. It means "Dharma-Counter" (*dharma-pratisaṃkhyā*), which refers to the Piṭaka of Treatises (*śāstra-piṭaka*).

Regarding the characters for *tāotuò*: the first, *tǎo*, is pronounced with the initial *tù* and the final *dāo* reversed; the second, *tiè*, is pronounced with the initial *tā* and the final *jié*. The *Zílín* states: "To covet wealth is called *tǎo*; to covet food is called *tiè*."

The character *huǐ* (詃) is used in the sense of "enticing" (*yòu*). The *Yùnyìlüè* states that it means "to entice through flattery or persuasion. The *Yùpiān* states it means "to mutually exhort and incite," and also "to instruct. Both are phono-semantic compounds (形聲字) derived from the radical for speech (言). The lower part of the character, *jué* (決), is pronounced with the rhyme *yǒu*. The *Yùnyìlüè* notes that it means "to entice and lead. The *Yùpiān* notes it means "to mutually exhort and move," and also "to teach. Both follow the radical for speech and are phono-semantic characters.

*The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School*, Fascicle One. *The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School*, Fascicle One. **Yù (禦)**: Upper radical *yú* (魚), level tone; the meaning is "to ward off," "to prohibit," or "to stop. According to the *Kǎoshēng* (Examination of Sounds), it means "that which ought to be. The *Erya* states: "Yù and yǔ mean 'prohibition. Guō Pǐng’s commentary says: "To restrain and control. The pronunciation of *yǔ* (圉) is as in *yǔ* (語); the lower character *hú* (胡) has the level tone, and *gān* (肝) has the departing tone. The *Yùpiān* (Jade Lexicon) states: "To resist and ward off. *Gàn* (旰) has the upper radical *gǔ* (古) and the level tone.

*Baiji* (敗績): The upper radical is *pu* (蒲) with the phonetic *mai* (邁). The *Guǎngyùn* states that "to destroy oneself" is called *bài*. The *Erya* states that *píbài* (圮敗) means "overturned. Guo’s commentary says it refers to being ruined and overturned. It follows the radical *wen* (文) and the phonetic *bei* (貝); the lower part is read as *zili* (子曆). The *Erya* states that *ji* (績) means "merit" (*gōngxūn*). Guo’s commentary says it refers to "labors and achievements. Lexicons define it as "accumulated deeds" or "accomplishment. The *Shuowen* writes this character as *zhao* (󱶚).
The eighth fascicle, "On Breaking the Sangha by Riding a Horse or Mounting an Ox" (御馬上牛), has already been fully explained.

Regarding "gǔgēng" (股肱): the upper character is pronounced as gōng (公) with the fanqie "hù fǎn" (戶反), meaning the thighs; the lower character is pronounced as hóng (弘) with the fanqie "gǔ hóng fǎn" (古弘反), meaning the arms. According to this, "gǔgēng" refers to the hands and feet. The *Shangshu* states, "The thighs and arms constitute a person," and the *Kongzhuan* explains, "Only when hands and feet are complete does one become a person. It also says, "Is the sovereign clear-headed? Are his ministers (the 'thighs and arms') excellent? This is what that means.

The character for "enmity" (yuàn) is pronounced with the upper radical *yuán* (袁) and the lower *shì* (市), according to the *Yùpiān* it means "to wrong," and according to the *Qièyùn* it means "resentment. The *Lǐjì* states: "One does not share the same heaven with the enemy of one's father. Zheng’s commentary explains: "The father is the son's heaven; to kill one's own heaven and yet share the same heaven with him is not the act of a filial son."

The *Veda* (薜陀; *Veda* in Sanskrit; formerly transcribed as 韋陁 or 吠陁; translated here as "Clarification") refers to the Four Treatises of Clarification (*Catur-vedāḥ*) of the Western Regions. "Veda" is the Sanskrit term; it is translated as "Clarification. It is also rendered as "Bright" (*Ming*). It corresponds to the four *Vidyā-sthānas* of the West. Note: "Pu" (蒲) is pronounced with the *ji* (計) tone as a variant reading for "wei" (韋). "Shi" (陁) is pronounced with the *fan* (反) tone as a variant reading for "di" (陁). "Jiu" (舊) means "formerly.
